en: Preface to the Combined Concordance of the Laṅkāvatāra and the Śūraṃgama Sūtras:
The *Laṅkāvatāra* was esteemed by Dharmatrata, and the *Śūraṃgama* was esteemed by Zhiyi; both are essential scriptures for the monastic community (*zhimen*).
Furthermore, the reasons for their respective degrees of circulation are also roughly similar. Mahāmati was the primary recipient of the *Laṅkāvatāra*'s teaching; from him—

The realm of noble wisdom is realized only through personal verification; yet the translator has rendered the terminology obscure and dark, causing readers to struggle with their words and stare blankly.
Reflecting upon this slowly, it is like a mosquito biting an iron ox—it finds no place of entry at all. Therefore, those of middling or inferior capacity do not respond with great enthusiasm.
As for one whose faculties are suited to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is Ānanda; he is the one who can cast aside preconceived notions and respond to the challenge.

Ordinary people may be somewhat close [to the truth], yet they have scholars polish their writings for them; when readers encounter such texts, it is like finding an itch and getting someone to scratch it—they each seek to understand through their own conceptual discrimination.
Even when they cite passages from sūtras and śāstras that appear similar as footnotes, though they may seem closer, they only increase their frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Thus far, at this lecture hall, regarding these two sūtras, we have done no more than maintain our teacher’s explanations.

Without falling into great error, [the tradition] remained stagnant until Master Xuelang appeared, who finally swept away the maladies of those who merely followed the gates and doors of others, producing everything from the direct realization (*pratyakṣa*) of his own mind.
Thus, he made the single assembly on Vulture Peak appear as if it were being opened anew. Yet, while the Master was eloquent in speech, he was sparing with pen;
he left behind but a single shadow for the sake of humans and devas. From that time onward, various masters have produced their own compositions.
For several years now, you have bared your sharp edge; it can truly be said that you hold the "Numinous Snake" in your grasp.

Your correct transmission of the *Zhijiao* (Ultimate Intersection) pulse is such that there has been almost no predecessor before you. Yet, regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, you have not yet had the leisure to do so.

Only Elder Master Hanshan and the present Master Yiyu have both provided illuminating expositions of these two sūtras. Having studied under Xuelang in your youth, you have long worn the "transmission of mind" upon your person.

His seal was not constrained by minor details; at one time, his disciples all wore fine garments and behaved with unrestrained license, yet the Master alone remained serene in a single robe for thirty years without change.
Possessing great eloquence and the capacity to travel throughout the world, he passed away after his mission was fulfilled.

Thereupon, the various disciples vied with one another to offer incense in homage to the Master. He declined their offerings with humility, yet the reputation that he graced the mountains and beautified the rivers spread far and wide.

That which is most profound cannot be concealed. Recently, he has constructed a thatched hut at the foot of Mount Tie, dwelling like a bird in its nest and subsisting on wild ferns; his quiet illumination has become even more penetrating.
Consequently, he has composed several fascicles of commentaries on two scriptures, entitled *The Convergence of the Tracks* (*Hezhe*).

Now that the transcription of the bamboo slips is complete, he has presented them to me, the unworthy one, requesting a preface. I, for my part, reflect that in the Unsurpassed Great Enlightenment, how could there be any tracks to be converged? Yet, considering the preservation of...
To deviate from the tracks is wrong; yet to fail to harmonize with the tracks while hastily wishing to abandon them altogether is even more so.

Are not the two schools of Nature (Dharmatā) and Characteristics (Lakṣaṇa) the two wheels for reaching the city of Nirvāṇa? As for the school of Destroying Characteristics (Poxiang), it is like the masters Wang Liang and Cao Fu:
they were not able to discard the two wheels and instead rely on some other singular skill. Perhaps someone wishes to do so by means of this...

To dismiss those [teachings] as errors is likewise a mistake. Speaking in terms of the two sutras, the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the two non-selves, the three categories, and the seven elements do not appear as clearly distinct as one might expect.

Yet, regarding the inquiry into the hundred and eight phrases and the inquiry into the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—when [the Master] picks up "seeing" and "not seeing," he says both are "is"; when he cites "causes and conditions" and "spontaneity," he says both are "is not."
If one applies the traditional style of the Chan school to this, even if one possessed a mouth all over one's body, could one utter a single word?
Thus, to claim that there is "Patriarchal Chan" apart from "Tathāgata Chan" is merely a secondary position.

Throughout his life, the Master’s thesis lay in correcting the biased extremes of these two schools and driving away the madness of superficial wisdom; examining what he has written, it is indeed detailed.
Ah! As for these words, they reach a point where language can no longer fully explain them; they draw back without being released, yet they leap forth with vitality.
The Master likely said: "I merely use my tracks to show the way; if there are those in the world who gallop far beyond the dust, I shall meet them morning and evening.
Thus, the circulation of this book is truly the afterglow of the Master’s legacy and the spiritual descendant of the Vulture Peak.
My family home is at Zhuwu, separated from Tie Shan by no more than the distance of a *kāṣāya*. For three years, I have attended my Master by the waterside and beneath the trees;
we have often conversed together on matters of which there was nothing to be said.

Now that this compilation has been completed, I feel a sense of private joy and have thus inscribed these few words at the end of the scroll, though I am not aware of being a man standing outside the gate.

On the Double Ninth of the Xinyou year of the Tianqi era, the Bodhisattva-Candala Wang Zhijian of Wuxia joined his palms and wrote this preface to the *Lengqie heyche* (The Concordance to the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra).
The *Yi* says: "That which fills the space between heaven and earth consists solely of the myriad things. Thus, as for these myriad things existing within heaven and earth...
Though they are numerous, their names and characteristics can be fully encompassed by a single word: those in the world today take that which is lofty and bright to be Heaven,
that which bears all things with thickness to be Earth, that which rises toweringly to be a mountain, that which is vast and level to be the ocean,
rivers, and streams, that which flies to be birds, that which leaps to be fish, and that which runs to be beasts— this is the multitude of beings.
That which is luxuriant and verdant is the appearance, while "grass" and "trees" are the names; that which is lofty and brilliant is the appearance, while "Heaven" is the name;
that which is broad and substantial is the appearance, while "Earth" is the name; that which rises up majestically is the appearance, while "mountain" is the name;
that which is vast and surging is the appearance, while "rivers," "seas," and "great streams" are the names; and that which flies and leaps is the appearance.
Fish and birds are names for their respective appearances; their darting and rushing are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the animals themselves are the names.

The vast multitude of beings is the characteristic, while plants and trees are the names. Thus we know that the greatness of heaven and earth and the profusion of the myriad things, when considered as a whole, all belong to the realm of names and characteristics;
there is no other dharma apart from this. Therefore, Heaven does not know itself as being lofty and bright, nor does Earth... [know itself as being vast].
The self does not know itself as being vast and profound; the mountain does not know itself as being abruptly emergent; the water does not know itself as being expansive and surging;
fish and birds do not know themselves as flying and leaping; beasts do not know themselves as galloping; plants and trees do not know themselves as being luxuriant.
Yet, that which is lofty and bright is necessarily taken as Heaven; that which is broad and profound is taken as Earth; and that which is abruptly emergent is [taken as the mountain].
That which forms the vast expanses of mountains becomes the rivers, seas, and streams; that which flies becomes birds; that which leaps becomes fish; that which gallops becomes beasts;
and that which throngs in dense clusters becomes grasses and trees. What is it that remains fixed and cannot be changed?
It is that which stands alongside Heaven and Earth as the most spiritual among all things—this is what is called "human. It is indeed so.
When humans and the myriad things of heaven and earth are established with various names and various forms, these are called "conceptual constructions" (*vikalpa*) and "objects of mental discourse.
In reality, the myriad things of heaven and earth have never from the beginning possessed various forms, nor have they ever possessed various names.
Once names and forms are established, thereupon do distinctions of low and high appear, and positions of noble and base are determined.
How could there not be partiality? From this emerge beauty and ugliness; from this arise "self" and "other"; from this spring forth right and wrong.
Thus, one clings to this name while condemning that name; one opposes this appearance while opposing that appearance.

Therein, "that" and "this," "self" and "other," "right" and "wrong"—right and wrong—stand thickly like a forest of brushwood between the heart and the eyes. Within this, there may be one who possesses the True Dharma Eye, who, by means of the Dharma...

With the eye of wisdom one observes and understands that the various names and forms of the myriad things in heaven and earth are originally established through the deluded thoughts of "self" and "person";
they are fundamentally not real, being inherently suchness (*tathatā*).

Therefore, although one may dwell alone amidst the myriad things of heaven and earth, the various names and forms of these things cannot dazzle or delude one’s ears and eyes, and one is thus able to harmonize with them.
Heaven, earth, and the myriad things all return to the self; one does not regard that as "that," nor this as "this"; one does not regard what is as "is," nor what is not as "not.
Thus, heaven and earth are as they are, the myriad things are as they are, and self and other are likewise so.
In this state, one may point to a mustard seed and call it Mount Sumeru, or regard an infant as long-lived, or even call a horse by another name.

One may take a cow to be heaven, or point to heaven as earth; because one is able to truly see that heaven and earth share the same root and all things are of one body, one does not perceive even a hair’s breadth of difference or distinct characteristics that could act as obstructions or hindrances.

Thus, one attains the mind-born body (*manomayakāya*), which acts with sovereign freedom according to the will, encompassing all within the myriad things such that no thing can constrain it; it is for this reason.

The Path is also known as that which realizes that names and characteristics all arise from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), yet understands that these names and characteristics are fundamentally not substantially real;
this is called "right knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*). It is for this reason that names and characteristics serve as the common thoroughfare for both ordinary beings and sages.

Although this sutra elucidates the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*) in addition to the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*), none of them—

The five dharmas that emerge are as follows: the five dharmas refer to name (*nāman*), appearance (*nimitta*), conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the eight consciousnesses: they refer to the eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the manas-consciousness, and the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Regarding the three natures: they refer to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). (2)

"Selflessness" refers to both the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). The eight consciousnesses are name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) and are conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
transforming the eight consciousnesses into wisdom is precisely correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), which is suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the eight consciousnesses are also the five dharmas:
dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is name-and-form; conceptual construction is the nature of delusion; and perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is correct wisdom.

Suchness (*tathatā*) is itself the three natures and also the five dharmas. To grasp at a self and grasp at phenomena upon the basis of names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) is false conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

This self and these phenomena are precisely names and marks. If one realizes through correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) that this self and these phenomena are fundamentally empty, one then realizes the suchness of the two kinds of emptiness and non-self;
thus, both self and non-self are also the five dharmas. Therefore, the five dharmas are cited here.
Thus, heaven and earth, the myriad things, and even all mundane, supramundane, and most excellent supramundane dharmas are comprehensively subsumed without exception.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness are all contained within the five dharmas.
It further states: "These five dharmas are the noble realization of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas."
The wisdom of the successive stages of the bodhisattva grounds encompasses all Buddha-dharmas within it.

This knowledge—that what fills the space between heaven and earth consists only of the myriad phenomena—is that which ordinary beings are deluded by; they are deluded because they take names and appearances to be real.
That which the noble ones have awakened to is precisely this. Why is this so? Because they grasp at names and appearances as being substantial reality.

To say that there is existence and thus distinguish this as arising and that as ceasing, or this as right and that as wrong, is entirely due to this and that; such right and wrong both belong to delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Because they arise from delusive conceptualization, they are called "delusion" and "ordinary beings. If one realizes that names and characteristics are fundamentally empty and that delusive conceptualization does not exist, then this is "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*) and "suchness" (*tathatā*). Because they arise from suchness and correct wisdom, they are called "awakening" and "the sages. This is...

Not only are names not fixed, but characteristics are also not fixed; thus, even the distinction between ordinary beings and sages lacks a fixed position, as it too belongs to the construction of names and characteristics.
With a single mention of names and characteristics, the five dharmas are established; with the establishment of the five dharmas, the one mind is revealed;
and with the revelation of the one mind, all Buddha-dharmas enter therein. As the First Patriarch Bodhidharma said: "The *Laṅkāvatāra* [is the teaching]..."
This scroll can be used to seal the mind; thus, this sutra serves as the "mind-seal" (xin-yin) transmitted hand-to-hand by Buddha after Buddha and from patriarch to patriarch.
Since it is the source from which both Tathāgata-dhyāna and Patriarchal-dhyāna emerge, it takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its primary tenet.

However, while this sutra encompasses all four teachings and harmonizes both nature (xing) and characteristics (xiang), although the two schools of nature and characteristics may appear equally majestic and without distinction, [they differ in their specific emphases].

Yet, as the doors and windows stand open, the various masters of antiquity who have interpreted this sutra have either relied upon the nature (xing) to explain the characteristics (xiang), yet those whose school is the characteristics cling to the characteristics to challenge the nature;
or they have relied upon the characteristics to explain the nature, yet those whose school is the nature cling to the nature to refute the characteristics.
Thus, those who take Asaṅga as their host denigrate Dharmapāla, while those who take Dharmapāla as their host revile Asaṅga.

What is called "brandishing spears within the chamber" or "calamity arising behind one's own door" refers to those who fail to understand that the doctrines of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*) and Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) are two yet one, and one yet two.

Therefore, whenever the Sūtras present the natures (*dharmatā*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as divergent paths, I shall cite both the nature and characteristic schools side-by-side to explain them together, as clearly as the stars and the moon, each with its own point of reference.
My aim is to ensure that the two schools of nature and characteristics remain like... [the sun and moon].
That two wheels of a carriage may travel side by side without conflict is my profound intention; therefore, I have named this work "Harmonizing the Tracks" (*Hezhe*).

If one ascends the road by means of these tracks, and from that road reaches the summit of Mount Laṅkā, which is otherwise inaccessible, one can arrive there in a single stride—what difficulty or danger could there then be? At that time...

Written on the third day after the Dragon Boat Festival in the fifth month of summer in the year of Xinyou of the Heavenly Revelation (Tianqi) era, at the Er-Leng-ʼan Hermitage in the Tianjie Lecture Hall;
respectfully recorded by the monk Tongrun. *The Lankāvatāra Sūtra*, Volume One: "The Harmonious Path."
**Exposition by the Monk Tongrun of Erleang Monastery** In general, the titles established for sutras are not uniform.
Some are designated by means of a person, some by means of a teaching (dharma), some by means of both person and teaching, and some by means of a metaphor for the teaching.
An example of a title designated by means of a person is the *Vimalakīrti*.
Those titles that manifest through both Dharma and person include the *Candrottarā-dārikā-paripṛcchā* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Those that manifest through both Dharma and metaphor include the *Śūraṅgama-rāja-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
This sutra, however, is titled according to its location; "Laṅkāpurī" is translated here as "The Unreachable," situated in the South Sea.
On the summit of Mount Malaya—*Abhataraka*, which means "Unsurpassed"—because both this mountain and this city are composed of unsurpassed varieties of precious jewels;
the Wei translation says: "Dwelling on the summit of Mount Malaya by the shore of the great ocean, within the city of Laṅkā.
That mountain is formed from various kinds of precious substances, with diverse gems interspersed, their radiance shimmering.

Brilliant and majestic, it was as if hundreds of thousands of suns were illuminating a mountain of gold, its interior and exterior transparently clear such that the radiance of the sun and moon could no longer appear.
This was the place where the sages, seers, and holy ones of antiquity contemplated the Dharma of reality and attained the Way.
As the World-Honored One emerged from the palace of the Naga King of the Ocean after preaching the Dharma, he raised his eyes and beheld Mount Ma...
At that moment, the Great City of Laṅkā on Mount Lakuṇḍaka smiled and spoke these words:

"In the past, all Tathāgatas taught within this city the Dharma realized through their own noble wisdom—a realm not accessible to the false views of externalists, nor to the spheres cultivated by those of the two vehicles. I, too, shall now reveal this Dharma for King Māpanda."

At that time, the yakṣa king Māvana, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, heard the Buddha’s voice, beheld the waves of the ocean, and contemplated the great ocean-like realm of the *ālayavijñāna* being stirred by the wind of the objective world, causing the waves of the *pravṛttivijñānas* to arise;
filled with joy, he requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma. Thus, this sutra was initiated by the yakṣa king Māvana.
Therefore, it is from the place where he dwells that his name is manifested. Some say that "Vaiḍūrya" is a precious gem;
the *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Mañjuśrī’s body is like a mountain of purple gold, and his crown is adorned with Vaiḍūrya jewels of five hundred kinds of colors.
Within each of these colors appear the sun, moon, stars, and various devas, nāgas, and so forth.
Furthermore, all things rare for beings in the world to behold appear therein. Moreover, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states that Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"When I wear a necklace of *śakrābhilagna-maṇi* jewels upon my body in the Sudharmā Hall atop Mount Sumeru, by their radiance the bodies of all the celestial hosts become invisible."

*Kāpiṅgala* is translated here as "Capable of Victory" (*Nengsheng*). It is also called the "Mirror of the Dharma" (*Zongjing*), and it is said that this city is composed of various jewels to symbolize the *Ratnakūṭa-samādhi*.
Thus, *Laṅkā* is also a name for jewels, though it does not necessarily refer to the eight-sided gems.
If one follows the two translations which both name it the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, then the meaning of the ancient translation [as *Kāpiṅgala*] cannot be discarded.
It is especially poignant that because there is no gate through which to enter, there is no path by which to pass;

it is where the yakṣas hold dominion, where all Buddhas abide, and where Bodhisattvas roam. As the former masters have said: "The ten directions have no walls, and the four sides likewise have no gates. And again:
"There is only a path for ascending, yet those who walk upon it are higher than others. Thus, within the various worlds...
All activities that involve the gateway of thought or the path of speech can be deliberated upon;

however, as for the Great Nature, self-nature, and the primary truth (*paramārtha*), they cannot be sought through a mind with intentional activity, nor can they be attained by a mind devoid of activity.

They cannot be constructed through words, nor can they be communicated through silence. As soon as one involves discursive thought, it becomes a superfluous dharma; as soon as one involves the lips and tongue, [it becomes conceptualization].
One must fall into the trap [of conventional understanding] unless one necessarily transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness, and cuts off the path of both sages and ordinary beings;

only then will study begin to correspond even slightly with the truth. Thus, the Great Master Bodhidharma said: "The *Laṅkāvatāra* takes the Buddha’s mind-essence as its core, and 'no-gate' as its dharma-gate.
And Layman Pang also said: "Mount Laṅkā is a precious mountain; on its four sides there are no paths for travel."

Only those who have attained the Way can travel through space coming and going of their own accord; this is what is meant by "there is no gate through which to enter and no path through which to pass.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states: "The World-Honored One preached the Dharma atop Mount Malaya on the southern sea, within the city of Laṅkā.
This mountain is five hundred yojanas high, overlooking the great ocean below, and there is no road [to it]."

One may ascend this city, which is composed of various jewels whose radiance outshines the sun and moon; it has no gates through which to enter, and only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are able to ascend.

Furthermore, the fact that this city, which has long been occupied by yakṣas, suddenly invites the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), precisely reveals that the *tathāgatagarbha* (the self-nature of sentient beings) is present within the Laṅkā city at all times throughout daily life.
There are yakṣas who appear, and at times there are Buddhas turning the wheel of Dharma; at times there are Bodhisattvas traversing these grounds.
Yet, being entangled by false imaginings and devoured by ignorance, they sink into the stagnant waters of death and fall into the turbulence of the present moment.
Thus, they transform the enlightenment sites of all Buddhas into the palaces of yakṣas. If one could turn the light back for even a single thought-moment, then those yakṣas— [would become Buddhas].
The entire palace is the site of enlightenment for all Buddhas and the true ground of the Bodhisattvas, without any interval between them; therefore it is said:
"Last night was the mind of a yakṣa; this morning is the face of a bodhisattva.

There is not so much as a single thread separating the bodhisattva from the yakṣa, for the ordinary and the holy dwell together and dragons and snakes are intermingled. Thus we know that the various Buddhas occupy the very place where the yakṣas reside.
The abodes and the spheres of activity of the bodhisattvas are all located in one place. Question:
This mountain is so high and steep that even those with the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the two vehicles cannot reach it; for what reason, then, can the yakṣas occupy this mountain? Answer:

This symbolizes the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate, which only those with Perfect and Sudden faculties are able to enter. Even if one’s faculties were sharp and keen, [if they were not of this type, they could not enter].
Even those as utterly evil as yakṣas, by suddenly entering the Dharma-realm through immovable ignorance, sit with their whole bodies upon the Jewel Mountain;
thus, when the butcher Wuguang laid down his cleaver, he said, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas.
If one's faculties are dull and one proceeds with lingering hesitation, even if one could move mountains, shake stones, and sit or lie within empty space, it would merely be a state of cessation.

Since the Sucao Hermitage is situated outside the gate, it is known that those who wish to traverse this path, enter through this gate, and dwell on this mountain need only concern themselves with whether their faculties are sharp or dull and the depth of their power of faith; they are not distinguished by being good or evil.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
The ruler of the Song state was surnamed Liu and named Yilong; he was the third son of Emperor Wu, who later ascended the throne as Emperor Wen.
Guṇabhadra, which means "Virtuous Merit" (Guǒdéxián) in Chinese, traveled from the land of India across the sea.

Emperor Wen arrived and, because Kumārajīva was thoroughly versed in the principles of both Buddhist and secular learning and proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit, he issued an edict for him to reside at Waguan Temple in the capital of Yangdu to translate various scriptures. This sutra was the first to be produced, consisting of four fascicles.

According to this, the full version of the scripture contains one hundred thousand verses, one million phrases, thirty-six thousand words, and one hundred and fifty chapters; that which is currently transmitted is but a portion thereof.
This is but a single chapter.

Regarding "The Chapter on the Heart of the Speech of All Buddhas," "all Buddhas" is a general term for the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the ten directions. Now, I shall briefly clarify this according to the five teachings.
First, in the initial teaching of the Hīnayāna, external objects are held to be substantially real, while "one mind" is established as a conventional designation;

this is because the various results experienced are produced by karma created by the mind. Second, in the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna, the *ālayavijñāna* of maturation is taken as "one mind," which negates the non-existence of external objects.
As the subsequent sutra states: "These two—the perishable and the imperishable aspects—are mutually causal, rooted in beginningless falsehood."
Third, the final teaching (niṣṭhā-naya) takes the Tathāgatagarbha, endowed with all merits, as the One Mind; the subsequent scripture states:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, just as an actor manifests various realms of existence.
Fourth, the sudden teaching (tada-naya) takes the state of total cessation and non-reliance as the One Mind; the following text says: "The three vehicles and the one vehicle are not [different]."
Riding upon what I have taught—the five aspects of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)—all phenomena are universally encompassed as the non-obstruction of thing-to-thing within the single mind.
As the subsequent sutra states: "The tenth stage is the first; the first is the eighth; the ninth is the seventh;
the seventh is likewise the eighth; the second is the third. Since there is nothing that exists, what sequence can there be? This is the fourth [point] of this sutra.
The teachings universally discuss the three roots; thus one knows that this mind is not merely the central tenet of this single sutra, but that the entire Great Canon enters into this very school.

Not only is it the sole school practiced, realized, expounded, and transmitted by a single Buddha, but it is also the only school through which Buddhas have successively conferred their realization and patriarchs have passed down the lineage.

Therefore, this sutra takes the mind of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-citta*) as its central tenet and the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of delusive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) as its aim.
As the subsequent sutra states: "This is the nature, the self-nature, and the mind of ultimate reality of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.
It further states: "That which was known by the former sages has been transmitted in succession; it is the lack of nature in delusive conceptualization."

Although these two statements differ in wording, their essential meaning is the same: because of the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*), deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) have no inherent nature;

and that which has no inherent nature is precisely the mind of the ultimate truth. Question: The subsequent scripture states that "all phenomena are unarisen" (*anutpanna*), so why should this be established as the central tenet?
Why instead take "the one mind" (*ekacitta*) as the tenet? Answer: All Buddhas of antiquity have transmitted [this teaching].
The Chan school also opens a single path through the gate of expedient means (*upāya*);

one must by no means cling to these expedients and become deluded regarding the Great Principle, nor may one discard expedient means and sever the continuity of the lineage. However, when the opportunity presents itself, there is nothing established as real;
should there be even a single understanding or a single word, these are all matters of the past, belonging to the second level. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: [With]...

For what reason, then, will they each divide into distinct categories in the future, such as the eighteen schools among the Buddha's disciples and the ninety-six types among the non-Buddhists?"
What is emptiness, and what is its cause? What is momentary destruction? What is birth from a womb? Why is the world unshakable?
What is the cause for [the world being like] an illusion, a dream, and a city of the Gandharvas; and for the world being like a mirage and the moon’s reflection in water?

For what reason are the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) and the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) taught? Why is there the disorder of the lands? And why is there the manifestation of the visible world?
"How is it that the world is neither born nor extinguished, like a flower in the sky? How does one awaken to the world?

This question concerns the distinctions between names and characteristics. While the world undergoes the phases of formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness, and the root-body (the psycho-physical organism) undergoes birth, subsistence, change, and extinction, here [the text] mentions "emptiness" and "destruction" while subsuming them under "formation" and "subsistence," and mentions "birth" while including "subsistence," "change," and "extinction. Since it has been said:
If the vessel-world perishes moment by moment, why do you further say that the three calamities cannot reach the worlds above the fourth dhyāna?
Since these are called "unmoving," they must be truly permanent; yet why does the Tathāgata further say they are like illusions, dreams, gandharva cities, mirages, and water-moons?
Furthermore, since the root-body is born from the womb, why does the Tathāgata [say it is otherwise]?
Furthermore, it is said that [these lands] arise from the seven factors of enlightenment and arise from the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.
Since the land is one and the same, why is what is seen so diverse and inconsistent? Some see an impure land undergoing transformation;
some see a pure land remaining undestroyed; some see it as being like a flower in the sky; and some see it as the world of Perfect Enlightenment.
What are the causes for these intervening states?

How is it explained that one is free from words and free from false conceptualization? Who says so? What is space like? For example, how many kinds of truly existent things are there? How many *pāramitās* are there?
By what cause does the mind transcend the various stages (*bhūmis*)? Who reaches the state of non-apprehension (the Wei translation says: "True Suchness has no sequence")? What is it?
How are the two kinds of selflessness [attained]? How many types of purified wisdoms are there? How many are the natures of sentient beings?
These questions concern the distinctions within suchness and correct gnosis (*tathatā-samyagjñāna*).

Since it has been stated that names, signs, and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are each distinct, why then is it further said that they are free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental objects, being ultimately like empty space?
Who is it that ultimately does not know equality as being free from the delusive conceptualization of names?

Having abandoned the delusive conceptualization of names and signs, one realizes right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, how many kinds of realized *tathatā* are there? How many kinds of minds reaching the other shore (*pāramitā*) are there?
And what are the causes by which one transcends the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to realize the *dharmadhātu*? As for this transcendent realization...

Ultimately, what kind of capacity is this? If names and characteristics are not empty, how many kinds of wisdom must one employ to minutely observe the grasping at self and the grasping at dharmas before attaining the two kinds of selflessness?
Furthermore, how many types of sentient beings' faculties and natures are there, and by employing how many kinds of disciplinary marks does one subdue them?
Who produces the various natures of jewels, such as mani-gems and pearls? Who produces the various languages and the diverse natures of sentient beings?
By whom are the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) and the arts (*śilpa*) revealed? How many kinds of *gāthā* are there?
How many kinds of long verses and short phrases are there that constitute them? What is called a *śāstra* (in Chinese: *tāolǐ*, meaning "principle")? How many kinds of explanations are there?
This question concerns from what source the various languages of sentient and insentient beings, as well as the sūtras and śāstras, are established.

For instance, when the world was first formed, from what did the various precious metals arise? And when sentient beings first emerged, from what did their various natures—and even the various languages of the ten classes of beings—originate?
The "fields of knowledge" (*vidyāsthāna*) refer to the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) are: first, grammar (*śabdavidyā*), which refers to the interpretation of glosses, the explanation of characters, and the classification of terminology;

second, the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*), which refers to technical skills, mechanical devices, and the calculation of astrology and calendrics; third, the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), which refers to incantations for warding off malevolent spirits, pharmacology, and the application of moxibustion and acupuncture;
fourth, logic (*hetuvidyā*), which refers to the examination and determination of the correct and the erroneous, and the investigation of the true and the false; and fifth, [the inner science].

Inner Science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) refers to the thorough elucidation of the subtle principles of cause and effect within the five vehicles; the former three are external arts, while the latter two are internal teachings.
The *gāthā* (verse) refers to the recitation of the *svatantra-gāthā* (independent verses). "Established" (*siddha*) refers to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature);

it is for this reason that the commentators explain this nature. O Mahāmati, do you not know that the jewel-nature arises from firm awakening? As for the word "speech" (*vacana*), it refers to the teaching.
It is said that speech issues from seven locations; thus, the internal and external sūtras and śāstras arise from language, yet there is an underlying intention.
As the former masters have said: "The magpie cries atop the tree, but its intent lies within the hemp field. Only those who forget both words and signs can grasp this.
How do beings arise with food and drink, and how do they give rise to various desires? What are called wheel-turning kings and minor kings?
How do they protect the kingdom? How many kinds of devas are there? What are called the earth, the constellations, and the sun and moon?
How many kinds of practitioners of liberation are there? How many kinds of disciples are there? And what is an ācārya?
How many kinds of Māras and various heterodox teachers are there, O Buddha? How many kinds of intrinsic natures and mentalities do they each possess?
Furthermore, how many kinds of each are there, and by what means are they established? We pray that the Most Victorious One will explain this.

This is a detailed inquiry into the names and characteristics of the distinctions among the ten realms. Since food, drink, and sensual desire are the fundamental roots of sentient beings, they are addressed first.
The *Āgama* Sūtras state that at the beginning of the kalpa, all sentient beings consumed the "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) and the exquisite rice of the fields;

they would eat when hungry and stop when satiated. However, there were those who took for themselves in excess, and because of this, strife and competition began, leading to the establishment of [social order].
The lord of the fields who rules over them is called a Kṣatriya and is named a king; this refers merely to a minor king who protects wealth.
As for a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), he possesses the seven treasures and travels through the air with sovereign ease to transform and guide sentient beings.

There are distinctions among these kings based on whether their wheels are made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, and there are differences among the kings according to whether they rule over four, three, two, or one world-system.

This person is the most honored among kings; even down to the minor "scattered-rice" petty kings within various lands, all of whom differ from one another—by what dharma do they protect their kingdoms?
As for the devas, from the fourth heaven below up to the Akaniṣṭha realm above;
as for the four continents below down to the hells; and as for the sun, moon, and stars.
That is to say, the liberation of the three kinds of deva-sons is for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), while their practice is for those still in training (*śaikṣa*).

Just as in the Hīnayāna, taking the second and third fruits as practice and realizing the fourth fruit as liberation, so too in the Mahāyāna, entering the stages (*bhūmi*) is practice and realizing wondrous enlightenment (*abhisaṃbodhi*) is liberation.
As for the disciples, how many kinds are there? They are categorized by their wisdom, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

Regarding the explanation of the Dharma, the Ācārya says: the "Master of Discipline" (軌範師) refers to the Teacher. There are several types of Buddhas: the Dharmakāya Buddha, the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha, and the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha. There are several types of birth:

namely, birth from the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*), birth from the mind (*manomaya*), and transformational birth (*nirmāṇaja*). As for Māra, this refers to the celestial Māras, the Māras of the defilements, and their like.
Regarding heterodox teachings (*tīrthika*), there are ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths. The self-nature (*svabhāva*) and the mind are themselves the Buddha.
Regarding the nature of the mind as taught by the non-Buddhists, there are three self-natures and seven kinds of natures.
As for the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-citta*), ordinary people, followers of the Lesser Vehicle, and non-Buddhists take existence and non-existence as its self-nature;

they take the physical heart-mass as the mind, the six consciousnesses as the mind, or the principle of primordial darkness (*pradhāna*) as the mind, and so forth, establishing various measures of the mind (*citta-mātra*) for each.
How is it that these various things come to be?
What is empty space, wind, and clouds? What is mindfulness and intelligence? What constitutes forests and trees? What constitutes creeping vines?
What are elephants, horses, and deer? How are they captured? What is base and lowly, and by what cause does one become base and lowly?
What are the six sections that encompass [the teaching]? What are the icchantikas—men, women, and those who are neither male nor female—and how are they all born?
What is the regression from practice? What is the arising through practice? By what dharmas does the Meditation Master establish [the path], and for what kind of people?
How are beings born into the various realms of existence? What are their characteristics and types? What constitutes wealth, and by what causes does one arrive at wealth?
What is the Śākya clan? By what cause does the Śākya clan exist? What is the Ikṣvāku lineage? O Supreme Honored One, please explain!
What is the Long-Suffering Rishi? How did he instruct the Tathāgata?

How is it that at all times and in all lands you appear surrounded by the most excellent sons, manifesting in various names and forms? Why do you not eat meat? Why was the eating of meat prohibited and severed?
Regarding the various species that eat meat, for what reason do they eat meat?
This is a detailed inquiry into the distinctions of their fundamental natures (*indriya-gotra*), names, and characteristics. Those who are unpredictable, shifting like empty winds and clouds;

those who possess mindfulness, intelligence, wisdom, benevolence, and knowledge of righteousness; those who have no perception or awareness at all, such as grasses and trees; and those that are merely insentient, such as elephants, horses, and deer.
However, among those who do not know propriety and righteousness, there are even some who, failing to understand benevolence and righteousness, go so far as to capture and eat [other beings].
There are also those who are lowly, base, and ugly; one does not know by what cause they have come to such a state.
Regarding the "six periods," the Western Regions reckon one period as two months; thus, the six periods refer to the time reckoned by the heretics (bāhyaka), namely the icchantikas.
This refers to those who lack faith and are extremely wicked. Regarding the "five types of non-males" (*pandaka*):
first, there are those born without male organs; second, those who have been castrated; third, those who are jealous of others engaging in sexual intercourse while being unable to do so themselves;
fourth, those whose gender alternates between male and female, changing into the latter due to intense jealousy; and fifth, those who are half-female, meaning they are not female.

The "conch-tendon drum-horn" refers to the *nāḍī* (channels). Regarding the regression of practice: it means regressing toward Māra and external paths, or [regressing] toward the various realms of existence (*gati*).

Regarding the advancement of practice: it means advancing toward the stage of abiding, the stage of conduct, and the stage of orientation. Thus, a Zen master who engages others through the matter of upward transcendence is like a person of wealth;
that is, one whose wealth and resources are sufficient does not know by what cause they have come to possess them. This is the explanation.
Regarding the origin of the lineage, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (or *Mahāmāyā-sūtra*) states that the Great King of Reed Grass attained the status of a royal seer (*rāja-ṛṣi*).
He was struck by a hunter’s arrow, and as his blood dripped onto the ground, two sugarcane stalks sprouted. Exposed to the sun, they opened to reveal one young boy and one young girl.
An astrologer established the name of the boy as Sujāta, who was consecrated as the Sugarcane King; the girl was named Sujātā.
The first consort was of the Gautama Śākya clan, from whom [the Buddha] is descended. "Long Kushen" refers to a rishi who practiced austerities;
that which he taught is the Dharma-gate of patience (*kṣānti*). "All times" refers to the three periods of time;
"all lands" refers to the ten directions; "name" refers to the title; and "form" refers to physical appearance. The Tathāgata did not permit the eating of meat and established this prohibition.
As for why those who abstain from meat [are so], it is because the yakṣas who delight in eating meat do not understand;
and as for why this section of empty space, wind, and clouds forms a pair with the grasses and trees of the forest, why intelligence forms a pair with elephants, horses, and deer,
why men and women form a pair with those who are neither male nor female, and why wealth forms a pair with the lowly and base— [these are all such pairs].
Advancement in practice and regression in practice form one pair; the Tathāgata and the icchantika form another pair;
eating meat and not eating meat form yet another pair.
What are these? There are worlds shaped like the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, lotuses, lions, or excellent signs; those situated sideways or inverted;
those like Indra’s net; or those composed entirely of various precious gems, lutes, hourglass drums, or various kinds of flowers;
or those that are free from the light of the sun and moon—such as these, they are immeasurable.
This is a detailed inquiry into the names and characteristics of the various worlds.
For example, the Sahā world is located within the thirteenth layer of the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpakaraṇḍaka-kṣetra*).
Its shape therein is like that of a sun disk, a half-moon, a lotus, a lion, a *vīṇā* lute, a *kettledrum*, or a cluster of flowers; some worlds are tilted, while others are inverted.
These worlds— some like the interpenetrating pearls of Indra’s net, some composed entirely of precious jewels,
and some that possess their own primary and secondary retributive radiance independent of the light of the sun and moon—
exhibit infinite varieties. By what causes are all these brought about?
What is a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*)? What is a reward-born Buddha (*vipākaja-buddha*)? What is a Tathatā Buddha (*tathatā-buddha*)? What is a wisdom Buddha (*jñāna-buddha*)?

Why does one not attain perfect enlightenment in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? For what reason does one attain awakening and the parinirvāṇa of the Sugata at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), having abandoned desire?
Who shall uphold the True Dharma? How long will the Teacher of Gods remain? And for how long will the True Dharma endure?

This extensively explains the names and characteristics of the various distinctions of *tathatā* (suchness). That which responds to the capacities and conditions of beings is called the *nirmāṇa-buddha* (transformation Buddha);
that which recompenses past causes is called the *saṃbhoga-buddha* (reward Buddha). Their essential nature (*dharmatā*) is non-dual; this is called *tathatā*.

The manifest illumination of original enlightenment is called "wisdom. *Tathatā* is itself the *dharma-kāya*; the *saṃbhoga-kāya* of Śākyamuni does not attain *bodhi* within the desire realm, but must do so [in the form realm].
The Akaniṣṭha Heaven is so called because it is the pure abode where those noble ones who have attained the three fruits reside.

"Sugata" means that he has already transcended the world and yet is able to enter the world; thus he is said to have attained "sugata-parinirvāṇa," which here is translated as "extinction and deliverance" (mie-du).
If one asks, "Now that the Buddha has attained extinction and deliverance, who shall uphold this Treasury of the True Dharma-Eye? the Teacher of Devas is none other than the Tathāgata.
The duration of this separate designation is still for some time. The True Dharma (Saddharma) remaining in the world indeed has a fixed period;
it shall perish only when human lifespan reaches forty thousand years, at the transition from this aeon of decrease to the next aeon of increase.
Only Kāśyapa shall maintain the Buddha’s robe, awaiting the descent of Maitreya to bestow it upon him, and only then will he enter parinirvāṇa.
How many kinds of *siddhānta* and views are there? What are the various divisions of the *vinaya* for bhikṣus?

By what causes and conditions do those most excellent sons, the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, exist? Why is there a hundredfold transformation? What is meant by the hundredfold absence of grasping (*anupādāna*)?
What is mundane supernormal power (*abhijñā*)? What is supramundane? And what are the seven stages (*bhūmi*)? I pray that you will explain these for me.
How many kinds of Saṃgha are there? What constitutes the schism of the Saṃgha? What is the science of medicine and its treatises?
By what causes and conditions did the Great Muni utter such words: "Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are I"?
Why did he speak of annihilation and permanence, as well as self and non-self? Why did he not always expound the true meaning?
Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, he analytically explains the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).

This is a detailed inquiry into the specific characteristics of correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*). *Siddhānta* is here translated as "universal bestowal," meaning that one universally bestows the four methods upon sentient beings:
first, the *loka-siddhānta*, which causes people to obtain the benefit of joy; second, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*... [the text continues].

1. *Adhigama-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth) enables people to attain the benefit of realizing the principle; 2. *Dṛṣṭi-anta-siddhānta* (the truth of views) enables people to attain the benefit of eliminating evil; 3. *Loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the worldly conventional truth) enables people to attain the benefit of increasing goodness; 4. *Pudgala-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the truth of persons) enables people to attain the benefit of generating goodness. Regarding the fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, it enables people to attain the benefit of awakening to the principle.

"Seeing" refers to the specific capacity of the recipient; that is, seeing such a person, one then preaches such a Dharma to them. How many kinds of such [capacities] are there? This is the Vinaya... [text fragment].
Regarding the statement that the *Bhikṣu-vibhaṅga* is the *Bhikṣu-caturvarga-vinaya*:
since both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are collectively referred to as *vinaya*, why is the Hīnayāna portion further divided into the *Caturvarga-vinaya*?

Furthermore, since both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are equally termed "transcending the world," why is it said that a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), having merely severed the grasping of conceptual discrimination, is immediately able to manifest a hundred Buddhas?

Regarding the two vehicles having already severed the innate [afflictions] within the realms and bodies (*dhātu-kāya*) such that they have nothing further to receive, they are only able to manifest eighteen supernatural transformations;

why is it that Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage, who penetrate conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to engage with the world for the benefit of sentient beings, while those of the two vehicles cannot engage with the world?
Why is it that only at the seventh stage is it called "transcending the world," whereby one attains right meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in every thought-moment?
Furthermore, since the followers of the Two Vehicles have already attained the hundredfold state of non-reception and aspiration, explain why this is so.
If one is called a *saṃgha*, it is by definition a "harmonious assembly" (*saṃgha*); how then can there be those who destroy the *saṃgha* or those who defile its ranks, such as the "lion-insects"?
Since the Tathāgata is called the Great King of Physicians, all the teachings he proclaims are capable of curing the ailments of humanity; these are thus termed medical prescriptions and treatises.
However, you are unable to exhaustively cure the illnesses of sentient beings; what is the cause of this?

World-Honored One, since the Dharma you preach has various distinctions, why do you further say that the three Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa are all me—Kakutsunda (translated as "That Which Should Be Severed"), Kanakamuni (translated as "Golden Silence"), and Kāśyapa?

This is called Kāśyapa. Since the present Buddha and the ancient Buddhas are one, and since the Way of all Buddhas is identical, why do they not expound the Dharma of the single characteristic and the single flavor?
Why do they distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, or speak of annihilation, permanence, self, and non-self?
Why do they not expound the true meaning, yet instead differentiate the various kinds of deluded thoughts and mental objects? All of these...
Because of the distinctions in right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), he inquired in detail:
"For what reason are the various mountains— such as Naran, Hālāhala, Āmalaka, Kīla, and Cakravāḍa-Vajra—
adorned with immeasurable jewels and filled with sages (*ṛṣi*) and *gandharvas*?"

This is the continuation of the discussion on the names and characteristics of the various divisions of the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*). The Forest of Men and Women (*Naranārīvana*) is also called the Śītavana (Cemetery).
Its fruits resemble the forms of men and women; when ripe, their color is radiant and beautiful, but before long they fall to the ground, appearing like corpses with an unbearable stench and filth.
The Buddha commanded his disciples to frequently rely upon this forest to practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*).
"Hārī" is fully transcribed as "Hārītaki," which means "brought down from heaven. "Āmalaka-phala" (the fruit of the *āmalaka*) is like a walnut.
From "Kīra" onwards, all are names of mountains—namely, those of the sages (*ṛṣi*) and *gandharvas*. Why do they not dwell among humans or in heaven, but instead reside on these mountains?
The one hundred and eight phrases above all proceed from the single state of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
The Bodhisattva discerns the various differentiated characteristics that flow forth from the mind; this is called "discriminating wisdom.
As the former masters have said, "The mind of nirvāṇa is easy to understand, but the principle of differentiation is difficult to clarify.
Therefore, Mahāmati questioned each point in detail, establishing it as the procedural framework for training in the Bodhisattva path.

The Unsurpassed Knower of the World, having heard those verses spoken concerning the gateways to the various perfections of the Mahāyāna—the foremost essence of the Buddhas—exclaimed, "Excellent, excellent!
Well asked, Mahāmati! Listen attentively; I shall now explain to you in due order that which you have asked."

Bodhisattvas on the fifth stage begin to study worldly dharmas; only the Tathāgata, because he has exhausted the nature of all things, is able to know worldly dharmas completely, and is thus called the "Knower of the World," which is one of the ten titles [of a Buddha].

This means that each and every one of the meanings of the one hundred and eight phrases you have asked about is a Dharma-gate for Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas to deliver sentient beings, and is also the teaching of all Buddhas.
Because it is the realized nature, the self-nature, and the ultimate mind, he praised his excellent questioning and granted this response:
"Arising and non-arising, nirvāṇa, emptiness, and momentariness all lead to the absence of intrinsic nature."
The Chinese translation states: "Whether arising or non-arising, nirvāṇa and the characteristic of emptiness, as well as saṃsāra, lack intrinsic nature.
Arising and emptiness, along with moments (kṣaṇa), are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); non-arising and nirvāṇa are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
By citing these two types, all mundane and supramundane phenomena are fully encompassed. However, when one investigates their ultimate limit, it is not merely arising [that is negated]."

The extinction of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), which are empty in their momentary nature, is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); this is precisely the unarisen and undying nature of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) likewise lack intrinsic nature. If birth and death possessed intrinsic nature, one could never enter nirvāṇa;
if nirvāṇa possessed intrinsic nature, one could never enter birth and death. It is solely because they lack intrinsic nature that [this is possible].

Regarding birth-and-death and nirvana, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally perceives all sentient beings entering nirvana;

they are all of one and the same nature, namely, the nature of non-nature. What is this nature of non-nature? It is the nature of signlessness, the nature of inexhaustibility, and the nature of non-arising."
The nature of things is without cessation; the nature of things is without self, and the nature of things is without non-self;

there is no nature of sentient beings, no nature of non-sentient beings, no nature of bodhi, no nature of the dharma-realm, and no nature of empty space; nor is there a nature of attaining perfect enlightenment.
Because one knows that all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature, one attains omniscience and, with great compassion continuously flowing, rescues [all beings].
To deliver sentient beings, one must know that the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is the essential secret of the Buddhas' discourse on the mind.
Because all phenomena arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature, neither the dharmas of ordinary beings nor the dharmas of sages can be apprehended.

Since they are conditionally arisen and devoid of intrinsic nature, the ultimate and the conventional do not become confused or intermingled; this is why this quiescent single mind possesses [all qualities].
Although there are various distinctions, these very distinctions are in reality entirely unrelated to the single mind of quiescent extinction.

This constitutes a single answer that simultaneously dissolves all [objections], rendering further explanation unnecessary; it is only for the sake of those with shallow understanding and dull faculties that I have added this further lamentation.
The Buddha’s various *pāramitās*, the sons of the Buddha, the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and those who practice in the formless realm;
likewise, all such diverse things as Mount Sumeru, the great oceans, mountains, continents, lands, stars, the sun and moon;
the non-Buddhists, devas, *asuras*, liberation, mastery, supernormal powers, dhyāna, *samādhi*, cessation, and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the wings of awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), the bodies, coming and going, meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),

the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the arising of the mind, and the discourse on mind, thought, and consciousness; the teaching of non-self (*anātman*) and the existence of dharmas, the notion of self-nature (*svabhāva*),

the perceiver and the perceived (where "the perceiver is the mind" and "the perceived is the object"), as well as the two manifest views (namely, the dualistic views of annihilationism and eternalism arising from the perceiver and the perceived), vehicles (*yāna*), and the various spiritual lineages (*gotra*).
Gold, silver, and mani-jewels; the great elements in chaos for those with icchantika-natures;

and the single Buddha-wisdom, which is attained like a blazing flame—this is the attainment of the four fruits and the progress toward the four stages (the "attainment" being the four fruits and the "progress" being the four paths). Regarding sentient beings, whether they exist or not, how could elephants, horses, or various birds and beasts be captured?

This is the analogy for the establishment of the *siddhānta* (doctrinal tenets) and the relationship between the agent and the action. The "dense forest of delusion" refers to the penetration [of truth] through the intellect, such as forests, trees, and creeping vines. This is the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).

There are no existing stages that mutually reach one another; there are a hundred transformations and a hundred absences of sensation, as well as medical prescriptions, crafts, treatises, arts, and sciences.
These all summarize the words asked by Mahāmati, which are uneven and do not necessarily require forced correlation.

How many *krośas* are there from one *yojana*, up to a *yojana* being equal to a *pippala*?
How many *aṇus* are there in what is called a *śalīśava*? How many *śalīśavas* make one *laitya*?
How many *laityas* make one *maṣa*? How many *maṣas* make one *dhāna*? Furthermore, how many *dhānas* make one *kāriṣāṇa*?
How many *karīṣaṇas* constitute one *pala*, and how many such *palas* accumulate to form Mount Meru?
These are what ought to be asked; why ask about other matters? How many are there in the bodies of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, Buddhas, and the supreme sons [of the Buddha]?
Why do you not ask this? How many *ratnis* are in a flame, and how many *ratnis* are in a wind?
How many *ārbuda* hairs are there on each root? How many are there in the pores and the eyebrows?
Generally, all material things within the three realms must have a definite number.

Now, Mahāmati, claiming to have attained mastery of the Mahāyāna and having profoundly investigated the myriad dharmas, inquires with these one hundred and eight questions; yet he remains seated within the *dharmadhātu*.
In their measure, they have not yet been able to exhaustively fathom the full extent of its quantity; this is because they have grasped the great while neglecting the minute.
Therefore, the World-Honored One supplements this teaching so that they may further investigate the subtle and examine the fine, lest they give rise to self-satisfaction.

Moreover, if one were to compare the wisdom of a Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment with the wisdom of the Tathāgata, it would be like comparing the soil on a fingernail to the earth of the great earth.
Because the earth of this bodhisattva is more extensive than that of others, he is called one of "Great Wisdom" (*mahāmati*); yet it is not yet "Immeasurable Wisdom.
It is only when one is a Tathāgata that one realizes immeasurable wisdom; thus the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable;
only by being immeasurable can its measure be fully exhausted. The first four lines summarize the receptacle world and the bodies of sentient beings.
Whether large or small, long or short, each and every one is an accumulation composed of a vast number of *paramāṇu* atoms.
Mount Sumeru dwells in the great ocean; it enters the water eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, and its emergence above the water is likewise.

As for the other mountains, they are like skulls made of the seven precious metals, while the oceans consist of varieties such as fragrant waters, sweet waters, and salt waters. The celestial palace of the sun is five [yojanas] in length and breadth.
Eleven *yojanas* in circumference, it is composed entirely of celestial gold and celestial crystal;
the moon palace is forty-nine *yojanas* in length and breadth, composed entirely of celestial silver and celestial blue lapis lazuli.
"Superior, middling, and inferior sentient beings" refers to the twelve classes of living beings. "One *kṣetra*" refers to a single Buddha-field, limited by the great trichiliocosm. One.
Regarding the first [section], which extensively enumerates the *kṣetra* as being as numerous as motes of dust:
it asks how many motes of dust are accumulated to form each individual *kṣetra*. Five feet make one *dhanus* (bow); two feet make one *hasta* (cubit);
two and a half feet make one *pada* (step); two steps combined make one *dhanus*; two *dhanus* combined make one *daśa* (ten); and twenty *daśas* combined make one [unit].
Eighty breaths combined constitute one *krośa*, which is one and a half *yojanas*. Twenty *krośas* make one *yojana*, and forty *krośas* make one *yojana*;
this is the measurement of distance for the world. Seven atoms (*paramāṇu*) form one window-dust particle (*vātāyanaraja*);
seven window-dust particles form one rabbit-hair-tip dust particle (*śaśaraja*); and seven rabbit-hair-tip dust particles form...
Seven particles of sheep’s wool hair (*ūrṇā-keśa-rajas*) make one particle of cow’s hair (*go-keśa-rajas*); seven particles of cow’s hair make one nit (*yūka*);
seven nits make one louse (*likṣā*); seven lice make one mustard seed (*sarṣapa*); seven mustard seeds make one large barley grain (*yava*).
One *yava* is one *pala*; ten *palas* are one *droṇa*; ten *droṇas* are one *āḍhaka*; ten *āḍhakas* are one *khāri*.
*Yana-khāri* is ten *khāris*; *ayuta* is one hundred thousand; *niyuta* is one hundred million; *vibhūta* is one trillion.

This refers to the accumulation of how many atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute a single barley grain, and how many barley grains constitute one *śu*, one *dou*, one *hu*, and so on, up to one trillion. *Aṇu-rajas* (dust mote); *śarkara* (gravel).
A *vāsa* is a mustard seed; a *yava* is a grain of *kuśa* grass; a *māṣa* is a bean; a *dharaṇa* is a *tola*;
a *karṣa* is two *tolas*; a *pala* is a *kārṣika*. This refers to how many atoms must accumulate to constitute one *tola*, one *karṣa*, and one *pala*.
A *meru* is Mount Sumeru. How many *parārdhas* of *merus* are there? This means how many *palas* must accumulate [to form a *meru*].
And thus Mount Sumeru is formed. All such quantities as these are things you do not know;
it was precisely these that you ought to have asked about, yet instead you ask about other matters you already know. Why is this?

From the Śrāvakas downward, it is clearly shown that although the physical dimensions of the bodies of the four types of noble ones differ—being large or small—their respective body sizes are all composed of accumulated atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Why is it that although you have achieved this, you cannot exhaustively calculate its number? Wind and fire constitute two of the four great elements;
it refers to how many atoms must accumulate to form the four great elements, the six sense faculties, and even down to the pores and eyebrows.
It is likely that while Mahāmati has already grasped the essentials regarding vast matters, he has not yet reached a thorough understanding of the subtle and minute details.
Exhort yourself to inquire into and investigate what ought to be asked and investigated. A former master said: "Because a single atom is empty, all atoms are empty;
because all atoms are empty, a single atom is empty. Within a single atom there are no all-atoms, and within all-atoms there is no single atom.
Therefore, when Sudhana entered into a single pore of Samantabhadra, he beheld worlds within worlds, infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
A sutra states: "There is a great sutra scroll, equal in size to the three-thousandfold world system, contained within a single mote of dust;
it is the same with all motes of dust. There is a person of wisdom whose pure eyes see this clearly; they break open the dust and bring forth the sutra scrolls to extensively benefit sentient beings.
Thus we know that if one wishes to exhaustively understand the sutra scrolls of the great trichiliocosm, one must begin by exhausting the minute motes of dust. We know this.
When even a single mote of dust falls away, one knows the vast, quiescent, and unified mind; this is why the World-Honored One was so earnest and repetitive.
O King of the Sovereign Lord of Wealth, what is the protection of a Wheel-Turning Sage-King? What is liberation?
The detailed exposition and the explanation of the verses are as you have asked: regarding the various desires and various foods and drinks of sentient beings;
what are the forests of men and women and the adamantine solid mountains; what is the analogy of illusions, dreams, and the thirst of wild deer;
what are the adornments of the mountain deities, celestial seers, and *gandharvas*; to where does liberation lead; and who is bound and who is liberated?
What is the transformation of the meditative realm? How do the non-Buddhists act without cause, and how do they act with cause?
How do they act with both cause and no-cause, and how do they act neither with cause nor without cause? What is it for that which has appeared to cease? How are all perceptions purified?
How do perceptions transform, and how are all conditioned activities transformed? How are all conceptualizations severed? And how does one arise from samādhi?
Who is it that breaks through the three realms of existence? Where, by what body, and in what manner? How is it that there are no sentient beings, yet one speaks of a "self"?

How is it that worldly convention speaks [of such things]? I pray that you will extensively analyze these questions: what are their characteristics, and what is the nature of the "non-self" that is questioned?
What constitutes the womb-essence (*garbha*) and the various diverse bodies? How are the views of eternalism and nihilism abandoned? And how does the mind attain meditative concentration?
How are speech, various forms of knowledge, ethical discipline, and the spiritual lineage established for the sons of the Buddha? How are the treatises, the teachers, and the disciples formed?
And how are these various sentient beings constituted? What constitutes food and drink? How are the brilliant and extensive arrangements established?
What are the trees and the climbing vines? O Supreme Son, what are the various realms, and the sages who practice long-term asceticism?
What is meant by "noble lineage"? From what teacher does one receive instruction? What constitutes being "ugly"? What kind of person practices within the desire realm?
Why is it that one does not awaken to the Akanistha heaven? What is mundane supernatural power (*abhijñā*)? What is a *bhikṣu*?
What is a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*)? What is a reward Buddha (*vipāka-buddha*)? And what is the Buddha of the wisdom of suchness and equality (*tathatā-samatā-jñāna*)?

"How do the sons of the Buddha among the assembly ask such questions? Regarding the lute, the waist-drum, the flower-adorned lands, the separation from light, and the ground of the mind—there are seven points of inquiry, all of which are according to reality; these and many other matters are what the sons of the Buddha should ask."
This concludes the summary citation of the words of inquiry, praising the appropriateness of what was asked.
"This" refers to that which was questioned by Mahāmati; "the many others" refers to those supplemented by the Tathāgata.

Your inquiry into the characteristics of the differentiation of the single mind is entirely discourse in accordance with principle and is by no means arbitrary. You should know that it is not only yours [that is so].
The questioner should ask and investigate not only what I have said, but also the many other matters that remain; they should likewise ask and investigate each and every point.
I shall now reveal the *siddhānta*—which is free from all views and errors, characterized by mutual correspondence, and beyond verbal expression.
O Son of the Buddha, listen well as I establish these phrases in their proper sequence.

What you have asked, though it involves the distinction between the noble and the ordinary, and the difference between the pure and the defiled—every one of these distinct characteristics is in accord with that which is without differentiation or distinction; that is to say, this very characteristic is itself devoid of characteristics.
Since these very things are not other than themselves, everything seen before one's eyes is nothing but the Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor;
how could there be any differentiation among various views? By these two phrases alone, one knows that quiescent, single-mindedness pervades all places;
therefore, the four modes of birth and the nine classes of beings all manifest within the self-nature body. Because of this...
Because the true mind is the nature of all phenomena, it manifests as form or emptiness, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
Following karma, its manifestations result in different retributions; for ordinary beings, karma and its fruits cause them to float or sink, continuing the cycle of birth and death.
For the sages, the dharma-body is perfected and its wondrous functions are inexhaustible. Although their concealment or manifestation differs, their single nature remains unchanged.
"Furthermore, all dharmas are from the very beginning quiescent and beyond verbal expression.
Now, within this state that is free from speech, we provisionally establish speech and sequentially construct various phrases. You should listen well so that you may attain what lies beyond words."
These one hundred and eight phrases are as taught by all Buddhas: the phrase of non-arising and the phrase of arising; the phrase of permanence and the phrase of impermanence;

the phrase of characteristics and the phrase of characteristiclessness; the phrase of abiding-change and the phrase of non-abiding-change; the phrase of momentariness and the phrase of non-momentariness.
It is said: "Regarding the one hundred and eight questions you have posed above, if all Buddhas perceive that every object encountered is *bodhi*, there is no other dharma whatsoever.
This is like merging the Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji Rivers into a single body of water, or melting a platter, a jar, hairpins, and bracelets into a single piece of gold.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary* states: "Since the nature is not external to phenomena, how could it ever conflict with their manifold variety?"

Since the emptiness of the *gotra* (spiritual lineage) is never at variance with the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*), the phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) possess four meanings in total:

first, because they arise dependently; second, because they are empty due to arising dependently; third, because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); and fourth, because they are empty due to lacking intrinsic nature.
Because that which lacks intrinsic nature arises dependently and is thus empty, it is not the emptiness of nihilism or non-existence; this is called "true emptiness" (*bhūtashūnyatā*).
Because that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature, existence is not the view of permanence; the existence of the view of existence is called "illusory existence.

Therefore, one attains the various forms of permanence and the single nature of permanence. What is now called "non-arising is itself arising" means that while there is no arising, the karmic fruits remain manifest.
What is called "permanence is itself impermanence" means that non-arising and non-ceasing is non-existence.
The meaning of "constant" (*nitya*) is that appearance is itself non-appearance; this is what is meant by the saying: "If one sees all appearances as non-appearances, one sees the Tathāgata.
That which is non-existent yet suddenly arises is called "arising" (*utpāda*); the temporary suspension of dharmas is called "abiding" (*sthiti*);

the differentiation of abiding before and after is called "change" (*anyathātva*); and the briefest moment of time is called a "kṣaṇa. Now, to contemplate arising is like a barren woman conceiving a child.
Contemplating abiding is like waves surging upon a mirage; contemplating difference is like the myriad transformations of floating clouds;
contemplating cessation is like wild flowers withering into space; and contemplating the momentary is truly such that not even a single hair’s breadth has ever moved.
Thus, from the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the eight phases of enlightenment up to his entry into parinirvāṇa, he never departs from the limit of the moment.
Because of samādhi, it is generally said that they are "not so. These include:
the phrase of self-nature, the phrase of being free from self-nature; the phrase of emptiness, the phrase of non-emptiness; the phrase of cessation, the phrase of non-cessation;
the phrase of extremes, the phrase of non-extremes; the phrase of the middle, the phrase of non-middle; the phrase of permanence, and the phrase of impermanence.
The *Inyuan Wuxing Lun* (Treatise on the Lack of Self-Nature in Causes and Conditions) states: "Ānanda and Devadatta were both younger brothers of the World-Honored One;
