Rāhula and Sunakṣatra were likewise both scions of the Tathāgata. Yet, while Ānanda constantly attended upon him with devotion, Devadatta repeatedly plotted to do him harm;
Rāhula protected the jewel so that it could not be violated, whereas Sunakṣatra broke the vessel and was difficult to reclaim. Inferring from this:
This can surely be understood. If you claim that each thing possesses its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and cannot be exchanged or transformed, this is most certainly not the case.
For instance, when a hawk transforms into a dove, its original essence is suddenly exhausted; when an orange becomes a *karka* (citron), its former flavor vanishes forever.
When one was poor in the past and wealthy now, the principle of a fixed nature is difficult to maintain; when one was noble before and base now, where is the talk of a predetermined fate?
Lu Wang, a butcher of oxen, ultimately enjoyed the rank of Grand Master; Yi Yin, a man who carried a tripod, finally ascended to the position of Prime Minister.

Dai Yuan was a source of concern for his neighbors, yet later established a high reputation; Zhou Chu was the origin of the "Three Evils," yet in his later years was celebrated for his exemplary virtue.
King Ashoka committed crimes of the Avīci hell, yet suddenly changed his course; King Kaniṣka committed faults of the utmost magnitude, yet abruptly [reformed].

If one were able to follow what is wholesome by relying on the principle of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could such a meaning be possible? Therefore, it is known that both sentient and insentient beings lack intrinsic nature;
they all undergo transformation according to the mind and arise solely in pursuit of conditions. Hence, it is said: "The phrase of intrinsic nature is the phrase of being devoid of intrinsic nature.
Because there is no intrinsic nature, there is emptiness; because there is the meaning of emptiness, all phenomena (*dharma*) are established.
Therefore it is said that whether a statement is about emptiness or not empty, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus;

yet to give rise to views such as annihilationism and eternalism, or extremes and middle, is like measuring space with a ruler or fathoming the ocean with a seashell. To speak of "annihilation" refers to the seven theories of annihilationism;

"eternalism" refers to the four theories of universal eternalism; and "extremes" refers to the two extremes of the provisional and the real in the Hīnayāna, and the two extremes of emptiness and existence in the Mahāyāna.

The "middle" refers to the provisional middle, the ultimate middle that does not rely on the provisional, the middle that is neither real nor unreal, and the middle that is neither existent nor non-existent.
One must understand that the middle is neither separate from the extremes nor identical to them.

If one seeks the middle apart from the extremes, the view of extremes has not been extinguished; if the middle were identical to the extremes, the conceptual understanding of the middle would still persist.
Therefore, it is said in general that they are "not. These are:

the phrase of conditions is not the phrase of conditions; the phrase of causes is not the phrase of causes; the phrase of afflictions is not the phrase of afflictions; the phrase of craving is not the phrase of craving;
the phrase of skillful means is not the phrase of skillful means; the phrase of ingenuity is not the phrase of ingenuity; the phrase of purity is not the phrase of purity. Thus it is established.
The phrase is not a phrase; the simile is not a simile; the disciple-phrase is not a disciple-phrase; the teacher-phrase is not a teacher-phrase;
the lineage-phrase is not a lineage-phrase; the three vehicles-phrase is not a three vehicles-phrase.
The afflictions and the conditions of passionate attachment are themselves the skillful means and the pure causes and conditions.
If defilement and purity possessed a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the mad would remain forever mad and the sages would remain forever sages.

Because they lack intrinsic nature, they become defiled according to defiling conditions and become pure according to purifying conditions; yet in reality, they are neither defiled nor pure. This is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Although the true nature is already fully present and perfected within all sentient beings, it is expounded and guided through various metaphors;

yet, because there is not a single metaphor that can truly illustrate it, one must provisionally establish those who can explain this Dharma as teachers and those who can listen to this Dharma as disciples.
Within this Dharma, the three vehicles of nature are established and the five types [of lineages] are opened.
In reality, because there is no distinction between speaker and listener, nor between the three vehicles or the five natures, it is collectively said to be "not so.

The phrase "aspiration" is not the phrase "aspiration"; the phrase "three wheels" is not the phrase "three wheels"; the phrase "characteristics" is not the phrase "characteristics"; the phrase "categories of existence" is not the phrase "categories of existence";
the phrase "both" is not the phrase "both"; and the phrase "the bliss of the present dharma manifested through one's own noble wisdom" is not the [ordinary] "present dharma."

The phrase "joyful expression" refers to when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by the power of their great vows, manifest supernatural powers through the three wheels of body, speech, and mind to preach the Dharma and discern the capacities of beings,
marking them with signs such as: "this is the mark of a self," "this is the mark of a person," "this is the mark of a sentient being," or "this is the mark of a life-span."
Having characterized them, he further designates them as: "this has marks," "this is markless," "this is both having and lacking marks," and "this is neither having nor lacking marks.
Yet, in reality, they are entirely free from the four positions and the hundred negations;
this very object of focus is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, wherein one presently attains the true enjoyment of the Dharma-joy. This, too, is it.
Since the mind is always divided, how could there ever be even a hair’s breadth of the mark of enjoyment? Therefore, it is said in general that it is "not.
The phrase "land" is not the phrase "land"; the phrase "rabbit" is not the phrase "rabbit"; the phrase "water" is not the phrase "water"; the phrase "bow" is not the phrase "bow";
the phrase "reality" is not the phrase "reality"; the phrase "number" is not the phrase "number"—it is clarified that the phrase "number" is not the phrase "number."

The phrase "non-illumination phrase," the "space phrase" and "non-space phrase," the "cloud phrase" and "non-cloud phrase," the "crafts phrase" and "arts-and-sciences phrase," the "non-arts-and-sciences phrase," the "wind phrase" and "non-wind phrase," the "earth phrase" and "non-earth phrase."
That which I have taught is that the great is subtle and the lands are like fine motes of dust; the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are themselves the real locus (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Even though earth, water, wind, clouds, and so forth are accumulations formed by the primary elements of fine motes of dust, when examined to the ultimate end, they all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for they are all manifested by sentient beings in accordance with their karma. Thus said Kāśyapa:
All worlds are composed of water-foam and arise from the inconceivable causes and conditions of the karma of sentient beings;

they do not exist as reality. As for what you have asked regarding the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and technical arts, they are all contained within the realm of names and words and possess no real meaning. Therefore it is said: "All numerical categories and non-numerical categories... and so forth.

Since my spiritual awakening has no involvement whatsoever, it is collectively termed "non-existence" (the two phrases refer to one as the number of calculation and the other as the quantity of measurement).
The phrase "mind" is not the phrase "mind"; the phrase "provisional designation" is not the phrase "provisional designation"; the phrase "intrinsic nature" is not the phrase "intrinsic nature";

the phrase "aggregates" is not the phrase "aggregates"; the phrase "sentient beings" is not the phrase "sentient beings"; the phrase "wisdom" is not the phrase "wisdom"; the phrase "nirvāṇa" is not...
The phrase "nirvāṇa," the phrase "fire," and the phrase "non-fire"; the phrase "non-Buddhist" and the phrase "non-non-Buddhist.

It is not merely that names and words are unreal; even the various designations you have asked about—such as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and "mind"—are all established according to sentiment and following after delusion through the setting up of various names. Yet, mind and nature are fundamentally not two.
When things are deluded, nature is bound to form the mind; when the mind is awakened, the mind is transformed back into nature.
It is just like water forming ice, and ice returning to water—how could there be two? Since this is the case for the mind and nature, so it is for the five aggregates and sentient beings.
Therefore, know that apart from the five aggregates there are no sentient beings, and apart from sentient beings there are no five aggregates. However...
That sentient beings within the five aggregates are still subject to delusion is inherently false;
yet, even the use of wisdom to observe and shatter the five aggregates, thereby purifying their flames, transcending birth and death, and realizing nirvana, is likewise false.
This is because what are called birth and death and nirvana are identical to last night’s dream; thus, it is said in general that they are "not. As for failing to realize one's own...

When the mind wanders outside the Way, it is called an "external way" (tīrthika); this also refers to the deluded mind pursuing external objects, yet "external" does not mean truly existing outside the Way.
The phrase "wild and chaotic" is not a wild and chaotic phrase; the phrase "illusion" is not an illusory phrase; the phrase "dream" is not a dream phrase; the phrase "flame" is not...
The phrase of flames, the phrase of images, the phrase of non-images; the phrase of wheels, the phrase of non-wheels; the phrase of gandharvas, the phrase of non-gandharvas.
All these are what you see: lands that are overturned, tilted, or slanted; some pure, some defiled, all in a state of chaotic disorder.

If things such as illusions and dreams are themselves illusions and dreams, how could those illusions and dreams truly exist? Furthermore, because they are manifested according to karma, this is also not the case.
[The term] "heaven" is not the term "heaven"; "food and drink" is not the term "food and drink"; "sexual desire" is not the term "sexual desire. To see [them thus]—
The phrase of views is not a phrase of views; the phrase of perfections is not a phrase of perfections; the phrase of precepts is not a phrase of precepts;
the phrase of sun, moon, and stars is not a phrase of sun, moon, and stars; the phrase of truths is not a phrase of truths; the phrase of fruits is not a phrase of fruits;
the phrase of cessation and arising is not a phrase of cessation and arising; the phrase of remedies is not a phrase of remedies; the phrase of characteristics is not a phrase of characteristics.

This is precisely what you have asked: how many kinds of devas are there? Although the various devas within the three realms differ in their relative status, they are all but the solidification of floating, empty, and deluded thoughts. If these deluded thoughts are removed, where would the devas be?

Furthermore, while food and sexual desire are said to be the fundamental roots of life, the four types of sustenance for the various devas differ; likewise, the nature of sexual desire among the six heavens of the desire realm also differs.
Who would say that the nature of food and form exists? As for your question regarding the arising of various views:

although these views are thorns difficult to extract and pits from which it is hard to emerge, if one realizes the self-nature of a single view, it shall—in a single thought—transform into unsurpassed awakening;

yet even this is not truly existent. Furthermore, as for your question concerning how many *pāramitās* and how many precepts there are: although there are ten *pāramitās*, there are [only] five precepts.

There are seven groups and three groups, and so forth; however, these are all established as teachings according to the capacities of beings and do not constitute a real "other shore" that can be reached, nor a "nature of precepts" that can be maintained.

This is because one speaks of a "reachable other shore" in contrast to this shore that can be abandoned, and speaks of "maintaining various precepts" in contrast to the violation of prohibitions that can be ceased; therefore, such views are also incorrect. As for the sun, moon, and stars—
Although each has a celestial son presiding over it, these are all merely the solidified congealment of eighty-four thousand confused thoughts of refined radiance;

how could they truly exist? Nevertheless, the Four Truths cultivated by the Two Vehicles and the Four Fruits realized therein, as well as the cessation and resurgence of thought within the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), though clearly distinguished as either false or correct, are in total not real.

Regarding the phrase "it is not so" because it is realized: the term "treatment" (zhì) refers to medical prescriptions (yīfāng). This is also like a physician administering a remedy in response to a specific ailment;
since the prescription is established in response to the ailment, once the ailment is gone, the medicine is discarded—how could one possibly cling to it?

Regarding the term "characteristics" (xiàng): this appears three times. The first instance states: "Characteristics" refers to the characteristics of names and forms (*nāmarūpa*); this is a general reference to the characteristics of the ten realms, encompassing both the holy and the ordinary.
Next, "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the characteristics that define [phenomena], meaning the establishment of characteristics such as existence, non-existence, self, and person.
This "characteristic" refers specifically to the characteristic of form; it is a general term for the forms of the various realms of existence (*gati*).
Since the former [the antidote] is not established, this [the characterized] is likewise not established. Because the former antidote is not real, that which is countered by it is also not real.

Likewise, there are phrases of the limbs and phrases not of the limbs; phrases of the fields of skillful knowledge and phrases not of the fields of skillful knowledge; phrases of dhyāna and phrases not of dhyāna;
phrases of delusion and phrases not of delusion; and phrases of manifestation and phrases not of manifestation.
"Factors" (*aṅga*)—translated in Chinese as "limbs"—refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the eight factors of awakening (*aṣṭamārgāṅga*).

These thirty-seven categories of factors conducive to the path (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are all points where the two vehicles skillfully practice and attain realization; therefore, they are called "places of skillful clarity.

"Meditation" (*dhyāna*) refers to the concentration (*samādhi*) that is practiced, while "manifestation" (*abhisamaya*) refers to realization. Although there was initial delusion followed by later realization, it is nonetheless [the case].
The joy of the journey is not yet the news of having arrived home; therefore, it is said: "No. The phrase of protection is not the phrase of protection;

the phrase of lineage is not the phrase of lineage; the phrase of the immortal is not the phrase of the immortal; the phrase of the king is not the phrase of the king; the phrase of gathering is not the phrase of gathering;
the phrase of the jewel is not the phrase of the jewel; the phrase of prediction is not the phrase of prediction; [and] the icchantika.
The phrase of non-one-sided-attachment; the phrase of woman, man, and neuter; the phrase of neither-woman-nor-man-nor-neuter; the phrase of flavor; the phrase of non-flavor;

the phrase of phenomena; the phrase of non-phenomena; the phrase of body; the phrase of non-body; the phrase of awakening; the phrase of non-awakening; the phrase of movement; the phrase of non-movement;
the phrase of faculties; the phrase of non-faculties; the phrase of the conditioned; the phrase of non-conditioned; the phrase of the unconditioned; the phrase of non-unconditioned.
The phrase of cause and effect, the phrase of non-cause and non-effect; the phrase of the ultimate form (Akaniṣṭha), the phrase of non-ultimate form;

the phrase of joints, the phrase of non-joints; the phrase of the *urubūka* creeper, the phrase of non-*urubūka* creeper; the phrase of mixture, the phrase of non-mixture; the phrase of exposition, the phrase of non-exposition;
the phrase of discipline (*vinaya*), the phrase of non-discipline; the phrase of the bhikṣu, the phrase of non-bhikṣu; the phrase of location, the phrase of non-location.
"Words and phrases, yet not words and phrases.

"Guarding" means protection. "Clan" refers to lineage. This means that within the three realms there are clans of similar kind, there are wandering sages, there are sovereign kings, there are laws for protecting the nation, and there are teachings for receiving and sustaining [beings].
There is precious treasure; there is one who receives a prophecy; there is a person of lack of faith; there are the distinctions of those who are neither male nor female;
there are flavors that are enjoyed; there are actions that are performed; there is a body composed of segments; there is conceptualization and deliberation;
there is movement that arises falsely; there are faculties that respond to sense objects; and there is the conditioned.
It possesses the dharma of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena; it possesses infallible causes and effects; it possesses unerring temporal sequences;
it possesses physical forms that ultimately belong to the abodes of noble ones (*ārya*); it possesses dense trees and vines that serve as dens for birds and beasts;
it possesses various mixed bodies; it possesses various distinct languages; it possesses those who maintain the *vinaya* and practice pure conduct; and it possesses those who dwell [therein].
Although these words are established in a state of stillness, they are all encompassed by false conceptualization and subsumed within the absence of intrinsic nature;
since they are entirely like illusions and transformations, it is said that they are "not so.
Mahāmati, these one hundred and eight phrases were spoken by the Buddhas of the past; you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should [master them].
Cultivation and study.

Calculating the preceding text, there are one hundred and four lines; however, the Chinese translation divides the "lines concerning existence" into "lines of existence" and "lines of non-existence," thereby reducing the count by one line, and divides the "arising and ceasing" into "lines of arising" and "lines of ceasing," thereby reducing [the count].

The "one sentence of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-pada*) up to the "sentence of the bliss of the present dharma realized by noble self-cognizing wisdom" (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-pada*) is divided into two in the Tang translation, whereas here they are combined into one.
Furthermore, there is one "sentence of certainty" (*niyata-pada*) missing; if this one sentence were added, the total number would be one hundred and eight.
As for why all these one hundred and eight sentences are said to be "not [existent]," it is because within the mind of quiescent extinction (*śānta-citta*), not only do all existing things...
Because defiled phenomena are unattainable, and because one must likewise not cling even to all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) pure phenomena, the *Dharmadhātudarśana* states:

"All are ungraspable; even 'ungraspability' is ungraspable. This statement cannot be accepted as a conceptual object, for it is a realm free from discursive thought (*nirvikalpa*), to be realized only through direct personal experience (*pratyātmavedya*). This is precisely what was taught by the Buddhas of the past.
The mind is the supreme realm of self-awakening; therefore, the *Prajñāmañjuśrī-vibhaṅga* states: "If one knows the absence of intrinsic nature, one knows the non-existence of phenomena (*dharma*).
If one knows the non-existence of phenomena, there is no objective realm. If there is no objective realm, there is nothing upon which to rely.
If there is nothing upon which to rely, there is no place of abiding. To be thus instructed and thus enter into faith in this is called [the realization].
Because the phrase "the word of reality" is synonymous with the "vajra-word," those who study the Mahāyāna should train themselves in this phrase.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of consciousnesses are there?"
Regarding arising, abiding, and ceasing:
Mahāmati first addressed the World-Honored One with one hundred and eight questions, which the Buddha collectively dispelled by means of the word "no.
Thus he directly revealed the essence of suchness, whereby the principle that the triple world is mind-only became as clear as the stars and the moon. Mahāmati!
Do you not know that within the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the Single Mind of Quiescent Extinction, not even a hair’s breadth is established?
Why, then, do you hastily ask how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing there are for the various consciousnesses?

This is because the essence of True Suchness (Tathatā) is unchanging and indestructible, utterly transcending arising and ceasing; yet the characteristics and functions of True Suchness are entirely present within arising and ceasing.
Within this consciousness, it is revealed that only the Buddha alone has perfectly realized the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.

From the stage of self-enlightenment (*svasaṃbuddha*) down to the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), if one considers the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*), the distance is as vast as the difference between heaven and earth;

yet if one examines their maturation (*vipāka*), which is not empty and still involves arising and ceasing, even those in the class of Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avakrānti*) remain seated within the cave of ignorance (*avidyā*).

If one does not request the Tathāgata to explain in detail, then one will remain muddled regarding True Suchness (tathatā) and falsely claim to speak with the wisdom of an All-Knowing One despite lacking such wisdom;

therefore, although Mahāmati understood the World-Honored One’s words, he urgently requested an explanation concerning the evolving consciousnesses precisely because he wished to clarify the distinctions between the characteristics and functions of True Suchness.
Thus, Aśvaghoṣa divided the single mind into True Suchness and the evolving [consciousness].

Because there are two gates, it is said that the aspect of this mind as *tathatā* (suchness) reveals the essence (*svabhāva*) of the Mahāyāna, while the aspect of this mind as the causal condition for arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) can reveal the essence, characteristics, and functions (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-kārya*) of the Mahāyāna itself.
Therefore, the World-Honored One first indicated the functions of the various consciousnesses, next set forth their characteristics, and finally manifested their essence; thereafter—

I have established the inference of True Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) to reveal the thesis that all phenomena are consciousness-only, ensuring that the mundane and the sagely, the heterodox and the orthodox, do not overlap by even a hair’s breadth.

I have done this so that one may directly observe the flowing stream [of consciousness], parching the habitual tendencies of the intellect, and thereby attain entry into the equality of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, I inquire into these matters in detail.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which cannot be known through discursive thought. The two kinds of arising of the consciousnesses are:
arising as a continuous flow (*pravṛtti*) and arising as a manifestation (*nimitta*). The two kinds of abiding are: abiding as a continuous flow and abiding as a manifestation.
The two kinds of ceasing are: ceasing as a continuous flow and ceasing as a manifestation."

Regarding the term "flowing stream" (*pravāha*): it refers to the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*, whose three characteristics are subtle and hidden; because it is the most subtle among the subtle, it is called the "flowing stream.
This flowing-stream consciousness is entirely the nature of true suchness (*tathatā*), which is neither arising nor ceasing.

Due to ignorance and non-awakening, it suddenly becomes conjoined with arising and ceasing, transforming into consciousness. It is named the "flowing stream" because it gives rise to and continues through the phases of kalpas.

The term "flowing and abiding" (*pravāha-sthiti*) refers to the period beginning from the initial arousal of the mind through right faith and observation, continuing until the realization of the *dharmakāya* where a small portion of cessation is attained, and extending up to the single moment of wisdom corresponding with the Vajra Path, at which point the ignorance of the characteristic of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) is suddenly severed. This is called the "cessation of the flow.

As for the term "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the three coarse and manifest characteristics of the preceding seven consciousnesses; these are [included here] because they are subtle among the coarse.

Because it is coarse within the coarse, yet subtle within the coarse, and even coarser than the coarse, it is called "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). This coarse characteristic is divided into three phases within the state of continuous flow (*pravṛtti-sthiti*):
the initial arising of the seven consciousnesses is called the "arising of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇotpāda*), which immediately unites with the preceding object and continues without interruption;
this is called the "abiding of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇasthiti*). From the stage of "conformity with faith" (*śraddhā-pratipatti-bhūmi*) onward, one abandons the grasping of these [characteristics].
The characteristic of marks (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*) is the most coarse among the coarse; its continuity is severed from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh.

The characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) is the subtle among the coarse; it is severed from the eighth stage onward. The manifest characteristic (*pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa*) is severed at the ninth stage.

The transforming characteristic (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) is the coarse among the subtle; its cessation is the extinction of names and characteristics (*nāma-nimitta-nirodha*). This is because the continuous flow (*pravāha*) is itself the characteristic within the flow, and the characteristic is itself the flow.
Because the characteristics [of arising, abiding, and ceasing] are noted therein, all consciousnesses possess these two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Although they differ in being coarse or subtle, as for their mutual perfuming and transformation, none know how this comes to be; thus, it is not something known through discursive thought.
Since all sentient beings have never been free from thought since beginningless time, if one attains non-thought, then one knows.
The mind gives rise to the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

All consciousnesses possess three kinds of characteristics, namely: the characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).

As for the characteristic of transformation, it refers to the first seven [consciousnesses], which are called the "discriminative consciousness of objects" (*vastu-vijñapti-vijñāna*) and also the "transforming consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); thus, its characteristic is termed "transformation."

The *Xianglun* (Treatise on Characteristics) states: "The second is called the 'evolving characteristic' (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), because it is based upon the moving mind and is able to perceive characteristics.
Thus, there are two evolving characteristics: if that which is moved by ignorance evolves to become the perceiver, it exists within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*);

if that which is moved by objects evolves to become the perceiver, it exists within the phenomenal consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). As for what is called the "characteristic of karma" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), it means:
The eighth is called the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), and its characteristic is named the "characteristic of karma" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). The *Treatise* states:

"First, because the mind moves through the power of ignorance without awareness, it is called the True Consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), and its characteristic is named the 'characteristic of reality' (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*). Question:

Since it has already been indicated that all consciousnesses possess two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, why is there a further indication of three characteristics? Answer: This is to reveal the transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Regarding the characteristics of karma, there are two kinds: arising, abiding, and ceasing. Yet, the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness) has never known arising, abiding, or ceasing.

An ancient commentary states: "These three characteristics apply to the eight consciousnesses; when the mind arises, it is called 'transformation,' and since all eight consciousnesses arise, they all possess arising and ceasing.
Thus, the movement of the mind is karma, for all eight consciousnesses are in motion. Regarding these eight:

Since both the true nature (*tathatā*) and the false nature are termed "true characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), the "evolving characteristic" (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) already encompasses the six coarse aspects;

furthermore, the "transforming characteristic" (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) also extends through the three subtle aspects. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Due to four causes and conditions, visual consciousness evolves," and further:

"The various waves of consciousness surge and evolve. Both of these refer to the transforming characteristic. Mind is called the "accumulating karma" (*saṃgraha-karma*), and it is also called the "evolving characteristic of karma" (*karma-pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*).
It is said that the waves are all marks of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), while constant purity and formlessness are the true mark (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).

Because the mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*)—which is quiescent and immutable—follows conditions without being defiled yet is nonetheless defiled, there are the two marks of the transformation of karma;
because the mind of True Suchness—which is quiescent and immutable—follows conditions without changing and is defiled yet remains undefiled, there is the true mark.
Mahāmati, briefly stated there are three kinds of consciousness; explained in detail, there are eight aspects. What are the three?

They are the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*), and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vasta-vikalpa-vijñāna*). Mahāmati, just as a bright mirror reflects all forms and images, so too does the manifesting consciousness appear in its respective locus.
The Treatise says: "The manifesting consciousness (ādarśa-vijñāna) refers to that which can manifest all objective realms, just as a clear mirror manifests forms and images;
the manifesting consciousness is likewise, appearing immediately as the five sense-objects encounter it, without sequence, because all dharmas arise spontaneously and are always present before it.
As for the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (vastu-vijñapti-vijñāna), it is termed [the seventh consciousness] in the Treatise.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is also called the "separating consciousness" because it discriminates the six sense objects by following after and grasping at phenomena;
herein, the true consciousness is the Tathāgatagarbha, the quiescent single mind, whereas this manifesting consciousness is the ālayavijñāna.
However, this manifesting consciousness has no separate self-substance other than the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, for due to non-awakening, it [appears as such].
All deluded thoughts possess the meanings of conjunction and non-conjunction. That which is conjunctive is capable of containing both defilement and purity;
it is designated as the *ālayavijñāna*. That which is non-conjunctive has a substance that is eternally unchanging; it is designated as *tathatā*, which is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Therefore, it is said that "that which is quiescent is called the One Mind. Since the One Mind is the *tathāgatagarbha*, a verse says: "The Buddha..."
The Tathāgatagarbha is taught as the ālaya; those of inferior intelligence cannot understand that the Garbha is precisely the ālayavijñāna.

Herein, regarding the three consciousnesses—if one considers the synthesis of the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing according to Aśvaghoṣa, and names this "ālayavijñāna"—it is the synthesis of the true consciousness, the manifesting consciousness, and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena.

Regarding the established tenet (*siddhānta*): if we follow Dharmapāla, the tenet is that the *ālayavijñāna* (manifest consciousness) and the *pravṛttivijñāna* (discriminating consciousness of phenomena) are in union.

Although each [master] has presented their own unique perspective, the ultimate meaning converges upon a single path. As the ancient masters said: "If one says that the nature of the mind of sentient beings is identical to the nature of the mind of the Buddhas, this is the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*).
In the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulyayāna*), the nature of the mind is one; it is the *Svabhāvakāya* (Intrinsic Radiance), where there is neither 'that' nor 'this'."
The limits of the Buddhas and sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time constitute one Great Perfect Mirror;
yet it is but a single mirror, devoid of identity or difference, for both Buddhas and sentient beings are merely images upon this single mirror. Question:

Is this mirror established according to the Dharma-character (Faxiang) school, or is it established according to the Dharma-nature (Faxing) school? Answer: If established according to the Dharma-character school, it is based on the principle of dependent origination through mutual correspondence.
The "gate" refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) acting as a mirror; this is what is established here.

If we refer to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is the Tathāgatagarbha—the quiescent single mind—that serves as the mirror, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*: "Furthermore, the aspect of awakening is equal to empty space, like a pure mirror.
Question: Why is it that in this context only the "manifesting consciousness" (*khyāti-vijñāna*) and "discriminating [consciousness]" (*vikalpa*) are mentioned?

The *ālayavijñāna* (the foundational consciousness) does not speak of the *manas*; the answer is that where there is the *darśanavijñāna* (the manifesting consciousness), there must necessarily be the *manas*, because it evolves depending upon it and takes it as its object.
Therefore, where there is the *manovijñāna* (the mental consciousness), there must necessarily be the *manas*, for the *manovijñāna* takes the *manas* as its root.

One should know that the subtle portion of the *manas* is common to the *darśanavijñāna*, while its coarse portion is common to the *manovijñāna*. Thus, when the *darśanavijñāna* and the *karmavijñāna* (the active consciousness) are mentioned, the *manas* is implied.

That is contained therein. Mahāmati, the manifest consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that discriminates objects (*viṣaya-vikalpa-vijñāna*)—these two have the characteristics of being destructible and indestructible, and they serve as reciprocal causes for one another.
Previously, all consciousnesses were designated with arising and ceasing as their primary principle; here, furthermore, their cause is revealed. "Destructible" refers to transformation (*parāvṛtti*).
That which is the characteristic of the *karma-lakṣaṇa* (characteristic of karma) yet remains undestroyed is precisely the *tathatā-lakṣaṇa* (characteristic of suchness).

Because these two characteristics serve as reciprocal causes for one another, they are able to establish the thesis of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). If this reciprocal causality is understood according to Aśvaghoṣa, it means that the *karma-lakṣaṇa* evolves based upon the *tathatā-lakṣaṇa*, which is the eighth consciousness;
and the *pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa* (evolving characteristic) evolves based upon the *karma-lakṣaṇa*. This refers to the [seventh] consciousness...
The seven consciousnesses revolve according to the aspect of the evolving basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), while the aspect of manifestation is precisely the first five consciousnesses.

Furthermore, the aspect of manifesting wisdom and the aspect of continuous grasping and calculating names and so forth constitute the discriminative consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñapti-vijñāna*); therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:

"Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, it refers to sentient beings revolving in dependence upon mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). Thus it is said.

The meaning is as follows: Why is it said that based on the *ālayavijñāna*, there arises ignorance (*avidyā*) and non-awakening, which gives rise to the capacity to see, the capacity to manifest, and the grasping of objects, such that thoughts arise in a continuous succession?
According to Dharmapāla, this refers to the eighth consciousness, which contains the seeds capable of producing the active manifestations (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) of the preceding seven;
thus, the actual manifestations and the seeds mutually perfume one another and serve as cause and effect for each other.
The *Śāstra* states: "All phenomena [act as causes] for the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and the store-consciousness likewise [acts as a cause] for all phenomena;

they mutually serve as the nature of cause and also constantly serve as the nature of effect. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "An impermanent phenomenon acts as a cause for another nature and also acts as a cause for its own subsequent moment;

this is the meaning of 'causal condition' (*hetu-pratyaya*). The term 'own nature' (*svabhāva*) indicates that within the same category of seeds, the preceding serves as the cause for the succeeding."
The term "other-nature" (*parabhāva*) clarifies the sense that seeds and manifest activities serve as causes for one another. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The storehouse consciousness and defiled dharmas serve as mutual causes and conditions, existing simultaneously like bundles of reeds.

This illustrates the difference between the two schools—the Nature School (*svabhāva-vāda*) and the Characteristic School (*lakṣaṇa-vāda*)—regarding their respective views on reciprocal causality. Thus, the Great Sūtra says: "Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental faculty..."

The various sense-faculties (*indriya*) thus flow on perpetually, yet there is no agent who causes them to flow; for the eight consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and the rest, act as both the perfuming agents (*vāsaka*) and the objects perfumed (*vāsya*), serving as mutual causes and flowing on perpetually without any separate self (*ātman*) or person (*pudgala*). Therefore, it is said that "there is no agent who causes them to flow.

It is only when their entire substance is realized to be empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*) that this perpetual flow is established; these very eight consciousnesses are what is termed "non-existence" (*anātman*).
The essential nature [of phenomena] lacks a real self or dharma as its master; if there were such a nature, it could not be perfumed or transformed, so how could it undergo transmigration?
Thus, by citing these successive causes, one specifically intends to refute the real self and real dharmas of the non-Buddhists and the Hīnayāna.
Mahāmati, the inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).
Mahāmati, the grasping of various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization are the causes of the discerning consciousness of phenomena (*nirūpaṇa-vastu-vijñāna*).
This specifically clarifies the causes by which the eight consciousnesses arise from one another in succession. There are two meanings of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*):

first, perfuming as cultivation, which refers to the perfuming of the substance of the mind to produce the defiled and pure [states]; second, perfuming as mutual support, which refers to the mutual support between the manifest mental objects and the various afflictions.
There are also two meanings of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*): first, manifestation; second, transformation. If one follows Dharmapāla, he takes only [the latter].

The single meaning of "perfuming and transformation" (*vāsanā-pariṇāma*) refers to taking the first seven consciousnesses as the perfumers (*vāsaka*) and the eighth consciousness as the perfumed (*vāsya*).

Taking the eighth consciousness as the transformer (*pariṇāmaka*) and the first seven as the transformed (*pariṇāmya*): that is, the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the images (*nimitta-bhāga*) and perceptions (*darśana-bhāga*) of the first seven consciousnesses perfume the eighth;
the eighth undergoes transformation into the seeds of the two parts—image and perception—wherein the first five [consciousnesses] perfume the seeds of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth.

The sixth [consciousness] perfumes the seeds of both the image and the seeing portions of the eighth [consciousness], while the seventh [consciousness] perfumes the seeds of the seeing portion of the eighth.
Thereupon, the eighth [consciousness] again transforms and gives rise to the active manifestations of the preceding seven.

Because this process of the perfuming and being perfumed, and the transforming and being transformed, occurs in such a manner without being consciously perceived, it is called "inconceivable perfuming" and "inconceivable transformation."

Regarding transformation, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Verses on Consciousness-Only) states: "By the power of all-seed consciousness (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*), it transforms in such and such ways;
through their mutual influence, various conceptualizations arise. This indicates that the first seven [consciousnesses] serve as the causes for the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, consciousness has many names; because it is able to store all seeds, it is called the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*), and it is that which is summoned by the karma of the preceding seven.

Because it is moved by conditions, it is called the *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*); because it can transform and give rise to various active manifestations, it is called the "manifesting consciousness" (*xiàn-shí*), with the character "manifesting" (*xiàn*) corresponding to the character "transforming" (*biàn*).

As for why the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*fen-bié shì-shí*) is able to grasp various sense objects, it is entirely due to the eighth consciousness containing the seeds of the preceding seven;
as these seeds are perfumed moment by moment, the eye is able to see forms, and so on.

The mind (*manas*) is able to apprehend phenomena (*dharma*). If there were no external perfuming by the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) manifesting, and no internal perfuming by the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā-bīja*), then the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, would be unable to differentiate the six objects.

Because there is uninterrupted mutual perfuming between the internal and external, the seventh [consciousness] is able to take an object that carries its own substance (*sadravyālambana*), the sixth is able to take three types of objects, and the first five are able to take [their respective] objects.
Since the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*) is the object-field, the eighth consciousness serves as the cause for the first seven;

according to Aśvaghoṣa, because they rely upon the *tathatā* (suchness), there exists ignorance (*avidyā*) which acts as the cause for all defiled phenomena. This is precisely the "phase of karma" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*).
Because this defiled phenomenon of ignorance exists as a cause, it perfumes the *tathatā*. Through this perfuming, the deluded mind arises. This is...

The mutual transformation occurs because the deluded mind immediately perfumes ignorance; failing to comprehend the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, one gives rise to non-awakening and conceptual thoughts, whereby false objects manifest.
This is the "manifestation phase" (*xiànxiàng*), which refers to what is called the "unawakened ignorance giving rise to the three subtle states.
Regarding the "inconceivable perfuming and transformation," it means that although *tathatā* is fundamentally incapable of being perfumed, it is [perfumed] by ignorance.

"Perfuming" (vāsanā) refers to inconceivable perfuming; the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) is fundamentally immutable, yet it now manifests all phenomena in accordance with the conditions of ignorance—this is called "inconceivable transformation.
This refers to the arising of the manifesting consciousness (pravṛtti-vijñāna) through mutual causality.
"Grasping at various objects" means grasping the six sensory objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) in the present. "Perfuming by beginningless false discrimination" refers to...
This refers precisely to the beginningless perfuming of views and attachments; therefore, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:

"The meaning of the perfuming of ignorance is twofold: first, fundamental perfuming, which is able to bring about the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), as described in the Sūtra as 'inconceivable perfuming';
second, the perfuming of the views and attachments that arise therefrom, which is able to bring about the discrimination of phenomena."

Because it is consciousness, this refers to what the Sūtra calls "the perfuming of beginningless deluded conceptualization"; that is, the various phenomenal consciousnesses (*vijnana*) arise through mutual causality.
Mahāmati, if those various unreal and false states are extinguished within that True Consciousness (*tathatā-vijnana*), then all sense-consciousnesses (*indriya-vijnana*) [will likewise cease].
The cessation of these is called the cessation of marks (*nimitta*). Mahāmati, as for the cessation of the continuity (*saṃtati*): when the cause of the continuity ceases, the continuity ceases;
when that from which it proceeds and its object (*ālambana*) cease, the continuity ceases. Mahāmati, why is this? Because they are its support.
"Support" refers to the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination (*vikalpa*); "object" refers to the objects of the consciousnesses, such as the manifestations of one's own mind. Falsehood.

[This is] the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). This is a detailed explanation of the causes for their mutual extinction. If one refers to the *Dharmapāla* [commentary], "covering" (*chādana*) has the sense of "obscuring";

it specifically points to a portion of the extremely subtle ignorance regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa-moha*) within the path of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*) of the path of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), because it is able to obscure the Truth.
Because of consciousness, up until the path of liberation, one employs the vajra-wisdom to suddenly sever [delusions] in a single thought-moment;

thus, the false habitual tendencies of the dual grasping at self and phenomena are simultaneously and instantaneously extinguished. Consequently, all consciousnesses that depend upon the sense faculties should, in that very moment, be entirely exhausted.

As before, the five consciousnesses depend upon the five faculties; the sixth depends upon the seventh as its faculty, the seventh depends upon the eighth as its faculty, and the eighth... [and so forth].
Because the seven [consciousnesses] take [the eighth] as their root, when that one part—the ignorance regarding the knowable—is empty, all consciousnesses that rely on the roots are also empty.
This is what is meant by: "If the bark no longer exists, where can the hair remain? It means that when the underlying flow (*pravṛtti*) ceases, the manifested characteristics (*nimitta*) also cease.
The term "continuity" (*saṃtati*) is merely a variation of the word "flow. That which is the cause is the "cause" (*hetu*).
That which serves as the support by way of association refers to the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) and the immediately preceding condition support (*samanantara-pratyaya-āśraya*);

that which serves as the support by way of the object refers to the objective condition support (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "that which is their support," this means that these three are the supports for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "All minds and mental factors possess supports; there are three types of supports. First...
The causal condition as support refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) which, being their own seeds, would necessarily not arise were they separated from their causal conditions.
The simultaneous support refers to the six internal bases (*ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana*), which would necessarily not function were they separated from their simultaneous supports.

The immediately preceding condition as support refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which would necessarily not arise were they separated from the opening and leading support. Thus, only the mind and mental factors possess all three types of supports.
These names have their basis; furthermore, these three all arise through the perfuming of beginningless ignorance.

As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it refers to the appearances of the five sensory objects grasped by the five consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, which are manifestations of one's own mind.
It is said that this continuous consciousness is fundamentally not substantially real; internally, it takes the seeds of ignorance as its direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Furthermore—

Taking the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and taking the opening-and-guiding support (*mukha-vijñapti-āśraya*) as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),

while externally taking the five sense objects as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), there is mutual permeation between the internal and external, continuing from moment to moment without interruption.
One must cause both the internal causes and external conditions to be simultaneously exhausted and eliminated, after which the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) ceases.
This means that as the characteristics cease, the continuous flow ceases as well. According to Aśvaghoṣa, because the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) exists, it can permeate ignorance;
by the power of the causes and conditions of this permeation, it can cause the deluded mind to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death and to joyfully seek nirvāṇa.
Because this deluded mind possesses the causes and conditions of weariness and seeking, it in turn permeates True Suchness.
Having gained confidence in one's own nature and realizing that the mind is deludedly active and that there are no external objects before it, one cultivates the dharma of detachment.

Because, in accordance with reality, there are no external objects, one employs various skillful means to initiate practices of conformity—neither grasping nor recollecting them—even until, through the power of long-term cultivation, ignorance is extinguished;
that is to say, the characteristics are extinguished and the continuous flow is also extinguished.
Furthermore, because ignorance ceases, the mind does not arise; because it does not arise, its objects of perception likewise cease.

When causes and conditions both cease and the characteristics of the mind are entirely exhausted, this is called attaining nirvana and accomplishing spontaneous karma—namely, that the continuous flow ceases and its manifestations also cease.
Mahāmati, it is like this: a lump of clay and its atoms are neither different nor non-different; so too it is with golden ornaments.
Mahāmati, if the lump of clay were different from its atoms, it would not be composed of them; yet, in reality, it is composed of them, and therefore they are not different.

If they were non-different, then there would be no distinction between the lump of clay and its atoms. Mahāmati, [this applies to] the evolving consciousnesses and the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).

If the true characteristic of consciousness were different [from its activity], the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) would not be its cause; if it were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cease, the store-consciousness should also cease.
However, its own true characteristic does not actually cease. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is not that the true characteristic of consciousness ceases, but rather that its karmic characteristic ceases.
If the true characteristic were to cease, the store-consciousness would perish; Mahāmati, if the store-consciousness were to perish, [it would not exist].
This differs from the heterodox views of the annihilationists (*ucchedavāda*).

Above, it establishes as its thesis that the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), together with their respective divisions, combine with the object-consciousness (*nimitta-vijñāna*) to form a single entity;

through this mutual interdependence of the perishing and non-perishing aspects, it demonstrates—by means of examples such as a lump of clay and its dust, or gold and its ornaments—that these are neither different nor non-different.
The establishment of the concordant example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) also establishes the thesis that the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing of Aśvaghoṣa are conjoined;
it likewise establishes the thesis of a true inference (*pramāṇa*) regarding the conjunction of the manifest-consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the object-consciousness (*nimitta-vijñāna*).

The atom (*paramāṇu*) and gold serve as metaphors for the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) and its true nature (*tathatā*), while the lump of clay and the ornamental objects serve as metaphors for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). As for the lump of clay...
If it were different from the atoms, then the lump of clay would not be composed of atoms; yet since the lump of clay is in fact composed of atoms, we know they are not different.
If the lump of clay were not different from the atoms, then when the lump of clay is destroyed, the atoms would also be destroyed, and there would be no distinction between them.
If the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) were essentially different from the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), then...
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) should not take the true nature of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) as its cause.
Now, since the storehouse consciousness is formed by the true nature of the evolving consciousnesses following conditions, it is known that they are not different.

If the true nature of the evolving consciousnesses and the storehouse consciousness are not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses cease, the true nature of the storehouse consciousness should also cease. However, the true nature of the storehouse consciousness...
Since the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are in reality not extinguished, one knows they are not non-different [from their essence]; therefore, he shows this again, saying:

"The previous statement that 'if the characteristics are extinguished, the continuity is extinguished' does not mean that the true nature (*tathatā*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) can be extinguished.

Because the true nature of the storehouse consciousness is itself True Suchness (*tathatā*), it has never even arisen; how then could it be extinguished? It is merely a portion of the storehouse consciousness that is beginningless..."
It is explained that it is the *karmic marks* (*lakṣaṇa*) that are subject to extinction, not the *intrinsic true nature*. Regarding what is called "intrinsic true nature":
the mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which does not depend on delusive conditions and whose nature is inherently spiritual and lucid, is termed "intrinsic true nature.

This is explained from the perspective of non-differentiation; even when following the winds of ignorance to undergo birth and extinction, the nature of spiritual lucidity does not differ from its original state.
"Named as the self-characteristic of reality" is stated here in the sense of non-difference. Thus, the three characteristics previously set forth are profoundly purposeful.
If the fruit of the self-characteristic of reality were subject to cessation, then the *ālayavijñāna* would also be subject to cessation.

This, conversely, demonstrates that the *ālayavijñāna* is formed through the conjunction of the real and the false; thus, although the false may cease, the essence of the real is not non-existent. Therefore, the Treatise says:
What is called "cessation" refers only to the cessation of the mind's appearances, not the cessation of the essence of the mind.
If the true nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) were truly subject to cessation, it would be no different from the doctrines of the nihilistic non-Buddhists;

in that case, who would be the one who realizes and what would be the object realized? Therefore, a verse in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata’s pure store and the worldly *ālaya* are like..."
Gold and its finger-ring are neither different nor not different. A verse in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The ultimate truth of these phenomena is also precisely suchness; because it is eternally as it is by nature, it is the true nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Clearly, Vasubandhu also took the *tathāgatagarbha* as the essence of consciousness. However, later commentators established only the unchanging [aspect] and...

It is permitted to follow conditions; now, according to Asvaghosa, a formal inference is set forth: the true consciousness (tathatā-vijñāna), the storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna), and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (pravṛtti-vijñāna) constitute the thesis (*pakṣa*) as being a combination of existent dharmas.
The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they mutually transform through the characteristics of the destructible and the indestructible.

The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "like gold and its ornaments. Furthermore, according to Dharmapāla, a formal inference is set forth: the storehouse consciousness and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena...

This is the thesis that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise through combination; the reason (*hetu*) is that the characteristics of destruction and non-destruction are mutually interdependent;
and the concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is like a lump of clay and its atoms. These two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are both pillars for erecting the banner of the Dharma.
If one differs from this, then the cognitions of "Mind-only" (*cittamātra*) and "Consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) will all fall into the arguments of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Mahāmati, those heterodox teachers propound such a doctrine as this: they claim that when the grasping of objects ceases, the flow of consciousness also ceases.
Mahāmati, if the flow of consciousness were to cease, then the beginningless flow would have to be severed.

Mahāmati, the heterodox teachers say that the cause for the arising of the flow is not produced by the meeting of the eye-consciousness, visible forms, and light; rather, there is another distinct cause. Mahāmati, as for that cause—
To speak of [the self] as being either supreme, or a person (*puruṣa*), or Īśvara, or time, or atoms—this is the nihilistic doctrine of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
They claim that when the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (the discerning consciousness that grasps objects) ceases, the eighth consciousness—the beginningless *ālayavijñāna*—also ceases;
they do not realize that the very essence of the eight consciousnesses is [the Tathāgata-garbha].
This true consciousness is called the "true, constant flow," which from beginningless time until now arises according to conditions and ceases according to conditions;
yet it is unaware that its essence has never once been born and never once ceased.
If one were to say that this flow can be extinguished, then the flow from beginningless time should have been severed; why then does it continue to flow without end until this very day?
Thus, it is clear that this true, eternal flow—extending through past and present, uninterrupted and indestructible—is the cause for the arising of all phenomena.

Yet the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are ignorant of this; on the contrary, they claim that the cause of the flow of arising is not like the way consciousness arises from the convergence of form and light, but rather that there is a distinct, separate cause that acts as a creator. As for what they call this "distinct cause":

They are like heterodox schools. What is meant by "heterogeneous causes"? It refers to those who hold that within the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), the Great Entity (*mahat*) and its conjunction (*saṃyoga*) constitute the cause as the agent (*kartṛ*), as is reckoned in the Vaiśeṣika school;

or those who hold that among the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the three qualities (*triguṇa*) constitute the cause as the agent, while the *puruṣa* (spirit) is the knower, the seer, and the enjoyer, as in the Sāṃkhya school.

Among these, some conceive of the person (*pudgala*) as the self (*ātman*), maintaining that Maheśvara is a real, omnipresent, and eternal entity who acts as the cause capable of producing all phenomena, like the followers of the Pāśupatas.

Others maintain that time (*kāla*) possesses functional activity and acts as the cause capable of producing all things, like the followers of the Kālavādins. Still others maintain that the ultimate... [is the cause].
The subtle reality (*sūkṣma-tattva*) is eternally the causal agent capable of producing phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), as conceived by the Lokāyatas;

because these [phenomena] do not take as their root either the disintegrating or the non-disintegrating characteristics, they are all mutually dependent causes, which are what are called "distinct causes" (*anyahetu*).
This is like the three samādhis of consciousness and mind cultivated by Maitreya, extending even to the empty lands of the Tathāgatas, whether pure or defiled.
Existence and non-existence are both manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind.

Because I realize that these are solely the products of mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*), the nature of consciousness flows forth as immeasurable Tathāgatas. Thus, the calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not go beyond this;
they fail to recognize that [the world] flows from this consciousness-mind, and instead take that which has flowed forth from consciousness as the cause.

How could this be the true cause? If it were indeed the flowing stream of consciousness (*vijñāna-srotas*) that could be extinguished, who then would be the "Born Man" (*puruṣa*), the "Sovereign" (*īśvara*), and so forth, whom you take to be the creator?
Furthermore, what you call the "creator" is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing, yet you falsely reckon it to be eternal;
conversely, the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), which is truly eternal and flows on, you instead treat as something that undergoes annihilation. Thus, you mistake the eternal for...
To claim that the impermanent is permanent is equally a discourse on the doctrine of annihilationism.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of self-nature (svabhāva): namely, the self-nature of accumulation, the self-nature of existence, the self-nature of characteristics, the self-nature of the great elements, the self-nature of cause, the self-nature of conditions, and the self-nature of accomplishment.
This is because non-Buddhists who advocate the doctrine of annihilationism regard the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as being without intrinsic nature;

therefore, it is represented by the seven kinds of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to demonstrate that all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature. How much more so for the "nature of all natures," which would itself be without intrinsic nature?
As for the "accumulated intrinsic nature" (*samudita-svabhāva*), it arises from the gathering together of the eye-consciousness, visible form, and light.
The gathering [of all things] is such that all sages and worthies gather herefrom, yet there are distinctions among them: the śrāvakas see suffering and sever the origin;
the pratyekabuddhas awaken to the gathering and dispersal of the origin and contemplate detachment; the bodhisattvas know that the origin is fundamentally non-existent and lacks conjunction;
and the Buddhas take the origin as the primary meaning (paramārtha). As for external paths, they give rise to views of existence and non-existence regarding the origin; this is the correct [view].

Just as gods and humans see rice while hungry ghosts see the waters of the Ganges, the rice appears differently to each and the water appears distinct to each, all because they manifest according to their own mental perceptions (*svacitta-pratyakṣa*).
Thus, although various collections appear with differences, the nature and essence (*svabhāva*) of those collections have never been different.
Although all phenomena arise through the gathering of causes and conditions, that which is produced...

The natures of the myriad things differ, and their characteristics vary; for example, the nature of Gu Sou was stubborn while the nature of Emperor Shun was filial, and the nature of Emperor Yao was compassionate while the nature of Dan Zhu was arrogant—thus, the natures they received each have its own inherent character.
The appearance of the Duke of Zhou was like a withered tree stump; the appearance of Gao Yao was like a carved melon; and the appearance of Fu Yue was—
The fish fin and the stature of Zhongni are both forms bestowed by nature, each possessing its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The solidity of earth, the moisture of water, the dryness of fire, and the movement of wind are the natures of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), each possessing its own intrinsic nature.
The pine is naturally straight, the thorn bush is naturally crooked, the crane is naturally white, and the crow is naturally black; these are their respective causal natures.
There is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). When a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) encounters the sun, it produces fire; when a moon-stone (*candramas*) encounters the moon, it exudes water;
when amber encounters grass, it becomes adhesive; and when a magnet encounters iron, it attracts it—these are instances where conditions possess their own respective intrinsic natures.
Likewise, ore is transformed into gold through smelting, raw jade into precious stone through carving, and wood into vessels through shaping.
Since the established nature (*dharmatā*) each possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the subsequent passage states: "All phenomena possess intrinsic nature and lack extrinsic nature.

How could this be intended as a doctrine of annihilationism? Question: Previously it was stated that one "attains the state of having no intrinsic nature," whereas here it is said that there "is intrinsic nature.
Is this not a contradiction between your earlier and later statements? Answer: This is because True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not abide in a fixed intrinsic nature.

Because they can manifest all self-natures according to conditions, they exist as causes when in a causal state, as conditions when in a conditional state, as gods when in the realm of gods, and as humans when in the realm of humans.

Outsiders are deluded regarding this; taking dharmas that lack self-nature, they formulate a doctrine of annihilationism, yet they further express it through the notion of having self-nature. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "All the grasses and leaves of the world..."
When one threads together and examines their origins, all things possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); how much more so the mind, which is the essence of all things?

That the mind itself lacks an intrinsic nature is precisely this point. Thus, the *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states: "To have an intrinsic nature is affirmative designation (*vidhi*), while to lack an intrinsic nature is negative designation (*pratiṣedha*).
This is because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to the existence of an intrinsic nature; therefore, the absence of intrinsic nature is used to negate it, as they are attached to such a notion.
Because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they are expressed by means of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*): namely, the realm of the mind (*citta-viṣaya*), the realm of wisdom (*jñāna-viṣaya*), the realm of insight (*prajñā-viṣaya*), the realm of vision (*darśana-viṣaya*), the realm that transcends the two views, the realm that transcends the stages of the sons [of the Buddha] and others, and the realm of the Tathāgata’s own realization.

The above has already explained that the seven kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*) are all *tathatā* (suchness); because they do not maintain their own nature, they are designated as the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
If one can comprehend this, it is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, having shown the seven kinds of self-nature, he further shows the seven kinds of ultimate mind. As for what is called the "sphere of the mind," it refers to whatever meets the eye.
All is the pure jewel-like awakening, with no other dharma whatsoever. As the subsequent text states: "The measure of the mind that is without mind" refers to the locus of self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the "sphere of wisdom" (*prajñā-viṣaya*): it is the observation of all dharmas, the thorough penetration of their non-existence, and the attainment of sovereign power;
this is what is called wisdom. Regarding the "sphere of knowledge" (*jñāna-viṣaya*): it is the gathering [of these insights].
Regarding the teaching on karma: it is that the mind does not accumulate [karmic seeds] through wisdom;

this is what is meant by seeing all forms as the form of the Buddha and all sounds as the sound of the Buddha—namely, what the Buddha knows and what the Buddha sees. Regarding transcending the realm of dualistic views:
it is to be free from existence and non-existence, identity and difference, bothness and neitherness. Regarding transcending the realm of the stage of the sons [of the Buddha]: it is bodhi...
The stage where [the Bodhisattvas] such as Śāriputra regard all sentient beings as their only child has now also been transcended; this is as stated in the subsequent text:
"I teach that these various vehicles are without vehicle and without a rider; there is no establishment of vehicles—I teach them as the One Vehicle.

That the Tathāgata has personally reached his own realm means that he has attained self-awakened noble wisdom (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna*) through his own realization, not by depending on others. He has thus penetrated the state of Buddhahood.
This is the Dharma.
Mahāmati, this is the mind of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present;
by means of this mind of the ultimate reality of the intrinsic nature, the Tathāgata brings about the manifestation of the world.
Regarding the mundane, the supramundane, and the most excellent supramundane dharmas, the noble eye of wisdom enters into the establishment of specific and general characteristics.
As they are established, they do not coincide with the evil views of the treatises of the outsiders. Mahāmati, why is it said that they coincide with the evil views of the treatises of the outsiders?

It is because they perceive their own realm through the vision of false discrimination, failing to realize that what appears is merely the manifestation of their own minds; thus, they do not penetrate the limits of reality. Mahāmati!
Ignorant ordinary beings (bālapṛthagjana) formulate dualistic views regarding the non-existence and existence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) as the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
These seven kinds of objective spheres are the ultimate truths that the Buddhas of the three periods have realized concerning the seven kinds of intrinsic nature;
by means of this mind of ultimate truth, they accord with ordinary beings to accomplish worldly phenomena.
One should accomplish supramundane dharmas through the three vehicles; one should accomplish the supreme supramundane dharmas through the Supreme Vehicle.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "By observing the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination with inferior wisdom, one attains the bodhi of a śrāvaka;
by observing it with middling wisdom, one attains the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha; and by observing it with superior wisdom, one attains the bodhi of a bodhisattva."
By contemplating the supreme wisdom, one attains the Bodhi of the Buddha; because one has attained the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the eye of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñācakṣus*) opens.
Thus, one is able to enter the absolute (*tattva*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), establishing all activities.

Whatever is established is entirely the realm of self-awakening through the mind of the ultimate truth; because it does not fall into dualistic views, it does not share in the evil views of external paths.
The individual characteristics are the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the common characteristics are the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Yet, as for what is called "commonality" regarding false views, how could there be a separate place of commonality? It is simply within the seven kinds of self-realized realms of the Tathāgata that one produces these false views through one's own deluded imaginings.
Due to such ignorance and confusion, one fails to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind.

The reflections in a mirror and the moon in water are fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent, yet one falsely establishes the boundaries of existence and non-existence, thereby creating self-generated obstructions that prevent penetration into the ultimate truth of the self-nature—the mind of the primary meaning. One mistakenly claims that the continuous flow has ceased and that all natures are devoid of nature;
conversely, one calculates that the creator is eternal. All of these are instances of being devoured by the evil views of ignorant ordinary beings regarding their own selves.

The mind of the ultimate reality of nature gives rise to these two views; yet one does not know that the mind of the ultimate reality of the self-nature of nature is the true aspect of the *ālayavijñāna*.
Without this, the Buddhas would have no means to accomplish the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane dharmas.
How could it be subject to annihilationism?

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the cessation of the suffering of the three realms of existence through the extinction of the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma, and how the illusory objects manifested by one's own mind are seen according to their appearance.
This refers to the non-Buddhists who, failing to realize that these are manifestations of their own minds, perceive them as real like illusions and thus cling to them as such.

Constantly calculating cessation and relying upon this to practice, one merely revolves further within the three realms; how could such a method—seeking to abandon suffering through suffering—possibly succeed?

If one can truly sever the causes of suffering within the three existences (*tribhava*) and extinguish the effects of suffering within the three realms, then one will be able to perceive, in accordance with reality, the various illusory manifestations of one's own mind.
One will certainly never again fall into the two views of annihilationism and eternalism; this is the correct [path].

I have taught this to you because it is the essential method for practicing the transcendence of suffering; this misplaced passage should instead appear before the words, "Furthermore, Mahāmati, if there are any other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who wish to cause the non-existent and the existent to manifest, and for things to abide in time.
Mahāmati, if there are any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who desire to cause the seedless and the seeded to appear, and for phenomena to endure through time...

“Mahāmati, regarding the arising and abiding of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas), or the claim that they cease after having arisen—whether it be a doctrine of continuity, of entities, of birth, of existence, of nirvāṇa, of the path, of karma, of its fruit, or of the truths—it is a nihilistic doctrine of annihilation. Why is this?
Because these are not apprehended in the present, and because seeing their beginning is impossible. Mahāmati, it is just as, for example,”
Just as a broken jar does not perform the function of a jar, and just as a scorched seed does not produce a sprout, so it is, Mahāmati: when the nature of the aggregates, elements,
