It is quiescence; they conceive of nirvana based on the cessation of the sense-faculties regarding future objects, yet it is not because they have realized the noble wisdom that proceeds toward the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism; having established these respectively, one attains the noble wisdom of self-realization.

Mahāmati, having abandoned the conceptual attachment to the existence of things apart from the two self-natures, and through the transformation of the mind, mentation, and consciousness, one severs all delusions regarding the grasped and the grasper within the manifestations of one's own mind.

For those who practice the noble wisdom of self-realization on the stage of the Tathāgata, they do not conceive of that state as being either existent or non-existent; such is the realm for those practitioners.
Mahāmati, when the perception of grasping at existence and non-existence arises, one thereby grasps at nourishment and grasps at a self and a person.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, if it is said that all such natures, intrinsic natures, and specific or general characteristics are spoken by a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) and not by a Dharma-Buddha, then all such verbal expressions arise solely from the hopes and views of the ignorant; they do not establish a separate realm of their own intrinsic nature.
The Dharma is that which attains the dwelling in the bliss of self-realized samādhi through noble wisdom; this is explained by way of analytical demonstration.
This critique, O Mahāmati, concerns those who are unskilled in meaning and who give rise to various forms of conceptual construction (*parikalpa*) by clinging to verbal expressions.

As for the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they are: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative testimony (*āptāgama*). Direct perception refers to the portion of the object that is realized through personal experience.

It is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is free from conceptual designations (*nāma-pada*), lacks the mind that calculates by means of signs (*tarka*), and directly realizes the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

This refers to the aforementioned ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)—the object of direct perception of the mind—which is free from existence and non-existence, free from objective referents (*ālambana*), and is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the sevenfold categories.
As for inference (*anumāna*), it is that which causes others to know through comparative reasoning by means of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

If the aforementioned three members of the syllogism and so forth constitute authoritative verbal testimony (*āptavacana-pramāṇa*), then one cites the Buddhas as evidence that they are not erroneous, as it is said:

"As the Buddhas have taught, regarding the phrase 'arising' and the phrase 'non-arising,' these are the nature and self-nature of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present; they are the foremost. Thus it is.

The five-part argument consists of the combination of the three members—thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—along with the application (*upanaya*) and conclusion (*nigamana*). As for establishing each [point] individually:

it is like establishing the internal and external teachings one by one through inference (*anumāna*), so that people may distinguish the false from the correct consciousness and avoid errors in practice or mistaken interpretations.

For instance, within the internal teaching, one establishes the arising and ceasing of the various consciousnesses as the thesis, and their successive transformation as the reason. The clay... [is the example].
Using the analogy of a mass of atoms, the non-Buddhists take annihilation as their tenet, asserting that there is a cause whether it possesses seeds or lacks them,
and employing analogies such as withered sprouts and broken jars; when I speak of establishing [the truth] through each of the three means of valid cognition and the five-membered syllogism,

it is precisely because I wish to lead people to recognize false consciousness, to attain self-awakened noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), and to remain far removed from the conditions of deluded thought.
Regarding the two kinds of self-nature—arising and being beyond verbal expression—how could one know them?

As long as one has not yet abandoned the false conceptualizations and attachments of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna-vikalpa-abhiniveśa*), one still considers the four positions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to be real and falls into these four positions.

If, however, one can indeed transform the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*), and transform the physical body into the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), then that which is manifested by one's own mind—the grasper and the grasped—[is realized].
Those who take up the severance of all false imaginings and attain the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom of self-realization as the causal-ground mind for their practice, are pure by nature;

regarding the objective realms of the particular and universal characteristics of that very nature, they certainly do not form dualistic notions of existence or non-existence, nor do they fall into the four logical extremes. Furthermore, if a practitioner, regarding those particular and universal characteristics...

If one gives rise to perceptions of existence and non-existence regarding objects and thereby engages in grasping, that is precisely the attachment to the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
Because the arising of thoughts and mental movements involves delusion and inversion, it is so called.
If this is so, for what reason does the Tathāgata speak of the "existence of intrinsic nature" and the "ultimate mind," and also speak of the Tathāgata’s noble eye of wisdom entering [into them]?
The self-characteristics and common characteristics are all spoken by the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha in response to the capacities of sentient beings;

they are not spoken by the *dharmakāya* Buddha, for the *dharmakāya* Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma transcends verbal expression. Nevertheless, even though the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha speaks in this way, it is done in response to the aspirations of deluded beings who seek something to be realized;
thus, he provisionally establishes nirvāṇa as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the unchanging true suchness (*tathatā*).
It is for the sake of those who follow conditions according to their own characteristics and common characteristics, so that they may know how to proceed;

it is not for the sake of true practitioners, for whom one does not separately establish the dharmas of the nature of their own inclinations, nor for those who have attained the bliss of the samādhi of self-realized noble wisdom, for whom distinctions are displayed.
For true practitioners, speech is severed and thought is extinguished; what is called "discourse" is merely a distinction.
The practice of reality is free from names and designations.
For example, when the reflection of a tree appears in water, it is neither a reflection nor not a reflection; it is neither the form of a tree nor not the form of a tree.
Likewise, the externalists, conditioned by their habitual tendencies and attachments to delusive thoughts, rely upon the notions of identity, difference, both, or neither.

Those who perceive existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence, as well as permanence and impermanence, are unable to know that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds.
This illustrates the unskillful discrimination of the manifestations of one's own mind, falsely conceptualizing the two divisions of subject (grāhaka) and object (grāhya) as truly existent.

The water is a metaphor for the ālayavijñāna, and the tree’s reflection is a metaphor for the two divisions of subject and object; in reality, they do not constitute such characteristics or perceptions.
Those non-Buddhists, being perfumed by their habitual tendencies of views, do not understand that the two divisions—the perceived and the perceiver—manifest from one’s own mind.

Like the two horns of a snail, which appear as a pair when extended and become a single unity when contracted, they are not truly existent; yet they falsely establish the four logical alternatives (*catuskoṭi*). One should formulate the following formal inference (*pramāṇa*):
The subject (*dharmin*) is the perceived and the perceiver; the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they manifest from one’s own mind; the reason (*hetu*) is that both are [simultaneously] present.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are like the reflection of a tree in water.

For example, as a bright mirror manifests all forms and images according to conditions yet remains free from conceptual construction—being neither an image nor a non-image, though it appears as an image—the foolish and deluded take it to be an image. Thus it is with the evil [views] of the outsiders.

Seeing the images of one's own mind appear, one gives rise to false conceptualizations and attachments based on views of identity or difference, both or neither, existence or non-existence, or being neither existent nor non-existent, as well as the views of permanence or impermanence.
This is like a clear mirror which the followers of the Two Vehicles fail to understand as their own mind; they falsely conceptualize that there truly exist the five sense objects outside the mind.
The metaphor of images appearing according to conditions illustrates how the first five consciousnesses appear according to conditions as the five sense objects;

these are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for they do not carry names or words and lack the mind that deliberates. They are not "images" in the conceptual sense, yet they are like images because one merely sees them as such without forming the thought "this is an image.
Thus it is said: "Just as a bright mirror manifests all forms and images, so too does the manifesting consciousness manifest."

The locus is likewise so. Because those non-Buddhists do not understand that this image is a manifestation of their own mind, they rely upon this image to give rise to various conceptual constructions (*parikalpa*) regarding existence and non-existence. One should formulate the following syllogism: "The five sense-objects are the subject (*dharmin*); they are manifestations of one's own mind, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*);
because they appear in accordance with conditions, this is the reason (*hetu*); like an image appearing in a mirror, this is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)."
For example, when wind and water come together, sound is produced; that sound is neither an intrinsic nature nor a non-nature.

In the same way, the false discriminations of the evil views of the outsiders rely upon the notions of oneness and otherness, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence.

This analogy illustrates how those of the Two Vehicles fail to realize that sound arises from four causes and eight conditions, and thus falsely cling to names, phrases, and syllables as being substantially existent.
Water represents the various consciousnesses; wind represents the eight conditions.
[Sound] arises from the internal causes of the eye-consciousness and so forth, and the external conditions of the eight factors such as the teeth; yet they do not understand this.
All that consists of speech is devoid of real meaning; yet the followers of the Two Vehicles and the non-Buddhists search through words and count the characters, chasing echoes and following sounds.
They cling to grammar to establish their treatises and take sound itself as the essence of the teaching, reckoning it as either existent or non-existent.

How could this not be a false view? One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "Speech" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is unreal" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); [this is] the reason (*hetu*).
It is said that because they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, they are likened to the sound of wind and water.
For example, where there are no plants or trees upon the great earth, hot vapors flow like rivers and waves, and clouds gather;

these are neither existent nor non-existent, for they are characterized by both craving and non-craving. Thus, foolish people are deluded by the false imaginings perfumed by beginningless habitual tendencies.

The attachment to the gates of phenomena—such as arising, abiding, and ceasing; oneness and difference; simultaneity and non-simultaneity; existence and non-existence; neither existence nor non-existence;
permanence and impermanence; and their dependence on conditions—is likewise like a mirage or a wave.

This metaphor illustrates how foolish people do not realize that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) manifests from True Suchness (*tathatā*), yet the seventh consciousness falsely clings to it as a self.
It is like a herd of deer, driven by thirst, who mistake a shimmering mirage for water in a place where there is no vegetation;
they see waves and clouds gathering, unaware that the mirage is neither an existent nature nor a non-existent nature, being merely a product of craving.
Because of greed, those who are greedy among a herd of deer see [the deer] but do not see that which is free from greed;

likewise, these deluded beings take beginningless, false ignorance as the perfuming agent (*paribhāvaka*) and True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the object perfumed (*paribhāvya*), whereby the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is transformed.
Then, the seventh deluded thought-giving consciousness greedily craves the *ālaya*, loves the *ālaya*, and stubbornly clings to it as a self.

Based on that storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which arises and ceases simultaneously with it, various forms of pervasive conceptualization arise through the gateway of its own-abiding object;
this is likewise like the thirsty deer’s craving for a mirage, which manifests as waves while the mirage itself is not water.
The "gateway of its own-abiding object" refers to the storehouse consciousness, because the seventh consciousness arises and ceases in dependence upon that storehouse consciousness.
Furthermore, because it takes that as its object, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Depending upon that, it evolves; taking that as its object.
For example, it is like a person using incantations or mechanical devices to cause a *piśāca* ghost—which is not a sentient being—to move and act through skillful means;
yet ordinary, deluded people falsely imagine and cling to it as coming and going. Such is the evil view of the non-Buddhists.

It is observed that they rely on false constructions based on the conceptual proliferations and attachments to identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and permanence and impermanence;
this is a metaphor for the foolish who, failing to understand their own minds, falsely grasp at the five aggregates, the body, and the mind as a real self. This is the metaphor.
Just as a magician, through the power of incantations and arts, can cause wooden mechanical figures to move—how could these truly be reckoned among the number of sentient beings?
Because those illusory persons, through the power of incantations, are formed by the attachment of ghostly entities, their movements and actions appear exactly like those of real humans.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "For example, a skillful magician conjures various [forms]..."

Although men and women see the movement of their various faculties, it is ultimately due to the drawing of a single mechanism; yet ordinary fools, unaware of this, cling to the notion that there is actual coming and going, giving rise to all manner of conceptual attachments.
The illusionist is a metaphor for True Suchness (*tathatā*), and the power of the mantra is a metaphor for the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Thus, these five aggregates—the body and mind—arise entirely from True Suchness following conditions; as the storehouse consciousness departs and returns, they follow.

Previously, they took it to be the root of birth and death; yet how could those various externalists, with their evil views and aspirations, establish diverse causes as the root of birth and death, claiming them to be non-illusory?

Mahāmati, for this reason, one who wishes to attain the reality of self-realized noble wisdom should abandon [the notions of] arising, abiding, and ceasing, as well as oneness, difference, both, and neither.
One should abandon the deluded conceptualizations of evil views—such as both existence and non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
This is an exhortation for those who practice true cultivation to naturally enter the noble wisdom of self-awakening by remaining free from the four extremes of birth and cessation.
This is because the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated; it is only due to...

Failing to realize that the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world before one’s eyes are all images manifested by one’s own mind—and that they are fundamentally not truly existent—one falsely clings to the five aggregates, the body and mind, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth as being a real self and real dharmas.

Consequently, views such as oneness and difference, existence and non-existence, arise; thereby, one transmigrates through birth and death without end, unable to realize entry into one’s own [true nature].

If noble self-aware wisdom can realize that the body, the sensory faculties, and the receptacle world are like a mirage or a city of the gandharvas, then one will not give rise to notions of arising and ceasing, nor to views of existence and non-existence; at that very moment, this is the perfected nature of noble self-aware wisdom.
How could there be deluded conceptualization apart from noble self-aware wisdom, or noble self-aware wisdom apart from deluded conceptualization?

"Awakened to noble wisdom indeed! By means of the Great Wisdom, you have asked about that which is not practiced by any outsiders, but is the domain of self-realized noble wisdom—free from the imagined nature of individual and common characteristics, and entering into the meaning of the supreme reality.
This seems as though it would divide the practices of outsiders from the practices of self-realized noble wisdom into two separate blocks; yet how could one know that outsiders...

That which is not traversed by the Path is precisely the sphere of activity of self-awakened noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). It is free from anything to be abandoned, for there is nothing to abandon; it enters nowhere, for there is no place to enter.
This is because the very state of freedom is entry, and the very state of entry is freedom. As the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*) says:
"To know illusion is itself freedom; to be free from illusion is itself awakening. How could noble wisdom be something obtainable apart from the cessation of birth and death?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Like a phantom, a dream, the reflection of trees in water, falling hair, a mirage in the heat—thus one should contemplate the three realms of existence (trisaṃsāra) to ultimately attain liberation.
Just as a thirsty deer, its mind deluded by shifting appearances, perceives a mirage as water though no actual water exists, so too does the seed of consciousness shift and revolve."

When objects are perceived, the deluded ordinary person gives rise to false conceptualization, just as one whose vision is obscured by a cataract clings to and grasps at the nature of beginningless birth and death.
Just as a wedge is driven out by another wedge, one abandons the grasping of craving;

by observing things as being like illusions, spells, mechanical devices, floating clouds, dreams, or flashes of lightning, one attains liberation and forever severs the three continuities. Regarding those [objects], there is no agent, just as...

Just as one perceives the flame in the sky, so should one know all phenomena; thus there is nothing to be known. Verbal teachings are merely provisional names, and even they possess no inherent characteristics;
yet, regarding them, one gives rise to deluded conceptualization. As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
"The mind is like a skilled painter who paints out various forms; from it, the five aggregates are entirely produced."
Because phenomena are uncreated, they are illustrated through metaphors such as illusions, dreams, reflections of trees in water, floating hairs, and mirages.
If one can observe these three [the subject, object, and their union] through various profound metaphors, one will attain ultimate liberation.
The reason one fails to attain liberation is precisely like a thirsty deer that does not realize that a mirage is fundamentally empty.
When the mind moves and thoughts shift, one becomes deluded and inverted, falsely conceiving water where there is no water and remaining unaware that no actual water exists.
In this same way, all phenomena within the three realms are fundamentally not real;

they arise from the seeds stored within the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) that give rise to various active manifestations (*pravṛtti*). Thus, while the moving and shifting mind perceives objective spheres, the foolish worldling takes them to be real.
Indeed, it is through the attachment to false conceptualization that the various views of existence and non-existence arise;

it is like a person with pure eyes who, when obscured by a cataract, falsely perceives falling hairs. This stems from beginningless time, where through birth and death, and death and birth, one clings to the grasped and the grasper and cannot achieve liberation for oneself—just as when a wedge is stuck in the eye, one cannot [remove it].
The Tathāgata himself appeared and taught him various profound metaphors, such as those of illusions and dreams, to cause him to apply his mind to observation and abandon the grasper and the grasped.
Just as one uses a wedge to extract a wedge, he taught that the grasper is like a magician, like a dream, or like a mechanical device activated by incantations;
and that the grasped is like a floating cloud, like what is seen in a dream, or like lightning.

If one can observe in this way, one attains liberation: namely, that the threefold continuity of the karmic fruits of worldly sentient beings is utterly empty and void. Who is the agent? What is the acted-upon?
It is exactly like a mirage, like space—fundamentally non-existent. Observing all phenomena with such an observation, throughout the entire day...
One discerns all phenomena without giving rise to conceptual notions, and thus is not obstructed by any dharmas.
Although these verbal teachings are like using a wedge to extract another wedge, they are nonetheless provisional names and lack any real characteristic.

Fools, failing to understand this, further cling to various names and phrases, giving rise to manifold deluded thoughts; how could they know that medicine is prescribed according to the illness? Now, furthermore—
Alas, taking medicine and contracting an illness!
The latent tendencies (anuśaya) are like falling hair, like a painting of falling hair, like a magical illusion, a dream, a city of the Gandharvas, a fire-wheel, or a mirage;

though non-existent, they appear to sentient beings. So it is with the notions of permanence and impermanence, identity and difference, bothness and neitherness—these are the continuous succession of faults from beginningless time.
Fools, through their deluded false imaginings, perceive various forms appearing within a bright mirror, water, clear eyes, or a wondrous mani-jewel,
yet in reality nothing exists there at all. All natures appear like the shimmering mirages of a hot day, manifesting in various colors, yet like a dream, they possess no existence.

It is said that not only are the three realms of existence like an illusion, but even the five aggregates, the body, and the mind are like falling hairs, like a painting, like an illusion, like a dream, like a city of the gandharvas, like a fire wheel, and like a mirage—all of which are provisionally manifested as existent from an original non-existence.
Fools, regarding these, calculate them to be existent or non-existent, establishing various propositions; this arises from beginningless emptiness.
When various deluded thoughts arise from the continuous succession of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false errors,
one must transform consciousness (*vijñāna*) into wisdom (*jñāna*). Once these habitual tendencies have been dissolved, the fundamental mind becomes pure— like a bright mirror,
like still water, like a clear eye, or like a *maṇi* jewel— in which various forms appear, yet there is not even the slightest atom of grasping or attachment therein.

In the midst of daily activities and movements, although all phenomena appear arrayed side by side, in reality they are like the various forms manifested by a shimmering mirage in the daytime, or like the objects appearing in a dream—truly non-existent.
This is what is meant by being naturally free from the four propositions and naturally severed from the hundred negations; this is called ultimate liberation. How could it be something external?

It is so. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is free from these four positions: namely, identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence;
it is free from permanence and impermanence, and it transcends the conceptual constructions of affirmation, denial, discrimination, and compilation regarding existence and non-existence.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma takes as its primary focus the true nature of dependent origination, the path, cessation, and liberation;

he does not teach that things arise from a primal nature (*prakṛti*), nor from a creator god (*īśvara*), nor from no cause, nor from atoms (*paramāṇu*), nor from time (*kāla*), nor from the continuity of self-nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, in order to purify the afflictions and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), he establishes one hundred and eight [categories] in successive order, just as a merchant leader [establishes his wares].
The phrase "non-existence of the four extremes" refers to the skillful discernment of the characteristics of the various vehicles (*yāna*) and stages (*bhūmi*).

This concluding statement clarifies that although the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma throughout the day, he does not fall into the four extremes, nor does he harbor the intention of establishing or denigrating through conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It is spoken for the purpose of compiling the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and pointing out the path of true practice.

The Dharma is designated as the True Reality (*tattva*), Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the Four Noble Truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*), and the Three Gateways to Liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*); these are its primary tenets.

It is not like the doctrines taught by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which take Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), the Sovereign Lord (*īśvara*), causelessness (*ahetu*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), time (*kāla*), or the continuity of self-nature (*svabhāva-saṃtati*) as their fundamental principles.
This [Dharma] is the domain of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*), whereas the non-Buddhists...
Since that which is not practiced is thus, by what means can one attain the true reality and liberation?

Although it is said that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is already free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), for what reason does he establish the one hundred and eight propositions to differentiate the various vehicles (*yāna*) and the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*)?

Therefore, the commentary explains: "It is for the sake of purifying the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) of the two vehicles and removing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the Bodhisattvas."
Because of obstructions, it is like a caravan leader who leads sentient beings to the place of jewels; proceeding from one *yojana* to another *yojana*, there must necessarily be a sequence.
Therefore, by establishing the hundred and eight propositions (*śata-aṣṭaka-pada*), the characteristics of the various vehicles (*yāna*) and stages (*bhūmi*) are distinguished.
To eliminate the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it is taught that there are four fruits (*phala*) in sequence for the purpose of purifying the objects of cognition (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Those who understand the obstacles explain that while there are ten stages (*bhūmi*) in their sequence, in reality there are one hundred and eight phrases;
these are not the phrases of the two vehicles, nor are they not the phrases of the two vehicles; they are the phrases of the ten stages, yet they are not the phrases of the ten stages.

Thus far, the three kinds of habitual tendencies have been extensively explained to reveal that true cultivation is free from the marks of mental objects, free from the marks of verbal expression, and free from attachment.
Following the conclusion of the [section on] marks, there is further clarification of the causes and effects of the heterodox and the orthodox.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four? They are:

the dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna that examines meanings, the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object, and the Tathāgata-dhyāna. What is the dhyāna practiced by fools? It refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...

The dhyāna practiced by ignorant worldlings consists of those practitioners who observe the selflessness of persons through the characteristics of specific and general traits, the chain of bones, impermanence, suffering, and impurity;
being primarily attached to such signs, they do not distinguish between the initial observation and the subsequent stages of progress, nor do they eliminate these signs—
this is called the dhyāna of ignorant worldlings.
This first distinguishes between the two causes—the false and the correct. Generally speaking, that which takes the mind of arising and ceasing as its cause is false;

that which takes the non-arising, non-ceasing mind as its cause is correct. "The Dhyāna practiced by foolish people" refers to the causal practices cultivated by the followers of the Two Vehicles and external paths, who merely observe the nature of the selflessness of persons, contemplating that each of the five aggregates possesses its own intrinsic nature.
The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the five aggregates are impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity; these are called common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Because they do not realize true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity, they cling to the four marks—headed by impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self—keeping them constantly present in mind without ever having a different perspective.

Entering the dhyānas and gradually progressing through them until reaching the sphere of non-conception and the meditative absorption of cessation, although one realizes the marks of nirvāṇa, these marks are not yet eliminated;

this is called "the dhyāna practiced by fools. This is because they are unskilled in the fact that external objects—whether existent or non-existent—are merely manifestations of their own minds, and thus their stage of practice is not truly real.
The *Zongjing Lu* states: "This refers to the differences in views held by the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists."
They mistakenly take the deluded mind to be real and recognize a false thief as their true son; they collect fish eyes to pass off as the pearls of the black dragon.
Consequently, they cause the ignorant to fall into the heavy gates of the prison of existence and the perverted to drown in the waves of craving within the river of views.

What is the dhyāna of examining the meaning? It refers to one who has realized the selflessness of persons regarding their specific and general characteristics, as well as the lack of intrinsic nature in the views of outsiders concerning self, other, or both;
having further examined the selflessness of phenomena, they progressively advance through the meanings of the characteristics of those stages—this is called the dhyāna of examining the meaning.
This is the dhyāna practiced by bodhisattvas of the Initial Teaching (śākyadeśanā). It means that these bodhisattvas,

having already been able to observe the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) cultivated by the two vehicles and having known the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), and furthermore having observed the externalist teachings on arising from self,

arising from another, or arising from both, and having known their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they are further able to observe the distinctions between names, meanings, and intrinsic natures (*nāma-artha-svabhāva*).
Discerning separately that external natures are non-existent and realizing that all phenomena are without self—this is all manifested by the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
By severing the dualistic grasping at a self and phenomena through discrimination, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Having entered the first stage, one sequentially observes the characteristics and meanings of the various stages, gradually progressing upward; this sequential observation of the characteristics and meanings of the stages is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

The meditation on examining meaning (*arthapravicaya-dhyāna*). What is the meditation on the object-condition of suchness (*tathatālambana-dhyāna*)? It refers to the non-arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) within the true state of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is the suchness of false conceptualization;
this is called the meditation on the object-condition of suchness.

This is the dhyāna practiced by Bodhisattvas of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-deśanā*). It means that while Bodhisattvas of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-deśanā*) distinguish between the non-self of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*) within the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), gradually severing and gradually realizing them, they still belong to the counteractive measures against delusive thought (*vikalpa*).

These Bodhisattvas directly contemplate the *dharmatā* (the nature of reality) as it truly is; since from the very beginning there is no person or phenomenon, nor is there mind or object, they do not give rise to discrimination.

Although this does not take the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) as its object, it nevertheless takes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as its object; therefore, it is called "clinging to the object" (ālambana).
In the two higher teachings of Dhyāna, both are cultivated gradually according to the stages and positions; thus, they are collectively termed "gradual."

What is the Tathāgata-dhyāna? It refers to entering the stage of the Tathāgata, attaining the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization, abiding in the three kinds of bliss, and accomplishing inconceivable deeds for the sake of sentient beings; this is called the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
This is the dhyāna practiced by Bodhisattvas of the Sudden Teaching. Merely the non-arising of a single thought is called "Buddha.
Because it is not taught according to the gradual sequence of stages and positions, it is called "Sudden.

This means that when these Bodhisattvas first give rise to the mind of enlightenment, they suddenly awaken to their own mind, directly transcending to the stage of Buddhahood, attaining the noble wisdom of the three voids through self-awakening, and abiding in the three kinds of tranquility.
The extinction of pleasure is like a dragon obtaining water, which enables it to raise clouds and spread rain to extensively perform Buddha-works and bring sentient beings to fulfillment;
this is called the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: “The dhyāna practiced by ignorant people is [merely] observation.”

The meditation on signs, the meditation on the攀緣 (ālambana) as it truly is, the Tathāgata’s pure meditation—just like the forms of the sun and moon, the padma lotus, the deep abyss, space, and the embers of fire—the practitioner observes these various signs.
Even the meditations of external paths and those common to worldly ways likewise fall within the realm of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; to abandon all of them is [the path].
With the inconceivable hand of non-existence, he simultaneously touched their crowns, causing them to enter accordantly into the mark of suchness (*tathatā*).
The severance of delusive thoughts by the foolish and the movement toward *tathatā* by the bodhisattvas are both not yet pure.

As for the practitioner of pure dhyāna, when the sentiments of both ordinary beings and sages are exhausted, the essence is as it is in *tathatā*. This is what is called taking non-arising and non-ceasing as [the basis].

Those who, through their original cultivation of causes, are able to fully realize the fruits of the stages of attainment—such as those non-Buddhists who, attached to signs, seek entry into meditative absorption and may see the sun and moon in the void, or see red lotuses in deep and perilous places;
or the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna, whose bodies are reduced to ashes and whose wisdom is extinguished, becoming like empty space; or the Pratyekabuddhas of the Yāna of the Solitary Realizers.
Gradually severing all conditions and further eradicating habitual tendencies, it is like reducing them to ashes.

When practitioners of the Way observe such various signs and meanings, because they do not eliminate these signs, they fall into the paths of externalists; even those who have attained the Way may likewise fall into the spheres cultivated by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
If one possesses the highest capacity, not only will they not practice the two vehicles, but [they will transcend them].
The meditation of the Way is the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s contemplation. Even when taking suchness as an object of focus, one does not habitually approach it;

because there is a meaning to be contemplated, the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) have not yet been forgotten, and because there is suchness to be taken as an object, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) has not yet been forgotten.

If both nature and marks are empty, then through skillful means they are all abandoned. When suchness is like an illusion, one is detached from it; being detached from the illusion is awakening, whereby one suddenly enters the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) without anything remaining.
Because there is a realm of purity, one is consecrated by the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously;
one enters the body of the Tathāgata and enters into suchness (tathatā), manifesting inconceivable deeds for the sake of sentient beings— this is called the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what you speak of as 'parinirvāṇa,' what dharma do you designate as nirvāṇa?

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Mahāmati, the transformation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all intrinsic natures within the *ālayavijñāna*, the *manas*, and the *manovijñāna*—this is called nirvāṇa.
The nature of nirvāṇa for all Buddhas and myself is the realm of the emptiness of all phenomena."

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): this distinguishes between the two fruits of the heterodox and the orthodox. Generally speaking, that which realizes the Tathāgata’s own-nature emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as the objective sphere is considered orthodox, whereas that realized by the followers of the Two Vehicles and non-Buddhists is considered heterodox.
Mahāmati’s intention was that meditative contemplation— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]
Question: Since those who have realized the same fruit should be different [from one another], what kind of dharma is called *nirvāṇa*? The Buddha replied:

The *nirvāṇa* obtained through pure meditation is that which is accomplished by the transformation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the self-nature of all consciousnesses—namely, the habitual tendencies of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the habitual tendencies of the manas, the habitual tendencies of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the habitual tendencies of the views of the first five consciousnesses. This is the one [nature].

All consciousnesses each have their own intrinsic nature and their own habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). If they do not undergo transformation and give rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*), they are the phenomena of birth and death.
If one can transform the eight consciousnesses and cause them to become the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*), I and all Buddhas call this "Nirvana.
This Nirvana is precisely the state in which the intrinsic nature of all consciousnesses is empty; its objective realm is solely the One.
When the self-nature of all consciousness is empty, then the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are all empty;
they are quiescent in their own place and in nirvana in their own place, with nothing further remaining.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is the realm of the self-realization of noble wisdom, free from the false imaginings of annihilation and permanence, and its nature is not...

Why is it that nature is not eternal? It is because the conceptualizations of self-characteristics and common characteristics have been severed; thus, it is not eternal. Why is it that it is not annihilated?
It is because all noble ones—of the past, future, and present—attain self-awakening; thus, it is not annihilated. Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither destroyed nor does it die.
If nirvāṇa were subject to death, it would follow that one must undergo the continuity of rebirth. If it were subject to destruction, it would fall into the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because it is characterized by such qualities, nirvāṇa is free from destruction and free from death; therefore, it is the refuge for practitioners.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither a relinquishing nor an attainment, neither a cessation nor a permanence, neither a single meaning nor a manifold meaning—this is called nirvāṇa.
This further clarifies the matter of the emptiness of intrinsic nature: Nirvana is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, which is free from both annihilationism and eternalism.
For those who hold to eternalism grasp at existence, while those who hold to annihilationism grasp at non-existence; both are equally mere conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

If it is that which is realized by noble wisdom, it is not so, because it is free from the various conceptual views regarding the specific and general characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and thus one does not cling to them.

Because it exists, it is not eternal; it is the noble wisdom of self-realization attained by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, whose radiance remains inexhaustible from antiquity to the present, and thus it is neither annihilated nor permanent—unlike the nirvana of the non-Buddhists who take the two views of annihilationism and eternalism to be nirvana.
Furthermore, nirvana is the eternal cessation of the two deaths, forever distinct from the conditioned, and is not a dharma subject to death or destruction.
If *nirvāṇa* were subject to death, then the Tathāgata would likewise be subject to rebirth and transmigrate through the three realms.

If *nirvāṇa* were subject to destruction, then the Tathāgata would be a phenomenon of arising and ceasing, and could not be called "quiescent extinction" (*śānti*). Therefore, *nirvāṇa* is free from destruction and free from death;
it is the ultimate ground of refuge for all practitioners, unlike the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), which are subject to death and [rebirth].
The point of dissolution is itself nirvāṇa. Therefore, as for nirvāṇa: because it is not separate from all phenomena, it is not "abandonment";
because it does not coincide with all phenomena, it is not "attainment. Because it is the constant illumination of constant awakening, it is not "annihilation";

because words are exhausted and thought is transcended, it is not "permanence. Because its nature is non-nature, it is not "one"; because non-nature is itself nature, it is not "different. It is free from these six [extremes].
The phrase refers to the reality of the Tathāgata’s own-nature emptiness as nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas consists in their awakening to the distinction between specific and general characteristics, their non-association with objective spheres, and their non-arising of deluded conceptualization through non-perverted views; they regard that state as the realization of nirvāṇa.
This clarifies the fruit attained by the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). It means that the *nirvāṇa* realized by these two vehicles is not at all ultimate;
rather, by perceiving the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as impermanent, suffering, empty, impure, and non-self, they do not give rise to craving and attachment toward their own characteristics.
Furthermore, observing the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*) as a place of turmoil, they take no pleasure in associating with it. This merely severs...
Having seen through the delusions of views, they do not give rise to inverted views; having severed the delusions of thought, they do not produce false imaginings.

Such individuals perceive within those states a realization of nirvana. From the perspective of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), this appears like a place of tranquility, and they take it to be true nirvana, yet it is not ultimate nirvana.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of characteristics of self-nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). What are the two?

They are the attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-abhiniveśa*) and the attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-abhiniveśa*). The attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of verbal expression arises from the attachment to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless false speech.
The attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of things arises from the failure to realize that [the world] is a manifestation of one's own mind.

[The text] speaks of "arising according to divisions. As for the previous statement that the transformation of the habitual tendencies of the intrinsic nature of all consciousnesses is itself the intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa—

why does it not mention the two kinds of intrinsic nature, namely, verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) and objective entities (*vastu*), which are precisely the two kinds of false conceptualization regarding names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*)?

The followers of the Two Vehicles fail to realize that names and appearances are fundamentally empty; they cling to names and fixate on appearances, asserting that there is birth-and-death to be abandoned and nirvana to be attained.
They do not know that this birth-and-death and nirvana exist merely as names, all arising from the habitual clinging to the false discourse of beginningless time.
Furthermore, they conceive of the intrinsic nature of discourse, which arises from non-awakening.
All phenomena arise from the manifestations of one’s own mind; the delimitation of their arising is termed the "nature of things" (*vastu-svabhāva*).
Because they are not empty of these two natures, people cling to various conceptualizations as being truly existent.

Not knowing that there are only empty names and no actual realization, the Tathāgata, understanding that verbal expression is like an echo, transforms the nature of verbal expression [into non-conceptual wisdom].
Although Nirvana is spoken of all day long, not a single word has ever been uttered regarding it.
The Tathāgata fully knows that all phenomena arise from the manifestation of one's own mind; like images appearing in a mirror, they are fundamentally not real.
Thus, by transforming the habitual tendencies of the self-nature of things, one attains Nirvana. Although one sees forms and hears sounds all day long, there is not a single atom of sound or form.
Because of these characteristics, one knows that the two kinds of self-nature serve as the common gateway between the false and the correct, and the shared path for both the holy and the ordinary;
thus, those who study the Way must first begin with the emptiness of the two self-natures.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata establishes Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas through two kinds of spiritual powers (*adhiṣṭhāna*) so that they may prostrate before the Buddhas and listen to and inquire about the meaning of the Dharma. What are these two kinds of spiritual power? They are:

the spiritual power of manifesting all bodies, faces, and speech through the meditative absorption of *samādhi*, and the spiritual power of the hand-consecration (*pāṇy-abhiṣeka*). Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva...
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva first dwells in the Bodhisattva stage through the Buddha’s spiritual power— namely, by entering the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna Illumination Samādhi—
and having entered this samādhi, all Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions, by means of their supernormal powers,
manifest for him all bodies, faces, and modes of speech, such as those of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha and others of similar appearance.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has accomplished merit possesses great wisdom; this is called the first bodhisattva stage.

Having attained the bodhisattva samādhi and its supernormal powers, through the cultivation of roots of goodness over hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he successively masters the stages, penetrating to the ultimate limit of the correspondence between the antidotes and the objects to be remedied, until reaching the Dharma-Cloud Stage.
Dwelling in a subtle and wondrous palace of a great lotus, seated upon a great lotus jewel lion-throne,
surrounded by a retinue of similar Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, their bodies adorned with various precious necklaces like golden campaka flowers and the radiance of the sun and moon—
these most excellent sons of the Buddha came from the ten directions and approached the seat within the great lotus palace.
And they sprinkle their crowns with water, just as the crown-princes of the sovereign Cakravartin kings and Śakra, Lord of Devas, are consecrated.
Mahāmati, this is called the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of hand-consecration. These, Mahāmati, are the two kinds of supernormal powers of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these two kinds of supernormal powers, he beholds the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, face to face. If...
If it were not thus, one would be unable to see them.
Because one realizes that the two kinds of self-nature are empty, one enters into communion with the spiritual essence of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;
thus, moved by the Buddhas through their two kinds of supernatural power, the Bodhisattva is established, and only then is he able to prostrate before the Buddhas and receive their teachings.
Regarding the two kinds of supernormal powers through which the Buddha answers questions on the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma:
the first refers to the Tathāgata personally manifesting his physical presence before the practitioner while they abide in samādhi and preaching the Dharma for them;

the second refers to the Tathāgata remaining silent and without speech, yet conferring the position of the Great Dharma King upon them by silently pouring water from his hand upon their crown as an empowerment. This is why he manifests his physical presence and speaks.

The "Expositor" refers to the Bodhisattva of the First Ground (Prathamabhūmi), who suddenly realizes the emptiness of the two kinds of self-nature and suddenly severs the dualistic attachments to a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

Having attained entry into the Mahāyāna-āloka-samādhi (the Samādhi of the Radiance of the Mahāyāna), they are able to give rise to the wisdom-light that illuminates and discerns the principles, teachings, practices, and fruits of the Mahāyāna.
Because they have for the first time attained the *dharmatā*, they evoke the manifestation of the Buddhas appearing before them to preach the Dharma, as described in the *Avataṃsaka*.
When the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha dwelt in the first stage (*bhūmi*), he immediately received the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power;

it was the same for the other bodhisattvas as well. Because the bodhisattvas possessed such bodily features, facial expressions, and modes of speech, the Tathāgata likewise accomplished those bodhisattvas through the merit of such bodily features, facial expressions, and modes of speech. This is called the bodhisattva of the first stage.
The supernormal powers attained within the meditative absorption of samādhi are obtained by this bodhisattva because he has accumulated roots of goodness throughout one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*;
thus, he achieves the empowerment of supernormal powers through samādhi, not by chance.
Departing from there, he proceeds gradually from stage to stage, each possessing the wisdom that remedies the afflictions to be remedied.

Thus, upon reaching the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*), one attains the severance of the obstacles to mastery over all dharmas and realizes the *tathatā* that serves as the basis for mastery over dharmas.
Having attained ultimate penetration, one enters the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) and manifests a vast body in the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*akaniṣṭha*),
seated upon a lion throne of immeasurable great precious lotuses within a palace of immeasurable great precious lotuses.
Bodhisattvas of the same class surrounded him at once as his retinue;
all were adorned with various precious necklaces, their physical forms were golden in color like the *campaka* flower, and their radiance was like that of the sun and moon.
Then, Tathāgatas from various Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions simultaneously poured water upon his head with their hands, whereby he succeeded to the rank of Buddha.

For example, when the crown prince of a wheel-turning sage-king receives the consecration, he immediately succeeds to the royal throne; this is called the power of the Bodhisattva’s hand-consecration.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage, by virtue of these two kinds of power, one is able to personally behold all Buddhas, listen to their teachings, and inquire about their meanings.
Without the sustaining empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, this would not be possible.

In the samādhi of suchness, one does not obtain face-to-face audiences with the Buddhas preaching the Dharma, nor does one see the Buddhas performing the empowerment by pouring water upon the crown of the head.
Furthermore, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, regarding all that is conceptually differentiated— namely, samādhi, supernormal powers, and the preaching of the Dharma—
Mahāmati, all who practice these [dharmas] abide entirely within the two kinds of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata.

Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were able to explain and discourse [on these matters] apart from the Buddha’s supernatural power, then all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) should likewise be able to explain them.
Why is this? It is because they do not abide in supernatural power. Mahāmati, mountains, stones, trees, various musical instruments, cities, and palaces...
Because of the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata’s entry into the city, musical sounds spontaneously issued forth from the palace; how much more so for those with consciousness!
Even those suffering immeasurable afflictions—such as the deaf, the blind, and the mute—all attained liberation.
The Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable spiritual powers to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings.

This is an objection: one might fear that it is difficult to understand why the Tathāgata’s spiritual power does not assist those of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-piṭaka-śaikṣa*), but instead favors only the ten stages of sages (*daśabhūmi-ārya*). Therefore, he further declares:

"Whatever practices of samādhi, psychic powers, and preaching the Dharma all bodhisattvas differentiate, these are all obtained through the secret empowerment of the two kinds of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power."
Unimpeded eloquence distinguishes all phenomena, yet one cannot perceive it directly.
If one were able to speak apart from the Buddha’s spiritual power (*buddhānubhāva*), then all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should also be able to speak; why then are they unable?

It is because ordinary beings do not abide in these two kinds of spiritual power that they cannot distinguish [the teachings] through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The nature of the Dharma is such that one might ask: by what power of the Buddhas can Bodhisattvas immediately distinguish samādhis, supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and preach the Dharma?
Therefore, the answer is given: it is by the power of their spiritual majesty (*ṛddhi-bala*).
If even insentient things such as mountains, stones, trees, and wood can produce wondrous sounds, how much more so those with minds who cannot fail to preach the Dharma?
By virtue of the Buddha’s supernormal powers, even those who are deaf, blind, or mute attain liberation;

how much more so can the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness not discern samādhi and liberation? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable supernormal powers to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings, he is able to secretly empower the Bodhisattvas to enter samādhi, manifest supernatural transformations, and preach the Dharma.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas bestow their spiritual power upon Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas when they abide in samādhi-samāpatti and at the time of consecration in the stages of supreme progress?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is for the sake of leaving behind the karmas of Māra and afflictions, and so as not to fall into the stage of the Śrāvakas."
Because they practice dhyāna for the sake of attaining the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization and for the sake of further advancing in the dharmas already attained,
the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas all establish the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
If they were not established by these supernatural powers, they would fall into the false views, delusions, and various māras of the external paths and the śrāvakas.

"May they not fail to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, sustain all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-bala*). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Honored One among Men, by his supernatural power, Has completely purified his great vows; Through samādhi, he receives the empowerment of consecration."
Regarding the first stage and the tenth stage, Mahāmati asked again:

"When Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages abide in samādhi and at the time of their consecration (*abhiṣeka*), they themselves already possess the sustaining power of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*).
For what reason does the Tathāgata further bestow his own spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*) upon them, so that they may attain the state beyond all comparison?"

Tianhuaye, although a Bodhisattva of the first bhūmi has initially attained the vision of the path and generated the bodhicitta, if they do not receive empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), they may forget the bodhicitta and fall into demonic activities, or become attached to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and fall into the stage of a Śrāvaka;
therefore, empowerment is necessary. Even upon reaching the tenth bhūmi, there still remains the most extremely subtle cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
If one is not sustained by empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one cannot progress toward the dharmas already attained, nor can one reach the stage of ultimate enlightenment;

therefore, empowerment is necessary. For this reason, when first entering the stages (*bhūmi*) and at the time of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the Tathāgata must necessarily sustain them with two kinds of spiritual power.
If one were not so sustained upon entering the first stage, one would fall into the state of an outsider (*bāhya*).
The *Śrāvakabhūmi* states that if one is not empowered (*adhiṣṭhita*) at the time of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one cannot attain perfect enlightenment;

therefore, the Tathāgata necessarily employs two kinds of spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*) to empower them. A verse from the Tang translation says: "The World-Honored One’s pure vows possess great power of empowerment;
[this applies to] the first stage through the tenth stage, as well as samādhis and consecrations. This verse more clearly expresses the intended meaning.
Both types of supernormal power flow from the Tathāgata’s pure vow-mind;

there is nothing therein that does not seek to cause Bodhisattvas to leave behind the paths of externalists and the two vehicles, to accord with *tathatā* (suchness), and to return solely to perfect enlightenment.

After Mahāmati had personally requested to practice without interruption, he first exhausted the investigation of conditions and causes, then exhausted the investigation of verbal expression, and thirdly, exhausted the investigation of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Regarding these causal conditions: the habit-energy of karma refers to the habit-energy of verbal expression; the habit-energy of conceptual proliferation refers to the habit-energy of the constituents of the self.
To cause practitioners of true cultivation to sever these three types of habit-energy is precisely what constitutes uninterrupted cultivation.
Once these three have been clarified, the subsequent differentiation between false and correct causes and effects serves to manifest clearly the emptiness of the marks of self.

That which has non-empty phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) pertains to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma*) of the Hīnayāna; that which has non-empty essential nature (*dharmatā*) pertains to the Bodhisattva;
and that in which both nature and characteristics are empty, with both existence and non-existence simultaneously negated, pertains to the pure cause and effect of the Tathāgata.
At this point, another conclusion is made.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, when the Buddha speaks of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), he is speaking of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and not proclaiming a self-originated path.

World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also speak of causes and conditions, asserting that all such natures arise from a Supreme Lord (*īśvara*), Time (*kāla*), or atoms (*paramāṇu*). Yet, World-Honored One, what you call the arising of all natures through causes and conditions—"
"You speak of the *siddhānta* with intervals and the *siddhānta* without intervals. World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also speak of existence, non-existence, arising, and non-arising;

the World-Honored One likewise speaks of non-arising, that what has arisen ceases, and as the World-Honored One has said: 'With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations,' up to 'old age and death.
This, World-Honored One, is your teaching of causelessness, not your teaching of causality. The World-Honored One establishes [the doctrine] in this manner."
To say that "because this exists, that exists" is not an established gradual arising; it is the teaching of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), not that of the Tathāgata. Why is this?

The World-Honored One [teaches] that the causes spoken of by the non-Buddhists do not arise from conditions yet produce something. The World-Honored One, however, teaches that when one contemplates the cause, there is the effect;
when one contemplates the effect, there is the cause. Such a confusion of causes and conditions leads to such a cycle of mutual dependence without end.

[This concludes] the section on the thorough differentiation between the causes and conditions of the heterodox and the orthodox. Furthermore, Mahāmati, fearing that the causes and conditions of our own internal teachings might be conflated with those of the non-Buddhists,
he again analyzes the underlying intent, meaning that the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) taught by the World-Honored One arises precisely from ignorance and karma.

It is not said that the fruits—consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth—arise with craving and the like as their causes, nor that they arise from a self-nature (*svabhāva*) or the manifestation of *tathatā*.

Non-Buddhists also speak of causes and conditions, asserting that such phenomena as these are produced by causes such as the Primal Nature (*prakṛti*), the Lord (*īśvara*), time, or atoms; yet, the cause that produces the fruit is what the Blessed One has taught.
"Is there a difference between the causal principle that produces effects as taught by the various non-Buddhists and these two kinds of Dharma-giving, or is there no difference?

The non-Buddhists also say that effects arise from no cause; the World-Honored One also says that all phenomena exist from a primordial state of non-existence, such that ignorance suddenly arises, and having arisen, suddenly ceases again."
This would not differ from the non-Buddhists' view that an effect arises from no cause. As the World-Honored One has said:
"With ignorance as the cause, volitional formations arise as the effect; with volitional formations as the cause, consciousness arises as the effect.

This [teaching] does not state that these are manifestations of one's own mind arising from the independent activity of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) produced by ignorance. This, then, is what the World-Honored One [taught].
Furthermore, it does not fall into the view of causelessness, nor does it fall into the view of having a cause.

World-Honored One, you have also taught that "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations" and "conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness," and so forth; this is the principle that "because this exists, that exists.

This is also the Tathāgata’s establishment of simultaneous arising (*sahaja*), not the establishment of gradual arising. However, the non-Buddhists reckon the Primal Nature (*prakṛti*) as the primordial source and Lord.
The *tattvas* arise from the *prakṛti*; the *buddhi* arises from the *prakṛti*; the *ahaṃkāra* arises from the *buddhi*; the five *tanmātras* arise from the *ahaṃkāra*;
the five *mahābhūtas* arise from the five *tanmātras*; and the eleven organs arise from the five *mahābhūtas*. These twenty-three principles constitute that which is experienced by the *puruṣa*.
Thus do the non-Buddhists establish a gradual process of origination; they do not establish simultaneous origination. However, when one examines these non-Buddhists...
What has been explained as arising gradually is superior to what the Tathāgata taught regarding simultaneous arising.

The reason it is superior is that the non-Buddhists hold that the single cause, the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*), is the producer; yet this Primal Nature does not arise from other conditions and is nonetheless able to produce all phenomena.
Thus, the cause acts as its own cause without depending on an effect, and the effect acts as its own effect without [depending on a cause]. This is untenable.

When one attends to causes in this manner, cause and effect are clearly distinguished without being confused. As the Blessed One has taught regarding the twelve links of dependent origination arising in succession:
taking ignorance as the cause produces volitional formations as the result; taking volitional formations as the cause produces consciousness as the result;
and so on, until taking old age and death as the cause produces ignorance once again as the result. This is...

If one phenomenon serves as a cause and then again becomes an effect—such that there is the effect within the cause and the cause within the effect—then they revolve in this manner in an endless, chaotic cycle, falling once more into the error of being both cause and effect. Therefore, I say that the superior teachings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are not something the Tathāgata can equal.
This inquiry has three parts: first, distinguishing how the internal teaching is entirely identical to the external teaching; next, distinguishing... [text continues].

The Tathāgata, on the contrary, falls into the threefold discrimination of causelessness; he establishes that which is co-arisen (*sahaja*), unlike the gradual arising [of phenomena] asserted by non-Buddhists.
O Mahāmati, if one’s Dharma-eye were clear and bright, how could one fail to foresee such a calamity of the final dharma? How could one possibly reach such a state?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not teach that things exist without cause, nor do I teach a confused theory of causes and conditions.

When I say 'because this exists, that exists,' I am referring to the non-existence of the grasped and the grasper, which is the realization that the magnitude of external objects is merely the manifestation of one's own mind.

Mahāmati, if one is attached to the grasped and the grasper and fails to realize that external objects—whether existent or non-existent—are merely the manifestation of one's own mind, such faults will arise; these do not apply to my teaching of dependent origination."
I have always taught that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and are not produced without cause.

This is shown through the non-arising of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to clarify that one does not fall into the view of causelessness, nor does it imply a confusion of causes and conditions.
Thus, what I teach is that the twelve links of dependent origination arise in succession; because this exists, that consequently comes to be.
That "existence" precisely reveals that the mind lacks both the cause of grasping and the effect of the grasped; therefore, it is said that "because this arises, that arises;
because that arises, this arises. Both are devoid of intrinsic nature, like an image appearing in a mirror, causing people to realize that they are the manifestations of their own mind.
It is merely that the manifestation follows conditions without changing, and it does not change while following conditions. Because of this...
Transforming while following conditions, one does not fall into causelessness; following conditions without transforming, one does not fall into confusion.

Those externalists cling to the grasping subject and the grasped object as being truly existent; they do not know that all phenomena are but mind, nor do they realize that external objects lack inherent nature.
Thus, they falsely grasp at all phenomena as existing from existence or non-existing from non-existence.
This arises from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false views since beginningless time, and from being permeated by evil teachers and false teachings;
thus this seed-nature (*gotra*) is transmitted from generation to generation and evolves upon the stage of conceptualization (*vikalpa-bhūmi*).

Because it possesses such faults, how can you claim that my explanation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is confused with [erroneous] causes and conditions, when in fact it is not? Furthermore, that which I have taught is...
Arising is not invariably non-arising, for it would otherwise be equivalent to annihilation. I have always taught that all phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions;
therefore, although they arise, in reality they have never arisen. Who could say they arise without cause?
The wisdom of the non-Buddhists does not reach this point, and they falsely claim that all phenomena arise without cause. Since there is no such arising...
If one asks, "By what cause is this produced? there would be no cause and no fruit; such would be true annihilationism.

How could this possibly be the meaning of my teaching on dependent origination and non-arising? The *Bai-men-yi-hai* (The Ocean of Meaning of the Hundred Gates) says: "To realize non-arising means that objects are the mind and the mind conditions objects.
When causes and conditions harmonize and combine, illusory appearances then arise. Because they arise from conditions, they necessarily lack self-nature."
Why is this so? Objects are not objects in themselves; they must depend on causes. The mind is not the mind in itself; it must depend on conditions.

Because they exist through mutual dependence, there is no fixed attribution. That which arises from conditions is non-arising; it is not that we negate arising by speaking of non-arising. It is precisely because of dependent origination that we speak of non-arising.
Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, does it not follow that because speech has an intrinsic nature, all things have an intrinsic nature?
World-Honored One, if there were no intrinsic nature, speech would not arise. World-Honored One, therefore, because speech has an intrinsic nature, all things have an intrinsic nature."

This argument addresses the objection that because the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one must assert that they possess intrinsic nature in order for verbal expression to function;

the intent is that worldly verbal expression possessing intrinsic nature necessarily requires that all the phenomena being expressed exist as actualities before one's eyes, serving as the basis for expression, after which verbal expression can arise. If...

If one knows that both the grasper and the grasped are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) is likewise devoid of intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is asked:

Is it the case that because verbal expression lacks intrinsic nature, all phenomena (*dharma*) also lack intrinsic nature? If all phenomena were indeed devoid of intrinsic nature, then verbal expression could not arise;
for since verbal expression does not arise in vain, there must be phenomena from which it arises, yet those phenomena do not manifest themselves [independently].

Since it must rely upon verbal expression to be manifested, wherever there is verbal expression, there must be something expressed; thus, that which is expressible and that which is expressed are not of the nature of being (svabhāva).
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "To speak of non-existence refers to such things as the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise, which are commonly spoken of in the world."
Mahāmati, it is said that neither existence nor non-existence exists; it is merely verbal expression.
If, as you say, verbal expressions possess existence and all things possess existence, then your own treatise is undermined. Mahāmati, not all Buddha-fields possess verbal expression;
verbal expression is merely a fabrication. In some Buddha-fields, the Dharma is revealed by a mere glance; in others, by gestures; and in others, by waving the hand.
The eyebrows may move, the eyes may blink, one may smile, yawn, cough, or contemplate buddha-fields; or there may be physical movements, O Mahāmati.

For instance, in the world-system of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra in the Gandhavatī universe, by mere gazing, all bodhisattvas attain the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and various supreme samādhis. Therefore, verbal expression does not possess intrinsic nature.
There is the nature of all things; Mahāmati, when one sees this world—mosquitoes, gnats, insects, and ants—one perceives that these sentient beings have no speech, yet each accomplishes its own task.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"As with space, a rabbit’s horn, and the pāṇḍara fruit, They do not exist, yet there is speech regarding them; so too is the nature of conceptualization the cause."

Ordinary, foolish people give rise to false imaginings regarding the combination of conditions; they are unable to know things as they truly are, and thus they wander through the three realms of existence.

The World-Honored One refutes both of these extremes, saying: "In the world there are also phenomena that lack intrinsic nature yet possess verbal designations, such as the horns of a rabbit, the hair of a tortoise, the wings of an ox, the hands of a horse, or the son of a barren woman. Although [these are non-existent],...

The essence of things such as a rabbit’s horn does not exist, yet the designation "rabbit’s horn" is applied; so too, while all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature, verbal designations are established.
If you claim that phenomena possess an intrinsic nature and yet verbal designations apply, then your own treatise is self-contradictory.
Thus Yongjia said: "Those who now apply names outside of an essence are merely naming that which has no essence. How could there be...?
Does the substance correspond to its name? For example, a rabbit has no horns, yet the name "horn" is applied to it;
this name merely refers to its lack of horns—how could there be a horn that corresponds to the name? When a name is applied where there is no substance, that name is a name without reality.
Since it is a name without reality, that which is named is not real; and since that which is named does not exist, the naming agent (the name) likewise does not exist.
Furthermore, if that which is named does not exist, then the name itself cannot exist; thus, both the speech and the object spoken of are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Who, then, could claim that both speech and the object spoken of possess intrinsic nature? Moreover, there are Buddha-fields that can manifest the Dharma without depending on speech;
