it is not the case that all lands possess speech. Therefore, we know that speech [is empty of intrinsic nature].
All these are produced through the causes and conditions of conceptual construction and do not possess a real intrinsic nature.

There are some Buddha-fields where looking straight ahead without blinking serves as a substitute for the Dharma-preacher; some where merely displaying a sign serves as a substitute for the Dharma-preacher;

some where moving the eyebrows serves as a substitute for the Dharma-preacher; some where rolling the eyes serves as a substitute for the Dharma-preacher; or [some] by means of laughter, or yawning, or...

Some may use coughing to represent the preaching of the Dharma; some may use mental intention to represent the preaching of the Dharma; and some may use bodily movements to represent the preaching of the Dharma.
If this is so, then all six sense faculties can preach the Dharma—why must one rely solely on the sounds produced by the mouth and tongue as the Dharma?
This is as it is in the world of Animiṣa, the world of Gandhavyūha, and the land of Samantabhadra.
The various bodhisattvas merely observe the Tathāgata with unblinking eyes and thereby attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) as well as immeasurable, sublime samādhis.
How could these be said to have a nature or a single essence through verbal expression? Yet, it is not only in other buddha-fields that this is so;
even here in this world, though mosquitoes and ants lack verbal expression, [they likewise attain such states].
Since each [of these] is capable of performing its function, why wait for verbal expression before the phenomenon can be manifested?

Therefore, one should know that all verbal expressions are merely conventional designations based on the false imaginings of sentient beings; they do not possess a real intrinsic nature. To further clarify this, it is stated in verse:
"Just as space, a rabbit’s horn, and the son of a barren woman—these all exist as names though they are fundamentally non-existent. This is what is meant by "words."

To say that there is no real intrinsic nature, yet through deluded conceptualization one reckons it to have a real intrinsic nature—by this very knowledge that verbal expression lacks intrinsic nature, one knows that all phenomena produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions likewise lack intrinsic nature.

Yet ordinary fools give rise to various deluded conceptualizations, falsely claiming that verbal expression has intrinsic nature and that all things possess intrinsic nature; this arises from their inability [to understand].
Because one does not know, as they truly are, that all phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind,

and that the grasping at external existence or non-existence and the objects expressed by verbal designations are all merely of a real nature, there is a reason why one cannot emerge from the three realms of cyclic existence on one's own.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of the 'eternal sound'? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It refers to delusive confusion (*bhrānti*). Although this delusive confusion appears even to the Noble Ones (*ārya*), it is not a state of inversion (*viparyāsa*).
Mahāmati, it is like the spring mirage, a fire-wheel (*alātacakra*), falling hair, a city of Gandharvas, an illusion, a dream, or a reflection in a mirror—such is the world."
"Inversion is not the mark of a wise person; yet, Mahāmati, it is not that this delusion does not manifest.
That delusion manifests in various ways, yet it is not the case that the delusion itself is impermanent. Why is this? It is because it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati, what is meant by being free from existence and non-existence? It refers to the various objective spheres of all foolish commoners, which are like the river Gaṅgā."
Because hungry ghosts see it while others do not, this delusion does not possess the nature of non-existence; yet because it appears to others, it is not of a non-existent nature.
Thus, this delusion is constant for the noble ones (*ārya*), who are free from inversion and are not inverted. This is because its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are never destroyed.

Mahāmati, it is not that the various characteristics of this delusion are destroyed through the characteristics of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); therefore, Mahāmati, this delusion is constant. Mahāmati said: [Why is this so?]

What is the delusion regarding reality? Furthermore, Mahāmati, when the Noble Ones encounter this delusion, they do not give rise to a perverted cognition, nor do they give rise to a non-perverted cognition.
Mahāmati, except for the Noble Ones, there may be some slight conceptualization regarding this delusion, but it is not the conceptualization of the activity of noble wisdom.
Mahāmati, whatever exists is merely the false speech of fools; it is not the speech of the Noble Ones.
This doubt arises from the question of whether that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is impermanent.
Since it is said that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and even speech lacks intrinsic nature, then both the speech and that which is spoken would both become impermanent.

If so, regarding that which the Tathāgata has taught as truly permanent and indestructible—what, ultimately, does he take as the basis for such a teaching? The World-Honored One then, by means of the Truth...
Because it constantly shatters the inverted views of impermanence, I say that what I teach as true permanence and indestructibility is distinct from the delusions and confusions of the non-Buddhists—
who falsely calculate existence and non-existence, identity and difference— and from the delusions and confusions of the followers of the Two Vehicles—
who calculate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity. Apart from these two kinds of delusion and confusion, there exists nothing else.
This is the characteristic of true permanence and indestructibility. "Delusion and confusion" refers to the mind and its objects;

because when the mind arises, the objects become confused, and when objects arise, the mind becomes confused, they are termed "delusion and confusion. However, how does one know that the locus of delusion and confusion is itself true permanence?
It is because although those various sages manifest within such delusion and confusion, they do not give rise to [the notions of] impermanence, suffering, or emptiness.
The views of non-self, impurity, and the various inversions are exactly like a springtime mirage, a whirling firebrand, falling hair, a city of the gandharvas, an illusion, a dream, or a reflection;

they are merely the false conceptualizations of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity held by deluded people of the world regarding these illusions, dreams, reflections, whirling firebrands, and falling hair. They are not [the truth].
This is what the wise have discerned. Those of clear intelligence do not mean that the confused states of mind and their objects do not appear at all;
rather, they skillfully discern that external natures—which are but manifestations of one's own mind—lack true existence, and thus they do not give rise to conceptual discrimination.
Therefore, although those confused appearances manifest in various ways, they do not form the notion of impermanence regarding the locus of that confusion. Why is this? Because...
Those phenomena of delusion do not themselves declare existence, nor do they declare non-existence, because they are free from both existence and non-existence.
How is it known that those delusions are free from existence and non-existence?

It is because fools perceive existence in all phenomena where there is no existence, and perceive non-existence where there is no non-existence; therefore, [the delusions] are free from existence and non-existence.
While abiding in various objective realms, one who is free from both existence and non-existence remains as they truly are.
It is like the water of the Ganges, which is fundamentally not fire, yet hungry ghosts perceive it only as fire and do not see it as water;
those whose deluded calculations regard the nature of things as impermanent are just like the hungry ghosts who see fire and do not see water.
This is a perversion; whereas other wise ones, though they appear [in the world], do not manifest the nature of impermanence, just as others see water but do not see fire—this is not a perversion.
Thus, because the noble ones do not engage in the various conceptual constructions (*parikalpa*) of ordinary beings and the small vehicles, they are free from perversion and are able to discern well.

Because external natures do not exist apart from what is manifested by one’s own mind, there is no inversion; for that which deludes ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles does not delude the noble ones.
Therefore, I say that delusion (*bhrānti*) is itself the true and eternal, because all phenomena (*dharma*) are truly real and indestructible.
This is not like the case of the two vehicles regarding the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) within delusion.
One contemplates impurity, suffering, emptiness, non-self, impermanence, and so forth; for this reason, I say that delusion (*bhrānti*) is itself the true permanence (*nitya*).
How is it known that delusion is the mark of true permanence and indestructibility?
It is because all delusions arise without departing from the conjunction of causes and conditions, being fundamentally unborn from the very beginning. Furthermore, regarding the sages...

When one does not give rise to the deluded, dualistic perceptions of existence and non-existence held by fools and those of the Two Vehicles regarding these phenomena produced by causes and conditions—which are themselves delusive—it is precisely this that constitutes non-inversion; for what else could non-inversion be?

Thus, to not form the notion of impermanence regarding delusive phenomena is itself true permanence. This is so because, apart from the various sages who have already realized the truth, [there is no other way].
Indeed, for one who does not give rise to discrimination, all delusive confusion is the very reality of the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

As for other forms of practice—such as those of Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Three Worthies (*trividha-śaikṣa*)—although they cultivate the six perfections, their discrimination has not yet been eliminated.

If one gives rise to even a slight conceptualization regarding delusive confusion, one deviates from the essence of the Dharma; such is not the reality of the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom. Therefore...

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Triṃśikā) states: "To manifest before oneself a slight object and claim it to be the nature of consciousness—because there is something apprehended—one does not truly abide in consciousness-only.
Therefore, any conceptual discrimination, however minute, that is impure causes one to fall into the worldly discourse of fools;
it is certainly not the speech of the Noble Ones, let alone the arising of various forms of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*)."
That delusion consists of the arising of two kinds of natures—erroneous and non-erroneous perceptions—namely, the noble nature and the nature of fools.
The noble nature is distinguished into three types: the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle.
How does the erroneous perception of fools give rise to the Śrāvaka vehicle nature? It arises from attachment to self-characteristics and common characteristics.
Hearing of the vehicle of the Śrāvakas is called the arising of the Śrāvaka-vehicle lineage from delusive conceptualization;

O Mahāmati, that very same delusive conceptualization arises as the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle lineage when one does not personally adhere to the specific and general characteristics of that same delusion.
How does the wise person arise the Buddha-vehicle lineage from that same delusion? It is said: [when they realize]...

To realize that the external world is merely the manifestation of one’s own mind, and that external entities neither exist nor do not exist, and thus to arise from the state of non-conceptualization—this is called the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle arising from that very delusion.
Furthermore, the arising of various conceptualizations regarding the nature of diverse phenomena in ordinary people is called the lineage of the foolish.
This is neither an existent thing nor a non-existent thing; such is the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*). Mahāmati, it is precisely that delusion...

The non-conceptualization of the delusions of the minds, mentals, and consciousnesses of the noble ones, as well as their habitual tendencies, intrinsic natures, and the nature of the transformation of phenomena—this is called "thusness" (tathatā).
Therefore, it is said that "like [the state of] being free from mind. This phrase demonstrates that freedom from conceptualization is itself the teaching of freedom from all conceptualizations.
It was stated above that the various sages do not give rise to inverted cognition regarding this delusive confusion;
they do not perceive it as non-inverted, for these inverted and non-inverted conceptualizations all arise based upon delusive confusion.

If one does not give rise to inverted cognition regarding that delusive confusion, one possesses the lineage of the sages. There are three kinds of such distinctions; regarding that delusive confusion, [if one] gives rise to...
Those with inverted cognition belong to the lineage of the foolish; this locus of delusion gives rise to the lineage of the sages and from it emerges the lineage of the foolish.
The followers of the Two Vehicles dwell between the foolish and the sages, within the realm of both the inverted and the non-inverted.

Although they observe the emptiness of nature through the three vehicles and so forth, they likewise possess the lineage of the sages; yet because their attachment to dharmas is not yet empty, they remain identical to the foolish.

It is well-founded that the "Noble Lineage" (*ārya-gotra*) is indicated by [the realization of] non-perversion and explained by [the absence of] delusion, while the "foolish person" (*bāla*) is indicated by [the presence of] perversion and explained by [the presence of] false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
That which is called the "Śrāvaka lineage" refers to one who, amidst the confusion of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), falsely conceives of birth and death as truly existent,
and thereby gives rise to the contemplations of impurity, suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, producing a sense of weary detachment and aspiring toward [liberation].

This joy in *nirvāṇa* arises from falsely conceiving attachment and aversion because the characteristics of phenomena have not yet been realized as empty; this is called the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle.

As for what is called the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha: it refers to one who thoroughly understands that the delusive five aggregates—whether characterized by self-nature or commonality—are dependently originated, false, and unreal;
such a person remains free from worldly clamor, takes no pleasure in social intimacy, and practices the path of returning [to the source].
The cessation [of these] is called the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna. Although these two have realized the emptiness of persons, they have not yet eliminated the cognitive obstructions;

thus they are merely called "fools" and not "wise ones. Once they enter the first stage (*bhūmi*), they are called "wise ones," because they have severed the dualistic grasping at a self and phenomena through discrimination.
That which is called the lineage of the Buddhayāna refers to that very same delusion.

To realize the true and eternal by awakening to the fact that all phenomena are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind, and thus not giving rise to discrimination regarding external existence or non-existence, such that they are quiescent in their very place—this is called the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna-gotra*).

Therefore, know that those who, within the realm of delusion, do not understand dependent origination and falsely give rise to longing and aversion are *śrāvakas*; even if they understand dependent origination, if they do not penetrate the absence of intrinsic nature, they remain [at that level].
"Nature" refers to the pratyekabuddha; if one realizes that dependent origination is without nature, and that what is without nature is dependent origination, this is called the Buddha-vehicle.
Therefore it is said: "Although there is but one dharma and no difference, the three types of persons perceive distinctions.

What is called the "nature of the foolish person" (bāla-gotra) refers to those who, regarding various phenomena and various natures, fail to understand that they are dependently originated and without nature, and thus give rise to inverted delusions.

To conceptually construct and falsely discriminate between existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence, identity and difference, and so forth, is called the lineage (*gotra*) of the foolish.
As for "lineage," it refers to that which follows conditions and is termed "lineage" (*gotra*), while that which does not change is termed "nature" (*prakṛti*).

It is neither existent nor non-existent, because fundamentally there is no fixed certainty. Thus, when it is perfumed by the Śrāvaka vehicle, it becomes a Śrāvaka; when perfumed by the Pratyekabuddha vehicle... [it becomes a Pratyekabuddha].
If awakened to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, one becomes a pratyekabuddha; if permeated by the Buddha-vehicle, one becomes a Buddha;
if permeated by the dharmas of foolish commoners, one becomes a foolish commoner. This is what is meant by the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*).

This lineage is that which is common to both the ignorant and the wise, yet it is also that which distinguishes the ignorant from the wise. Therefore, while entangled in afflictions, it is called "lineage"; when free from entanglement, it is called "Reality."
As before, he points this out by saying: "Even within that state of delusion, there are those who do not give rise to false conceptualization.

When the various evil habitual tendencies within the eight consciousnesses are transformed by the sages into the four wisdoms, they realize the nature of nirvana—the reality of the emptiness of self-nature.
When there is no longer the perfuming of false conceptualization, these very seeds are transformed and named *tathatā* (Suchness); it does not mean..."

Apart from the lineage (gotra), there exists a separate suchness (tathatā). Therefore, I speak of this phrase "suchness," and furthermore, I reveal that suchness is free from conceptual discrimination (vikalpa-saṃjñā).
This means it is not only free from perverted conceptions, but also free from non-perverted conceptions;
thus it is said that one speaks of being free from all conceptions—meaning to utterly eradicate ordinary sentiments and sever [all attachments].
Because the noble ones lack such deluded thoughts, they do not perceive these things as such. Thus, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:
"All dharmas exist with their distinctions solely based upon deluded thought; if one is free from deluded thought, then there are no appearances of any objective realms.
Therefore, all dharmas have, from the very beginning, been free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of names."
"Because it is free from the marks of mental objects, ultimately equal, without change, and indestructible—being solely the one mind—it is called *tathatā* (Suchness).
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, is this delusion existent or non-existent? The Buddha told Mahāmati, "It is like an illusion; it does not exist."

If there were a characteristic of attachment within delusion, then the nature of that attachment would be indestructible, and dependent origination would be like the causal production of phenomena as taught by the non-Buddhists. It is objected:
if you say that delusion exists, then it contradicts your previous statement that the grasped and the grasper are without intrinsic nature; yet if you say [it does not exist],...

Furthermore, it is said that delusion (*bhrānti*) is itself the eternally real; since these [statements] are mutually contradictory regarding its prior and subsequent states, one asks whether delusion is existent or non-existent.
The Buddha replied: "All phenomena of delusion are merely images manifested by one’s own mind;
they cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said not to exist. They are just like the illusory objects manifested by a magician. Therefore, the preceding verse says "all."
Dharmas are like illusions and are far removed from mind and consciousness; wisdom cannot apprehend them as either existent or non-existent.

Since they are said to be like illusions, how could they be reckoned as having existence or non-existence? Therefore it is said that there is no attachment to signs, for attachment to signs arises from deluded conceptualization and does not arise within the dharmas themselves.
If the phenomena of confusion were truly existent such that they possessed signs to which one could become attached, then [it would be otherwise].
If there truly exists a nature that can be grasped through conceptual attachment, how could it be extinguished?
Since it cannot be extinguished, it is fixed as death and permanence; one is unable to transform consciousness into wisdom or transform ignorance into sainthood.

Such dependent origination would then be identical to the "causes as creators" asserted by non-Buddhists—namely, the Primal Nature (*prakṛti*), the Lord (*īśvara*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), or the Person (*puruṣa*)—from which all things are produced.
"How do all phenomena differ? Is the dependent origination taught by the Tathāgata not like this?
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if delusion is like an illusion, it would further act as a cause for other delusions.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Illusion is not the cause of delusion, because it does not give rise to faults. Mahāmati, illusion does not give rise to faults; it has no [faults]."

"O Mahāmati, that which is like a magical illusion arises from another source of illumination; it does not arise from the locus of one's own delusive conceptualization or from the latencies of past habits.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, it does not give rise to faults. This is a delusive attachment of the minds of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The Noble do not perceive delusion, nor do they perceive anything in between."
If there were no real intermediate state, then delusion would be reality itself;

yet, if one truly abandons all delusions, then the appearance of any characteristic is likewise delusion and impurity, like a visual impairment. Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is not that illusion does not exist, but rather that all phenomena are seen to be similar to an illusion.

An objection is raised: "Even if delusions are like illusions and are inherently devoid of self-nature, they still differ from the views of non-Buddhists who claim things are produced by causes and conditions;
therefore, these delusions should still act as causes for other delusions, leading to further conceptual attachment.
Why, then, do you say there is no characteristic of attachment? The Buddha replied: "Illusory phenomena cannot serve as the cause of delusion, because illusory phenomena..."
Because they give rise to faults, [the mind] does not give rise to them; that which does not give rise to faults is because all illusory phenomena are apart from mind and consciousness.

That they are apart from mind and consciousness is because all illusory phenomena arise based on incantations and arts, rather than arising from the attachment to the habitual tendencies of one's own deluded thoughts.
Therefore, they cannot give rise to various faults and evils. Thus, the *Awakening of Mahāśrī* (*Mahāśrī-viśeṣa-cintā-brahma-paripṛcchā-sūtra*) says: "All manner of illusory transformations..."
The Tathāgata’s perfectly awakened, wondrous mind is like a flower in the sky, which exists only from within space.
Once one knows that all phenomena are like flowers in the sky, one realizes that external natures have no inherent nature; how then could they serve as causes for other delusions?
Since they cannot even act as causes for other delusions, how much less could they delude people? It is only because the minds of foolish people are already [previously]...
Deluded by one's own illusory objects, one clings to them as real, giving rise to inverted perceptions and all manner of faults and evils;

it is just like a small child playing with a shadow—playing with the shadow, not with the person. Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "Failing to realize that dependent origination is unreal, one falsely gives rise to pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
Although it is said that this deceives and deludes the foolish, in truth, the fool is merely deceiving himself. Just so.
The monkey grasping at the moon is not the moon grasping at the monkey; therefore it is said that "the myriad dharmas are fundamentally tranquil, yet people themselves create the clamor.

Thus, if the sages and worthies were not deluded by confusion, then not only would inverted views constitute attachment, but even non-inversion would likewise be attachment; not only would confusion itself be confusion, but...
Reality is also delusion. As Master Rong said: "If there were even a single dharma superior to nirvāṇa, I would say that it too is like a dream or an illusion.
Therefore, the verse dispels both simultaneously, stating: "The Sage does not perceive delusion, nor is there reality in between.
If there were a characteristic of reality within delusion itself, then this delusion—
If there were a real intrinsic nature, then ordinary beings could not be transformed into sages, nor could the ignorant be transformed into the wise.

If one were to abandon delusion and confusion for the arising of a truly real characteristic, that very reality would itself be a delusion—just as when a film suddenly appears before the eyes of one who is pure and clear. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: [text follows]
Since false appearances manifest as true and both the true and the false are equally illusory, it is further stated that among all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms,
there is not a single thing that can serve as a comparable analogy other than the metaphor of illusion. Therefore,
although the sages perceive all phenomena as they would see an illusory person or an illusory horse, how could they ever harbor affectionate attachment toward them?
Ah! Layman Pang said: "If I have no mind toward the myriad things, it does not hinder the myriad things from constantly surrounding me.
An iron ox fears not the lion's roar; it is like a wooden man seeing flowers and birds. The wooden man’s essential nature is itself devoid of sentiment;
the flowers and birds, meeting a person, do not know how to startle. When the mind and its objects are thus in suchness—what worry is there in this?"
He said, "If one does not achieve the path and is like a householder, then they have truly realized that all things are like an illusion.

Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, when it is said that 'all dharmas are like an illusion,' is this because of attachment to various illusory appearances, or is it because of attachment to distinct characteristics?
If it is because of attachment to various illusory appearances that one says all dharmas are like an illusion..."
“World-Honored One, it is not the case that the nature of existence is like an illusion. Why is this? It is because the various marks of form are not caused by the world;

World-Honored One, there is no cause for the manifestation of the various marks of form other than being like an illusion. Therefore, World-Honored One, there is no attachment to the similarity of various illusory marks with the nature of reality.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: “It is not that the various illusory marks are attached to as being similar to one [another].”
All phenomena are like illusions, Mahāmati; they are not real. All phenomena perish as swiftly as lightning; thus they are like illusions.
Mahāmati, for example, a flash of lightning appears for a mere instant and, having appeared, immediately vanishes. It does not appear to the foolish.

In this same way, all natures are observed through one's own false imaginings to be devoid of self-nature and common characteristics. They are not appearances of form, nor are they objects of attachment.

Then the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Since there is nothing that is not an illusion, the nature of dharmas is said to be like an illusion—unreal and as swift as lightning; therefore, they are said to be like an illusion."

This further profoundly investigates the root of illusion. Because the preceding passage generally indicated that all mundane and supramundane phenomena are entirely like an illusion, [the question is asked:

"Does the World-Honored One’s teaching that things are 'like an illusion' refer to the various illusory phenomena manifested by the true mind of the various sages as being like an illusion, or does it refer to the karma of deluded commoners who cling to them?"

Are the various different appearances manifested by consciousness like illusions? If you mean that the various illusory appearances manifested by the true mind of the sages—which they point to and do not cling to—are like illusions, then it may be so;

however, if you mean that the various different appearances manifested by the karmic consciousness of ignorant people—which they point to and cling to—are like illusions, this cannot be, for even that which possesses a nature [of existence] cannot be like an illusion.
This is because there exists a nature that is not like an illusion. Why is this so?

It refers to form that is without cause, which arises from another luminous source and cannot serve as a cause for other delusions; because it does not give rise to conceptual attachment, it can be called an illusion.
But would one also call an illusion that which has no cause yet manifests with various characteristics? This is indeed because...
Form that is without cause is manifested from the true mind of the noble ones; like a mirror reflecting an image, it gives rise to no grasping or attachment.
Therefore, seeing form is not seeing form, and hearing sound is not hearing sound. Because it does not act as a cause for other delusions, it can be described as being like an illusion.
If form has a cause, it is the manifestation of the self-realization of the ignorant man’s *karmic consciousness*, and is thus named [delusive form].
Internal form is called the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition) because it is that which is apprehended and relied upon by visual consciousness and the other [sensory] cognitions.

This [internal form] can act as a cause for other delusions, producing them through a continuous succession; it is thus comparable to an illusion. Therefore, when the various illusions perceived by the noble ones (*ārya*) are conceptualized and clung to, they may be called "illusions.
However, if one conceptualizes and clings to a distinct characteristic that lacks the various characteristics of illusion, how could that possibly be so?
The Buddha said: "When I speak of things being like an illusion, the meaning is manifold;
it is not merely that the various illusory appearances manifested from the clinging mind—which are forms without a cause—resemble an illusion.
To say that all phenomena are like an illusion also refers to those internal forms with causes produced by the evolving consciousness of karma, even though these differ [from external illusions]."
The various consciousnesses arise from one another in succession; because they shift and perish with every moment as swiftly as lightning, they are like illusions.

For example, a flash of lightning appears in an instant and perishes at the very place it appears. This is not like the attachment of the foolish who take these various appearances to be truly existent.
Therefore, the text below states: "When things arise, they are subject to cessation; this is not for the sake of the foolish."
I teach that all such phenomena are merely one's own false conceptualizations and discriminations; thus, one perceives that self-characteristics and common characteristics can be apprehended.

If one can skillfully contemplate that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent, then since even self- and common-characteristics are not seen to manifest, how could there be any characteristic of form to be grasped through attachment? For this reason, I say that all phenomena are like [a reflection].
Since there is not a single thing that can serve as a metaphor for an illusion other than an illusory phenomenon itself, it is said that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is like an illusion.

Not only do various illusory appearances resemble illusions, but their lack of reality—arising and ceasing instantaneously—and their lack of substantial nature, being inherently unborn like a flash of lightning, are also like illusions; how could this not be so?
"How singular is this path!

Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying: "Regarding what the World-Honored One has taught—that all natures are unarisen and like illusions—will there not be a contradiction between what the World-Honored One has previously said and what he now says? Is it not that you speak of unarisen natures being like illusions? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
Wisdom is not what I call the fault of contradiction between prior and subsequent statements regarding the nature of non-arising being like an illusion. Why is this?
It is because the realization that arising and non-arising are merely the manifestation of one’s own mind—whether existent or non-existent—is the non-arising of external natures and non-natures.

Mahāmati, it is not that I am guilty of the fault of contradiction between prior and subsequent statements; rather, it is to refute the causal arising of the outsiders that I say all natures are non-existent.
Mahāmati, you and the other outsiders are a mass of delusion who wish to give rise to existence and non-existence through birth; this is due to various attachments to your own false imaginings.
Mahāmati, I do not hold that there is birth from existence or non-existence. Therefore, Mahāmati, I speak by means of the teaching of non-birth.
Mahāmati, when I speak of "nature," it is for the purpose of gathering in those in saṃsāra, and to destroy the view of non-existence and the view of annihilationism for my disciples.
Because it encompasses the various karmic bases for rebirth, Mahāmati, it is spoken of as having the nature of sound;
it is spoken of as having the nature of illusion because its own-nature and characteristics are intended to be free from the characteristics of own-nature.

It speaks of illusions and dreams to counteract the attachment to the characteristics of self-nature produced by causes and conditions—attachment that arises from the ignorant clinging to the signs of evil views and the failure to understand that all is merely the manifestation of one’s own mind.

"Mahāmati, regarding the characteristic of self-nature, one should not cause foolish people with evil views to harbor hopes for or become attached to all dharmas—whether to oneself or to others—but rather see all dharmas as they truly are in their actual state, thereby avoiding incorrect doctrines. Mahāmati, seeing all dharmas as they truly are in their actual state means transcending the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: [Verse omitted per instructions]

To claim that "arising" is not a real nature, yet is subsumed under the nature of existence, and to observe birth and death as being like an illusion and so forth, without conceptualizing their marks—this objection suggests that the Tathāgata’s teaching involves a contradiction between its earlier and later parts. The meaning is this:

since the World-Honored One has already stated that all phenomena are unarisen, he should not further state that the causes and effects of good and evil within the triple world, along with the cycle of rebirth, truly possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Since you have already stated that there is an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet you also say that all phenomena are like illusions—because they do not understand that while arising is non-arising, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is serene and non-arising, yet karma and its fruits arise;

and that while birth and death are like illusions and dreams, those karmas are not destroyed because one is mired in verbal expression—it is for this reason that this question was asked. The Buddha said: "The Dharma I teach..."
All these are words spoken in accordance with the intentions of others; they do not possess the fault of internal contradiction between earlier and later statements.
When I say "unborn," it does not mean that there is an absolute non-arising. Rather, the very place of arising is itself non-arising.

Through my own realization of the manifestation of the mind-only (*cittamātra*), I have examined all existing phenomena and non-phenomena; when one investigates their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is found to be utterly unobtainable from the beginning.
Since that which is unborn manifests birth by following the unborn, it is said to be like an illusion;
how could there be any fault of contradiction between what I have previously stated and this? Furthermore, my teaching on the unborn does not stop at that alone.
Moreover, in order to refute the non-Buddhists' view of production through causes—since those foolish crowds of non-Buddhists claim [the self] to be one—[I have taught this].

All phenomena arise from existence through seeds; they do not arise from non-existence through the absence of seeds, nor do they arise from the conditions of one's own various deluded imaginings, attachments, and habitual tendencies.

Since arising from existence or non-existence is not what is taught by those external paths, I teach that all phenomena are unarisen in order to refute such views; therefore, I speak using the discourse of non-arising.

Now, since I have already stated that all phenomena are unarisen, yet also stated that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature, why do the non-Buddhists claim that all phenomena arise conditioned by various attachments to their own conceptual constructions, arising from various distinct causes?
Because they do not know the origin of birth and death, they fall into the view of annihilationism; therefore, I speak of good, evil, and so forth.
If dharmas that induce birth and death all possess a real intrinsic nature, then cultivating virtuous causes must necessarily induce virtuous fruits,
and creating non-virtuous causes must necessarily induce non-virtuous fruits— just as a shadow follows a form without the slightest error.

This would cause them to perceive the three realms as being entirely due to the grasping of birth and death through their own virtuous and non-virtuous karmic actions, leading them to destroy and annihilate [the teachings] by repudiating evil.

Because I see this, I have made such a statement for my disciples: that all dharmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome, truly possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because they are able to encompass and receive various karmic fruits and retributions.

Although I have stated that all dharmas truly possess an intrinsic nature, I have also stated that their nature and essence are like an illusion; this too is for the purpose of causing those foolish people to abandon their attachments.
Because they perceive that there is a truly existent intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), those foolish people fall into wrong views;

failing to realize that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are merely manifestations of mind and are fundamentally uncreated and devoid of intrinsic nature, they falsely imagine a creator as the cause of birth.
Clinging to the characteristics of intrinsic nature as being truly existent, they aspire to attain the fruit [of their actions] for the sake of a self.
Because they destroy the production caused by those [erroneous] causes and eliminate attachment to the nature of self-nature (*svabhāva*),
it is taught that the aggregates and all other phenomena arise from conditions and are fundamentally devoid of self-nature, being like illusions and dreams.

This is done so as not to allow foolish people to harbor attachments to the imagined existence of specific or common characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa/sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) with a real self-nature, nor to allow them to turn away from reality (*yathābhūta*).
To hold views and engage in improper discourse while dwelling in the state of suchness—that is, seeing all phenomena as merely the manifestations of one’s own mind—is already a transcendence;
how much more so is it to see them as having a truly existent nature, self-nature, or characteristics? Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata, abiding in samādhi, sees that both the seer and the conditions for seeing, along with all perceived characteristics, are like empty space."
Empty flowers are fundamentally non-existent; this seeing and its conditions are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi.
How could there be "is" or "is not" within them? Therefore, know that only by abiding in the place of suchness does one see things as like an illusion;
only by realizing they are like an illusion does one see their non-arising. What contradiction could there be? One should formulate the syllogism thus: all dharmas are... [non-existent].
The thesis, reason, and example are stated as follows: "Because it is comprised within the nature of existence and because it undergoes birth and death, it is like a magical illusion.
In this verse, the same meaning is further elaborated: all phenomena arise from the manifestation of one's own mind; therefore, they are unarisen. Because they are unarisen, they are uncreated.

Because they are uncreated, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The reason for speaking of their being "unarisen" is to refute the non-nature of phenomena produced by causes, as asserted by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Furthermore, when it is said that there is "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), it is intended to let disciples know that wholesome and unwholesome karma truly possesses its own nature which governs birth and death;
this is precisely for the purpose of destroying the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

When it is said that things are "like an illusion," it is because non-Buddhists, through their evil views, harbor hopes and attachments, reckoning that the aggregates (*skandha*) and other phenomena possess real specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); therefore, I [teach them] in such a way.
By observing [them] as being like illusions and so forth, one intends to cause them not to give rise to false conceptualizations or attachments regarding the characteristics of self and other.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall explain the characteristics of the body of names, phrases, and syllables; a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who skillfully contemplates the body of names, phrases, and syllables...
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters accordingly into the meanings of words and their formal bodies, they quickly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having thus awakened, they awaken all sentient beings. Mahāmati, what is called the "name-body" (*nāma-kāya*) refers to the establishment of names based on things.

What is called the "phrase-body" (*pada-kāya*) refers to phrases that possess meaning; when the self-nature of a phrase is determined and its ultimate limit is reached, that is called a "name. (This is called a "phrase.")
The "body of form" (*rūpakāya*) refers to the manifestation of names and phrases; thus it is called the body of form. Furthermore, the body of form refers to length, shortness, height, and depth.
The "body of phrases" (*padakāya*) refers to tracks, such as the tracks left by elephants, horses, humans, beasts, and so forth;
these are given the name "body of phrases. Mahāmati, as for "name" and "form," it is because one explains the four formless aggregates (*skandhas*) by means of names that they are called "names."

Because their own characteristics appear, form is spoken of; the bodies of names, phrases, and forms are spoken of as the distinct limits of the characteristics of the bodies of names, phrases, and forms—this should be studied.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The distinctions between the bodies of names, phrases, and forms—foolish ordinary people cling to them, like an elephant sinking into deep mud."

After Mahāmati had requested an explanation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), seven successive challenges were raised: 1. The first challenge: If there is a nature in verbal expression, then all things must possess a nature;

it should not be said that the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) are non-existent. 2. The second challenge: If both the expression and that which is expressed lack any nature, then this results in the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*);
who then could be said to be eternal? 3. The third challenge: Delusive confusion (*bhrānti*) exists; it should not be [denied].
To say that the delusion of non-nature is non-existent would be incorrect, for it should not be said that the True and Eternal is thus.

Question: Is this delusion existent or non-existent? These are four difficulties. Furthermore, delusion is like an illusion; it must also serve as the cause for other delusions—this is a sixth difficulty. Among all phenomena, some are illusory and some are non-illusory;
one should not exhaustively use the analogy of being "like an illusion" for all of them—this is a seventh difficulty. That the nature of non-arising is like an illusion [is the response].
These contradictions between what precedes and what follows all stem from clinging to names and phrases and failing to penetrate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);

therefore, I urge you to skillfully observe the bodies of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and syllables (*vyañjanakāya*). If you can skillfully observe them, you will not be deluded by names and phrases, nor will you falsely raise questions and difficulties;
rather, you will enter into the meaning through words, attain the meaning and forget the words, and swiftly realize unsurpassed *bodhi*. Thus is awakening.

Furthermore, by means of awakening all sentient beings to the meaning that transcends verbal expression: what is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) refers to the establishment of names based on things;
it is that which expresses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such as establishing the names "bowl" or "pitcher" based on objects like bowls and pitchers.
Because these names themselves constitute a body, they are called "name-bodies. How could these names truly exist? As for a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), it refers to individual phrases...
There are definitive meanings that can express distinctions, such as a copper jar or a silver jar among jars, or a ceramic basin or a wooden basin among basins;
because these various distinctions are fixed, ultimate, and never confused with one another, they constitute the "body of names" (*nāmakāya*).
As for the "body of phrases" (*padakāya*), how could it ever truly exist? The "body of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*) refers to written characters, consisting of dots, strokes, slants, and so forth.
By pressing [the fingers] into shapes, names and phrases are manifested; because they serve as the basis for names and phrases, they are called "vocalic bodies" (*vyañjana-kāya*).
How could these letters ever truly exist? Furthermore, regarding the vocalic body: it is said that characters possess four tones and eight rhymes.
Because these phonetic rhythms have inflections and curvatures, their long and short, high and low pitches constitute the vocalic body. Furthermore, there is the "syntactic body" (*pada-kāya*).
Because it is definitive and ultimate, it is likened to a track; for a track is that which emerges from the footstep.
Thus, by following the track one knows what kind of creature it is, and by following the words one knows what their meaning is. Therefore it is said:
"To seek the ox, one must inquire after its tracks. Furthermore, "name and form" refers to the four formless aggregates, which are profoundly devoid of any manifest characteristics.
Because there is only its name, it is called "name" (*nāman*); yet since its name exists, its form can also be manifested through syllables, and thus it is called "form" (*ākṛti*).
In this way, names and forms not only manifest matters pertaining to the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), but can also manifest matters pertaining to the formless realm (*arūpa-dhātu*).
If one thoroughly understands the boundaries of names, phrases, and forms, one will then be able to enter into their meaning accordingly.
They possess identical forms; thus, among the three kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the habitual tendency for names and words (*nāma-vāsanā*) serves as the primary seed.
This is why the root of name is so difficult to uproot. Therefore, once the root of name is uprooted, one swiftly realizes *bodhi*.
A former master said: "Seeking light out of craving, one drills into paper; though there are many ways to fail to penetrate, suddenly one stumbles through."
"Only upon returning and retracing my path do I finally believe that my entire life has been deceived by my own eyes.
Is this not one who, while skillfully observing the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*), is no longer deluded by them?

The verse states that although there are distinctions among the bodies of names, phrases, and forms, these are nothing other than means intended to reveal the ultimate meaning that transcends words; they merely serve as conduits for entering the meaning through the bodies of phrases and forms. Yet, ordinary beings—
To be submerged in names and phrases and unable to extricate oneself is like an elephant stuck in deep mud; unable to save itself, how can one hope for it to trample its way out?

Furthermore, Mahāmati, in future ages, those with wisdom will, by means of being free from the views of oneness, difference, both, or neither, [perceive] the characteristics of the self and what belongs to the self.

The one who asks about the general meaning of non-intelligence immediately replies: "This is not a correct question. For instance, whether form (*rūpa*) and so forth are permanent or impermanent, whether they are different or not different;

likewise, regarding nirvāṇa and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*), the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), the primary element (*bhūta*) and the derivative element (*bhautika*), the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and the seen (*dṛśya*), gross objects (*sthūla*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the cultivator (*bhāvaka*)—such things as these are mutually related in this manner."

When asked such questions, the Buddha spoke of them as "unexplained" (*avyākṛta*) and ceased the discussion; this is not because those foolish people are capable of knowing it, but rather because they lack the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, spoke of them as unexplained so as to cause them to leave behind terrifying phrases and did not provide an explanation for their sake.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, he did not speak of them in order to cease the speculative views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The Tīrthikas speak thus, asserting that "the life-principle is the very body," and so forth; such are their indeterminate doctrines (*avyākṛta-vāda*), Mahāmati.
Those foolish outsiders formulate these indeterminate doctrines regarding causes, but they are not my teaching. What, Mahāmati, is my teaching?

It is the departure from the false discrimination of the grasped and the grasper, wherein such conceptualization does not arise. How, Mahāmati, is that [discrimination] ceased? It is by ceasing attachment to the grasped and the grasper.
Because they do not understand that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats,

and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the four kinds of categorical explanations (*vyākaraṇa*). Mahāmati, as for those who withhold categorical explanations, I say from time to time that this is for those whose faculties are immature,
and not for those whose faculties are mature.
This chapter addresses the Southeast while its intent lies in the Northwest; though it ostensibly rebukes the non-Buddhists, its true purpose is to offer a profound censure of Mahāmati himself.

Its meaning is this: you are named "Great Wisdom" and are thus called a wise one, yet when I speak to you using the Dharma that transcends the four propositions, you are still unable to comprehend it.
Instead, you cling to names, phrases, forms, and bodies, giving rise to false discursive arguments.

How much more so for one who lacks wisdom, when they are interrogated regarding the meaning I have mastered—the Dharma that transcends the four propositions—and yet they do not believe it, instead claiming that what I have asked is not correct?

They maintain that one should distinguish between the five aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest, as being either permanent or impermanent, and likewise [distinguish] whether *nirvāṇa* and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are different or not different from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Thus [they speak].
That which arises is the producer; that which is produced is the produced. The realizer is the dependent; the realized dharma is the basis.
The four great elements are the creators; the [derived] four great elements are the created. That which sees is the faculty; that which is seen is the object.
That which is coarse is the gross particle; that which is subtle is the atom. Cultivation is the act of cultivating; the cultivator is...
When one practices in such a manner, these successive categories all possess the characteristics of being both permanent and impermanent, as well as different and non-different;
it is by means of such questions that one asks correctly. Yet, if one conversely says, "This which was spoken by the Buddha, I do not know;
I do not understand; it cannot be recorded," if a wise person were to encounter such a person, they would certainly [reject them].

One should desist and not debate further; it is inappropriate to engage them in discussion using the method of transcending the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*), for this method of transcending the four propositions is beyond the comprehension of such ignorant persons.

These deluded people, having long been devoid of the cultivation of wisdom through hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), are suddenly confronted with this teaching and become utterly bewildered and filled with fear. Thus, the Tathāgata [commands]:
Because he is free from the phrases of fear, even if he were to utter the words of the Tathāgata, they would be beyond recording;

a wise person should certainly set them aside and not attempt to analyze them. Furthermore, since beginningless time, those non-Buddhists have been conditioned by various false views and conceptual proliferations through the influence of evil teachers and evil teachings, never departing from the four extremes. If one employs the Dharma that is free from these four extremes—
If one engages in clear debate with such a person, not only will it fail to dispel their delusions, it will instead further increase them;

therefore, one should desist from speaking and cause them to reflect in silence and examine themselves. This is also a form of "instruction through disdain. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"For example, if someone asks how many pecks of milk can be obtained by milking a cow's horn, this is not a valid question; therefore, one should not respond."
Answer: It is like a person asking about the height, stature, beauty, or ugliness of a barren woman’s son or a eunuch’s son;

this should not be answered because such sons do not exist. What are called the views and theories of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) mean that they do not understand that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a functional capacity established as a designation—consisting of vitality, warmth, and consciousness—which is drawn forth by karma and serves as the eighth seed to maintain the continuity of matter and mind without interruption.
To falsely claim that what is called the "life-faculty" (jīvitendriya) is identical to the body is truly a neutral (avyākṛta) doctrine.
Those heterodox teachers (tīrthika), being ignorant and lacking wisdom, are deluded regarding cause and effect;

they do not know that this body arises from the attachment to one's own false imaginings and from the union of the two drops—red and white—from one's parents—and yet they falsely claim that an autonomous person (puruṣa) or other such entities are its creator.

Consequently, they possess this body while denying cause and effect; such talk is truly beyond the ears, a doctrine of nihilistic annihilation that is indeed a "neutral" (*avyākṛta*) theory. Yet, what they call "neutral" is surely not what I teach.
What I teach is free from the four propositions and transcends the hundred negations; within, there is no mind that grasps, and without, there is no...

When the objects of grasping no longer give rise to false conceptualization and the pathways of the mind are cut off, this state of "indeterminacy" (avyākṛta) is none other than the pure consciousness (amala-vijñāna), which is the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is beyond verbal description and cannot be recorded; yet, it is not comparable to the nihilistic annihilationism of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Therefore, [the Buddha] remained silent and did not answer, thereby bringing that discourse to a halt. That which was being discussed by them concerned the internal...

If one truly maintains that there is a mind capable of grasping and that there is an external object to be grasped, yet— due to ignorance of the fact that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind—
one falsely constructs this discourse regarding the existence or non-existence of external natures, then even if one were to attempt to cover it with a round lid and fit it with a square base,
they would certainly not match. It is better to simply cease such discussion and likewise cause their discourse to cease, waiting for [the realization of truth].
If this spiritual mechanism is triggered, perhaps there may arise a mind of repentance and awakening?
Furthermore, this discussion is not intended solely for non-Buddhists; rather, the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma to sentient beings through four modes of answering:
there are those given direct answers, those given by means of counter-questions, those given with detailed analysis, and those set aside without answer. Its...

To set aside [the question] without answering is precisely to cease the discussion. This is as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable.
This cessation of discussion is for those whose faculties are not yet mature, so that they may wait for the right time before it is taught.
If one's faculties are mature, then even if one speaks all day long, one never truly speaks; why then would one need to cease? Therefore, [this approach] is provided.
The wise say that speaking is itself not speaking, and for those without wisdom, not speaking is itself speaking;

since both speaking and not speaking are nothing other than the manifestation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one should not harbor any attachment to the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are free from being produced by causes and conditions; because there is no agent, all dharmas are unproduced.
Mahāmati, why are all natures devoid of intrinsic nature? Because when one examines them through self-awakening, neither their specific nor their general characteristics can be apprehended;
therefore, it is said that all dharmas are unproduced. Why are all dharmas ungraspable?
That which comes cannot be brought, and that which goes cannot be taken away as a common characteristic. If one wishes to bring it, there is nowhere from which it comes;
if one wishes to take it away, there is nowhere to which it goes. Therefore, all phenomena are free from bringing and taking away. Mahāmati, why is it that all phenomena do not perish?
It is because their intrinsic nature and characteristics do not exist, and because all phenomena are unattainable; thus, all phenomena do not perish.

Mahāmati, for what reason are all dharmas impermanent? It is because their characteristic of arising is the nature of impermanence; therefore, it is said that all dharmas are impermanent. Mahāmati, for what reason are all dharmas eternal?
It is because the characteristic of arising is the nature of non-arising, and since non-arising is eternal, it is said that all dharmas are eternal.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: [The Verses on the Exposition]
There are four kinds of categorical interrogation, analytical questioning, and the cessation of debate used to restrain the various non-Buddhists.
Regarding existence and non-existence, the teachers of the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika schools all maintain that [these] are indeterminate.
By thus demonstrating that the self-nature discriminated by the Perfectly Awakened One cannot be apprehended because it is free from verbal expression, one speaks of the absence of self-nature.
For this reason, because Mahāmati clung to the nature of non-arising as being like an illusion— which was internally contradictory—

and because the World-Honored One had already rebuked his attachment to words and phrases as being like an elephant sinking in mud, he further used the views of external paths to censure him. Therefore,
he again synthesizes these various meanings to conclude by stating that not only are the meanings of non-arising and illusion not mutually exclusive, but furthermore...
This does not contradict the meanings taught in the sūtras regarding non-extinction, neither coming nor going, permanence, and impermanence.
How could one perversely cling to mere terminology without relying on the comprehensive meaning established by me?
Therefore, that which I call "unborn" is so because all phenomena are devoid of an agent and lack anything produced; for phenomena born of causes and conditions are themselves non-existent.
Because they arise, it is said that all phenomena are unarisen and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

This means that although all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature that could be relinquished, foolish people, not knowing that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds, falsely claim that all phenomena have obtainable intrinsic natures, both specific and general.
If one examines all things with the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), [they are seen as unarisen].

Since phenomena possess neither specific nor general characteristics, and furthermore, no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or commonality can be apprehended, it is said that "all things are devoid of intrinsic nature.
This absence of intrinsic nature is precisely what is meant by non-arising.
Why is it that all phenomena neither come nor go? If all phenomena possessed a real intrinsic nature, they could be brought here or taken away.
Because both specific and general characteristics are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), they have nowhere from which to depart and nowhere to which they go; thus, there is no coming or going.
This absence of coming and going is precisely non-arising. Why is it that all phenomena (*dharma*) are not extinguished?

Because all phenomena can only be extinguished if they possess a self-nature (*svabhāva*) that can be apprehended; since all phenomena are devoid of any self-nature that can be apprehended, they are necessarily [non-extinguishable].
There are no dharmas that can be extinguished; this non-extinguishing is precisely non-arising. Why is it that all dharmas are impermanent?

If the characteristics of dharmas do not arise, they may be said to be permanent. Now, the characteristics of dharmas arise and perish in an instant, abiding for no moment and lacking any nature of permanence.
This very nature of impermanence is precisely non-arising. Why is this so? All [dharmas are thus].
If dharmas were always characterized by the arising of their marks, then one could say they possess a real nature of birth and are thus impermanent.
Now, although the marks of dharmas arise, they in reality lack a nature of birth; therefore, that all dharmas suddenly arise and suddenly perish is precisely true permanence.
This true permanence is itself non-arising. Thus, the two characters "non-arising" do not merely negate self-arising and other-arising.
Co-arising and arising without cause—its reality neither comes nor goes; its meanings of permanence and impermanence are such that nothing remains unpenetrated.
How could it be fettered by words and names? One must certainly enter through words to attain the meaning, yet once the meaning is attained, one forgets the words.
In the verse, the four types of categorical explanations (*vyākaraṇa*) are clarified: a "direct answer" is to respond in accordance with the question asked, as follows:

If one asks, "What is the Buddha? and answers, "The mind itself is the Buddha," this is an answer by way of a counter-interrogation (*prativākya*). An example of an answer by way of analysis (*vibhajya-vākya*) is as follows:

if a non-Buddhist takes "non-acceptance" as his tenet, one counters by asking, "Do you accept this view [of non-acceptance]? An example of an answer by way of classification (*vibhaṅga-vākya*) is as follows:
if one asks about the heavens, one answers, "In the desire realm there are six; in the form realm there are eighteen; and in the formless realm there are four."
Regarding the "argument of cessation" (*sthāpanā-vāda*): it is like when a non-Buddhist asks whether one speaks of existence or non-existence, and the World-Honored One remains silent;
among these four types of arguments, only the argument of cessation is the method for subduing the heterodox views of existence and non-existence.
The *Sāṃkhya* refers to the followers of the *Sāṃkhya* school; because their doctrine calculates [existence], they establish twenty-five *tattvas* (principles) to demonstrate it.

The Vaiśeṣika masters maintain that all phenomena are real; because their doctrine calculates that [the self] is non-existent, they establish six categories to demonstrate that all phenomena are non-existent.
All of these do not transcend the false conceptualization of existence and non-existence, and thus ultimately result in a theory of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
As for that which is discerned by Perfect Awakening, it is not merely a matter of having a nature or lacking a nature, nor is it both.

The absence of intrinsic nature is neither existence nor non-existence; it is unapprehendable. Thus, the buddha-nature, the dharma-nature, the bodhi-nature, and the nirvana-nature are all unapprehendable.
Because they are unapprehendable, they transcend verbal expression. Because they transcend verbal expression, they are devoid of intrinsic nature.
This absence of intrinsic nature is precisely non-arising and non-non-arising, and non-ceasing and non-non-ceasing.
That which is not eternal is precisely not discontinuous; that which is not discontinuous is precisely not coming; and that which does not come is precisely not going.

Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Neither arising nor ceasing, neither eternal nor discontinuous, neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going—those who can thus explain dependent origination effectively extinguish all conceptual proliferation. Thus, one knows that dependent origination is non-existent [in its own right].
Since all phenomena that arise are universally pervasive, how can one be mired in names and phrases and restrict them to a single meaning?

From this point, up to the "Chapter on Difficulties in Dependent Origination," these sections all serve to clarify the doubts regarding the three chapters on conditions, causes, and conceptual proliferation (*parikalpita*).
From here below, until the beginning of the third fascicle, the "Flower Adornment of Sovereignty" provides an extensive refutation of heterodox views.
This clarifies the four types of false and correct causes and effects mentioned in the preceding text.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the specific distinctions and general characteristics of the various types of *srotāpanna* and their paths, as well as how a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva may skillfully understand the *srotāpanna*.”

Having distinguished and understood the general characteristics of the various paths of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), as well as the specific characteristics of the means for the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),
non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and arhat, they teach the Dharma to sentient beings in such and such ways— namely,

the characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness and the characteristics of purifying the two obstacles and traversing the stages (*bhūmi*)— until they ultimately penetrate and attain the inconceivable, ultimate realm of all Tathāgatas.
The realms are like a mani jewel of manifold colors, excellently able to benefit all sentient beings;

through the inexhaustible body and wealth of the sphere of all dharmas, they sustain and nourish all Buddhas. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall now speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! Indeed, we shall listen and receive it."
This question concerns the specific characteristics of the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*) and the preparatory methods for the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*).

Regarding what is called the "general characteristic of the distinctions," it means that the causal practices cultivated by those in the stage of *srotāpanna* and those proceeding toward the stage of *srotāpanna* (*srotāpattipratipannaka*) possess both commonalities and differences.

As for the distinctions: while the fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa*) are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior, their abandonment likewise possesses superior, middling, and inferior aspects.

Regarding the ultimate characteristic, all are called *srotāpanna*. Regarding the provisional characteristic, although the name is the same, there are those who manifest provisional means, such as the category of "secret within and manifest without.
Once one has discerned these two types of distinct characteristics, one should preach the Dharma to sentient beings in such and such a manner.
Having attained the purity of the two kinds of selflessness— of persons and of phenomena— one eradicates the two obstacles of afflictions and the known,
transcends all ten stages, and reaches the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata. Manifesting forms in accordance with sentient beings like a mani jewel displaying various colors,
one sustains and nourishes all living beings through inexhaustible bodies and wealth.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three types of *srotāpanna* and distinctions regarding the fruit of *srotāpatti*.
What are the three? They are the inferior, the middling, and the superior. The inferior [attains parinirvāṇa] after seven births at most; the middling attains parinirvāṇa after three or five births;
the superior attains parinirvāṇa in that very same birth. These three types have three kinds of fetters—inferior, middling, and superior. What are they?"

The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Through these three distinct fetters, one progressively ascends to attain the state of an Arhat.

A *srotāpanna*—translated here as "Stream-enterer"—is described in other passages as one who, by means of the sixteen moments of mind of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), abandons [the afflictions] of the three realms.
The eighty-eight afflictions of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are first termed the "fruit of stream-entry" (*srotāpanna-phala*) when one initially enters the stream of the noble ones.

Subsequently, by being born seven times in the heavens and seven times among humans, one eliminates the eighty-one grades of the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) within the three realms and attains the state of an Arhat.

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Among the seeds of the ten afflictions of the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), those abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) are [abandoned] by the vision of the Three Vehicles."
Regarding those seeds of the innate afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) to be abandoned through cultivation that are severed all at once within the stages of the Path:
depending on whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, there is both simultaneous and gradual abandonment. For a certain class of dull-facultied practitioners, abandonment occurs over seven births;

they divide the three realms into nine levels (*bhūmi*), and each level into nine grades (*prakāra*), resulting in eighty-one grades in total. A person who has attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) abandons [the first grade] of the desire realm.
The abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) up to the fifth grade is called the stage of the candidate for the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*).

The abandonment of the sixth grade is called the fruit of the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), so named because three grades of afflictions of thought in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) remain unabandoned, causing one to return to the human world.

When the abandonment reaches the eighth grade, it is called the candidate for the Non-returner (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*). When the abandonment reaches the ninth grade, it is called the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala*), because the afflictions of the desire realm are exhausted.
Because they do not return to the human realm, they dwell in the fourth dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, by severing the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) in each of the eight higher stages, up to the seventy-first grade, they are called "candidates for arhatship" (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*). When the final grade is severed, they are called "arhats.

This refers to those of dull faculties who abandon [afflictions] gradually. Furthermore, there is another class of those with sharp faculties who, regarding the nine [grades of afflictions] of the three realms...
The eighty-one categories of afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are combined into a single aggregate and collectively divided into nine grades.
Although there are nine grades, because they are severed individually over the course of one lifetime, only two fruits are established: namely, the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and the Arhat.

Regarding the statement that there are three types of *srotāpanna*, this refers to the fact that the *srotāpanna* themselves possess three grades of faculties (*indriya*). Among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), [the first] pertains to the body...

Regarding the three fetters of view and doubt, categorized as superior, middling, and inferior, they are further distinguished according to the exhaustion of seven births, five births, or one birth before realizing *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to the *srotāpanna* of dull faculties who exhausts innate delusions;
since the latter two fruits have not yet attained *nirvāṇa*, they are collectively subsumed within the first fruit. One contemplates the abandonment of innate *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.
This can be understood; therefore it is said that by ascending higher and further advancing, one attains Arhatship. One asks:

"The afflictions of the ten fetters (*daśa-ānuśaya*) must be completely severed before one finally exits the triple world (*traidhātuka*); why now do you speak only of three? It is because when the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is severed, the three poisons (*triviṣa*) naturally cease to arise.

Therefore, pride is not mentioned. Furthermore, since the four fruits [of the śramaṇa] have not yet been fully realized, it is not mentioned. This was because he had not yet entered the Buddha-Dharma."
Initially, the honored one, Māra, harbored doubts toward the Buddha; now that he has entered into right faith, he no longer doubts the Buddha-dharma.

Therefore, among the five dull faculties, only "doubt" is mentioned as being severed. As for the five sharp faculties, the other three are not mentioned because they all pertain to the false views of external paths, whereas since he now relies upon the Buddha, those are not discussed.
Mahāmati, there are two kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity): namely, that which is innate (*sahaja*) and that which is conceptualized (*parikalpita*).
Just as with dependent origination, so it is with the conceptualized nature of things; based upon the dependent nature, various attachments to the conceptualized nature arise.

Because these are neither existent nor non-existent, and because they lack the characteristics of a real conceptualized form—being neither existent nor non-existent—fools conceptually construct them in various ways.

Attachment to the self-nature and characteristics of perceptions—such as the perception of water by a thirsty deer in a mirage—is the false imagination of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of a *srotāpanna*.
By means of the realization of the non-self of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), they grasp at the absence of intrinsic nature and sever their long-standing attachment to ignorance.

O Mahāmati, that which is innate is the *srotāpanna*’s view of a self-body; because the four aggregates (*skandhas*) of oneself and others are devoid of the characteristics of form, [they perceive] form.
