Because they are both primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), because they are mutually dependent causes and conditions for one another, and because the primary elements and derived matter do not aggregate [independently], the *srotāpanna* contemplates the categories of existence and non-existence;
thus, when the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) no longer manifests, it is severed. When this view of a self-body is severed, craving does not arise.
This is called the characteristic of the view of a self-body.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) refers to the grasping at a self or what belongs to a self within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*);
its function is to serve as the basis for all modes of speculative views. There are twenty aspects of this view: namely, (1) the self is large and form is small, with the self being within form;
(2) the self is large and form is small, with form being within the self; (3) form is the self; (4) the self is apart from form. These four [aspects] apply to each of the [five] aggregates.
The five aggregates combined comprise twenty propositions; if these are traversed through the three periods of time, they become sixty.

If one further adds the existence and non-existence of the unconditioned as the fundamental basis, they are subsumed within the sixty-two types of conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*). Among these, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is divided into two kinds:
that which falsely identifies the four great elements as one’s own body is called the "delusive view of a self-body," while that which falsely identifies the objects of the six sense-fields...
That which takes the shadow to be one's own mind is called the innate view of self (sahaja-satkāya-dṛṣṭi).

Dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva) is metaphorically compared to the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), while the nature of false imagination (parikalpita-svabhāva) is metaphorically compared to the discriminated view of self (vikalpita-satkāya-dṛṣṭi).

Just as the discriminated view of self arises based upon the aggregate of form, so too does the nature of false imagination arise based upon the nature of dependent origination. This is because they do not understand that the aggregate of form consists of the four great elements (mahābhūta).
These provisional combinations are fundamentally illusory; they cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said not to exist.
Since they are neither existent nor non-existent, one knows they lack reality. All arise from ignorance, with karma and craving as their cause, resulting in these appearances.
Foolish people, lacking wisdom, give rise to deluded views; they recklessly calculate that there is a real self-nature therein and cling to it as a real self, just like one who is thirsty.
A deer pursues a mirage in a place where there is no water, falsely imagining it to be water; this is what is called the "view of a self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of a *srotāpanna*.
By observing this view of a self-identity with wisdom, one finds that solidity is earth, moisture is water, warmth is fire, and movement is wind.
Since these four great elements are each separate, where now does this delusory body reside?
Thus one knows that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is fundamentally without real nature; by not giving rise to grasping and attachment, one eliminates long-standing ignorant discrimination.
This is called "being far removed from the view of a self-body" (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). Although discriminative [afflictions] have been severed, innate [afflictions] still remain.

Therefore, one further applies the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) to observe again that, although within one's own and others' bodies there is the reception of sensations and the movement of cognitive objects, [they are ultimately empty].

Flowing through the discrimination of the four aggregates, one finds that while there is no characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), there is a name without a substance, which arises simultaneously with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Now, when observing the arising of the aggregate of form, it further arises by depending on the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its creators;
these arise through mutual causation, yet they do not know one another. One understands form by discerning who has combined to produce this form.
The aggregates (*skandha*) originally lack intrinsic nature; thus the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is empty. Since the aggregate of form is empty, the other four aggregates are also empty.

When the four aggregates are empty, who is there to act as a sovereign? When one contemplates in this way, one knows that the aggregate of form is without self and that its categories do not manifest;
furthermore, one knows that the four aggregates are without self and that their categories do not manifest. This is collectively termed "severing the body" (*kāya-prahāṇa*).
If the characteristic of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed, then craving for the desire realm is forever severed and does not arise or manifest;
this is called the *srotāpanna* because they have severed the characteristic of the view of a self-body.

Thus, the *Xian shi lun* (Treatise on Manifesting Consciousness) names this consciousness "the consciousness of the self-body" (*ātmabhāva-vijñapti*), because it is covered by the craving of the view of self, and thus undergoes birth within the six destinies. This consciousness is...
If this consciousness exists within the body of birth and death, then there is bodily consciousness. If this consciousness is exhausted, then the body of birth and death is exhausted.
Because the view of self gives rise to all delusions regarding flesh, and craving gives rise to all delusions regarding skin, the body of birth and death exists.
If one is detached from craving and the view of self, then there are no afflictions of skin or flesh; if there are no afflictions of skin or flesh, then [the body of birth and death ceases].
Because there is no body of the three realms, the body-consciousness does not undergo birth and death.

Mahāmati, the characteristic of doubt refers to the attainment of the characteristic of the correct vision of dharmas, as well as the cessation of the two previous kinds of false discrimination regarding the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi).
Thus, doubt regarding dharmas does not arise; one does not give rise to a view of a "Great Teacher" elsewhere concerning purity or impurity. This is called [the absence of doubt].
The characteristic of doubt is severed by the *srotāpanna*.
Doubt is defined as having a nature of hesitation regarding the principles of the truths; it functions as an obstacle to non-doubting, certain conviction.

There are three kinds of doubt: doubt regarding the principle, doubt regarding the Dharma, and doubt regarding the teacher. Now, one observes with the wisdom of *pudgala-nairātmya* (the selflessness of persons).
Because one perceives the true reality (*tattva*) through the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one has no doubt regarding the principle;
furthermore, since the two aforementioned types of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have already been abandoned, one also has no doubt regarding the Dharma.

Since one has no doubt regarding the principle or the Dharma, nor regarding whether the person who expounds the Dharma is pure or impure, one has no doubt regarding the teacher. This is called the characteristic of doubt abandoned by a *srotāpanna*.

Mahāmati, as for the attachment to precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*), why does the *srotāpanna* not cling to them? It is because he clearly perceives the painful nature of the places where one is reborn;
therefore, he does not cling to them. Mahāmati, "clinging" refers to the fool who, determined to undergo ascetic practices, seeks rebirth in those realms for the sake of various pleasurable things;
thus, he clings. This is excluded, except for that which is dedicated toward the excellence of self-realization and is free from delusive discrimination.

The practice of upholding the factors of morality through the application of skillful means regarding the characteristics of untainted dharmas is called the "taking up of the marks of morality" by a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).

This constitutes the abandonment of the three fetters; for the stream-enterer, greed and delusion do not arise. If a stream-enterer were to think, "I have not accomplished the abandonment of these fetters," there would be two faults:
falling into the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the failure to abandon the various fetters.
"Adherence to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) refers to the attachment to various views, precepts, and observances, as well as the aggregates upon which they depend,
as being supreme and capable of bringing about purification— such as, for example, observing the precepts of cattle or dogs as a cause for rebirth in heaven.
A *srotāpanna* does not grasp at such false precepts, for they clearly perceive that those who observe these precepts will inevitably be born in states of suffering at the time of their next rebirth.
Therefore, one does not adopt the practices of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The reason for adopting [the Buddha's path] is that they lack knowledge;

they believe that by practicing asceticism, the suffering of this life will be exhausted and they will surely be reborn in heaven to experience various pleasures. Consequently, they fumigate their noses, pluck out their hair, smear themselves with ashes, lie upon thorns, and observe the precepts of cows and dogs.
Not knowing this—that they are merely using suffering to abandon suffering—how could they ever attain true happiness? They must...

The srotāpanna perceives this; therefore, he does not grasp it, but rather upholds those branches of morality (śīlāṅga) for the sake of dedicating [merit] toward the supreme state of self-awakening and for the sake of abandoning the marks of conceptualization and the characteristics of outflow-free phenomena (anāsravadharma).
Thus, he undertakes and maintains the categories of precepts, yet not for the sake of seeking the fruits of human or celestial rebirth. This is called the abandonment of the srotāpanna.
Regarding the grasping at precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*): once the three fetters have been severed, greed and delusion do not arise, and the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are purified.
Nevertheless, one should not form the notion that "the fetters have been severed. If such a notion arises, there are two views: first, falling into the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*);
second, failing to sever the various fetters. Thus, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "A stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) might think: 'I have attained the fruit of a stream-enterer.'"
"Is there, Subhūti, a fruit of stream-entry? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?

One is called a 'stream-enterer' because they have entered the stream, yet in reality there is nothing entered. They do not enter into forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or objects of touch; thus they are called a stream-enterer."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken of many kinds of desire. Which among these is the desire that must be severed?

The Buddha told Mahāmati, “It is the love and longing for women, being entangled in and greedily attached to them through various means, committing evil deeds of body and speech, and experiencing pleasure in the present while planting the seeds of future suffering. That [desire] is what does not arise. Why is this? Because one attains the correct reception of samādhi.”
Because it is pleasant, its abandonment does not constitute the cessation of craving for *nirvāṇa*.

Although craving is manifold, only sensual craving (*kāmarāga*) is singled out here; for by means of this craving, the mind is not without attachment toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
Thus, even while experiencing pleasure in the present, one plants the seeds of future suffering; this refers to the first fruit [of the path].

Having severed the mind of craving, one does not give rise to attachment toward the six sense objects, because by abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one attains the bliss of right reception (*samyaksamādhi*).
Consequently, one no longer remains entangled in the five worldly desires; therefore, that severance is certainly not the severance of the craving for Nirvana.
This is because the *srotāpanna* has not yet attained Nirvana and is still truly seeking to proceed toward it.

Because of this turning back, Mahāmati, what are the characteristics of a Sakṛdāgāmin? It refers to one who, through sudden illumination, realizes that the characteristics of form, the characteristics of the arising of deluded thought, and the characteristics of views do not arise;
because they have well perceived the characteristics of the stages of dhyāna, they return once more to this world to reach the end of suffering and attain nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is so named.

The Sakṛdāgāmin. The preceding section concluded the gradual realization for those of inferior faculties who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna; this section concerns those of middling faculties who realize the second fruit instantaneously within a single lifetime.
For example, Ānanda suddenly severed the subtle afflictions of the three realms cultivated by the mind and instantaneously realized the second fruit.
This type of person, by severing discursive views regarding the body and realizing the fruit of *srotāpanna*, no longer gives rise to craving toward the six sensory objects.
Furthermore, through the power of wisdom, they suddenly illuminate the subtle craving that arises in relation to present objects;

by means of this power of wisdom, they permanently sever the six grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-kleśa*) and the innate view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which remain forever suppressed and do not arise.
Therefore it is said: the characteristic of birth and the characteristic of seeing do not arise.

Because one has well perceived the meaning and purpose of the dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the coarse and debased six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are unable to move the mind or alter its nature.

However, because the residual thoughts of the desire realm have not yet been fully purified, one must return once more to this realm to sever the remaining three grades of thought; once these are entirely eliminated, the experience of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) ceases.
Attaining the bliss of nirvana is the characteristic of a *srotāpanna* who attains the second fruit in this very life.

Mahāmati, why is one called an *anāgāmin*? It is because they see the faults of the arising of the characteristics and natures—whether existent or non-existent—of past, future, and present form, and because their delusive imaginings no longer arise; furthermore, because their fetters are severed, they are called an *anāgāmin*.

This refers to a Srotāpanna of superior capacity who realizes the three fruits instantaneously in a single lifetime, such as the Bhikṣuṇī Śrīguptā, whose desire was exhausted and who instantaneously realized the three fruits.
Previously, one merely observed that the manifest forms and appearances are illusory and lack intrinsic nature;
here, however, one exhaustively investigates the forms and appearances of the three periods of time and finds them all to be without self-nature, thereby becoming entirely free from attachment.
Because the innate view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the nine grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) no longer arise, and because the three fetters have been permanently severed,

there is no further arising of objects or conditions; thus, while dwelling in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), this *srotāpanna* attains the third fruit in one lifetime— this is the characteristic mark thereof.

Mahāmati, an Arhat is so called because they have realized that the various dhyānas, samādhis, liberations, powers, and clarities are devoid of the nature of afflictions, suffering, and false conceptualization; thus they are named Arhats.
This is the characteristic of a Srotāpanna of the highest capacity who attains the four fruits in a single lifetime, like the novice monk’s play.

The elder bhikṣu struck the leather ball four times and immediately realized the four fruits of arhatship—this being called "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), also "slayer of thieves" (*arhan*), and also "worthy of offerings" (*arhat*).
Of the preceding two fruits, only the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) were severed;
because he now suddenly exhausted all afflictions of the two higher realms at once, he attained this name and abided therein.

In this stage, one fully accomplishes the nine meditative concentrations, the three samādhis, the three liberations, the six supernormal powers, and the three insights; reaching the fourth stage of abiding,
one extinguishes without remainder the suffering of conditioned birth-and-death brought about by afflictions,
no longer undergoes future existence, and realizes the bliss of nirvana— this is the characteristic of a Srotāpanna attaining the four fruits in a single lifetime.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One speaks of three kinds of arhats. To which of these does this refer?

World-Honored One, is it the śrāvaka who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility, or is it a bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifesting as an arhat through skillful means, or is it a transformation buddha created by a buddha?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “It is the śrāvaka who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility.”

It is not for others; rather, it is because those who practice the bodhisattva path and those emanated by the Buddha employ skillful means and fundamental vows that they manifest birth within the great assembly to adorn the Buddha’s retinue.

Mahāmati, in the realm of conceptual construction, various teachings are proclaimed—such as attaining fruits and attaining dhyāna—but since the practitioner of dhyāna is entirely free from them, one manifests the attainment of self-mastery.

The attainment of the fruit through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the mind is called "attaining the fruit. Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who wish to transcend the realms of the dhyānas, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless (*ārūpya*) should abandon the marks of the direct perception of their own mind.
Mahāmati, it is not the case that one transcends the direct perception of one's own mind by means of the meditative attainments of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-samāpatti*);
why? Because there still exists the measure of the mind (*citta-mātra*).
Mahāmati, having heard that one could attain the fruit of Arhatship in a single lifetime, feared it might be a manifestation of the Buddhas or Bodhisattvas;
therefore, he inquired in detail: "What kind of being is this Arhat? The Buddha said:
"This one who has been described is one who has attained cessation (nirvāṇa) yet aspires to the Single Vehicle (ekayāna). He is not a Bodhisattva transformed by the Buddhas or Bodhisattvas."

Because they are endowed with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and the power of great vows (*mahā-praṇidhāna-bala*), they are able to conceal their inner reality while manifesting outwardly to bring sentient beings to maturity.
Those who are emanations of the Buddha manifest among human beings to adorn the Buddha’s retinue;
they enter into realms of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and teach various dharmas, speaking of the attainment of the four dhyānas and the attainment of the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
In truth, there is no person who can practice dhyāna and no dhyāna that can be entered, because all that is capable of being entered and all that is entered are utterly transcended.
It is merely a manifestation for the sake of humans and devas, employing the means of "harmony through common activity" (*samānārthatā*):

within the realm of non-mental-measurement (*acitta-mātra*), one manifests the mental-measurement (*citta-mātra*) and speaks of the signs of attaining the fruit, though in reality nothing is attained. Therefore, it is urged: "Desiring to transcend the four..."

Those who practice the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) of dhyāna and transcend the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), yet desire to bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn the Buddha’s retinue, should abandon the measure of what is manifested by their own minds (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*).
Only then will they not be restricted by such measures and become addicted to quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).
For those who take quiescent extinction as their goal become intoxicated by that very extinction and are thus unable to transcend the measure of what is manifested by their own minds.
Those who extinguish sensation and perception to attain right concentration have all yet been unable to transcend the mind-measure (*cittamātra*).
Because they still possess a mind-measure, they have not yet reached the point where the measure of numbers has been extinguished;
only the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not fall into these categories, and thus they are able to enter among beings according to their types to transform them, unhindered by such measures.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The various dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the formless attainments, and samādhi;
the cessation of all sensation and perception—all these are merely the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). They do not exist [independently].

The fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship—these are likewise delusions of the mind. For the practitioner of dhyāna, when dhyāna and its objects are severed, they are known [to be empty]."
To perceive the ultimate truth is merely the measure of conceptual construction; if one awakens to this, there is liberation.

This refers to the four dhyānas of the form realm, the four immeasurables, the four concentrations of the formless realm, up to the cessation of sensation and perception—all these are fundamentally devoid of various mental measures.
They are all the result of the delusive confusion within the minds of those who have attained the four fruits of the path.
Within the immeasurable, one manifests a measure for oneself and claims:

"I am a practitioner of dhyāna," "This is the dhyāna I have cultivated," "This is the object of clinging I have severed," "This is the accumulation I have severed," "This is the suffering I have known," and "This is the truth I have seen. All of these are termed delusions.
If one’s contemplation is such that the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) arises, one immediately attains liberation;
it is just as when one is in a great dream and does not wake, yet once awakened, the dream-scene vanishes entirely.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of cognition: the cognition of investigative examination (*pravicaya-buddhi*) and the cognition of establishing through the grasping and attachment to the marks of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa-saṃgraha-abhiniveśa-vyavasthāna-buddhi*).

Mahāmati, as for the cognition of investigative examination, it refers to the cognition that investigates the nature and characteristics of self-nature, which, being free from the four extremes (*catus-koṭi*), cannot be apprehended;
this is called the cognition of investigative examination. Mahāmati, those four extremes refer to being free from [the notions of] identity, difference, both, and neither.
"Not both existing and non-existing, neither non-existing nor non-non-existing, and neither permanent nor impermanent"—this is called the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), Mahāmati.
That which is free from these four propositions is called all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), Mahāmati. One should study the investigation of all phenomena by means of these four propositions.
This demonstrates the method of awakening, which is twofold: causing one to realize that "this is so" and "that is not," thereby abandoning the non-true and entering the true.

Regarding what is called "observing awakening," it means directly perceiving that the nature and self-nature of all phenomena are entirely the ultimate mind (*paramārthacitta*), and that when each is individually examined and sought, none can be found.

To reckon that things exist, to reckon that they do not exist, to reckon that they both exist and do not exist, or to reckon that they neither exist nor do not exist—all such reckonings are termed slandering the Dharma.
If one observes that all phenomena transcend these four positions, this is called truly awakening to the selflessness of all phenomena.
Mahāmati, what is the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false discrimination?

It refers to the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination—namely, solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—which are unreal; it is the establishing, through the attachment to the characteristics of the four great elements as thesis, reason, and example, of that which is unreal.
This is called the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false discrimination.

These are called the two kinds of characteristics of awakening. If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes these two characteristics of awakening—the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and phenomena—and thoroughly understands skillful means, they attain the awakening of non-existence;

observing the stages of practice, they enter the first stage (*bhūmi*), attain one hundred samādhis, and obtain the distinguished samādhi. They see one hundred Buddhas and one hundred Bodhisattvas, and know the limits of the past and the future.

Each illuminates the events of a hundred kalpas and shines upon a hundred buddha-fields; one knows the characteristics of the progressively higher stages (*uttarottara-bhūmi*), the excellence of great vows, and mastery over spiritual powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*).
Through the empowerment of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharma-megha-abhiṣeka*), one shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

With the mind firmly bound to the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣaya-pada*), one matures sentient beings through various transformations, adorned with light, and attains the samādhi of the noble bliss of self-realization.

"Feeling," "appropriation," "clinging," "establishment," and "discernment" refer to the fact that within the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the self-nature of things (*dharmatā*), where nothing can be apprehended,
one establishes through false imagination (*parikalpita*) the notion of a truly existent self-nature— such as saying the nature of earth is truly solid, or the nature of water [is truly fluid].
The nature of water is truly moist, the nature of fire is truly warm, and the nature of wind is truly mobile.
Furthermore, these are established as the four great elements (mahābhūta). They are established as both the creators (bhūta) of all phenomena and the created (bhautika).

Each is established with three branches as the standard, as when the Hīnayāna formulates a syllogism: "The four great elements are the subject; they truly possess intrinsic nature is the thesis; because..."

Because they can produce the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they are like space producing form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya teachers establish that the five subtle potentials (*tanmātra*) produce the five great elements:

the subtle potential of odor produces the earth element; the subtle potential of taste produces the water element; the subtle potential of color produces the fire element; the subtle potential of touch produces the wind element;

and the subtle potential of sound produces the space element. They also formulate a formal inference (*prayoga*) as follows: "The five subtle potentials are the subject (*dharmin*); they are presently existing..."

One may attempt to establish a thesis through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), using the reason (*hetu*) that "the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) are capable of being produced," with the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of "cloth being produced from threads.
All such [arguments] are established by following the deluded mind (*vikalpa-citta), taking an unreal nature to be a real existent nature.

One does not realize that the four great elements originally arise from the four kinds of deluded thoughts—namely, cutting and severing, moistening and lubricating, capacity and adaptability, and drifting and moving—which constitute the four [elements].
The great elements arise from the primary natures, yet they are separately established as solidity, moisture, heat, and motion;
to take these as the primary natures is called the conceptualization of grasping and attachment, which establishes cognitive awareness.

If a bodhisattva accomplishes these two aspects of cognitive awareness, they can abandon the aspect of establishing cognitive awareness and reach the ultimate state of the two kinds of selflessness. Being well-versed in skillful means, they thereby become free from [attachment].

Because one observes all phenomena through the realization that the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are non-existent, one enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) from the stage of the four preparatory practices (*catur-prayoga-bhūmi*) and immediately attains one hundred samādhis and so forth. The *Saṃgrahaṇī* states:

"When a bodhisattva enters the first stage, they realize ten sets of one hundred gates of clarity (*vidyā-mukha*). First, in a single kṣaṇa, they realize one hundred samādhis; second, by means of the pure devas...
1. With the eye of wisdom, one sees a hundred Buddha-fields; 2. By the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), one can shake a hundred Buddha-worlds;
3. One can travel to a hundred Buddha-lands to teach and transform sentient beings; 4. One can, with a single body, manifest a hundredfold forms so that sentient beings may behold them;
5. One can bring to maturity a hundred classes of sentient beings to be transformed; 6. If for the sake of benefiting others, one can remain [in the world].

9. He can know the events of a hundred eons regarding the past and future limits; 10. He can, through wisdom, enter the gate of illumination of a hundred dharmas, penetrating and understanding them thoroughly;
11. He can, by means of the contemplation of the body, perceive a hundred classes of kinsmen;

in the subsequent stages, these qualities increase manifold until the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*), where, by the power of great vows, he employs the four [immeasurables]...

Having attained unimpeded eloquence, extensively transformed sentient beings, gained mastery over the mind, and achieved self-mastery over the Dharma, one reaches the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) and receives the position of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Therein, one shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realized wisdom (*svayaṃbhū-jñāna-bhūmi*) by properly binding the mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣayamukha*), namely:
the inexhaustibility of sentient beings, the inexhaustibility of worlds, the inexhaustibility of space, the inexhaustibility of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the inexhaustibility of nirvāṇa.
The appearance of inexhaustible Buddhas; the inexhaustible wisdom of the Tathāgatas; the inexhaustible objects of the mind; the inexhaustible entry into the wisdom of Buddha-wisdom;
the inexhaustible turning of the wheel of Dharma; and the inexhaustible [turning]—by means of these ten inexhaustible wisdoms, they deliver inexhaustible sentient beings;
therefore, they are able to manifest various transformation bodies to transform ordinary people and those of the two vehicles, and to manifest the light of retributive fruition.
Adorning their bodies, they transform all bodhisattvas so that they all attain the sublime bliss of the noble wisdom of self-realization—namely, the realization of discernment.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in the four great elements and derived matter; how does a bodhisattva become skilled [in this]?
Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who realizes this awakening regarding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) perceives that those primary elements are unarisen.

Having observed that those primary elements are unarisen, he investigates the limits of names, marks, and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), as well as the limits of what is manifested by one’s own mind.
He realizes that external natures have no intrinsic reality; this is called the limit of the conceptual construction manifested by the mind.

This refers to the contemplation of the three realms wherein one observes that the nature of the four great elements and derived matter is free from the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). It is pure, free from "I" and "mine," and abides as the true characteristic (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and in distinct segments. Through the self-characteristic of non-arising, Great Wisdom (*mahāmati*) is perfected. Regarding those four great elements, how do they give rise to derived matter? It is said: the element of internal and external water arises from the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of moisture; the element of fire arises from the conceptualization of capacity; the element of wind arises from the conceptualization of motion; and the element of earth arises from the conceptualization of solidity. Thus, through these four types of conceptualization regarding the great elements, the various categories of derived matter are produced. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the four great elements are neither born nor destroyed, for their nature is eternally quiescent. They are like the horns of a hare or a horse—unborn and unceasing. Because they are not subject to birth or destruction, they are called "great elements. Mahāmati, it is because they transcend the four propositions that they are called "great elements. They are like the horns of a tortoise or a snake, which are non-existent and cannot be grasped by the mind or mental factors. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should cultivate the practice of non-attachment toward all dharmas. Do not grasp at the characteristics of the four great elements, nor at the characteristics of the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, or the twelve sense bases. Why is this? Because all such characteristics are merely names and conventions established by the Tathāgatas for the sake of teaching sentient beings. They are not real entities. If one clings to the characteristics of the four great elements, one will fall into the views of eternalism or nihilism, and will never be able to transcend the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should abandon the views of existence and non-existence, and should not grasp at the characteristics of the four great elements. You should train yourself in the realization of the non-self of both persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*). This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means in the contemplation of the four great elements. If a Bodhisattva can thus contemplate the four great elements, he will quickly attain the stage of a Buddha and will not fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means in the contemplation of the four great elements. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the four great elements are neither born nor destroyed, for they are devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing. They are like the horns of a tortoise or a snake—non-existent and beyond the reach of thought. The primary elements (mahābhūta) that give rise to the internal and external fire element are the conceptualization of flickering; the primary elements that give rise to the internal and external wind element are the conceptualization of the cutting off of form;
and the primary elements that give rise to the internal and external earth element are the attachment to both form and space as false truths.

Mahāmati, when the five aggregates are gathered and the four great elements produce derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), consciousness arises because one takes pleasure in various traces and objective realms. The rest is as before.

The continuities of the realms, the great elements such as the earth, and derived matter have the four great elements as their conditions, yet they do not have those [great elements] as their conditions.
Why is this? It is because of the absence of nature (*svabhāva*), form, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), place, action, and means; the great elements do not arise without these.
Mahāmati, it is through the conjunction of nature, form, characteristics, place, action, and means that they arise, and not from that which lacks form. Therefore, there are four.
The externalists' false imaginings regarding the characteristics of the great derived forms are not the self.
This clarifies that the four great elements are not created by primary elements, as they arise from four kinds of false imaginings;
thus, one should skillfully contemplate the great elements and their derived forms. One who skillfully contemplates derived forms should not observe them within the four great elements.

One should observe from the standpoint of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since that ultimate truth is fundamentally devoid of even a single thing, one knows that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are inherently unarisen.
If the four great elements are fundamentally unarisen, from what could those four great elements possibly exist?
Having performed such observation, one realizes that the names and characteristics of the four great elements originally arise from—
The darkening obscuration of false conceptualization transforms the realm of ultimate truth into the appearances of the four great elements.
Furthermore, upon these various appearances, one establishes the names of the four great elements: "this is earth," "this is water," "this is fire," and "this is wind.
Within this state that is originally without boundaries, one falsely gives rise to the notion of boundaries; yet one does not realize that these boundaries originally derive from oneself.
What is manifested by the mind does not come from outside; once one knows that it is manifested by one's own mind, one knows that external natures have no inherent nature.
This is called the limit of the false discrimination manifested by the mind, not the limit of the actual existence of external natures. What is this so-called "limit"?
It is precisely the various names and characteristics of the triple world. Thus one observes the fundamental nature of the four great elements and derived matter.
When no self-nature can be apprehended, one is detached from self-nature; when the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are fundamentally unapprehendable, the four propositions are purified.
When one does not perceive the five aggregates, body, or mind within, one is detached from "I"; when one does not perceive mountains, rivers, or the great earth without, one is detached from "mine.
Since there is nothing but the single true mark of *tathatā* (suchness) and not a single dharma that confronts the mind, one knows that which was previously [clung to].
The internal four great elements (*mahābhūta*) grasped as such, and the external four great elements, are by nature originally unarisen;
they have from the beginning resided within the self-characteristic of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and are established therein.

If this is so, how could those four great elements possibly create the form of the four great elements? It is not known that there are inherent four great elements capable of producing the four [elements].

Furthermore, regarding what are called the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): when one’s own mind of attachment encounters objects of the six sense-fields that are agreeable to its desires, it takes exquisite delight in them, clings to them with longing, and refuses to let go;
the entire body becomes lustrous and moist—this very deluded thought perfumes and forms seeds that give rise to the internal and external water element.
When one’s own mind of anger encounters objects of the six sense-fields that are disagreeable to its desires...

A surging sense of hatred arises, with eyes wide open in rage as if capable of tearing them apart; this very deluded thought perfumes and forms seeds that give rise to the internal and external fire elements.
One's own ignorant mind, regarding the objects of the six sense-fields, suddenly arises and suddenly ceases, rushing about in flight, drifting and moving without stability;
this very deluded thought perfumes and forms seeds that give rise to the internal [fire element].
The external wind element arises when one’s own grasping mind firmly clings to the objects of the six sense-fields, demarcating boundaries and severing them from one another;
this very deluded conceptualization perfumes and forms seeds that give rise to the internal and external earth elements.
Thus, the seeds of the four great elements are rooted in deluded conceptualization; therefore, it is said that the limits of what appears to one's own mind are not external natures.
Those of such a nature, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), do not skillfully examine the truth of non-arising; they do not know that external natures are without intrinsic nature.

They falsely speculate that *avyakta* (the Unmanifest) in conjunction with the three *guṇas* is the productive cause: from the Unmanifest arises *buddhi* (Intellect); from *buddhi* arises *ahaṃkāra* (I-consciousness);

from *ahaṃkāra* arises the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); from the five sense-objects arise the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*); and from the five great elements arise the ten [faculties].

The "one root and five great elements" refers to the four great elements together with space; the "eleven roots" refers to the five sensory faculties, the five faculties of action, and the mind-faculty (manas).
How do the five sense objects give rise to the five great elements, and how do the five great elements give rise to the five faculties?

It is said that the sense object of sound gives rise to the great element of space, and from the great element of space, the ear faculty arises. Therefore, the ear in turn hears sound. [Likewise for] the sense object of touch.
From the element of wind (*vāyu-dhātu*) and the great wind element, the body faculty (*kāya-indriya*) is produced; therefore, the body in turn perceives the objects of touch and form.
From the element of fire (*tejo-dhātu*) and the great fire element, the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is produced; therefore, the eye faculty in turn illuminates the objects of form and taste.

From the element of water (*ap-dhātu*) and the great water element, the tongue faculty (*jihvā-indriya*) is produced; therefore, the tongue in turn knows the object of taste. From the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and the great earth element, the nose faculty (*ghrāṇa-indriya*) is produced.
Therefore, after the nose returns to smelling odors, there arise next the five organs of action: first, the organ of speech; second, the two hands; third, the feet;
fourth, the organ of excretion; and fifth, the organ of defecation. Next arises the organ of mental equanimity, which takes as its essence the discernment of the components of the five sense objects;
thus it is able to universally perceive all objects. This is precisely the calculation of those non-Buddhists who do not comprehend the True Truth of non-arising.

Adhering to false truths, they falsely claim that form (*rūpa*) and space (i.e., the five great elements) and the aggregation of the five aggregates (i.e., the eleven faculties) are all produced from the derivative matter of the four great elements (i.e., the five subtle particles).

Therefore, he rebukes them, saying: "Even if the five great elements could produce the five [sensory] faculties and the five faculties of action, it might still be acceptable for a material seed to produce material phenomena; however, as for that mind..."
How could the seeds of form be produced by the equalizing faculties? Furthermore, that mind’s equalizing faculty is not a separate entity;

it is the eighth ālayavijñāna. From this arise the discerning consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) which, due to craving for the objective realms that are images of the five sense-objects, give rise to delusions and create karma, thereby inducing the fundamental consciousness to revolve through the various realms of existence. Yet...
The "Cutter" (the Tathāgata) is he who can give rise to the five great elements and the various realms of existence; how could the five great elements themselves possibly give rise to them?

Therefore, one should know that the four great elements such as earth, as well as the derived forms (i.e., the five subtle atoms), possess four kinds of false conceptualization which serve as conditions for their arising;
it is not that those five subtle atoms serve as conditions for those four great elements to arise.

Why is this so? It is because when one investigates the nature, characteristics, locations, and the functional applications of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), each is found to lack inherent nature and is utterly unobtainable; how then could they give rise to the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Even if one were to claim that the five sense objects possess nature, characteristics, locations, and functional applications through their combination—
That which is capable of producing can only produce the material aggregate (rūpa-skandha) that possesses form; it is absolutely incapable of producing the four aggregates that lack form.
Therefore, it is said that the five aggregates are a collection [of elements] produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta).

Such a "producer" is a conceptual construction and attachment based on false establishment, belonging to the deluded imaginings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika); it is not what I call the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
This refers to the non-arising of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates (*skandha*). What are the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates? They are the five aggregates. What are the five?

They are form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Among these, the four aggregates that are not form are sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Mahāmati, as for form (*rūpa*), the four great elements and the derivative matter each have distinct characteristics.

Mahāmati, it is not that non-form (*arūpa*) possesses a numerical count like space. For example, just as space transcends numerical characteristics and is detached from number, yet through false conceptualization one speaks of "one space," so too, Mahāmati, the aggregates (*skandha*) transcend numerical characteristics and are detached from number;
they are free from existence and non-existence, and detached from the numbers of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are what are spoken of by the discourse of foolish commoners; they do not belong to the noble ones (*ārya*).

Mahāmati, for the noble ones, the various forms and images are like illusions, free from the conceptualization of difference or non-difference; they are also like dreams, reflections, or the body of a person, being free from difference or non-difference.

Therefore, Mahāmati, the fact that noble wisdom proceeds toward the appearance of the same as the false discrimination of the aggregates (*skandha*)—this is called the characteristic of the self-nature of the aggregates. You should eliminate it.

Having taught the Dharma of tranquility through the cessation of all cessations, Mahāmati spoke of the purification of the view of selflessness in phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) which severs all heterodox views regarding the Buddha-fields.
When he taught this Dharma of tranquility, [beings] entered the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Having entered the Immovable Stage, they attained mastery over immeasurable samādhis, the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*), and the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), thereby penetrating the ultimate power and clarity of their own nature.
Just as the great earth sustains and nurtures all sentient beings,
so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally rescue and benefit all sentient beings.
The preceding section explained in detail that the four subtle elements cannot produce the four great elements;

the following section explains in detail that the four subtle elements cannot produce the five aggregates (*skandhas*), and thus describes the essential characteristics of the nature of these aggregates. What are called the five aggregates?

Those possessing form and substance—earth, water, fire, and wind—are termed the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, which lack form and substance, are termed the non-form [aggregates].

Furthermore, among the five aggregates (*skandha*), the single aggregate of form (*rūpa*) consists of both primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*bhautika*), each having distinct characteristics.
Thus, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility are the derived matters, while earth, water, fire, and wind are the primary elements.

Yet, how could the four non-material aggregates (*arūpaskandha*)—which likewise possess these four numerical categories—not also be produced by visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility? For these four aggregates are, in their essence, like empty space.
How could that which is immeasurable be suitably divided into four? Manifesting forms according to the capacity of beings, how could it be harmonized to become one?
Since you know that space is neither one nor different, you know that the four aggregates are neither one nor four.
Since you know that the four aggregates originally possess no number of four, you know that the aggregate of form likewise possesses no distinct characteristics; therefore, it is said: "Thus."

Since the aggregates (*skandhas*) transcend numerical quantity, and having transcended numerical quantity they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning, how could they be sought through the four propositions of existence and non-existence?
Thus, the calculation that the aggregates are substantially existent is merely the deluded conceptualization and verbal expression of fools;
how could it be the teaching of the sages and worthies? If a sage observes with wisdom the seeds present before them...
All varieties of forms and characteristics are like illusory phenomena; one should not establish views of existence or non-existence, identity or difference, and so forth.
They are just like the body of a person manifested in a dream, or like the reflection of a person’s form in a mirror—how could they be considered either different or not different?
It is just as in space, which has no measure or location, yet appears to have measure and location. Thus it is.
Thus, how could the realm manifested by noble wisdom exist apart from the delusive thoughts of the five aggregates?
In reality, it is identical to the very locus where the five aggregates and delusive thoughts manifest; it is merely that what the noble and the ordinary perceive differs.

Therefore, one knows that the self-nature of the five aggregates is fundamentally unborn; how could they be produced by the four subtle elements (*catur-aṇu*)? How then could one say that each [element] exists separately?
Because they are of the nature of self-existence, it is said: "You should eliminate the self-nature of the aggregates (*skandha*);
once they are eliminated, you shall then preach the Dharma of quiescence (*śānti*) to sever the views of birth held by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Furthermore, when you personally attain the pure view of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), you will enter the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). Having entered the Immovable Stage, you will immediately attain immeasurable samādhis and realization."
The Dharma-nature body of the mind-born (manomaya-kāya) follows wherever the mind turns, never failing to accord with its intent;

furthermore, one attains the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) and manifests transformations according to the various types of beings, even entering the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) and penetrating the ultimate goal of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

Regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the three knowledges (*trividyā*), there is nothing—whether mind or phenomena—in which one does not attain mastery, extensively benefiting all sentient beings.
Just as the great earth sustains all things and nurtures all beings without exception, so too is the Bodhisattva’s universal salvation;
that is to say, for those who attain awakening and liberation, it is just like this.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvāṇa taught by the various non-Buddhists. What are these four? They are: (1) the nirvāṇa of the self-nature of things being neither existence nor non-existence;
(2) the nirvāṇa of the existence and non-existence of various characteristics; (3) the nirvāṇa of the realization that the self-characteristics of self-nature are neither existence nor non-existence;
and (4) the nirvāṇa of severing the continuity and flow of the aggregates' own and common characteristics. These are called the four kinds of nirvāṇa of the various non-Buddhists.
Nirvāṇa is not what I teach, Mahāmati; what I teach is that the cessation of the discriminating consciousness is called nirvāṇa.
Having already caused them to realize the cause of differentiation, I further cause them to realize the fruit of differentiation. This is the nature of things itself.

Regarding "nirvāṇa as the non-existence of intrinsic nature": this refers to the view of the Sāṃkhya teachers, who maintain that when the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) perceives that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and the twenty-three principles produced by the three *guṇas* are subject to transformation and impermanence, it develops revulsion toward them and practices the path.

When the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) withdraws its manifestations and ceases to appear, and all phenomena no longer arise, the self attains liberation; this state of various characteristics is called nirvāṇa.

Regarding "nirvāṇa as existence and non-existence": this refers to the Vaiśeṣika school’s reckoning that the three categories—substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*)—and all their various characteristics arise through the conjunction with the universal property of "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*). If there were no conjunction with this Great Existence, all phenomena would be non-existent.
This Great Existence is called nirvāṇa. Regarding "nirvāṇa as the awakening to the self-characteristic and self-nature of non-existence": this refers to...
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) establish that among the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), the state after death being devoid of characteristics is called nirvāṇa;

they claim that when the continuity and flow of the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates are severed, that is nirvāṇa. This is precisely what is conceived as nirvāṇa by those in the four formless realms (ārūpyadhātu), specifically the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
However, these four types of nirvāṇa are all merely the suppression of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), preventing it from arising; they falsely claim this to be [true liberation].
Nirvāṇa is the proclamation of the nature of exhaustion within the inexhaustible; that which is conceptualized through false discrimination as nirvāṇa is not the nirvāṇa I teach.
What I teach is called nirvāṇa when the discriminating consciousness is forever extinguished and does not arise again.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, do you not establish the eight consciousnesses? The Buddha replied, “I do, Mahāmati.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “If they are established, why is it that one is liberated from the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) and not from the seven consciousnesses?

The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Because of those causes and those objects of perception (*ālambana*), the seven consciousnesses do not arise. As for the *manovijñāna*, it arises from attachment to the segmented divisions of its objective realm and from the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of birth.”

The wind-energy nurtures the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which, together with the mental faculty (*manas*), arises through the conditions of conceptualization that clings to "I" and "mine," producing the indestructible marks of the body.
Because the store-consciousness takes as its object the realm manifested by one's own mind and clings to it, the collection of minds arises, mutually dependent upon one another;
it is like the waves of the ocean. When the wind of the realm manifested by one's own mind blows upon them, they arise and cease in the same manner. Therefore...
When the mental consciousness ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease.
Mahāmati, having heard that the cessation of the conceptualizing consciousness is called *nirvāṇa*, he gave rise to a doubt, thinking:

"The World-Honored One has already stated that when the self-nature, habitual tendencies, and the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—along with the mind (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the views and habits—are transformed, it is called [nirvāṇa]."
If one asks, "Since you establish eight kinds of consciousness, does it not contradict [your claim] that what is called 'nirvāṇa' is simply the cessation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?

The answer is: "We do indeed establish them. Furthermore, if one asks, "Since you have established eight kinds of consciousness, why do you speak only of being free from the mental consciousness and not of being free from the other seven?
The answer is: "It is because that mental consciousness is capable of planting seeds for the future."

Because the [seventh consciousness] takes present objects as its conditions, the other seven do not transcend this; they arise from the arising of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and, being unable to arise by themselves, they cease through the cessation of that mental consciousness without depending on further cessation. How is it known that those seeds of the mental consciousness serve as the causes and conditions for future [consciousnesses] while taking present objects?
It is because the active manifestation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-pravṛtti*) grasps and conditions the five present sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
When one discriminates and grasps at the characteristics of segmented objects, seeds accordingly flow into the field of the eight consciousnesses and nourish the *ālayavijñāna*.

Consequently, the *manas* arises simultaneously with it, engaging in moment-to-moment deliberation and clinging to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as "self" and its image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) as "mine. Thus, the *manas* arises from the *ālayavijñāna*.
The growth [of the ālayavijñāna] truly relies upon the manovijñāna as its causal condition;
therefore, since the manas has no distinct essence or characteristic apart from the manovijñāna, it refers only to the manovijñāna and does not mention the manas. The Tang translation states:

"When the manovijñāna discriminates objects and gives rise to attachment, it produces various habitual tendencies (vāsanās) that nourish the ālayavijñāna; from this, the 'self' associated with the manas [arises]."
The clinging to "mine" and the mental deliberation that follows it have no separate essence or characteristics;
yet, why is it said that they do not exist apart from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) or apart from the first five consciousnesses?

It is because the storehouse consciousness contains the seeds, and it is through the manifest activity of that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—which, by grasping at the objects of the five sensory realms manifested by one's own mind—that attachment arises and the preceding [consciousnesses] are induced.
When the five mental aggregates simultaneously apprehend objects together with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), these serve as the cause for the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);

likewise, the six consciousnesses serve as the conditions for the first five consciousnesses. Therefore, one speaks only of the "six consciousnesses" and not of the storehouse consciousness or the first five consciousnesses.
Thus, it is known that the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, existing only in dependence upon the six consciousnesses.
Due to causes and conditions, within the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*, various waves of consciousness are successively produced by mutual causation and induction.

Among these eight consciousnesses, the seventh consciousness (*manas*) is nourished by the six consciousnesses; the seventh consciousness gives rise to the view [of self] because of the six consciousnesses;

the five consciousnesses grasp objects because of the six consciousnesses; and the sixth consciousness clings to and discriminates objects because of the five consciousnesses. If one investigates the reason for this:
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is inherently clear and still; it is only because of the six consciousnesses grasping at various objects that the various waves of consciousness arise.
Thus, when the six consciousnesses arise, all the consciousnesses arise; when the six consciousnesses cease, all the consciousnesses cease.
It is like the great ocean, which gives rise to waves only when stirred by the wind; if the mental consciousness does not arise, the winds of objects will not stir it.

When the drum [of the mind] is struck, the ocean of the mind naturally becomes tranquil and the waves subside together; thus, when the *manovijñāna* (consciousness) ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease.

According to Dharmapāla, the seventh [consciousness] functions only within the internal sphere (*antarmukha*), while the first five function only in the external sphere (*bahirmukha*), and the sixth functions in both spheres.
Because it functions within the internal sphere, it is able to share in the portion of objective apprehension (*ālambana*) with the first five consciousnesses.
When the seeds of perfuming arise from the objects of the six consciousnesses, they are stored within the *ālayavijñāna*.

Because the seventh consciousness (*manas*) firmly grasps and maintains them so that they are not lost, the cause of the *ālayavijñāna* arises from the six consciousnesses as they grasp external objects;
since it has no separate essence of its own, it is said that the indestructible characteristic of the body is produced through causes and conditions based on the external.

Because the gates revolve, the seeds of the *ālayavijñāna* give rise to the sixth [consciousness] in its active manifestation (*pravṛtti*), which grasps the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and draws forth the first five consciousnesses.
Thus, through the active manifestation of the sixth consciousness, there exist the seeds of the eight consciousnesses;

and because the seeds of the eight consciousnesses exist, there is the active manifestation of the sixth consciousness. This is what was previously called the "manifesting consciousness" (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*).
This is the meaning of the mutual causality among the various consciousnesses.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The nature of my nirvāṇa is not something produced by action, nor is it characterized by marks or conceptualization;
it is the cessation of the *vijñapti*-consciousness. That [nirvāṇa] is caused by that [cessation], and the mind (*manas*) takes that as its object of attachment."
Regarding the equality of the body and its causes: the mind is the support for consciousness, just as when the great flow of water ceases, waves do not arise;
likewise, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is extinguished, the various forms of consciousness do not arise.
This means that the nirvāṇa conceived by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) is entirely characterized by activity and marks;
it is not the nirvāṇa that is without activity or marks, and therefore it is said, "It is not what I have taught. What I have taught is as follows:

when the *vijñapti-mātra* consciousness (*er-yan-shi*) ceases and no longer gives rise to the grasping of dharmas (*dharma-grāha*), this is called nirvāṇa. This is because that *vijñapti-mātra* consciousness currently manifests as active攀缘 (*pān-yuan*, objective clinging).
The objects of the five sense-fields draw in and seize their shadows, which flow into the *ālayavijñāna*;

because the *ālayavijñāna* receives them as seeds, the various bodies of consciousness arise. Furthermore, that which serves as the cause for the various consciousnesses and gives rise to their active manifestations (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is the *ālayavijñāna*, because it collects all seeds within itself and brings forth all active manifestations; therefore, it is the basis for all consciousnesses.
That upon which [the seeds] rely is that all manifestations in the present life arise from causes and conditions;
thus, the six consciousnesses, by grasping at the six sense objects, give rise to active manifestations that flow into the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to become seeds.

Furthermore, from these seeds in the storehouse consciousness, the preceding seven consciousnesses arise as active manifestations. Therefore, one knows that only after the active manifestations of the six consciousnesses exist can the [seventh] subsequently arise.
The seeds of the eighth consciousness are the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*; the six consciousnesses are like the great current, and the remaining consciousnesses are like the waves.
Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can encompass the waves of all the other consciousnesses, it is called the "great current. Thus, when the great current is exhausted, the waves cease;
when the mental consciousness is exhausted, the various consciousnesses do not arise. If that is so, when the mental consciousness is transformed...
Question: "Are all consciousnesses not to be transformed? Answer: This, too, is a teaching given according to the capacity of the listeners.

Here, because it is addressed to those who hold the views of non-Buddhists regarding nirvana, it is said that the cessation of deluded consciousness is called nirvana; this is because they have not yet extinguished their deluded consciousness.
However, if it were addressed to those of the Two Vehicles, it would say that the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) constitutes nirvana. Thus it is.

Since he has already extinguished the consciousness of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), yet the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is described as a "great stream," one knows that a subtle flow still persists;
how, then, could it not continue to evolve?

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the general characteristics of the differentiation of the self-nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). If the self-nature of conceptual construction...

Having thoroughly distinguished the common characteristics [of all things], you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will be well-discriminating, free from false imagination, and reach the stage of noble self-realization.
You will clearly perceive that the external paths of non-Buddhists are merely the grasping of what is grasped by false imagination;

thus, you will sever the various marks of dependent origination and the activity of the imagined nature of false imagination, no longer engaging in such conceptualization. Mahāmati, what is the thorough penetration of the discrimination of the imagined nature?

The characteristics of conceptualization (vikalpa) are said to be: conceptualization of verbal expression, conceptualization of the objects described by words, conceptualization of marks, conceptualization of benefit, conceptualization of self-nature, conceptualization of cause, conceptualization of views, conceptualization of accomplishment, conceptualization of arising, conceptualization of non-arising, conceptualization of continuity, and conceptualization of bondage and non-bondage.
These are called the general characteristics of the differentiation of the self-nature of conceptualization.
This is a detailed analysis of the consciousness of deluded thought (*vikalpa-vijñāna*).

Since that which is encompassed by the consciousness of deluded thought is extremely vast, although it is said that the six consciousnesses plant seeds for future causes and the six consciousnesses take present objects as their conditions, it does not stop at this alone.

Setting aside the attachment to worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) as being deluded thought, even if there is the slightest attachment to supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*), it is likewise so.

If one does not recognize the characteristics of this delusive conceptualization as it manifests, there is a danger of mistaking a thief for one's own son; therefore, I shall further explain it in detail.
If a Bodhisattva thoroughly understands this meaning, they will be able to transcend all delusive conceptualizations and reach the state of self-realization (*pratyātma-gati*).

They will clearly perceive the tendencies of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) toward distancing themselves from the discrimination between the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*), and [they will understand] the various aspects of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Among these characteristics, one does not further grasp at the falsely imagined characteristics; nevertheless, the distinctions among false imaginings total twelve kinds, which in general do not go beyond what was previously mentioned:
attachment to the nature of verbal expression and attachment to the nature of things.
Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of verbal expression? It refers to the attachment to various wonderful sounds and the melodies of songs;
this is called the discrimination of verbal expression. Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of the object expressed?

It refers to the fact that there is an object expressed which has its own intrinsic nature known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*); based upon that, the discrimination of verbal expression arises. This is called the object expressed.
Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of signs (*nimitta-vikalpa*)? It refers to the attachment to the very things spoken of, just as a deer is attached to the notion of water in a mirage;
that is, the attachment to all natures through their characteristics of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion. This is called the discrimination of signs.

Discursive conceptualization regarding verbal expression refers to the arising of attachment to the perception of beauty and pleasure upon hearing various subtle and wondrous sounds of worldly instruments such as the *vīṇā*,
*paṇava*, *veṇu*, and *vaṃśa*, as well as the sounds of songs, amorous lyrics, and flowery, winding, and elegant speech.
Discursive conceptualization regarding the objects expressed refers to hearing the explained nature of the supramundane ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If awakening, nirvana, suchness, the Buddha-nature, and so forth are all objects known by the noble wisdom of self-realization,
and one becomes attached to them as having a real intrinsic nature, thereby giving rise to various verbal expressions— namely, the "establishment of a nature where no nature exists"—
this is called the delusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*). As for the delusion of phenomena (*nimitta-vikalpa*), it refers to hearing the various matters of worldly conventional truth.

What is called solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—the earth, water, fire, and wind elements—possessing the real intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of both the primary and derived [elements], arises from the conceptual attachment to the "thirst of a deer" (a mirage). This refers to the establishment of characteristics where no characteristics exist;

these three are all the deluded imaginings of attachment to the intrinsic nature of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-svabhāva*). The following eight types are all attachments to the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*vastu-svabhāva*).

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Mahāmati, what is the conceptual construction of benefit? It refers to delighting in various kinds of gold, silver, and precious treasures; this is called the conceptual construction of benefit.
Mahāmati, what is the conceptual construction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*)? It refers to the false view that holds that intrinsic nature is thus, not otherwise, and is unchanging.
Mahāmati, this is called the conceptualization of self-nature. Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of cause?

It refers to the arising of signs based on the discrimination of existence and non-existence regarding causes and conditions; this is called the conceptualization of cause. Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of view?

It refers to the conceptualization, attachment, and false imagination of evil views held by outsiders—such as [the notions of] existence and non-existence, unity and difference, both and neither; this is called the conceptualization of view.

Mahāmati, how is the conceptualization of "accomplishment" (pariniṣpanna-vikalpa) formed? It refers to the conceptualization of "I" and "mine" which establishes a definitive doctrine; this is called the conceptualization of accomplishment.
The conceptualization of "advantage" (lābha-vikalpa) refers to the arising of craving due to being deluded by the eyes regarding worldly treasures and the mind being infatuated by gain and desire.
Pleasure arises from not knowing how to employ the treasures of one's household to benefit others, instead coveting external objects for one's own profit.
The delusion of fame and profit and the delusion of self-nature refer to the firm and persistent grasping that all phenomena possess a real intrinsic nature;

it is the demarcating of boundaries and distinctions between "this phenomenon" and "that phenomenon," such as grasping at the eye as having the nature of seeing, or the ear as having the nature of hearing.
"Because hearing has the nature of being able to hear, and the nose has the nature of being able to smell, and so forth, the former masters said: 'A single face is as large as a plate;
the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue divide up their respective domains, yet they do not know what is inside the skull. Tell me, you who are outside—how can you act so strangely?
Because you do not know that all-encompassing penetration is the nature of all things, this nature is called the cause of deluded conceptualization.'"
Conceptualization (*vikalpa*) refers to the false discrimination that because existence arises with existence as its cause and non-existence arises with non-existence as its condition,
all phenomena in the world are produced from these two types of causes, existence and non-existence; thus,

one fails to understand that all phenomena arise through the successive causality of the eight consciousnesses, and falsely establishes other causes— this is called the view of false conceptualization regarding causes.

"Conceptualization" (saṃjñā) refers to the adherence to the four positions of existence and non-existence, each regarding one's own view as correct and the views of others as incorrect, resulting in opposition and contradiction;
this is what is called the "proliferation of views" (dṛṣṭi-prapañca).
"Forming conceptualization" means reckoning the first aggregate (skandha) as the self and the other four aggregates as "mine," thereby establishing one's own tenet.
To establish the definitive doctrine, the verse states: "One self as self, and four selves as mine; each of these four possesses three aspects, totaling twelve.
Self and what belongs to the self thus combine to fifteen. Discussing the five aggregates in mutual relation results in sixty-five.
Not knowing that the source of the Way is originally without a self, one falsely calculates it to be a self; thus the Great Way is obscured by the small, and deluded conceptions are formed."
Mahāmati, what is the delusion of arising? It refers to the attachment to the arising of the nature of existence and non-existence;

this is called the delusion of arising. Mahāmati, what is the delusion of non-arising? It refers to the fact that all natures are fundamentally unarisen and lack seeds or causal conditions for arising, being a body without cause;
this is called the delusion of non-arising. Mahāmati, what is the delusion of continuity? It refers to those two together... [text ends]... being both.
The continuity that is like a golden thread is called the妄想 (vikalpa) of continuity. Mahāmati, what is the妄想 of bondage and non-bondage?
It refers to the attachment to the causes and conditions of bondage and non-bondage, such as the skillful means of a person who either binds or releases;
this is called the妄想 of bondage and non-bondage.
The conception of arising refers to the calculation that all phenomena arise from the two conditions of existence and non-existence, either instantaneously or gradually.

"Instantaneous arising" means that the effect exists within the cause; "gradual arising" means that the effect does not exist within the cause. Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* refutes this, stating:

"Prior to the conditions, the effect is neither existent nor nonexistent. If it were previously nonexistent, for what would the conditions act? If it were previously existent, what use would the conditions have?"
Not understanding that there is no intrinsic nature in dependent origination, they falsely establish the name "arising" as being truly existent; this is what is called the delusion of arising.
As for the delusion of non-arising, it means that prior to the arising of all phenomena, there is first a substance of non-arising.
This substance has no seeds and does not arise from causes; because it is produced without cause, they reckon that all things arise spontaneously and without cause.

There are those who, because they do not understand that all phenomena arise by relying on causes and depending on conditions, speculate that things are produced without cause and thus fall into views of annihilationism;
