The trembling agitation of the foolish is just like this. If a noble one were possessed of noble knowledge, noble vision, and noble wisdom, [they would not be thus].
The eye is not thus; being free from the marks of delusion and confusion, what is seen is pure, and one attains the three liberations.
Remaining far removed from birth and death, though wandering through the three realms, one does not give rise to fear.

Because that practitioner cultivates the realm of signlessness and does not perceive even a single dharma as being before the mind, they are free from both existence and non-existence; their nature is inherently equal, and from this point on—

Upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one immediately gives birth to the fruit of sainthood (*ārya-phala*). Yet, if fundamentally this is but a single Dharma, why do ordinary beings perceive existence and non-existence?
How is it that the continuity of karmic results persists for them, while for the sages everything is equal, such that they give rise to the fruit of sainthood?
It is because those deluded ones do not understand that all phenomena within and without the triple world are manifestations of one's own mind, originally quiescent from the very beginning.
Yet, by giving rise to false attachments toward the internal body and external objects, one becomes extremely agitated and falls into the two views;

thus, through false vision, one revolves in saṃsāra. If one can destroy those various conceptualizations and cognitive views so that not a single thought arises and all phenomena are simultaneously stilled, then what is seen will have no dual characteristics and all will be equal. Who, then, could be said to exist or not to exist?
"Who is it that is non-arising?

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, when wisdom does not apprehend an object of perception, this is the establishment of the measure of designation (*prajñapti-mātra*).
It is included within the measure of designation; it is neither the grasping of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor the grasping of non-nature."
Because nature is without grasping, cognition does not arise; it is merely a conventional designation.
Why, Blessed One, is cognition unable to apprehend because the particular and universal characteristics of nature are neither different nor non-different?

Or is it because cognition is unable to apprehend due to the obscuration of the various natures and self-natures of the particular and universal characteristics? Or is it because of mountains, crags, stone walls, earth, water, fire, or...?
Is it because of an obstruction by wind that knowledge does not arise? Is it because of being too far away or too near that knowledge does not arise?

Is it because of being old, young, blind, or having impaired faculties that knowledge does not arise? World-Honored One, if knowledge does not arise because one does not perceive whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or not different, then one should not speak of "knowledge," but rather of "non-knowledge," since there is an object that is not apprehended.

Furthermore, if wisdom does not apprehend various phenomena because their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are obscured by their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that too is non-wisdom;
it is not true wisdom, O Blessed One, for such an obstacle exists. Wisdom arises when there is no absence of nature, as it accords with such conditions;

therefore, it is called wisdom. This applies even to mountains, crags, stone walls, earth, water, fire, and wind, whether extremely distant or extremely near, or to the aged, children, the blind, and the ignorant.
If one whose faculties are incomplete does not attain wisdom, this too is not wisdom but rather a lack of wisdom, because there is an object that cannot be attained.
Since the previous position held that suchness exists while the holy wisdom does not exist, this objection is raised by referring back to that prior position.
It is said: As the Buddha has taught, all objects of deluded conceptualization are established and designated by various forms of deluded conceptualization;
they are not the domain attained by those with noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom. However, only when there is an object to be grasped does there arise a mind that grasps.
If there is neither a grasper nor an object to be grasped, then both subject and object are absent. Since they are absent, cognition (*jñāna*) does not follow.
If one asks what arises [from this], it is known that the wisdom realized by the Noble Ones is also a provisional designation; how could it be truly existent?
If wisdom were truly existent yet unable to apprehend the characteristics of objects, why would it be called "wisdom"?

Since it would be entirely of the nature of non-cognition, it would be unable to know whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are existent or non-existent, different or not different, permanent or impermanent.
Is it because the self-characteristics and common characteristics of these five aggregates, as well as the seven kinds of intrinsic natures, are obscured such that wisdom cannot know them?
Or is it because external objects—such as mountains, cliffs, rocky walls, earth, water, wind, and fire—are variously obstructed such that wisdom cannot know them?
Or is it because they are too distant or too near for the power of vision to reach them?
Is it that wisdom cannot know? Or is it that because of old age, youth, blindness, or darkness, one cannot fully know;
or because the faculties are incomplete, there is fundamentally no capacity to know? Are these all cases where wisdom fails to reach the object, such that wisdom cannot know?

If one does not awaken to the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—whether they are permanent or impermanent, different or non-different—and thus fails to attain [realization], is this not so?
One should say that there is wisdom, and one should say that there is non-wisdom. Because [the mind] does not know the characteristics of objects and remains indistinguishable from wood,
tiles, or stones— since this mind does not illuminate objects— if, moreover, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*),
and the sevenfold nature of self-nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) are hidden, concealed, and obstructed such that they are called "unattainable," that too is non-wisdom and not wisdom.
The Venerable One possesses an object of knowledge, and the wisdom that is able to know it arises; it is not devoid of the nature of knowing.
It is named "wisdom" because it encounters the object of knowledge. If this object did not encounter the mind, it would not be wisdom.
If one were to claim that wisdom does not penetrate places obstructed by mountains, crags, stone walls, or barriers, or those that are extremely distant...

When an object is nearby yet beyond the reach of one's vision, or when one is aged, young, blind, or lacks the integrity of the sense faculties such that wisdom is incomplete—in all these cases, it is equally improper to designate this as "wisdom," for although there is an object present, it cannot be apprehended.

What is truly esteemed as wisdom is the ability to discern the objects before one; if one were to consider the failure to apprehend an object before one as wisdom, I truly do not understand such a claim.
This Great Wisdom [Maitreya] raises this objection because he fears that worldly people know only that having discrimination is wisdom, but do not know that non-discrimination is wisdom;
they take the arising of the mind in response to objects to be wisdom, but do not know that the absence of mind in response to objects is wisdom.
Thus, he poses this difficulty.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not as you say. It is that which is non-intelligence which should be intelligence, and not non-intelligence. I do not speak thus by way of concealment regarding the objects of perception.

Wisdom does not attain them; this is the establishment of the measure of designation. One awakens to the fact that the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind is neither existent nor non-existent.
Knowing that external natures and non-natures do not exist, yet not attaining the objects because they are unattainable—this is how wisdom remains free from calamity therein."

Even the wisdom that accords with the three liberations cannot be attained as anything other than false imagination; for since beginningless time, the nature of things—whether existent or non-existent—is a deceptive habit-energy of cognition.

To produce such a cognition is to know that which is not truly known. Consequently, because one does not sever the false imagination regarding the self-nature and characteristics of external objects and locations, one establishes the measure of one's own mind (*svacittamātra*) and remains attached to the grasping and conceptualization of the marks of "self" and "mine."

One awakens to the fact that what appears to one’s own mind is merely a mental construction (*vikalpa*) arising from the radiance of gnosis (*jñānālīka*). Because it is a mental construction, external natures have no real existence;
thus, when one investigates them, they cannot be apprehended, and one should not rely on the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Mahāmati, that which does not differentiate the objects of discourse is not considered wisdom; rather, it is the differentiation of the preceding objects that constitutes wisdom.
Therefore, the World-Honored One rebuked him, saying: "It is not so; what you have said differs from what I have taught.
You take discriminative wisdom to be wisdom and non-discriminative wisdom to be non-wisdom; I hold that non-discriminative wisdom is indeed wisdom and not non-wisdom.
However, as for what I have taught regarding the wisdom that takes objects as its support (*ālambana*), it is not [as you claim]."
Those who attain this establishment of the measure of designations are all speaking with clarity; it is not a half-lit, half-dark, or cryptic discourse.

Why do you not understand it thus? Because I have realized that within the manifestation of one’s own mind, whether phenomena exist or do not exist, they are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
therefore, although I perceive them through noble knowledge, noble vision, and the eye of noble wisdom, [they are ultimately empty].
In all phenomena, not even a single phenomenon can be apprehended, because there is no objective realm to be apprehended.
When wisdom does not give rise to grasping toward the objects of knowledge, it is able to accord with and enter the three gates of liberation;
thus, no wisdom itself can be apprehended. Therefore, I take the non-apprehension of objects to be wisdom, which is not like the deluded conceptualization of ordinary worldlings.

Since beginningless time, those who have habituated themselves to false and deceptive knowledge regarding all phenomena, reckoning them as either existent or non-existent and engaging in such conceptual discriminations, claim to know them;

yet they do not truly know them. The reason they do not know is that they merely give rise to false conceptualizations regarding the intrinsic and common characteristics, and the existence or non-existence of natures, within the objects of external phenomena.
The continuity of separate streams does not cease; within the sphere of what is manifested by one’s own mind, they establish various constructs.
Where there is originally no self, they establish a self; where there is originally no "mine," they establish "mine.
Where there is originally no grasper or grasped, they cling to grasper and grasped, giving rise to the view of permanence. Therefore, this is called "knowing that while not knowing."

Furthermore, there are those who do not realize that what appears is the manifestation of their own mind, and being ignorant of its primordial emptiness and stillness, they give rise internally to the cognition of a knower and externally encounter the objects of knowledge. Due to this discrimination, they fail to comprehend that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent;
they falsely claim things exist and then vanish, and though they investigate them, they find nothing at all. Thus it arises.
The reason the view of annihilationism is so named is that it knows this while being ignorant of that; thus Master Zhao said: "Deluded wisdom has knowing, yet there is that which it does not know;
true wisdom is without knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know."

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "When there are various objects of attachment, if wisdom does not discern them—this is not ignorance, nor is it wisdom;
this is what those of false imagination say. To say they are not different from the nature of phenomena, yet wisdom does not discern obstructions, distance, or proximity—this is called false wisdom.
When the faculties of the old and the young are dull, their wisdom [is likewise obscured]."
To claim that wisdom does not arise yet its objects (ālambana) truly exist is also called false cognition.
When wisdom fails to apprehend any object of perception, this is the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) in which both subject and object are forgotten;
to instead regard this non-conceptual wisdom as "not wisdom" is the work of those who possess the habitual tendencies of deluded thought.

Thus it is said that the ear [is limited] because it knows only that which possesses conceptualization as being wisdom, while failing to know that which is free from conceptualization as being wisdom.
That [ear] cannot discern whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or not different;

it cannot discern what is obstructed by mountains or walls, nor what is extremely distant or extremely near—all such [cognitions] are merely the false wisdom that pursues external objects, and are not [true wisdom].

This is the correct wisdom that transcends objects. Furthermore, the wisdom of the elderly, children, and those who are blind or dim-sighted—those whose sense faculties are incomplete—and the wisdom that knows the objects of knowledge, is also false wisdom and not correct wisdom. If it were correct wisdom, the faculties and objects would not be involved;
how then could stone walls, distance, proximity, or the state of being old, young, blind, or dim-sighted obstruct or separate it?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, ignorant ordinary beings are turned around by beginningless, false, evil, and perverse conceptualizations.

As they are thus turned around, they do not properly understand their own tenets or the universal accessibility of the teaching. Because they are attached to the external natures and characteristics manifested by their own minds, they cling to the provisional teachings and fail to correctly discern the pure, universal characteristics of their own tenets within the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Rebuking Mahāmati for being entangled in the two views of existence and non-existence— both of which arise from failing to understand the two-fold penetration of the fundamental tenets—

he addressed him again, saying: "The aforementioned reckoning of *tathatā* (suchness) as existent and of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) as nonexistent is all due to the deluded ordinary person being driven by the beginningless habit-energy of false knowledge and evil, perverse conceptualization."
The inability to overturn those false conceptualizations arises entirely from a failure to properly understand the two types of penetration (*prativedha*).

Because one does not understand the penetration of the self-nature (*svabhāva-yukti-prativedha*), one fails to realize that external natures have no intrinsic reality and is thus turned by external objects.

Because one does not understand the penetration of the teaching (*deśanā-yukti-prativedha*), one clings to expedient teachings and generates understanding merely according to the literal words; consequently, regarding one's own school, one remains bound by the four [extremes].
Since the hundredfold negations of the phrases pertain to the universal characteristic of purity,
it is appropriate that one who engages in improper conceptual discrimination should regard non-conceptualization as non-wisdom and conceptualization as wisdom.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “It is truly as Your Majesty has taught. I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for my sake, analyze and explain the *sūtra-vehicle* (the teaching) and the *principle-vehicle* (the realization), so that I and other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may become skilled in these two vehicles and not allow ordinary people, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas of future ages to find fault with them.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this.”
"Keep this in mind, and I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of teachings: the teaching of the common discourse (*deśanā-prativedha*) and the teaching of the self-nature of the school (*sva-āgama-prativedha*).

As for the teaching of the common discourse, it refers to preaching various collections of sūtras according to what is thought by the minds of sentient beings; this is called the teaching of the common discourse. As for the teaching of the self-nature of the school..."

"Penetration" refers to the practitioner who is free from the various delusive imaginings manifested by their own mind; who does not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither;
who transcends all mind, thought, and consciousness; who personally realizes the realm of the noble ones;

and who is free from the nature of views established through causes—this is what I call [penetration], which cannot be known by any non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas who have fallen into the two extremes.
“Mahāmati, this is called the characteristic of the penetration of one’s own school and the penetration of verbal expression;
you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should practice and study them. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“I speak of two kinds of penetration: the penetration of the school and verbal expression. Verbal expression is for the instruction of the ignorant; the school is for those who practice.”
This was because he had been reprimanded by the World-Honored One and thus requested the two supernormal powers once more. An ancient worthy said:
"Though scholars are many, not one has attained awakening; the fault lies in seeking the path of another’s tongue.

If you wish to forget words and obliterate traces, strive with diligence in walking through empty space. Therefore, those who seek head and brain along the path of another’s tongue are all unskillful."

The second is one who is skilled in the two penetrations (*dvividha-prativedha*). One who is skilled in these two penetrations remains silent and self-knowing, resolutely refusing to search for the shortcomings of others at the corners of their mouths;
therefore it is said that being skilled in the two penetrations means "not finding their faults. The World-Honored One told him:

"What is called the penetration of teaching (*deśanā-prativedha*) refers to speaking according to the intentions of others regarding the ten wholesome paths of action, the four noble truths, and the twelve links of dependent origination."

Even regarding the various teachings of the six perfections and myriad practices that accord with principle and adapt to capacity, those who are able to use these teachings to illuminate their own minds are said to possess "teaching penetration" (*shetō*).
If one speaks of emptiness while clinging to emptiness, or speaks of existence while clinging to existence, such a person has fallen into the trap of literal words;
how can they be called one who possesses teaching penetration? What is called "the penetration of one's own school" (*jishūtsū*) refers to...

The person of true cultivation leaves behind the various delusive imaginings manifested by their own mind and does not fall into the four positions of existence and non-existence held by externalists and followers of the Small Vehicle; this is the emptying of the parikalpita (imagined) nature.

To transcend all mental activity and enter the realm of noble self-realized wisdom is to transform the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms. This is to be free from views produced by causes and conditions.

Regarding the two aspects of characteristics, one realizes the perfected nature by means of the dependent nature being empty [of the imagined]. If the fruit can be such as this, even the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot know it;
how much less could non-Buddhists or those of the Two Vehicles know it? Furthermore, because it is known only by oneself, there is nothing that is not known;
this is called the "penetration of one's own school" (svayam-āgama). If a single thought-moment just arises, then [the truth extends] across thousands of miles and ten thousand...

How could one say that Li An had attained self-communication? Therefore, we know that for those at the initial stage, he cleared away the thickets of ignorance like a child’s, using provisional verbal teachings to facilitate their understanding.
However, for practitioners of true cultivation, he directed them to sever speech and cease discursive thought, so that they might personally behold their original nature.
Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "One looks up to the great purport of the various scriptures to directly perceive one's own [nature]."

With the mind following the subtle words of the sages, one suddenly opens the precious treasury; casting aside views of supernatural powers and dispelling feelings of perverse attachment, one gains deep faith in the orthodox tradition.

This makes it known that the moon does not reside in the finger pointing at it; by turning the light back upon oneself, one perceives the nature of reality without following the mere text. Only when realization accords with the truth is this the original intent.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One once said:

'Regarding the various treatises and diverse expositions of worldly discourse, you must be careful not to associate with them; for if you do so, they will engender craving and not lead to the grasping of the Dharma.
World-Honored One, why did You speak thus? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Worldly discourse is of many kinds..."
By means of phrases, meanings, causes, conditions, parables, and collections of ornaments, they entice and delude foolish, ordinary people who do not enter into reality or their own self-realization;
unaware that all phenomena are but the false imaginings and inversions of their own minds, they fall into the two extremes.

Thus, these ignorant and deluded ones destroy themselves, continue through the succession of various realms of existence, fail to attain liberation, and are unable to realize that [all things] are manifestations of their own minds.

Because means of valid cognition do not transcend the false conceptualization and attachment to the intrinsic nature of external objects, the various discursive explanations of worldly discourse fail to escape birth,
old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, remaining instead deceptive, delusive, and confused.
Since it is said that "teaching the uninitiated" involves explaining the path, then speech and written characters are certainly unavoidable.
For what reason, then, did the World-Honored One further admonish his disciples within the inner teaching not to associate with worldly treatises?

He stated that those who associate with them will only acquire greed and attachment, and will not obtain the true flavor of the Dharma. The Buddha said: "Worldly discourse collects all manner of things."

With various phrases, diverse meanings, manifold causes and conditions, and numerous metaphors, they produce speech that is flowery and elegant, with sharp and novel wording, speaking in a way that is glib and deceptive. They speak contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the meaning;
they lack genuine personal realization and have no connection to it, and thus they cannot enter. Because they do not enter by themselves...
Although they have attained penetration, they are still unable to comprehend the "penetration of teaching.

Failing to realize that all phenomena are merely expedient words used to guide and lead others, they give rise to deluded thoughts and inverted views, reckoning non-existence as existence and falling into the two extremes.
Due to their ignorance, they destroy the Buddha-dharma and fall into the three miserable realms, failing to attain liberation; if one investigates the root of this...

Because they all fail to realize that all phenomena arise from the manifestations of one's own mind, and because they fail to realize that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent, they grasp at the self-nature of external things as being truly real.

This is due to their habituation to worldly treatises and their failure to enter into their own internal realization. Therefore, although worldly discourse possesses various forms of eloquent explanation, it cannot bring about [liberation].
Those who have emerged from the sorrow and suffering of birth and death can only delude the mental consciousnesses of the foolish and cause them to become confused;
therefore, I say that they do not embrace the True Dharma.
Mahāmati, Śakra Devendra extensively explained various treatises and composed his own work on phonology; among those proponents of worldly theories, there was one...
The disciple took an image of a dragon and went to the palace of Śakra-devendra to establish his essential tenets of debate.
He vowed, "If you do not follow me, I shall sever each of your thousand-spoked wheels as a recompense for your defeat. Having made this vow, he immediately used the teachings of Śakra to subdue him;
Śakra was defeated, and his chariot was destroyed wherever it went. He then returned to the human realm. Thus it was.
Mahāmati, worldly discourse is adorned with causes and analogies;
even animals can, through various phrases and expressions, delude the gods and asuras, causing them to become attached to views of arising and ceasing—how much more so for humans?
Therefore, Mahāmati, one should distance oneself from worldly discourse, for it brings about the causes for the arising of suffering; be careful not to practice it.
Mahāmati, those proponents of worldly treatises speak only of the body, sensation, and their objects. Mahāmati, there are hundreds of thousands of such worldly treatises;
however, in the future—specifically during the final five hundred years—they shall be destroyed because the views based on evil perceptions will flourish during that period of compilation.
Consequently, evil disciples will receive these various phrases of worldly treatises that destroy the true compilation.

"Mahāmati, the teachings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) regarding the causes of flavors and the like, which are explained through metaphors and ornaments, are attachments to their own specific causal conditions and lack any self-validated principle.

Those non-Buddhists have no self-validated doctrine; they extensively expound immeasurable hundreds of thousands of categories of worldly treatises, yet these lack any self-validated principle, and they themselves do not realize that these are merely foolish worldly discourses."
This is the fault of the Lokāyata (Worldly) doctrine. It is said that Śakra, having extensively mastered various treatises, further composed a work on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*).
A disciple of the Lokāyata, appearing in the form of a nāga, went to Śakra’s palace and established the fundamental tenets of the Lokāyata he had studied, making this vow:
"I shall debate with you; if your position fails and falls into error, I shall destroy your thousand [eyes]."
"By means of this wheel with its spokes, I shall manifest my victory over you; since you have been defeated and fallen, I shall cut you limb from limb to atone for your submission.
Having made this vow, he immediately used the treatise on grammar (*śabda-śāstra*) created by Śakra to subdue Śakra.
Śakra was defeated and fell; his chariot was destroyed, and he reverted to his dragon form and returned to the human realm. Thus it was.
The worldly treatises adorn their words with causes and analogies; their arguments are logical and their facts are well-supported.
Even animals can be deluded by such various phrases and meanings, leading them to destroy the Asuras and give rise to the dual views of arising and ceasing—how much more so for humans?
Who among them would not be deceived and confused by them? For this reason, the world...
The treatise states that one should distance oneself from that which brings about the causes for the suffering of future births;

how could one ever cultivate or approach it? That which brings about the causes of suffering is merely the teaching of this body’s illusory objects of sight, hearing, awareness, and cognition, while failing to understand that external natures—whether existent or non-existent—are but manifestations of one's own mind. That world...
The proponents of these doctrines are not of a single kind, but number in the hundreds and thousands.
During the final five hundred years, a time when strife will be firmly entrenched, they will each establish their own tenets and form their own factions, thereby destroying the True Dharma.
Due to the flourishing of their evil realizations, they will each cling to their own causes and maintain their own views to mark out their tenets, [leading] all the evil disciples...
If one receives and upholds that Dharma, transmitting it from one to another as a family treasure, such worldly discourse destroys the [true] compilation.
Although it is adorned with various phrases, flavors, causes, and analogies, all that is spoken concerns the matters of external paths;
it is an attachment to a self, and its claims that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions merely give rise to various theories in total.
Emerging from the body, the realm of sensation reaches the fundamental source of self-nature (*zixing zongtong*). This does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing;
it does not belong to causes and conditions; nor does it belong to the view of a personal body (*shenjian*). How, then, could it be known?

Yet, since those non-Buddhists lack their own fundamental realization, even if they expound immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates, they speak only of the present perceptions, cognitions, and movements of the senses.
Taking form after form as the sovereign and manifesting it as one's own enjoyment, yet failing to investigate the ultimate reality beneath one's own heels—
lacking any self-realization and practicing this throughout one's life without knowing it is erroneous—
this is precisely what the Tathāgata calls "those who are to be pitied."

At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if the various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies used by non-Buddhists in their worldly treatises—which lack any self-attained realization and are merely attachments to their own specific matters—are not [the truth], then why does the World-Honored One also speak of worldly treatises?
You have extensively expounded immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions for the sake of the diverse assemblies of devas, humans, and asuras gathered from all directions."
"Is this not my own established doctrine? Does it not also enter into the wisdom, speech, and teachings of all the non-Buddhists?

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not speak of worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*), nor of coming and going. I speak only of neither-coming-nor-going. Mahāmati, 'coming' refers to gathering, meeting, and arising;
'going' refers to dispersing and destruction. That which is neither-coming-nor-going is that which is neither-arising-nor-ceasing; this is what I teach."

One does not fall among the categories of the delusory imaginings of worldly discourse. Why is this? It is because one does not cling to external existence or non-existence, which are the two extremes of delusory imagining within the sphere of what is manifested by one's own mind.
When one realizes that the characteristics of objects have no inherent nature and are merely manifestations of one's own mind, then the delusory imaginings of one's own mind do not arise.
When delusory imaginings do not arise, one enters the three gates of liberation: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
The gates of liberation are called "liberation.
Mahāmati asked again: "Worldly treatises have no self-attained realization; one must be careful not to study or associate with them.

Yet, World-Honored One, you also extensively expound various phrases and meanings for the assembly of gods, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings who have gathered here; these too do not constitute self-attained realization."
"Does this enter into the category of the wisdom and discourse of the non-Buddhists?

The Buddha said, "For the sake of the assemblies gathered from various regions, although I speak with various phrases and expressions, I do not speak of worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*). What they speak of involves the dharma of coming and going;
what I speak of is the dharma that neither comes nor goes. That which 'comes' arises through the convergence of conditions; that which 'goes' [ceases] through the [dissolution of] conditions."
If dispersed, they cease; yet if there is neither coming nor going, there is neither birth nor cessation.
What I teach is the dharma of non-birth and non-cessation, and therefore it does not fall within the categories of worldly discourse or deluded conceptualization. Why is this?

Because they fail to realize that what appears is but the manifestation of their own minds, and do not understand that external natures have no inherent existence; thus, they engage in deluded discrimination regarding external objects.
Because one is driven by the two views of "existence" and "non-existence," there is coming and going;

yet, I do not cling to the existence or non-existence of external natures, for I realize that existence and non-existence are merely the false imaginings manifested from one's own mind, which cannot be overturned.

Because one realizes that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent and understands that they are manifestations of one's own mind, false imaginings do not arise. Through the non-arising of false imaginings, one is able to enter the three liberations.
The "gate of liberation" is called liberation; because one realizes liberation, there is neither coming nor going.
Mahāmati, I recall that once, while staying in a certain place, a world-theorizing Brahmin came to where I was.
Without first requesting a private audience, he asked me: "Gautama, is everything created? At that time, I replied to him: "Brahmin..."
"O Brāhmaṇa, 'everything is created' is the first worldly doctrine. He asked again, "Is everything uncreated?
I replied, "'Everything is uncreated' is the second worldly doctrine. He asked again, "Is everything eternal?
Is everything impermanent? Is everything born? Is everything unborn? To this, I replied:
Regarding these six types of world-theorists, Mahāmati, he further questioned me, saying: "Are all things identical? Are all things different?

Are all things both identical and different? Are all things neither identical nor different? Do all things manifest through various modes of rebirth? I replied to him: "These are the eleven types of world-theorists.
Mahāmati, he further questioned me, saying: "Are all things indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Or are all things determinate (*vyākṛta*)?"
Is there a self? Is there no self? Does this world exist? Does this world not exist? Does another world exist? Does another world not exist?
Is there liberation? Is there no liberation? Are all things momentary? Are all things non-momentary? Is there space?
Is there analytical cessation? Is there nirvana? Is it created by Gautama? Is it uncreated? Does existence exist?
"Is there an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or is there no intermediate state, Mahāmati? At that time, I replied: "Such statements are all merely worldly treatises;

they are not my teaching. Your are a worldly treatise. I teach only that beginningless false conceptualization and habitual tendencies are the various causes for the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Failing to realize that these are the manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to false conceptualizations and clings to external objects."
"Mahāmati, the arising of cognition through the conjunction of the three—the external object, the sense faculties, and the self—is not as the non-Buddhists conceive it.
I do not teach a cause, nor do I teach no-cause; I teach only the dependent origination established by the nature of the grasped and the grasper, which is a construction of false discrimination.
This is not something that can be realized by you or others who fall into the continuity of the view of a self. Mahāmati, this is nirvāṇa.
The cessation of space does not actually possess three types; it is merely that there are three enumerations.
This passage extensively cites worldly treatises to refute such errors, demonstrating to future generations that they should not study or associate with them.
"Brahmin" (婆羅門) is translated here as "Pure Conduct" (淨行). They claim their ancestors were born from the mouth of Brahmā and are born of eloquence in debate.
Because he was conceited in his own eloquence, he did not wait for the World-Honored One’s leisure but suddenly posed a question.
That which is "created" (*saṃskṛta*) is the conditioned; that which is "not created" (*asaṃskṛta*) is the unconditioned.

Permanence and impermanence, arising and non-arising, identity and difference, both and neither—these are the four positions (*catuṣkoṭi*). All causes that manifest through various forms of rebirth are "differentiated causes."

Furthermore, he asked about the determinate and the indeterminate, the existence of a self and the non-existence of a self, this world and other worlds, liberation and non-liberation, the momentary and the non-momentary,
the three unconditioned phenomena, the created and the uncreated, and whether there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or no intermediate state.

Because they do not realize that [all things] are manifestations of their own minds, do not realize their own spiritual penetration, and have not transcended worldly dharmas, he collectively dismisses them as "worldly."
The treatise states that those who have transcended the three realms do not hold such views; therefore it says: "This is not what I have taught.
I teach only that beginningless, false, delusive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and various kinds of unwholesome manifest activities are the causes of the three realms.
Because they do not know that these are the manifestations of their own minds, and fail to realize that external natures have no intrinsic reality, [these views] arise."

"False imagination clings to external natures as the cause of all things, giving rise to various births and appearing like the doctrines of the non-Buddhists who speak of a self (ātman) and a soul (puruṣa).
They claim there are eleven faculties, all of which arise from the combination of the three qualities (guṇas), such as cognition and so forth.
This is your view, but I do not teach it in this way. I speak only of false imagination, whether there be a cause or no cause."

If one clings to the grasping subject and the grasped object as being the causal condition for the arising of all phenomena, then since all phenomena arise from conditions and are fundamentally rootless—
being entirely like illusions and transformations— how could one see them as existent, and how could one see them as non-existent?
This is not the way of the Brahmins or the followers of other worldly treatises who fall into the acceptance of the view of self and cling to a personal soul (*ātman*).

That which is known by those who continue through the cycle of birth and death—whether they maintain that there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or that there is no intermediate state—is merely worldly discourse (*lokavāda*).
Even those who maintain that the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) exist as substantial entities fall into worldly discourse;
for while the enumeration of the three unconditioned phenomena exists, their unconditioned essence does not even admit of duality, much less plurality.
Therefore, clinging to the three unconditioned phenomena is also worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time the Brahmin of worldly discourse again asked me:
"Is the existence of the three realms of being caused by ignorance, craving, and karma, or is it without cause? I replied to him: "These two [positions] are also merely worldly discourse. He—
He asked again: "Do all natures enter into self-characteristics and common characteristics? I replied: "This too is worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*), O Brahmin;
even the false conceptualization of external objects by the flow of the mind is all worldly discourse.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time the Brahmin of worldly discourse asked me again: "Is there anything that is not worldly discourse? I said: "Yes."
"All the systems of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) explain various phrases, flavors, causes, conditions, and parables as adornments. I replied:
"That which 'is not yours' is not a non-system, nor is it a non-explanation; it is not that various phrases and flavors do not exist, nor that they are not adorned by causes and parables.
The Brahmin asked: "What is it that is not the worldly doctrine (*loka-vāda*), yet is not a non-system, nor a non-[doctrine]?"

When I spoke of "self," I said at that time: "O Brahmin, there is a non-worldly doctrine that you followers of external paths cannot know, because you are attached to false imaginings and deceptions regarding the unreality of external natures.
When such imaginings do not arise, one realizes the presence or absence of what is merely the manifestation of one's own mind;
when imaginings do not arise, one does not receive external objects, and imaginings are forever stilled—this is called [the non-worldly doctrine]."
"This is not the worldly doctrine; this is my teaching, not yours, O Brahmin.

Briefly stated, that consciousness—whether coming or going, dying or being born, pleasure or pain, the ocean of suffering, seeing, touching, or clinging to various marks, the conjunction and continuity of marks, or the attachment to sensation and its causes—O Brahmin, such as these are [not my teaching]."

"Your worldly treatises are not mine; I possess great wisdom. When the Brahmin of the worldly treatises asked me such a question, I answered him thus, whereupon he fell silent and withdrew without further protest.
He reflected upon his own position and thought to himself: "The Śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has strayed outside of the established systems;
he speaks of non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness, asserting that one awakens to what is merely one's own deluded imagination and that what appears is false."

Mahāmati, the non-arising of conceptualization is precisely what you asked me just now: "For what reason do you associate with worldly treatises and various forms of eloquent discourse that embrace desire rather than embracing the Dharma?"
Because the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) had seen that the World-Honored One had refuted each of their views as mere worldly discourse (loka-vāda),
they asked the World-Honored One whether the three realms of existence arise from the causes of ignorance, craving, and karma—

just as he had taught— and further asked about "all" in reference to his teaching on how the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) enter into all phenomena.
"Are all phenomena included within the specific and general characteristics? The World-Honored One replied:
"That which I have taught is now in your mouth, yet it is still worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). Moreover, it is not only that which is expressed in words that constitutes worldly discourse;
even the slightest movement of thought or the false conceptualization of external objects is all worldly discourse. [End of] Brahmin One.
Once pressed down by the World-Honored One, his stratagems were exhausted and he found no words left to speak;
he then made a request regarding the Lokāyata doctrine, saying: "I am the founder of all non-Buddhist schools.
All the scriptures of the various non-Buddhists, adorned with manifold causes and analogies, flow forth from my teaching. How could there be a 'Lokāyata' (worldly discourse) apart from this?"
Therefore, he asked: "Is there perhaps that which is not worldly discourse? The World-Honored One replied: "There is indeed that which is not worldly discourse;
however, it is not yours, it is not your doing, it is not your tenet, and it is not what you have spoken.

Yet, it is not that various phrases and expressions are not spoken therein, nor is it that causes and similes for adornment are not spoken. He asked again: "What is this that is not worldly discourse?"
"Is it that what you argue is not a non-thesis but is your thesis; that what you speak is not a non-exposition but is your exposition?
The Buddha said, "There is a non-worldly discourse which is not known by you, because you give rise to false conceptualizations through your attachment to external natures and all unreal dharmas.
What is called 'non-worldly discourse' refers to the absence of deluded imagination."

Because one realizes that all phenomena appearing before one—whether existent or non-existent—are manifestations of one’s own mind and that no phenomenon exists outside the mind, delusive thoughts do not arise.
Furthermore, by being able to penetrate the fact that external natures lack inherent existence, one does not grasp at external objects;
thus, there is no mind apart from phenomena, and delusive thoughts arise of themselves no more. When both mind and object are forgotten, the foundation is secure.
In truth, I do not engage in the pursuit of speech nor do I employ empty and ornate rhetoric; this is called "non-worldly discourse.
However, this is the Dharma realized by me, which you have not attained. To speak briefly of what you have attained:
that consciousness possesses the characteristic of coming and going, the appearance of birth and death, the retribution of suffering and pleasure, and the state of being submerged.

Yet, they do not transcend the view of existence, the discrimination of the sensation of existence toward external objects, the grasping of objects within, the characteristic of the conjunction of consciousness, the characteristic of the continuity of mind, the feeling of reception, and the cause of attachment;
because all such categories are the spheres of perception for your own bodies, they are collectively termed "worldly discourse. If I...
"Since one seeks within one's own school [of thought] and finds the characteristics of past and future, birth and death, suffering and pleasure, etc., utterly unobtainable, they are not my own.
Upon hearing this teaching, the Brahmin did not take leave but departed;
returning to reflect upon the doctrines he himself mastered, he instead regarded the Buddha’s words as erroneous and thought to himself: "The views held by this śramaṇa are extraordinary."
Beyond my own understanding, you have taught that all phenomena are unborn, signless, and causeless, thereby falling into the view of nihilism;
yet, having stated that all phenomena manifest from one's own deluded thoughts, you further claim that these deluded thoughts do not arise.
This is what I cannot comprehend. Upon careful consideration of its meaning, it appears you merely cling to the realm of bodily sensations and are unable to believe or accept [the truth].
Regarding the principle that dependent origination is non-arising, it is said that "great words do not enter the ears of villagers.
Therefore, I say that those who study the discourses of recent times merely grasp at craving and do not grasp the Dharma; this is precisely what serves as an example.
Thus, the preceding text states: "If, in a future age, a wise person were to use the Dharma that transcends the four propositions as that through which I have attained penetration..."
When one asks about the meaning [of a doctrine] to those who lack wisdom, they will reply, "This is not a correct question.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of the phrases 'grasping at desire' and 'grasping at the Dharma'?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! You are able to contemplate and inquire about such phrases for the sake of future sentient beings."
"Listen attentively, Mahāmati; listen attentively and reflect well upon this, for I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "That which is called 'craving' consists of grasping or rejecting, touching or tasting external objects, becoming bound by attachment to them, and falling into the views of the two extremes.
From this, there arises the aggregate of suffering—birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction."
All afflictions arise from craving; because of this, the study of worldly treatises and association with those who propound such treatises—I and all the Buddhas call this "greed.
This is called "embracing greed and not embracing the Dharma. Mahāmati, what is meant by "embracing the Dharma"?

It is the skillful realization of the manifestation of one's own mind, seeing the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, and [the cessation of] false conceptualization.
Not giving rise [to discursive thought], possessing superior knowledge of the higher and higher stages, being free from mind, thought, and consciousness,
receiving the empowerment of the wisdom of all Buddhas, fully embracing the ten inexhaustible phrases, and attaining sovereign mastery over the non-arising of all phenomena—
this is called the Dharma; that is to say, not falling into any views, any falsehoods, any delusions, or any notion of a single nature.
"O Mahāmati, there are many foolish outsiders who fall into the two extremes of either eternalism or nihilism; they are not wise.
Those who accept the doctrine of no-cause give rise to the view of eternalism, while those who deny external causes and the nature of causal conditions give rise to the view of nihilism.
O Mahāmati, because I do not perceive arising, abiding, or ceasing, I call it 'Dharma. O Mahāmati, this is called craving."
"Desire and the Dharma—you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train yourselves in them.

Although it was stated above in general terms that one who associates with worldly treatises embraces desire and does not embrace the Dharma, it did not specifically point out what constitutes desire and what constitutes the Dharma;
therefore, he asked about them again. The Buddha said: "That which is called 'desire' is as follows:"
That which was previously described— having grasping and rejecting, having contact and relishing, being fettered to external objects, and falling into the views of existence and non-existence—
takes this as its cause to further give rise to the various bitter fruits of birth, old age, sickness, death, suffering, and pleasure;
all of these arise from craving, due to that attachment to words and phrases, and the study and association with worldly treatises and those who follow such worldly treatises.
That which is brought about is what is called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*); failing to eliminate it, one accumulates learning and thereby creates a fault.
I and all the Buddhas perceive this affliction and point out that such people belong entirely to greed; they consume only the food of sensual desire and do not eat the flavor of the Dharma.

What is called "Dharma" means skillfully knowing that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone, that external natures have no inherent reality, and that one has severed conceptual discrimination.
When the false imaginings of the dualistic attachments to self and phenomena no longer arise, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Progressing from stage to stage, one gradually exhausts the innate attachments to self and phenomena, thereby entering the higher and higher stages. Having distanced oneself from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), one attains the four types of wisdom.
All Buddhas then pour the water of wisdom upon one’s crown, and one receives the rank of Tathāgata.
That is to say, one possesses the ten inexhaustible phrases and attains great mastery over all phenomena without depending on further revelation;
this is called the Dharma. Specifically, it does not fall into the views of existence, non-existence, annihilationism, or eternalism;

it does not fall into any seeds of false habitual tendencies; it does not fall into the manifestation of any deluded thoughts; and it does not fall into any notion of self-nature or [the extreme of] unity.
Regarding these two extremes, because many foolish non-Buddhists fall into them, they conceive of permanence and annihilation;

these are not states into which the wise fall. Only the ignorant, associating with proponents of causelessness and accepting their doctrine of no-cause, conceive that the four great elements do not arise from causes, and thus imagine that humans are born from humans and birds are born from birds.
Because there is no alteration or shifting, one gives rise to the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

Alternatively, if one sees that the four great elements and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) perish due to external causes and are never born again, one gives rise to the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṣṭi*).

Since I do not see anything arising, abiding, or ceasing, I do not fall into any views, nor do I fall into any of the two extremes; this is called "consuming the food of the Dharma" and not "consuming the food of sensual desire."

This is called the twofold meaning of the phrases "craving" and "the nutriment of phenomena. You should study this so as to instruct future sentient beings and enable them to clearly know the location of the nutriment of phenomena;
[otherwise] the mother will transform into the nutriment of desire.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "All worldly treatises and the false teachings of the non-Buddhists are based on deluded views regarding cause and effect;
they possess no school of their own. I alone have my own school, which is free from cause and effect.
For the sake of my disciples, I teach the departure from all worldly treatises; the mind-only (cittamātra) is invisible and cannot be perceived."
Investigating the two minds—the grasping subject and the grasped object—one finds they lack intrinsic nature and are free from both extremes of annihilation and permanence.

Even the flow of the mind is merely worldly discourse and conceptual construction; for one who does not engage in such [discourse], this person sees that what comes is but the arising of phenomena within their own mind, and what goes is but the non-appearance of those phenomena.
Clearly understanding that the conceptual constructions of coming and going do not arise again, there is neither permanence nor impermanence regarding what is produced.
The absence of action regarding this world, the next world, and so forth—all these are encompassed by worldly discourse (*lokāyata*).
Whether one embraces desire or embraces the Dharma, it is entirely due to the penetration of the principle of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it is not a matter of penetrating the [worldly] tenets.
If one first attains the penetration of the principle of intrinsic nature, the foundation is firm and stable; even if one speaks of worldly discourse all day long, it is no longer worldly discourse.

If one does not realize the intrinsic nature and one's footing remains unsteady, then even if one speaks all day long of what is not worldly discourse, it still becomes worldly discourse—what is called "the marvelous becoming putrid and the putrid becoming marvelous. Therefore, the verse reiterates this point:
all worldly discourse is the false speech of non-Buddhists, for by means of their false views, they treat the agent as the object.
This is because it is impossible to establish a school based on the *pratyātma-gati* (the realization of one's own nature). Only I have personally seen the original face;
taking the *pratyātma-gati* as primary, I know that all phenomena are manifestations of one’s own mind and that external natures have no inherent reality.
Thus, being unattached to the agent and the acted-upon, and free from the habitual tendencies of false views, I teach the heterodox paths for the sake of my disciples.
Worldly discourse merely embraces desire and does not embrace the Dharma; be careful not to study or associate with it.
It is called "worldly discourse" because those who engage in it do not perceive that all is a manifestation of their own mind, nor do they investigate the non-duality of the mind.

Seeing no duality between subject and object, and clinging to extremes such as annihilationism or eternalism, they speculate on birth and non-birth, permanence and impermanence, and so forth, even regarding the mind itself.
Consciousness flows in a single moment, falsely conceptualizing external objects; all such views ultimately belong to worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*).

Only those who do not flow with deluded thoughts perceive that which is the manifestation of their own mind (*svacitta-dṛśya-mātra*), which is without coming or going and without movement—this is what is called "one's own fundamental doctrine" (*sva-siddhānta*).
However, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who conceptualize coming and going define "coming" as the arising of a fruit and "going" as the cessation of a fruit.
Because they do not know from where they come or to where they go, they give rise to various kinds of false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*).

If one can thoroughly understand the place of coming and the place of going, then false conceptualizations will have no basis from which to arise. That false conceptualizations do not arise is precisely the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing.
What is called "one's own fundamental school" (*sva-siddhānta*) is like this. As for those who calculate...
Adherence to views such as permanence and impermanence, agency and non-agency, or even this world and the next, never departs from the characteristics of coming and going;
these generally belong to the worldly doctrines (*loka-vāda*) and do not constitute the penetration of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Disciples of the inner teaching should be careful regarding what they study.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what you have called 'nirvāṇa,' what kind of dharma is designated as nirvāṇa?
For the various non-Buddhists each give rise to their own deluded imaginings. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall explain it for you. The nirvāṇa imagined by those various non-Buddhists is not their [true] delusion."
Wishing to inquire further regarding Nirvāṇa, Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
Since the preceding section clarified that worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*) is not the cause of non-worldly discourse, this section now distinguishes that it is not the fruit of non-worldly discourse;
therefore, he asks: what kind of dharma is designated as Nirvāṇa, and for what reason do the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) speak of Nirvāṇa?
The term "each giving rise to deluded thoughts" means that the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) all rely on deluded thoughts while claiming for themselves what they call *nirvāṇa*;
this is not like the Tathāgata, who accords with *nirvāṇa* by means of those very same deluded thoughts.

Thus, the fruit of the Tathāgata is called *nirvāṇa*, whereas the *nirvāṇas* of the non-Buddhists are all termed deluded thoughts. Therefore, the subsequent text identifies each of these as being false.
I have considered this, yet I have not yet shown it to you through the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"There are certain non-Buddhists who perceive the cessation of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas) as the realm of detachment from desire; they see all phenomena as impermanent, such that the categories of mind and mental factors do not arise.
They do not contemplate the realms of the past, future, or present, and they hold that the exhaustion of all sensations and aggregates is like a lamp going out."
When the fire is extinguished like a destroyed seed, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise; those who perceive this state conceive of it as *nirvāṇa*.
Mahāmati, it is not by the destruction of views that one names the realm of *nirvāṇa*. It is like the ceasing of the wind when the movement of thought has ceased.
Some take the cessation of movement from one direction to another to be liberation; others take the destruction of the perception of the perceiver and the perceived to be liberation; or they see...
They conceive the notion of liberation regarding the permanent and the impermanent, or perceive various marks and notions that bring about the causes for the arising of suffering.

Having reflected thus, they fail to discern through skillful awareness that these are merely manifestations of their own minds; fearing these marks, they perceive the markless and develop a profound attachment to it, conceiving the notion of nirvana.

The non-Buddhist practitioners of the "Non-conceptual" (asaṃjñika) school calculate that by extinguishing the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and the six sense bases, they sever the fetters of the desire realm;
by not craving the coarse and base six objects, they do not give rise to thoughts of desire.

Seeing all phenomena of the desire realm as impermanent, they subdue the six consciousnesses—the sovereign mind and its mental factors—as a meditative concentration, not recollecting the objects of the three periods of time. They claim this to be the cessation of perception and feeling.

Having exhausted [all things], they never arise again; taking the non-acceptance of all things as their tenet, like the extinguishing of a lamp or the destruction of a seed—such heterodox practitioners reckon the state where sensation is exhausted to be *nirvāṇa*.
These are merely their own deluded views, which they falsely claim to be *nirvāṇa*, yet are not true extinction.
They call this deluded view *nirvāṇa*, not realizing that it is the cessation of the characteristics of objective realms.

This is not true cessation; it is merely like the temporary stilling of the wind. By the power of the concentration of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*), there is extinction for five hundred kalpas—extinguished during the first half-kalpa and then arising again during the latter half of the four hundred and ninety-nine kalpas.

How could it be that once a lamp is extinguished or a seed destroyed, they never arise again? Regarding the statement that "reaching from direction to direction is called Nirvāṇa," this is a discussion concerning directions.
The teacher calculates that first the four directions arise; from the directions, humans arise; from humans, heaven and earth arise.
When heaven and earth perish and dissolve, they return to those very places. He asserts that the directions are eternal and calls this the cause of Nirvana.
Regarding the claim that "the destruction of what is perceived by the perceiver is called Nirvana," the teachers of the Vedas say that from the navel of the god Nārāyaṇa, a great lotus flower arises.
From the lotus arose Brahmā, the progenitor; from that Brahmā were produced all sentient and insentient beings.
From the mouth of that deity was born the Brāhmaṇa; from his two arms, the Kṣatriya; from his two thighs, the Vaiśya; and from his two feet, the Śūdra.
This great earth is a field of merit and a site of precepts, from which all flowers and grasses grow to serve as offerings.

They transform themselves into wild animals of the mountains and fields, as well as humans, pigs, sheep, donkeys, horses, and the like, and by slaughtering them within the site of the precepts (*sīmaṇḍala*) to offer them to Brahmā, they attain rebirth in that realm, which they call *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, the teachers of the Vedas claim that Brahmā is eternal and is the cause of *nirvāṇa*; yet, they perceive that both the subject of cognition and the object of cognition are subject to destruction.
Regarding those who conceive of the eternal and the non-eternal as *nirvāṇa*, the followers of the Īśvara theorists say:
"The form and appearance of the Venerable Īśvara cannot be seen, yet he pervades all places.
Although he has no physical form, he is able to produce all sentient and insentient things; this is called *nirvāṇa*. Because Īśvara can produce the myriad things, [he is so named]."

That which is constantly arising is impermanent. Those who fear conditioned marks (*nimitta*) yet delight in unconditioned marks, conceiving them as *nirvāṇa*, include various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
They perceive the various marks of humans and devas in the desire realm as the cause of the suffering of birth;

or they reckon that it is the cessation of the body, the cessation of desire, the cessation of suffering, the cessation of extreme bliss, or the cessation of extreme equanimity—this is their reckoning.
The seventh [stage] is extinction as nirvāṇa; the remaining four empty heavens, along with the dull-natured arhats, are all included in this category.
This is because they do not skillfully realize that external objects—whether existent or non-existent—are merely the manifestation of one's own mind;
consequently, they fear the presence of signs and crave the signless.

There are some who, perceiving that the individual and general characteristics of all internal and external phenomena exist as an indestructible nature throughout the past, future, and present, conceive the notion of Nirvana;
or there are those who, seeing the destruction of all phenomena—including self, person, sentient being, and life-span—conceive the notion of Nirvana;

or there are those of the non-Buddhist paths whose wisdom is scorched by evil, who perceive a primal nature (*prakṛti*) and a person (*puruṣa*), and [believe] that between these two there is an interval, or that the person exists within them.

That which arises is called self-nature (*svabhāva*), like the primordial darkness (*prakṛti*). Comparing it to the transformation of the *guṇas*, they conceive of the *guṇas* as the agent and imagine them to be nirvāṇa;
or they claim it is the exhaustion of merit and demerit; or they claim it is wisdom; or they see Īśvara as the true creator of saṃsāra and imagine him to be nirvāṇa;
or they claim that saṃsāra arises through mutual succession and that there is no other cause.
This is precisely the attachment to causes; because those who are deluded cannot awaken to this and do not understand it, they falsely conceive of it as *nirvāṇa*.

To claim that internal and external phenomena possess an indestructible intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is to reckon that the internal body and external objects are substantially real rather than provisional.
He thinks thus: "If a phenomenon remains established in its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), this phenomenon truly exists.
If it were non-existent in the future, it would then not yet have received its characteristic; if it were non-existent in the past, it would then have lost its own characteristic.
If this were the case, the own-characteristic of all phenomena could not be established. This is precisely the view of the eternalist outsiders (*śāśvatavādin*).

In total, there are four types of eternalism proponents; they maintain that the four great elements and the six sense organs are all eternally substantial and never disperse or perish, because they exist eternally throughout the three periods of time.

Those who conceive of the destruction of the self, persons, sentient beings, life-span, and all phenomena as being nirvana—this is the nihilistic view (uccheda-dṛṣṭi) held by non-Buddhists, who reckon that after death there is no further existence, just like this place.

The Pūraṇa-kāśyapa school calculates that when a person dies, both body and spirit are utterly extinguished; even if one were to subject them to cutting, burning, pounding, or grinding, what could possibly be done to them?
The followers of Udraka Rāmaputra seek that which is the "maker" (kartṛ), conceiving of nirvāṇa as such; they seek the false subtle atoms (paramāṇu).

The Vaiśeṣika masters calculate that these subtle atoms are eternal and capable of producing all things, and that they are the cause of nirvāṇa. They claim that [all things] arise from these subtle atoms.
Coarse objects such as the self (puruṣa) and so forth arise from *prakṛti* because all selves originate from atoms and *prakṛti*.
Just as *prakṛti*—which exists as two distinct states—can produce the twenty-three principles beginning with *mahat*, so too can atoms and *prakṛti* produce the self;
therefore, they calculate that atoms and *prakṛti* undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Because they can produce coarse objects and, by gradually analyzing coarse objects down to the subtle, they abide in them; therefore, coarse objects are impermanent while atoms are permanent.
This is the cause of nirvana according to certain non-Buddhists, yet this is the most erroneous among them, and thus it is called "badly burning wisdom.
"Exhaustion of merit and demerit" refers to those non-Buddhists who negate cause and effect. "Afflictions" (kleśa).

"The exhaustion [of afflictions] is itself wisdom" means that, as translated by Tang [Xuanzang], one does not rely on wisdom to cultivate abandonment, yet all afflictions are exhausted of their own accord.
This is what the naturalists (Nirgranthas) calculate: that when the number of threads in a ball reaches its limit, it ripens and one attains the Way.
Or, seeing that the essence of Maheśvara is real, pervasive, and eternal, and governs the birth and death of humans, they themselves suspect that their own bodies and minds flow forth from him.
That all the empty spaces of the ten directions arise together—this is the calculation of the master Mādhava.
Regarding "arising through successive production," the master Nirgrantha calculates that at the beginning of the kalpa, one man and one woman were born;
from the union of these two, all things animate and inanimate were produced, and later, they dispersed and returned [to their source].
Because that state is called nirvāṇa, they say that there is no other cause for saṃsāra;

yet they do not realize that such conceptual attachment itself is the cause of saṃsāra. Because of their ignorance, they are unable to perceive this, and due to this lack of knowledge, they consequently reckon saṃsāra to be nirvāṇa.
Or there are non-Buddhists who, having attained the path of true reality (*satya-mārga*), conceive of it as *nirvāṇa*;
or who, seeing the qualities (*guṇa*) and that which arises from those qualities—whether as identical, different, both, or neither—conceive of that union as *nirvāṇa*;

or who, seeing the nature (*svabhāva*) arising as the variegated patterns of a peacock’s plumage, various kinds of jewels, thorns, and so forth, and having perceived these natures, conceive of them as *nirvāṇa*. O Mahāmati! Or...
There are those who, perceiving twenty-five principles, or being protected by a king, or receiving the treatise on the six virtues, conceive the notion that this is *nirvāṇa*;
or upon seeing [these], they conceive the notion that this is *nirvāṇa*—whether regarding the agent, time, or the world.

Such perceivers conceive the notion that this is *nirvāṇa*, or they claim it is *prakṛti*, or they claim it is not *prakṛti*, or they claim it is the nature of knowledge, or they claim it is not the nature of knowledge, or they perceive a distinction between consciousness (*caitanya*) and *nirvāṇa*.
The notion of nirvāṇa held by such various types of conceptual constructions taught by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) is unestablished and rejected by the wise.
Mahāmati, all such [notions] fall into the two extremes and are conceived as nirvāṇa;
yet within those conceptualizations of nirvāṇa held by such non-Buddhists, there is absolutely no arising or ceasing. Mahāmati, each one of those non-Buddhists...
Regarding the path to nirvāṇa, when examined through the wisdom of their own treatises, nothing at all is established;
for those whose minds and thoughts wander, drift, and flow according to their delusions, none among them can attain nirvāṇa.
Those who have attained the path of true reality are the Saṃgha masters who reckon the *mūlatattva* (the primal principle) as true reality.
They maintain that the twenty-three factors, beginning with *mahat* (the Great One), are produced from *prakṛti* (primordial nature).

Therefore, by practicing according to the specific nature of whatever object one encounters among the twenty-five principles, and by knowing them as they truly are, one returns to *prakṛti* and is able to achieve liberation.
Because all birth-and-death attains nirvāṇa, it is said that the self-nature (*svabhāva*) is eternal and capable of producing all phenomena;
this is the cause of nirvāṇa. Some say that the producer and the produced are neither different nor non-different, and this constitutes nirvāṇa;

this is precisely the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) postulated by the Vaiśeṣika school: (1) substance (*dravya*), (2) quality (*guṇa*), (3) activity (*karman*), (4) universal (*sāmānya*), (5) particularity (*viśeṣa*), and (6) inherence (*samavāya*).
The nature of the sixfold conjunction of distinct categories—within this, the attributes (guṇa) are the nature of "Great Existence" (mahāsattā) and so forth;

that which is produced by these attributes consists of substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), and action (karman). That is to say, the nature of Great Existence is conjoined with substance, quality, and action in a single locus;
it is neither identical nor different, neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous. Thus, these six categories of meaning (padārtha) serve as the cause for nirvāṇa. Or, one may perceive the self...
Regarding that which arises from nature (*prakṛti*), those who reckon self-nature to be *nirvāṇa* are proponents of causelessness (*ahetuvādin*).

They maintain that all things arise spontaneously (*svabhāvaja*) without depending on causes and conditions; for instance, they observe that the variegated patterns on a peacock’s feathers are naturally so, various precious jewels are naturally luminous and pure, and various thorns are naturally sharp and pointed, and having seen this, they consequently conclude [that all things are likewise].
All phenomena arise spontaneously; consequently, they reckon this spontaneity to be *nirvāṇa*. As it is said: "Who opened the rivers and seas? Who filled the mountains and peaks?
Who trimmed the thorns and brambles and painted the birds and beasts? This is the Spontaneity Heresy (*svabhāva-tīrthika*).
Alternatively, there are those who perceive the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*) and accept the doctrine of the six qualities (*ṣaḍ-guṇa*) as *nirvāṇa*; this is the Sāṃkhya school.
Regarding the followers of the two masters, the Vaiśeṣika and the Sāṃkhya, their respective tenets are as follows:

they claim that by merely knowing the meaning of the twenty-five *tattvas* and accepting the doctrines of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), one can protect the nation in the present life and attain *nirvāṇa* after death.

As for the proponents of Time (*Kālavādin*), they maintain that time is the creator; these teachers of Time reckon that the seasons and temporal divisions are the cause, and that time creates all things.

It destroys all things; just as when a person is struck by a hundred arrows, they do not die until the time arrives, yet once that time comes, they die even upon touching a blade of grass—so it is with all things.
At the time of birth, at the time of ripening, and at the time of extinction, [all things perish]; the time that is contrary to these is impossible.
All things in the world are impermanent, yet this time is eternal. Because it gives rise to all things, it is called the cause of Nirvana. Or, some say:

Regarding "nature" (*prakṛti*), the proponents of the theory of "existence through transformation" (*pariṇāma*) hold the view that there is a substance named *nirvāṇa*. This refers to the followers of the Water-Consumption Theory (*udakapāna-vāda*), who reckon that water can produce things and water can destroy things;

they claim that water is eternal and is the cause of *nirvāṇa*. Alternatively, those who propound the theory of "non-nature" (*aprakṛti*) hold the view that the absence of substance is named *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to the followers of the Oral-Power Theory (*mukhabala-vāda*), who reckon that empty space (*ākāśa*) is the cause of all things.
All dharmas arise from emptiness and return to extinction in emptiness; emptiness is eternal and is the cause of nirvāṇa.
Or, some claim that knowing the nature of existence and non-existence—specifically, seeing that there are no such things as "existence" or "non-existence"—is the cause of nirvāṇa.

This refers to the calculation of the Āndhaka masters, who maintain that at the beginning of the kalpa there were originally no sun, moon, stars, planets, empty space, or earth, but only a great expanse of water.
The Great Peace Tea grows like a chicken egg, golden in color all around. When it is ripe, it breaks into two parts:
that which is above becomes heaven, and that which is below becomes earth; in the middle, the Brahma Heaven arises.
All sentient beings are born from the Brahma Heaven and return to that place, which is called Nirvana. Or, one may see that there is a distinction between awakening and nirvana.
The notion of *buddhi* (intellect) as *nirvāṇa* refers to the realization that because *buddhi* can lead to *nirvāṇa*, it is not itself *nirvāṇa*.

This is also a conception held by the followers of the *Vaiśeṣika* school, who maintain that since *buddhi* arises from *tamas* (darkness), and *buddhi* gives rise to the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃkāra*), they reckon that while *buddhi* can produce [the self], *nirvāṇa* does not;
