thus, there is a distinction between them. All twenty-two types mentioned above are merely false conceptualizations.
What they conceive cannot actually accomplish what is to be accomplished, yet they claim it can;
though this is accepted by fools, it is truly rejected by the wise. Why is this so? Because they all fall into the two extremes and do not transcend duality;
it is merely a deluded fabrication, a self-constructed nirvana. Such is the delusion of these foolish people.
They imagine that they will personally attain nirvana, yet they themselves fall into birth and death; however, that nirvana has never actually fallen into birth and death.
Because they conceive of nirvana according to their own treatises, if one observes them with the eye of wisdom, they are all merely delusive thoughts with nothing established.
This is because they have not been able to eliminate the mind and its perceptions, and thus they drift, falsely grasping at external objects.
Because they scatter and disperse without cessation, although there are many types of beings, not a single person attains nirvāṇa;
these are all the fruits realized through worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*).
Mahāmati, as for the nirvāṇa I have taught, it means the thorough realization of the manifestation of one’s own mind and non-attachment to external objects.

By nature free from the four extremes of conceptualization, seeing things as they truly are, one does not fall into the false imaginings of the mind’s own manifestations—the duality of grasper and grasped—which cannot be apprehended.
One does not perceive any established reality through any form of measurement; for such a person, the ignorant should not be accepted as true.

Having abandoned that [ignorance], one attains the noble Dharma of self-realization, knows the two kinds of non-self, becomes free from the two afflictions, and completely purifies the two [obscurations].

"Mahāmati, when one is forever free from the two deaths, abides in the higher and highest stages, and reaches the stage of the Tathāgata—wherein there are profound samādhis such as those like shadows and illusions—and is free from mind, thought, and consciousness, this is called Nirvāṇa. You and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should practice and study this;
you should swiftly distance yourselves from all views of Nirvāṇa held by the various non-Buddhists."
This demonstrates that the great fruit of *nirvāṇa* is not realized through worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). I alone have thoroughly mastered the manifestation of my own mind;
I do not grasp at external objects, remain far removed from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*), abide in the vision of reality as it is, and do not fall into the two sides.
Being free from the grasped and the grasper, I do not enter into the various measures of false conceptualization (*vikalpa-pramāṇa*)—this is what constitutes *nirvāṇa*. Because of that delusion...
Since nothing is established within reality that could serve as an object of proof, one should not grasp at it; having abandoned that,
one attains the noble self-realized wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) which knows the two kinds of selflessness— of persons and phenomena— and, being free from both fundamental and derivative ignorance,
severs the two obstacles of afflictions and the cognizable, thereby severing the two types of birth and death— the intermittent and the transformative— and gradually traverses the stages (*bhūmi*).
Upon reaching the supreme Buddha-ground, one attains the Illusion-like Samādhi and transforms illusory sentient beings throughout the limits of the future;
this is the Great Nirvāṇa realized only by those for whom mind, thought, and consciousness have been purified and exhausted without remainder.
How could one hope for a nirvāṇa that is merely a product of false imagination and deluded calculation? Therefore, bodhisattvas who wish to practice and study should do so with haste.
By abandoning the false imaginings of nirvāṇa held by non-Buddhists, one immediately attains the realization of this Great Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The views of nirvāṇa among non-Buddhists each arise from false imaginings;
These are born from mental conceptions and lack the skillful means for liberation. The foolish are bound by their own fetters; those who distance themselves from them are truly free."
Those of external paths who possess skillful means yet harbor notions of liberation will ultimately never give rise to the various wisdoms;
those of external paths who follow divergent paths and whose views extend even to them all lack liberation, because they are mired in delusion and false conceptualization.

Thus, all foolish externalists, through their false views regarding the agent and the acted-upon, and their discourses on existence and non-existence, are entirely devoid of liberation. The ignorant delight in false conceptualization and do not hear [the truth].
The speech of true wisdom is the root of the cessation of the three kinds of suffering; it is the cause for truly extinguishing suffering.

Just as an image in a mirror appears yet does not exist, so too do fools see duality within the mirror of the deluded mind. Failing to recognize the mind and its objects, they give rise to the two-fold delusion.
When one understands the mind and its spheres, delusion no longer arises. The "mind" refers to that which is variously detached.

The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized objects (*lakṣya*) appear yet do not appear, just as the deluded imaginings of the ignorant [conceive] the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) to be mere imagination;
external referents (*bāhyārtha*) do not exist at all. Various things appear through imagination, which the ordinary and foolish cannot comprehend.
The sūtras state that imagination never transcends names (*nāman*); if one is separated from speech, there is nothing whatsoever to be expressed.
The preceding verse stated that the various nirvāṇas of the non-Buddhists all arise from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
as these are the causes for the continuity of birth and death, they lack the means for liberation—how, then, could liberation be attained?
Because they are bound by such conceptualization, and furthermore, because they claim "I have attained nirvāṇa," those who are thus bound by these two fetters must distance themselves from them.
Although they employ the means of liberation and conceive the notion that they have attained liberation, liberation ultimately does not arise.
Furthermore, the inclinations of the wisdom of those non-Buddhists differ; some reckon [existence] as eternal, while others reckon it as annihilated.

Each, relying on their own particular views, claims to have attained liberation, yet in reality none of these are liberation—they are all merely false imaginings. Why is this so? It is truly because of their wisdom.
Only by destroying ignorance can truth be realized, and only by removing delusion can it be eliminated.
Since they are ignorant regarding bondage, they cannot be free from it; being adrift in deluded thoughts, they likewise cannot be free from falsehood.

Lacking the wisdom of suchness as the means of realization and lacking the principle of suchness as the object of realization, how could they ever attain liberation? It is for this reason that ignorant non-Buddhists engage in false conceptualizations.
Those who falsely conceptualize causes and non-causes regarding the agent and the acted-upon establish various worldly doctrines, none of which lead to liberation.

Because those fools delight only in false discrimination and do not hear true wisdom, they merely employ causes and analogies to adorn their speech, giving rise to idle discourse; how could they know that such discourse is the root of the three sufferings?
How could one transcend the three realms and attain liberation? Therefore, it is clear that those who fall into worldly discourse can never achieve the fruit of true liberation.
If one does not construct various doctrines and give rise to various conceptualizations, then conditioned thoughts will be exhausted and speech will be cut off;
only then can the state of true liberation be realized and the three types of suffering be extinguished. However, as for these three sufferings—
Fundamentally, even speech and discourse are not real; they all manifest spontaneously from the mind, like reflections in a mirror, which can neither be said to exist nor be said not to exist.

It is only because foolish people create these two views regarding the images manifested in the mirror of their own deluded thoughts that they fail to recognize the essential nature of their own being and do not realize that external phenomena have no inherent reality.

By nature, delusion gives rise to two views: one does not know that while the images have coming and going, the mirror has neither arising nor ceasing; while conditions have coming and going, the mind has neither arising nor ceasing.
If one can realize that the image is identical to the mirror, and that conditions are identical to the mind, then from where could delusive thoughts possibly arise?
Therefore, know that the mind is precisely the various kinds of mind, and the various kinds are precisely the mind’s various kinds. If...

Since being able to detach from the mind is itself the ability to detach from objects, one who has detached from both mind and object does not perceive even a single phenomenon as corresponding to their own mental state, despite facing objects all day long;
how could such a person be like the foolish who cling to existence or non-existence?

Furthermore, everything that exists within the three realms is merely established by deluded conceptualization and possesses no real meaning at all; ordinary fools, failing to understand this, falsely give rise to distinctions.

Because they are distinct, various signs falsely appear; therefore, the sūtras repeatedly state that wherever there is conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it is revealed to possess only empty names and no real meaning whatsoever.

If one can indeed depart from both speech and the meanings expressed by speech, then the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata will be realized spontaneously, without being sought. Thus, those who wish to realize the Tathāgata...
Those who come to the Great Nirvāṇa should depart from both speech and that which is spoken.
*The Combined Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Fascicle Six;
*The Combined Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
Explanatory Notes by the Śramaṇa Tōrun of Ryōryōan. Composed by Tōrun.
The Fourth Chapter on the Heart of All Buddha-Speech.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I only pray that you will explain for me the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
“I and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to be well-versed in the self-nature of the Tathāgata, awakening ourselves and awakening others.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “Ask whatever you desire; I shall explain it to you according to your questions.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, a created thing, or is he uncreated? Is he an effect, or is he a cause?”
Is it the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or that which is characterized (*lakṣya*)? Is it the teaching (*deśanā*) or that which is taught (*deśya*)?
Is it awakening (*bodha*) or that which is awakened to (*boddhavya*)? Are such terms and phrases different or not different?
*Samyaksaṃbuddha* is translated here as "Perfectly All-Knowing. The self-nature of the Tathāgata is precisely suchness (*tathatā*), the equality of Buddha-nature.

Previously, when the World-Honored One was questioned by non-Buddhists regarding whether all phenomena are created or uncreated, he rejected each of their views as mere worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*).
Nevertheless, within the Tathāgata’s equal dharma-nature, there is no phenomenon that is not [included].

If one thoroughly understands this intrinsic nature (*tathāgata-svabhāva*) of the Tathāgata, one can personally realize the realm of self-awakening and can also cause others to reach that realm of self-awakening.

Therefore, Mahāmati asked: "Is this intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata that which is attained by practicing the six perfections and the myriad deeds, or is it that which is spontaneously attained without practicing the six perfections and the myriad deeds?"
Is this the self-nature of the Tathāgata? Is it the fruit that is realized which is the self-nature of the Tathāgata?
Or is it the cause that is cultivated which is the self-nature of the Tathāgata? Is it the visible characteristic which is the self-nature of the Tathāgata?
Or is it the invisible characteristic which is the self-nature of the Tathāgata? Or is it the speaker who is the self-nature of the Tathāgata?
Is it the self-nature itself, or is it the dharmas that are taught which are the self-nature?
Is it the wisdom that realizes which is the self-nature, or is it the principle that is realized which is the self-nature?
Regarding these terms, is the Tathāgata’s self-nature different from these terms, or is it not different from these terms?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither a thing (*vastu*) nor a cause (*hetu*) in such expressions as these.
Why? Because both [positions] entail faults. Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were a thing, he would either be produced or impermanent;
because he would be impermanent, all things would be the Tathāgata—a conclusion that neither I nor other Buddhas accept."
If that which is uncreated is non-apprehendable, then skillful means are empty, being like the horns of a rabbit or the son of a barren woman;
because they do not exist, Mahāmati, if there were no object and no cause, it would be neither existent nor non-existent.
If it were neither existent nor non-existent, it would transcend the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). These four propositions are worldly discourse; if one transcends the four...
As for "phrases," they do not fall into the four propositions; because they do not fall [into them], the meaning of the phrases of all Tathāgatas is likewise grasped by the wise.
The wise should know that, as I have taught, all dharmas are without self (*anātman*); one should know that this meaning is such that the nature of being without self is itself non-self.
All dharmas possess their own-nature (*svabhāva*) and lack other-nature (*parabhāva*), like a cow or a horse, O Mahāmati.

For example, the nature of a cow is not that of a horse, and the nature of a horse is not that of a cow; in reality, they are neither existent nor non-existent, for they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In this same way, Mahāmati, all phenomena do not lack their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), yet they possess specific characteristics;

however, they are devoid of selfhood (*anātman*) such as can be known by the ignorant through their false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Thus, all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature.
One should understand the nature [of reality] in this way.
This statement means that the self-nature of suchness (*tathatā*) is not a phenomenon of cause and effect, nor does it fall within the realm of cause and effect.
If it were to fall within cause and effect, both positions would entail faults: if the self-nature of the Tathāgata were a produced result, it would be identical to conditioned phenomena.

Furthermore, it is impermanent; if one were to take impermanence as the Tathāgata, then all impermanent phenomena would be the Tathāgata, which belongs to the view of annihilationism—a position neither I nor the Buddhas permit.

If one claims that the self-nature of the Tathāgata is not a produced effect, then the Tathāgata would be utterly devoid of any obtainable self-nature, despite the various [attributes] attributed to him.
The practice of skillful means is empty and without attainment, identical to the horns of a rabbit or the son of a barren woman;
it is ultimately non-existent and belongs to the category of annihilationism, which neither I nor the Buddhas permit.

Therefore, one should know that the self-nature of the Tathāgata exists within cause and effect yet does not fall into cause and effect; since it does not fall into cause and effect, it likewise does not fall into the four logical extremes (*catuskoṭi*).
The fourfold propositions are worldly conventional discourse and conceptual construction; the wise do not grasp them.
That which transcends the four propositions does not fall into the four propositions, but is uniquely manifest as the true and eternal—this is what the wise grasp.
My own nature and that of all Tathāgatas, the self-nature of the Dharma-body as taught by me, are all free from the laws of cause and effect and free from the four propositions. They are complete.

Those with the eye of wisdom should understand this: that which I have previously described as the meaning of "all phenomena are without self" is precisely what those possessing the eye of wisdom must also understand. What is called "without self" means that all phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind;
since there is no sovereign master, and because they lack the nature of a self as imputed by pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), they are termed "without self."
It is not that there is no true self in the dharma-body; rather, it is because all phenomena each possess their own true intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
While they lack the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is like when one speaks of a cow while mentioning a horse:

this does not mean that the nature of a horse exists within the nature of a cow, nor does it mean that the nature of a cow exists within the nature of a horse, for both the horse and the cow each have their own [true nature].
To chew grass and drink water, standing on its hind legs—this is the true nature of a horse. To think only of water and grass and know nothing else—this is the true nature of an ox.
Regarding the true nature of an ox, one cannot say that the nature of a horse exists or does not exist;
regarding the true nature of a horse, one cannot say that the nature of an ox exists or does not exist. This is because each possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The absence of the horse’s intrinsic nature is just like the case where, regarding the second moon, one cannot say it exists or does not exist;
yet, because the real moon is not non-existent, it is said that in reality it is neither existent nor non-existent. That [absence] is not the non-existence of an intrinsic nature.

Thus, one should know that all phenomena merely lack the nature of being conceptually imputed (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), but they are not non-existent phenomena.
The nature of the body is likewise thus: where there is a nature, there must be characteristics; since the nature is such as this, existence (*bhāva*) should also be so.

All phenomena (*dharma*) merely lack the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), yet they are not without the true characteristic of suchness (*tathatā-svalakṣaṇa*).
This is illustrated by the fact that while fire does not exist within wood, the true nature of water is not non-existent [within it]. Nevertheless, all phenomena possess [this true nature].

The nature and characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness) cannot be known by those who have attained the selflessness of persons, nor by the ignorant followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), because their attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not been emptied and they have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); thus, they do not see the true self.
Since all phenomena are without self, it follows that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); this should also be understood accordingly.
This is known by analogy: it means that while the nature of the self (*ātman*) is empty, its own-being (*svabhāva*) is not;
while the self-nature does not arise, its own-being does not arise; and while the imagined self lacks own-being, the true self lacks no own-being. Question:
Since this sutra states that there is no self-nature, no own-being, and no other-nature, yet also speaks of the existence of own-being, how is this so?
"Does this not also constitute the fault of evasive equivocation? He replied: "Although these [arguments] are interwoven, each possesses its own systematic order.

When it is said that there is no self-nature (*ātman*) and no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this refers specifically to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of universal imagination). This is because, within the *parikalpita-svabhāva*, one clings to the *dṛṣṭi-bhāga* (the subjective aspect of perception) as having a real self-nature that acts as a sovereign, and further clings to the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect of perception) as having a real dharma-nature."
Because one gives rise to the two views of self and phenomena by grasping at tracks and supports, it is called "self-nature" and "intrinsic nature.
Now, because these two kinds of thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) do not exist, it is said that there is "no self-nature" and "no intrinsic nature.
As for "other-nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*), this refers to all dependent phenomena; for all dependent phenomena rely upon causes and depend upon conditions.
Because arising has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the treatise states that the *paratantra-svabhāva* arises from conditions through conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Since it is now said that this *paratantra-svabhāva* does not exist, it is called "the absence of other-nature" (*parabhāva-abhāva*). When it is said that "intrinsic nature exists," this refers to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*.
This clarifies that while the *parikalpita* and *paratantra* are non-existent, the *pariniṣpanna* is existent.
In this way, the Tathāgata is neither different from nor non-different from the aggregates (*skandha*). If he were not different from the aggregates, he would be impermanent;
if he were different, skillful means (*upāya*) would be empty. If there were these two [possibilities], there would have to be a difference, as in the case of the similarity of a cow's horns.
Yet, while they are non-different, there is a difference in their length and proportions. All phenomena are likewise, Mahāmati. It is like the right horn of a cow being different [from the left].
The left corner is different from the right corner; likewise, long and short, and various colors, each pair is distinct.

Mahāmati, in this way the Tathāgata is neither different nor not different from the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas). Likewise, the Tathāgata is neither different nor not different from liberation.
If the Tathāgata were to be designated by the name "liberation," yet were different from liberation, he would possess the characteristics of material form (rūpa-lakṣaṇa).
Because they are established through the mutual establishment of form and characteristics, they should be impermanent;

yet if they were not different, the practitioner’s attainment of realization would be without differentiation, whereas the practitioner perceives differentiation. Therefore, they are neither different nor non-different. In this way, wisdom and the cognitive object (*jñeya*) are neither different nor non-different.
The preceding statement that the *dharmakāya* is without delusion implies that it is not without a true self (*ātman*).

The following clarifies that the true self of the *dharmakāya* exists within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) yet does not belong to the five aggregates; it exists within liberation (*vimukti*) yet does not belong to liberation;
it exists within *prajñā* yet does not belong to *prajñā*. Therefore, it is neither different nor non-different [from them]. If the *dharmakāya* were not different from the five aggregates, then...
If the aggregates (*skandhas*) possess the characteristic of flux, then the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) should be impermanent.

If the Dharma-body were distinct from the five aggregates, then while the aggregates would have characteristics, the Dharma-body would be without characteristics, resulting in a nihilistic emptiness and a lack of skillful means (*upāya*).
If the Dharma-body and the fruit of the five aggregates were two separate entities, then the Dharma-body would exist independently apart from the five aggregates. [Apart from the Dharma-body...]

In the case of a physical body, one may speak of it as being distinct from the five aggregates (*skandhas*). However, in the present case, the Dharma-body is not separate from the five aggregates, nor are the five aggregates separate from the Dharma-body;
how then can they be said to be different? It is like the two horns of an ox, which, because they are both part of a single body, are not different;

yet, there is a distinction between their left and right positions, and between their length and shortness. Since this is the case with the horns of an ox, one should know that the same applies to the five [aggregates].
The aggregates (*skandha*) are all equal because they are the Dharma-body; thus, they are not different [in essence].

However, the manifested characteristics of the aggregates differ in length, shortness, magnitude, and smallness, and are therefore said to be different—just as the right horn of an ox differs from the left horn, and the left horn differs from the right horn.
These are called "different" only because their dimensions and color-forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) are distinct, yet both horns equally arise from the ox.
The essence has never been different. Thus, one knows that the Dharma-body and the five aggregates are neither different nor not different.
If the Dharma-body and the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are neither different nor not different, then one knows that the Dharma-body and liberation are neither different nor not different;
for it is because the Tathāgata realizes liberation that he is called the Tathāgata. If [it were otherwise], then...
If the Tathāgata were different from liberation, then the Tathāgata would necessarily be composed of physical form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
If the Tathāgata were composed of physical form, then the Tathāgata would be an impermanent phenomenon (*anitya-dharma*). How could one say that [the Tathāgata] is different [from liberation]?
If the Tathāgata is not different from liberation, then when practitioners attain the mark of liberation, they would be able to realize the [Tathāgata].
If realization were non-conceptual, then how could we now see the realizer and the realized so clearly and without confusion?

How can it be said that the Dharmakāya is not different [from these]? Since one knows that the Dharmakāya and liberation are neither different nor non-different, one should know that the Dharmakāya and Prajñā—and the object known by Prajñā—are likewise neither different nor non-different. This is because Prajñā...

If this is the wisdom-dharmakāya, then wisdom is the principle of initial awakening (shijue) and the principle is original awakening (benjue); because the initial and the original are one body, they are not different;
yet because they are two names for the initial and the original, they are not non-different.
Mahāmati, wisdom (*jñāna*) and its radiance (*jyotis*) are neither different nor not different; they are neither eternal nor impermanent; neither agent nor object;

neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); neither the subject of awakening nor the object of awakening; neither characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor that which is characterized (*lakṣya*);

neither the aggregates (*skandha*) nor distinct from the aggregates; neither the teaching (*deśanā*) nor that which is taught; neither identical nor different; neither both nor neither; neither one... [nor many].

Because difference is neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous, it is entirely free from all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Being free from all means of valid cognition, there is no verbal expression; being without verbal expression, there is no arising;
being without arising, there is no cessation; being without cessation, there is quiescence; being quiescent, there is *parinirvāṇa* by nature (*prakṛti-parinirvāṇa*).
Being *parinirvāṇa* by nature, there is no objective entity and no cause; being without objective entity and cause, there is no object of apprehension (*ālambana*).
When there is no objective support (*ālambana*), one transcends all falsehood; to transcend all falsehood is to be the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is the Samyaksaṃbuddha, Mahāmati. This, Mahāmati, is called the Samyaksaṃbuddha Buddha.
Mahāmati, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Buddha is free from all sense organs and all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
From this point downward, it is generally refuted that all things are subsumed within the self-nature of the Tathāgata.

Because the Dharmakāya Tathāgata is neither different nor non-different from the five aggregates (*skandhas*), neither different nor non-different from liberation, and neither different nor non-different from *prajñā*, he is already endowed with the three virtues within the causal state;
thus, one knows that because he is "immutable while following conditions," he is not eternal, and because he is "following conditions," he is not impermanent.
Because it is subject to transformation, it is not non-constant; because its fundamental nature is immovable, it is not an agent, nor is it created by another, nor is it a product.
While demonstrating the unconditioned nature within conditioned phenomena, it does not destroy the characteristics of the conditioned, and thus does not fall into [the extreme of] the conditioned.
While demonstrating the characteristics of the conditioned within unconditioned phenomena, it does not conceptualize the nature of the unconditioned.
Therefore, one does not fall into the unconditioned, for there is no nirvana; nor is there a Buddha, for there is no nirvana of a Buddha.

Because there is no subject that awakens and no object to be awakened, there is neither the characteristic of the seer nor the characteristic of the seen. Therefore, one does not fall into the characteristic or the characterized.

One is neither identical to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) nor separate from name-and-form. Therefore, one does not fall into the aggregates (*skandha*), nor are they non-aggregates. This is the path of meaning beyond words and conceptual boundaries.
Therefore, it does not fall into the trap of speech or that which is spoken, for it transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.

Because it does not fall into the extremes of identity, difference, both, or neither, and because it is free from the four propositions, it is free from the conditions of the mind. Being free from the conditions of the mind, it is free from verbal expression.
Being free from verbal expression, one sees that all phenomena are originally unarisen; being unarisen, they are unceasing; and being unceasing, [they are quiescent].
When quiescence reaches the point where both arising and ceasing have been extinguished and quiescence manifests before one, then one perceives the self-nature of pure nirvāṇa.
Upon perceiving the self-nature of pure nirvāṇa, one abandons the ālayavijñāna; thus, one transcends the triple world and does not fall under the sway of cause and effect.
When cause and effect have vanished, mind and consciousness are also severed; therefore, there is no grasping at objects, and when there is no grasping at objects, then [all] ceases.
Because habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been transcended, both the manifest and the seeds of all falsehood have been eliminated; this is precisely the immovable *tathatā* (suchness).
This immovability of *tathatā* is itself perfect, equal, and right awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Thus, above, it is equal to all Buddhas, and below, it is equal to all sentient beings;
this is called the fruit of equality realized by perfect, equal, and right awakening, which is termed *Samyak*.
Since the Buddha is himself a *saṃbuddha*, one should know that a *samyaksaṃbuddha* is free from all measures of the senses and cannot be subsumed by the calculations of deluded thought.

If there remains even the slightest measure of mind, and one falsely discriminates external objects, one immediately flows into the nature of others rather than abiding in one's own nature; this must be until the measure of deluded thought is exhausted and [the mind] becomes level.
The Dharmakāya is thus omnipresent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Completely free from the measure of the sense organs, Without objects and without causes, Already detached from the perceiver and the perceived, And likewise detached from characteristics and the characterized, Regarding the aggregates, conditions, and so forth— The Perfectly Enlightened One is neither one nor many."
None can see it; since there is no seer, how could one differentiate it? It is neither made nor unmade, neither an action nor without cause;
it is not the aggregates (*skandha*), nor does it reside within the aggregates, nor is it something else apart from them, nor is it possessed of various natures.

As it is seen through such false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one should know that it is not non-existent either. This is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): because of existence there is existence, and because of non-existence there is non-existence.
Therefore, one should not accept that existence is like non-existence, nor should one conceptualize it as existent;

nor should one linger or become immersed in the two extremes through the conventional expressions of "self" or "non-self. To destroy all faults by liberating oneself and the world through correct observation of the self as it truly is—this is called right contemplation, which does not disparage the Great Teacher.

This verse summarizes how the Dharmakāya is free from all faults. Since the measures of the faculties do not extend beyond seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, when one is detached from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, one realizes the pure Dharmakāya.

Therefore, it does not fall into the characteristics of cause and effect, nor does it involve the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived, nor does it involve the characteristic that manifests and the characteristic that is manifested. Thus, although the Tathāgata exists within the five aggregates and the twelve [bases], [he remains free from them].

In the midst of conditions, one attains equal and perfect enlightenment; yet, not perceiving any marks such as identity or difference, even this very perception does not exist—how then could there be conceptual discrimination?
Thus, one knows that the Dharmakāya is pure, falling neither into the categories of "action" nor "non-action," nor into cause and effect;
it is neither separate from the aggregates, nor does it reside within the aggregates, nor is it mixed with other things.

It is not that there is existence within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and non-existence within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), as is the case with the various deluded views of the followers of the Lesser Vehicle and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, one should know that it is not that the self-nature of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) does not exist.
Once one knows that the Dharma-body is sovereign and fundamentally without a self, it becomes clear that all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise without a self. Thus it is understood.
Existence, non-existence, and so forth are all conceptual constructs arising from mutual opposition; they are fundamentally not real entities.

Therefore, one should not form the notion of existence regarding what exists, nor should one form the notion of non-existence regarding what does not exist, because both existence and non-existence are other-natures (*parabhāva*) and not self-natures (*svabhāva*).
Alternatively, some understand these two views of existence and non-existence to be the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Taking this as the nature of the self and failing to see that non-falling into dualistic views is the very nature of non-self, one becomes attached to the conceptual constructs of verbal proliferation;
lingering therein and unable to relinquish them, one remains submerged and fails to attain liberation.
Having already ruined oneself, one also ruins the world; the faults are immeasurable. Therefore, those who wish to liberate themselves from all faults should, by means of...

To observe correctly by means of contemplation that which I have taught—the penetration of the principle of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-siddhānta*)—and thereby perceive the equal Dharma-body without giving rise to discriminative thought, is called correct contemplation. This does not slander the Tathāgata’s true wheel of Dharma. Therefore, the preceding text states:
"The Sage observes with tranquil stillness; this is to be far removed from birth. This is called non-appropriation of this world and the world beyond."

If one is not pure in this way—reckoning existence, reckoning non-existence, lingering, and failing to relinquish—all such persons are destroyers of the Buddha and slanderers of the Dharma; how can they not exert themselves?
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, the Sūtras encompass..."
Regarding the non-arising and non-ceasing of sensation, the Blessed One further stated that "non-arising and non-ceasing" is another name for the Tathāgata.
How is it, Blessed One, that you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing as another name for the Tathāgata because of the absence of intrinsic nature? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I teach that all dharmas are non-arising and non-ceasing because the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear."

This refers back to the previous chapter’s statement that where there is no verbal expression, there is no arising; where there is no arising, there is no cessation; and where there is no cessation, there is quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
It continues up to the point where it says that to transcend all falsehood is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth.
This is intended to mean that [the notion of] non-arising and non-cessation is a re-emergence of the dualistic views of existence and non-existence.
The principle realized is the Tathāgata, who is the person that realizes it; therefore, one should not regard "non-arising" and "non-ceasing" as alternative names for the Tathāgata.
[The opponent] asks: "World-Honored One, in various places throughout the sūtras you have taught that non-arising and non-ceasing encompass all phenomena;
yet this sūtra also states that non-arising and non-ceasing are alternative names for the Tathāgata."
What do you think? Is it because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature that they are said to be neither arising nor ceasing?

Or is it that "neither arising nor ceasing" is spoken of as another name for the Tathāgata? If one says that the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena constitutes their lack of intrinsic nature, then since this would fall into the extreme of nihilism, it should not be called another name for the Tathāgata. If, on the other hand, one says [it refers to the Tathāgata]...
To say that "coming" is a different name [for the Tathāgata] would mean falling into the view of existence (*bhava*); one should not then say that he is neither born nor extinguished.

This implies that the Tathāgata does not fall into non-existence (*abhāva*). Since non-arising and non-extinction are non-entities (*abhāva-dharma*), whereas the Tathāgata is an entity (*bhāva-dharma*), one should not designate "non-arising and non-extinction" as a different name for the Tathāgata. The preceding section has thus manifested this through the Dharma.
In this chapter, because the person is used again to manifest the Dharma, this question arises. The Buddha said: "The Tathāgata has taught that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing;
this is simply another name for the Tathāgata. Furthermore, they do not fall into existence or non-existence. Because the complete person is this Dharma, one does not fall into existence;
because the complete Dharma is this person, one does not fall into non-existence. Therefore, it is said that they do not belong to the categories of existence or non-existence."

[The Buddha] manifested [this]. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if all dharmas are non-arising, then the apprehension of dharmas cannot be obtained, because all dharmas are non-arising.
If there were any dharma within names, I pray that you would explain it for me. The Buddha told him:
“Excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your teaching. The Buddha told Mahāmati: “I say that the Tathāgata is not without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), nor is he something that is neither born nor extinguished.
He encompasses all phenomena (*dharma*), and because he does not depend on conditions, he is neither born nor extinguished.”
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, cessation is not without meaning. I speak of the 'mind-born Dharma-body' as a name for the Tathāgata;
that which is 'unborn' is not within the realm of any outsiders, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage, Mahāmati.
That 'unborn,' Mahāmati, is simply another name for the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, it is like Indra, Śakra, and Purandara [being different names for the same deity]."
Such things as these also each have many names; yet it is not because they have many names that they possess a multiplicity of natures, nor is it that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Mahāmati, because phenomena are non-arising and non-ceasing, one should not conceive of them as being merely different names for the Tathāgata; this is precisely what is feared.
Because those in the final age regard annihilation as the Tathāgata, he asks again:

"If all phenomena are called 'unborn' because they lack intrinsic nature, then since the unborn and the unceasing would encompass all phenomena such that nothing could be apprehended, this would result in total annihilation.
Where, then, would there be a Tathāgata, and how could one speak of this as another name for the Tathāgata? If...
That is to say, if there were a distinct existent phenomenon that is neither arising nor ceasing which serves as another name for the Tathāgata, I pray that you would explain it for me.
Therefore, the Tang translation says: "If a phenomenon does not arise, it cannot be grasped; there is not even the slightest phenomenon—what then is the Tathāgata? The Buddha said:
"The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is neither a non-existent thing, nor is it subsumed under that which neither arises nor ceases. This constitutes one section.
All dharmas are ungraspable; to say they fall into annihilation is not to rely on causes or depend on conditions for their arising.

To speak of non-arising and non-extinction while falling into the view of existence is likewise not the case. It is not that my teaching of non-arising and non-extinction is a false statement consisting of mere names without meaning.
What I call the "mind-born dharma-body" (manomaya-dharmakāya) arises yet does not arise; that which does not arise is precisely...

This is another name for the Tathāgata. It refers exclusively to the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage who, having severed the mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), have realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and attained the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) that realizes the self-nature of dharmas.

Because arising is itself non-arising and non-arising is itself arising, no distinct characteristic can be found. This applies to all non-Buddhists, followers of the Lesser Vehicle, and Bodhisattvas up to the seventh stage.
The realized realm has not yet abandoned the *ālayavijñāna*, and the arising and ceasing still persist;
because one cannot yet know this realm of non-arising, there is the designation "non-arising" based on the *manomayakāya*. Based on the meaning of non-arising, there is the name "Tathāgata.
Therefore, I say that "neither arising nor ceasing" is an alternative name for the Tathāgata; it is not without meaning. Thus, the *Vajra*...
The Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas. For example, Śakra has one name, Śakradevendra;
another, Purandara; and another, Kauśika. Even down to earth and space, or hands and feet—each of these things has many names.
Just as it is with Śakra, so it is with all these things and likewise with all Buddhas.
Thus, it is not that there are multiple entities because there are many names, nor is it that the true nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is lost in nihilistic annihilation;
for who would say that "non-arising and non-ceasing" has different names?
In this way, Mahāmati, I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names in this Sahā world;
all foolish people hear them and each speaks of my name, yet they do not understand that these are different names for me, the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, there are some sentient beings who know me as the Tathāgata, some who know me as the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*), some who know me as the Buddha, and some who know me as the Savior.
In this world, some know him as the Self-Awakened One; some know him as the Teacher; some know him as the Broad Guide;
some know him as the Universal Guide; some know him as the Seer; some know him as Brahmā; some know him as Viṣṇu; some know him as Maheśvara;
some know him as the Victorious One; some know him as Kapila; some know him as the Limit of Reality; and some know him as...
There are those who know the moon; there are those who know the sun; there are those who know birth; there are those who know non-birth; there are those who know non-extinction;
there are those who know emptiness; there are those who know suchness; there are those who know the truths; there are those who know the limit of reality;
there are those who know the nature of phenomena; there are those who know nirvana; there are those who know permanence; there are those who know equality; there are those who know non-...
Second, there are those who know the signless, those who know liberation, those who know the path, and those who know the mind-born (*manomaya*).
Mahāmati, these and other such names—three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya*s in number—are neither increased nor diminished;
in this world and in all other worlds, everyone knows me as being like the moon in water, neither emerging nor entering. Yet those foolish people do not [understand this].
Because they know that I have fallen into the two extremes, they all revere and make offerings to me;
yet they do not skillfully understand the meaning and intent of words and phrases, do not discern names, and do not understand self-realization.

They are attached to various verbal expressions and textual passages, forming notions of "non-existence" regarding the unborn and undying, and failing to understand the distinctions among the Tathāgata’s titles, such as Indra.
Rāśīka and Aparāntaka do not understand that these [names] ultimately converge and return to the same point: the conceptual attachment to all phenomena according to how they are described.
This explains in detail that although there are many names, their essence is not different. *Sahā* was formerly translated as *Saha*; *asaṃkhyeya*.
Regarding the term "innumerable Tathāgatas": because they have come from the path of suchness (yathābhūta) to achieve perfect enlightenment, they are called Tathāgatas.

Their noble wisdom is the great emptiness that awakens to all phenomena; this is termed "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā). Because they have awakened by themselves and awakened others, and their practice of awakening is perfected, they are called Buddhas.
Because they enter into lands as numerous as motes of dust to liberate sentient beings, they are called Saviors of the World who have attained the wisdom of self-awakening.
One who realizes the dharma of the true mark is called a Self-Awakened One; one who leads sentient beings out of the sea of birth and death is called a Guide of Beings;

one whose names are universally proclaimed according to the infinite varieties of beings is called a Universal Guide; one who manifests bodies and preaches the Dharma in every land and within every atom is called a Guide of All;
one who is able to practice patience and remains unattached to worldly appearances is called a Rishi of Pure Conduct.
"Vimala" (Dàng) means "free from even the slightest speck of dust. "Brahman" refers to Viṣṇu; this is translated as "Great Power" (*Mahābala*).

Being endowed with the ten powers and remaining unmoved by all phenomena, he is called "Great Power. Having no thing that is not himself and being present everywhere, he is called "Sovereign" (*Īśvara*).
Transcending all and having no equal, he is called "Victorious One" (*Jina*). "Kāpila" means "Golden-Hued"; he practiced various ascetic austerities.
Possessing the mark of golden hue, he realizes the true Dharma and abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); thus he is named "The Limit of Reality.
He can destroy darkness and bestow coolness upon others; thus he is named "The Moon. He can perform beneficial deeds for sentient beings; thus he is named "The Sun.

Being endowed with innate virtues, he gives rise to wholesome dharmas; thus he is called "Arising. Because unwholesome [dharmas] do not arise and wholesome dharmas are not extinguished, he is called "Non-arising."

The non-extinction and departure from subtle thought, the severing of the outflows of ignorance, is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That which accords with conditions while remaining unchanging is named suchness (*tathatā*).

Realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is named the truth (*satya*). Reaching the limit of true thusness (*bhūtakoṭi*) is named the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Attaining the self-nature of phenomena is named the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Transcending the two deaths is named nirvāṇa. That the essence of awakening is indestructible is named permanence (*nitya*). Viewing all sentient beings with equality is called...
Equally realizing the path of the One Vehicle is called "Non-duality"; not perceiving any marks is called "Formlessness"; being eternally free from fetters is called "Liberation";
reaching all things without exception is called the "Path"; appearing universally according to the mind is called the "Mind-born.
Although there are thus hundreds of thousands of such names, though they have many names, their essence does not differ; it neither increases nor decreases. This—
Furthermore, throughout all other worlds, they know me to be like the moon in water—neither emerging from nor entering the water.

The water is a metaphor for the minds of sentient beings, and the moon is a metaphor for the body of the Tathāgata. If the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflection of the Tathāgata naturally appears;
yet, in reality, there is no coming or going. Nevertheless, those foolish people do not understand this meaning and fall into the two extremes, even though they offer worship.

I do not understand the phrasing, nor do I comprehend the underlying meaning. Since I do not recognize the reason for these names, nor do I grasp their intrinsic nature or the penetration of the ultimate principle (*tathatā*), I am attached to mere words, phrases, and chapters.

Regarding that which is neither arising nor ceasing and transcends the realm of existence and non-existence, I have formulated a doctrine of non-substantiality and nihilism; having taken "non-arising" to mean non-existence, I further [misconstrue] the Tathāgata...
There are those who do not know that this "neither-arising-nor-ceasing" is a distinct name for the Tathāgata,
just as Śakra has various names. Because they fail to realize their own inherent penetration and cannot resolve it within their own ultimate state,
they instead follow the literal words and produce interpretations, claiming that "neither-arising-nor-ceasing" should not be considered a different name for the Tathāgata.
Why is this so? Mahāmati, those deluded people speak thus: "The meaning is identical to the expression; there is no difference between the meaning and the expression. Why is that?
Because they claim that since meaning has no substance, there is no meaning whatsoever apart from the expression; it is merely the expression itself.
O Mahāmati, those whose wisdom is scorched by evil do not know that the nature of discourse is beyond cognition; they do not understand the meaning of the arising and ceasing of discourse.
To the Great Wisdom, all discourse falls into the realm of words, yet its true meaning does not fall therein, for it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Therefore, there is no rebirth and no body. O Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not speak of dharmas that fall into words, for words are neither existent nor non-existent.

Because they are unattainable, they exclude falling into words. Mahāmati, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata teaches a dharma that falls into words, this would be a false teaching, for the Dharma is free from words.
Therefore, Mahāmati, neither I nor the various bodhisattvas have spoken a single word, nor have we answered a single word. Why is this? Because the Dharma is free from words; it is not [otherwise].
Mahāmati, those who speak of doctrines that do not lead to benefit do so because of the conceptual constructions of sentient beings.
Mahāmati, if all dharmas were not taught, the teaching would perish; if the teaching perished, there would be no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas.
If these did not exist, who would teach and for whom? Therefore, Mahāmati, let Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas not cling to verbal expressions.
According to what is appropriate through skillful means, I have extensively expounded the Dharma of the sutras;

for because the hopes and afflictions of sentient beings are not uniform, I and the various Buddhas have taught various dharmas for those beings of diverse understandings so that they may become detached from mind, thought, and consciousness.
It is not for the sake of attaining the state of self-realized noble wisdom, Mahāmati, but rather for the realization that all dharmas are non-existent.
The direct perception of the mind is free from the two kinds of false conceptualization; therefore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas rely on the meaning and not on the words.

Those who derive understanding merely by following the words are deluded persons who do not understand the relationship between names and meanings, falsely claiming that meaning exists apart from words and that words exist apart from meaning.
[They fail to see that] meaning is itself the word, and the word is itself the meaning. Why is this so? It is because:
Meaning has no intrinsic substance; it exists only through verbal expression. Apart from verbal expression, there is no further meaning.
Therefore, where there is no verbal expression, there is no arising; where there is no arising, there is no cessation; and where there is no cessation, there is quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

As for this state of quiescent extinction, it cannot be further designated by another name such as "Tathāgata. Those whose wisdom is scorched by evil do not know that verbal expression is ultimately non-existent.
Furthermore, one does not realize that while conventional expressions undergo arising and ceasing, their underlying meaning is without arising or ceasing.
The reason conventional expressions undergo arising and ceasing is that they fall into the realm of language and letters;

because they allow for the grasping of two extremes, the perception of marks of arising, and the apprehension of a fixed essence, they possess the sense of arising and ceasing. Therefore, [the ultimate] is not...
That which arises and ceases is manifested by means of words as its cause, yet in reality it does not fall into words;
therefore, there are no two extremes to be grasped, no marks of arising to be seen, and no self-nature to be found—this is the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Thus, while the words may come to an end, the meaning is inexhaustible. Who would say that beyond verbal expression there is no further meaning?
Therefore, although the Tathāgata speaks all day long, there is not a single word; for if he were to speak, he would fall into the dharma of words and letters.

The reason he does not fall into words and letters is that the Dharma transcends existence and non-existence, and words and letters likewise transcend existence and non-existence, being ultimately unobtainable.
Thus, by remaining free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, one does not fall into the dharma of words and letters.
The Tathāgata has constantly taught that if anyone says the Tathāgata speaks of dharmas that fall within the realm of words, such a person slanders the Dharma;
for the Dharma is fundamentally apart from words and cannot be reached by speech.
Therefore, although all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma throughout the day, they have never spoken a single word themselves, nor have they answered others with a single word.

All dharmas are devoid of words and letters; nevertheless, one desires to benefit sentient beings through these meanings, and it is not the case that one does not speak in accordance with those meanings.
Thus, all speech is spoken out of necessity in response to the deluded conceptions of sentient beings.
If one does not provide instruction by adapting to their various capacities according to their circumstances, there would be no teaching of the Dharma.
If there is no Dharma, there is no Buddha; if there is no Buddha, there is no Sangha. If these three are all absent, who would preach the Dharma, and for whom would it be preached?
Therefore, only when there is a person who preaches the Dharma and an assembly that listens to the Dharma does the Dharma that can be preached exist.
Thus, the teaching of the Dharma arises from conditions; it is like the yellow leaves used to stop a child's crying—how could it be anything real?
Therefore, a bodhisattva should thoroughly investigate the ultimate truth that transcends words and must not cling to verbal expressions;
for even the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures are all provisional means (*upāya*) suited to the specific occasion and capacity of beings.

Since the aspirations of sentient beings differ and their afflictions are manifold, I and the various Buddhas provide remedies according to their illnesses in response to those beings of diverse understandings.

The teaching on medicine that causes one to be free from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not for those who have attained the noble realization of self-awakening through true cultivation;

it is not taught to them because they have, regarding all phenomena, understood them as they truly are—realizing there is nothing to be found, that they are merely the manifestation of their own minds, and are thus free from the two kinds of false discrimination between speaker and spoken. These are the Bodhisattvas.
All possess the capacity for the Mahāyāna; they rely solely on the meaning and not on the words, for there is no substantiality in verbal expression.
Thus the Sūtra says: "The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to liberate all minds; since I have no mind, what use have I for all dharmas?"
If a son or daughter of good family relies upon the literal words, they will destroy the ultimate truth for themselves and be unable to awaken others;
they fall into a succession of evil views and preach to the assembly, failing to properly understand all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics,
nor do they understand the phrasing and sentences— even though they claim to thoroughly understand all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics.
One who masters the chapters and verses and possesses the nature of the meaning can then delight themselves with the true joy of signlessness (*animitta*).
By establishing sentient beings in the equal Mahāyāna, one who possesses great wisdom (*mahāmatis*) embraces the Mahāyāna;
and by embracing the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, one embraces the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
To embrace all sentient beings is to embrace the True Dharma; to embrace the True Dharma is to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
To ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed is to be able to understand and attain the sublime place of entry.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who understands and attains this sublime place of entry will always attain birth by transformation and establish the ten self-natures of the Mahāyāna.
By means of power, manifesting various forms and images, one penetrates the physical types, aspirations, and afflictions of sentient beings to teach the Dharma according to reality.
That which is "according to reality" is not different from reality; that which is "according to reality" has no coming or going.
All falsehoods are stilled—this is called "according to reality. Mahāmati, sons and daughters of good family should not grasp at or adhere to what is said according to these descriptions.
Reality is free from names and designations;

therefore, one does not rely on words. This is because reliance on words not only obstructs the ultimate meaning for oneself, blocking the gate of self-realization, but also fails to clear away the thickets of ignorance in others, thereby preventing them from attaining awakening. True awakening arises precisely through one's own fundamental realization.
Failing to penetrate [the truth], one falls into wrong views and teaches the Dharma to the assembly based on one's own personal opinions.
One does not properly understand all the dharmas to be cultivated, all the stages to be realized, or all the characteristics to be abandoned;
nor does one understand the three types of phrases that express these meanings. Thus, if one cannot even awaken oneself, how can one awaken others? If one is skillful...
Having thoroughly understood all phenomena, all stages, and all characteristics, and having further attained mastery over the chapters and verses as they converge upon the ultimate nature—
which is inherently endowed with immeasurable wondrous meanings and does not rely on words—
one is then able to delight in the true formless bliss through the noble wisdom of self-realization; this is precisely the signless, equal Mahāyāna.
One who establishes sentient beings in this Dharma is called one who upholds the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
One who upholds the teachings of the Mahāyāna is able to uphold the four types of noble ones—the realized Dharma, the teaching Dharma, and so forth.
By upholding these four types of noble ones, one is able to transform that which arises and ceases into the non-arising and non-ceasing; therefore, one is able to uphold it.
If the six classes of ordinary beings can be gathered and led toward non-arising and non-ceasing, then all false and delusive phenomena will be unable to shake them;

thus they can gather and uphold the Tathāgata’s True Dharma. If they can gather and uphold the Tathāgata’s True Dharma, they can practice according to the teachings so that the Buddha-seed is not severed. As for "the Buddha-seed being not severed," it means:
One is able to be born into the family of the Tathāgatas; one understands the sublime points of entry and succeeds to the rank of the Buddha.
One who understands these sublime points of entry can manifest infinite bodies to transform all sentient beings and establish them in the Mahāyāna;
by means of the ten powers, they manifest various forms and images, penetrating the diverse physical types, the diverse inclinations, and the diverse aspirations of sentient beings.
One should teach the Dharma of reality as is appropriate for each affliction.

That which is called the "Dharma of reality" refers to the Dharma of equality and non-duality, the Dharma that neither comes nor goes. Because it quiets the empty and quiets the false, it is called "reality.
Therefore, one should embrace the Dharma of reality and should not embrace attachment to conventional descriptions; this is because of the true Dharma.
This is because it is fundamentally free from names and words.
Mahāmati, it is like a fool who, when pointed at an object by another with a finger, looks only at the finger and fails to grasp the actual reality of the object.

In this same way, fools follow the fingers of verbal expression, grasping and becoming attached to them, never relinquishing them until the end; thus, they can never attain that which transcends words.
Mahāmati, it is said that regarding the ultimate reality, it is like a small child who should eat food that has been cooked and should not eat raw food;
if he were to eat raw food, it would cause him to go mad because he does not know the sequential methods for cooking it.
Mahāmati, in the same way, that which is neither born nor extinguished is not wholesome if it is not cultivated through skillful means; therefore, one should cultivate skillful means well.
Do not follow after verbal expressions, just as one does not look at the tip of a finger; therefore, Mahāmati, you should skillfully cultivate the true meaning.

That which is the true meaning is subtle and tranquil, and it is the cause of nirvāṇa. Verbal expression is conjoined with false discrimination, and false discrimination is that which accumulates birth and death.
Mahāmati, the true meaning is obtained from those who have heard much. Mahāmati, "those who have heard much" refers to—
One who is skilled in the meaning, rather than merely skilled in verbal expression, does not fall into the scriptures and treatises of any non-Buddhist schools;
they do not follow them themselves, nor do they cause others to follow them. This is what is called being "virtuous and learned.

Therefore, those who seek the meaning should draw near to the learned—namely, those skilled in the meaning—and should avoid those who are the opposite, namely, those who are attached to mere verbal expression.
This is for the purpose of distancing [oneself from such views]. To clarify by means of an analogy why one should not grasp at or adhere to what is merely said:
it is like a fool who, unable to see an object, is pointed toward it by a finger; the fool looks only at the finger and does not look at the object.
In the end, they do not obtain the object; thus, these foolish people merely contemplate verbal expressions and, being attached to them, do not relinquish them.
They ultimately fail to see that which transcends verbal expression—the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Therefore, they are called "fools.
However, those who preach the Dharma should especially guide them according to their areas of clarity. For example, an infant should be fed cooked food and not [raw food].
If one eats raw food—that is, if one consumes living beings—it will inevitably cause madness, because one does not know the sequential skillful means for gradual ripening.
Likewise, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is neither born nor extinguished and is free from the characteristics of verbal expression;
yet, if the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of names and words are too ripe, and one does not gradually temper and ripen them through skillful means, one will become attached to them.
Yet, if one does not transform [the mind] and instead acts unskillfully, one must certainly employ the four kinds of skillful means to cause that [mind] to cultivate goodness thoroughly;

thus, the place of birth gradually matures, and from the matured state, birth gradually arises. Then, one will no longer follow mere verbal expressions, for it is like looking at the tip of a finger and failing to see the object itself.
Therefore, regarding the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), one should practice, but one should not be attached to verbal expressions. Furthermore, as for the truth...
The reason why the ultimate meaning (*tattvārtha*) should be cultivated is that this ultimate meaning—unborn, undying, subtle, and quiescent—is the direct cause of *nirvāṇa*.
Since the wondrous fruit of *nirvāṇa* cannot be realized apart from this, those who wish to realize the fruit of *nirvāṇa* must cultivate the ultimate meaning as the cause for *nirvāṇa*.
As for verbal expressions, one should not become attached to them.
This is because all verbal expression is conjoined with false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); since false conceptualization exists, one accumulates birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Thus, verbal expression is the cause of birth and death; therefore, those who wish to sever the cause of birth and death must take the severing of verbal expression as their foundation.
Furthermore, the true meaning (*tattvārtha*) is necessarily attained through extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), and "extensive learning" refers to hearing.
One contemplates, and through contemplation practices; through practice, one attains the single realization that hearing one thing is equivalent to hearing all things.

This is what is meant by a person of "virtuous meaning" (*śubhārtha*); it does not refer merely to words leaving the mouth and entering the ear. Therefore, a person of virtuous meaning is able to practice through personal application and is not swayed by the various sūtras and śāstras of external paths.
Not only do they themselves not follow the flow of verbal discourse, they do not cause others to do so either.
If a person merely follows the flow of words, they are called a "virtuous one of great learning" (*bahuśruta*);
therefore, those who seek the true meaning should draw near to such a virtuous one of great learning, for he is what is meant by "one skilled in the meaning.

If one speaks of emptiness with every word yet clings to existence in every thought, there is a discrepancy between name and reality; if one's speech and practice are at odds, then even if one possesses much learning, it is of no avail.
"One should remain far removed from that which is to be approached.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, further empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, there is nothing extraordinary about your teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is this? Because even all the external paths do not [acknowledge] causes..."
The Blessed One has taught that space (*ākāśa*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the realm of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇadhātu*) are neither born nor extinguished.

The Blessed One has also taught that the heterodox claim that causes give rise to the various worlds, whereas [he] teaches that ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), karma, and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) serve as conditions for the arising of the various worlds;
these are merely differences in names for those causes and conditions. External causes and conditions are likewise [the same].
In this way, there is not even a grain of difference between the World-Honored One’s discourse and that of the non-Buddhists;
for regarding these nine things—such as the Supreme Lord (Īśvara), the Self-Master (Puruṣa), and so forth—the non-Buddhists likewise assert that they are neither born nor extinguished.

The World-Honored One also teaches that all natures are neither born nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended. Furthermore, the non-Buddhists also assert that the four great elements are indestructible and that their intrinsic nature is neither born nor extinguished.
"The four great elements are always the four great elements, even as they circulate through the various realms of existence without abandoning their own nature;
the teaching of the World-Honored One is likewise so. Therefore, I say there is nothing extraordinary about it.

I only wish that the World-Honored One would explain the distinction by which it is extraordinary and surpasses all non-Buddhists; for if there were no extraordinariness, then all non-Buddhists would also be [the same]."
Because the Buddha is neither born nor extinguished, the World-Honored One has declared that it is impossible for many Buddhas to appear in a single world-system, as was previously stated;
for if there were many Buddhas in one world-system, they would be indistinguishable from one another.
Previously, because you identified non-arising and non-ceasing as annihilationism, you did not allow it to be a synonym for the Tathāgata;
this conception takes non-arising and non-ceasing to be a "death-permanence" (a permanent state after death) and conflates them with the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

Therefore, it is said that what the World-Honored One taught regarding non-arising and non-ceasing possesses no extraordinary quality. Thus, each point is recounted in succession to question you: first, there is the calculation of the non-Buddhists.

The agent is the cause by which all phenomena arise and cease, yet the agent itself neither arises nor ceases. This non-arising and non-ceasing is no different from the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) taught by the Blessed One.

Second, the non-Buddhists reckon that the principle of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), through the causal conditions of the combination of the three qualities (*guṇas*), gives rise to all sentient beings;
this is also the same as what the Blessed One teaches regarding birth through the causal conditions of ignorance, karma, and craving.
In all worlds there is no difference; it is only because of those causes and conditions that names differ while the reality remains the same.

Whether it be the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense-bases (*āyatana*), or even various external objects such as jars, clothing, grain, or grass—all must arise by depending on causes and conditions.
Thus, the causes and conditions taught by the Blessed One and those spoken of in the treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are not at all different.
The third difference is that the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon nine things—such as atoms, time, space, atoms, the great elements, Brahmā, Viśeṣa, Mahādeva, Īśvara, and the Self—as creators;
they are all collectively termed "creators" and are held to be neither born nor extinguished.
This is no different from the World-Honored One’s teaching that all natures are neither born nor extinguished. The fourth [difference] refers to the non-Buddhists...

If one calculates that the four great elements do not perish but circulate through the various realms of existence without abandoning their own nature, this is no different from what the World-Honored One has taught regarding the true nature of the four great elements being real and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. Thus, what the World-Honored One says is identical to what those non-Buddhists say;
what is so extraordinary or superior about it that it excels that of the non-Buddhists? We only pray that you will explain for us what is truly extraordinary.
If there were no distinction between them, then even non-Buddhists would all be Buddhas, for they equally realize that which is neither born nor extinguished.
World-Honored One, you have previously stated that there are not many Buddhas in a single world-system.
Furthermore, as previously explained, "neither born nor extinguished" is another name for the Tathāgata; now, you again enumerate thirty-two distinct titles. Now...
If it were said that non-Buddhists are the same as the Tathāgata, then there would be many Buddhas in a single world-system;
would this not be truly extraordinary?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The 'non-arising and non-ceasing' that I teach is not the same as the 'non-arising and non-ceasing' of the non-Buddhists; therefore [it is not the same]."
Why is this? Those various non-Buddhists maintain that there is a self-nature (*svabhāva*) which is unarisen and immutable;

I do not hold such a view, as I would fall into the categories of existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, my "self" is free from the categories of existence and non-existence, and free from arising and ceasing;

it is neither a nature nor a lack of nature, because it manifests like various illusions and dreams. It is not a lack of nature. Why is it not a lack of nature? Because form possesses the characteristic of being without self-nature.
Because they encompass both the manifest and the unmanifest, and because they encompass both the grasped and the ungrasped, all natures are neither existent nor non-existent;
rather, it is simply the manifestation of one’s own mind. When false discrimination does not arise, there is peace and happiness, and worldly affairs are forever stilled.
The activities of deluded ordinary people are the products of unreal discrimination, like a city of the *gandharvas*, whereas this is not the case for the noble ones.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is like a conjured person, a city of the Gandharvas, or various beings created by magic;
foolish people, through their deluded imaginings, claim there is real coming and going, yet in reality there is no one who comes or goes—it is merely due to those deluded imaginings.
In this same way, Mahāmati, ignorant ordinary people give rise to the confusion of birth and non-birth, and they likewise [err].
There is no such thing as a conditioned or unconditioned being born from illusion; in reality, there is neither birth nor cessation, because their nature is non-existent and they possess nothing.

All phenomena are likewise thus, free from arising and ceasing. Foolish ordinary beings fall into the false view of arising and ceasing by giving rise to deluded conceptualizations that do not accord with reality;
this is not the case for the noble ones, who do not perceive things as they are not. It is according to their true nature.

The conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) is not different [from it]. If it were different from conceptualization, one would be attached to all things as having an intrinsic nature;

failing to see tranquility, and failing to see tranquility, one would never be free from conceptualization. Therefore, Mahāmati, the vision of signlessness (*animitta-darśana*) is superior, not the vision of signs (*nimitta-darśana*).
Signs are the cause for the taking up of birth; therefore, they are not superior. Mahāmati, signlessness is not conceptualization.
“Mahāmati, I teach that Nirvāṇa is the non-arising and non-ceasing of birth. Mahāmati, as for this Nirvāṇa: it is seeing according to the true meaning;
