it is being free from the prior deluded thoughts of the mind and mental factors; it is attaining the noble self-realized wisdom of the Tathāgatas. This, I say, is Nirvāṇa.”
The Buddha said to me: "My teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing is not the same as the non-arising and impermanence theories of the non-Buddhists.
Why is this? What the non-Buddhists conceive of as non-arising and non-ceasing is that all phenomena possess a substantial essence that neither arises nor changes;
they call this 'dead permanence. Though they claim it is unchanging, in reality it falls into nihilism. I do not teach such a thing."
Thus, what I have taught is that phenomena follow conditions without changing, and do not change while following conditions;

they are free from existence and free from non-existence, and free from arising and ceasing. This is not the teaching that things possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or lack intrinsic nature. Why is it not "without nature"?
Because they manifest like illusions and dreams. Why is it not "with nature"? Because all phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, lack the characteristic of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, there is neither the characteristic of the grasper nor the grasped; they are like illusions and dreams. Although they appear, they have never truly appeared;
although they are grasped, they have never truly been grasped. Therefore, I say that all dharmas are free from existence and free from non-existence.

One should simply realize that all dharmas are manifestations of one's own mind, like the moon in water or a reflection in a mirror, fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent. Do not [cling to them].

Because all phenomena arise from the view of existence and non-existence, when deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise, one immediately attains the bliss of peaceful extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), and worldly affairs are forever stilled.

What, then, would there be that is not liberated? Those various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), failing to realize their own minds and being deluded regarding all phenomena, engage in various activities through deluded conceptualization; they are attached to and grasp at [theories of] non-arising and non-cessation.

Transformation is not [the domain] of the noble ones (ārya), because they regard what is unreal as real through false conceptualization (vikalpa), and they falsely regard cessation and permanence as non-transformation.

They do not understand that the objects perceived by false conceptualization—such as the appearance of conjured people in a city of the Gandharvas, or the coming and going of merchants—are merely the false conceptualizations of fools; they are said to truly come and go, yet in reality, there is no such thing.
There are those who enter and those who emerge; yet they merely cling to their own false imaginings, taking them to be the marks of the unarisen and the immutable.
How could they know that what they conceive as "unarisen" and "immutable" refers to such things as the *puruṣa* (Self), atoms (*paramāṇu*), or the *pradhāna* (Primal Nature)?
Furthermore, they conceive of *pradhāna* as the creator, whereas the *puruṣa* is not the creator.
This experiencer is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not know that; furthermore, there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned.

Just as one might conceive of an illusory person who has birth and cessation, yet in reality such birth or cessation does not exist—because both existence by nature and non-existence by nature are unattainable—so it is with all phenomena: they are likewise devoid of [birth and cessation].

Ignorant ordinary beings, deluded regarding arising and ceasing, do not see their own minds as they truly are; falling into what is unreal, they give rise to the false discrimination of arising and ceasing.

Therefore, know that it is not only those who calculate arising and ceasing who are subject to arising and ceasing—those who calculate non-arising and non-ceasing are likewise subject to arising and ceasing.
All of these are the inverted discriminations of fools; how could they belong to the noble ones?

This refers to those noble ones and sages who, having realized the true state of what appears to their own minds as mere mental construction (*cittadṛśya-mātra*), are not deluded by illusory phenomena;
therefore, they are called "wise. Those who fall into unreal conceptualization (*ayoniśo-vikalpa*) are not so;

for they claim there exists a self-nature (*svabhāva*) that is unarisen and immutable, which they believe to be distinct from the conceptualization of arising and ceasing. Yet they do not realize what it is they are calculating.
That which is unborn and undying is not different from the deluded thoughts of birth and death. If, because the self-nature of things is unborn and unchanging—
distinct from the deluded thoughts of birth and death— one clings to all self-natures as being unborn and undying,
one fails to realize that this very moment of clinging does not perceive the original quiescence of all phenomena.

This is the characteristic of tranquility. Because they do not perceive the characteristic of tranquility, although they claim to have attained the characteristic of non-arising and immutability, they ultimately do not transcend the deluded conceptualization of arising and ceasing.

Therefore, know that seeing original tranquility and not perceiving the characteristics of a self-nature or inherent nature is called the vision of signlessness; it is superior and not like being attached to all phenomena as truly existent.
"Self-nature" refers to that which does not perceive what is originally quiescent; this is a comparison.

To speak according to reality, if one perceives a mark of non-arising and non-ceasing, this is the cause of birth and death, not true non-arising and non-ceasing, and because one does not attain nirvana, it is not superior.
If one does not perceive a mark of non-arising and non-ceasing, this is deluded imagination.
Because quiescence is not a cause for rebirth, I call it true *nirvāṇa*. That which is called *nirvāṇa* refers to seeing all phenomena as they truly are:

being originally quiescent, free from the deluded thoughts of non-Buddhists, and having attained the realm of the Tathāgata’s noble self-realized wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). This realm of noble wisdom is the foremost.
"The ultimate truth of the meaning that I have taught is this: Nirvana. If it is that which is grasped by outsiders as having characteristics or views, it is a false imagination and not Nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "He eliminates their theories of arising and establishes [the truth]."
I teach this Dharma of non-arising, which the foolish cannot understand: that all phenomena are unarisen, without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and non-existent.
Like a *gandharva-city*, a magical illusion, or a dream, they have no intrinsic nature; being without cause, they do not arise. Why are they empty? I shall explain:
because they are free from conjunction, the nature of cognition does not manifest; therefore, I teach that they are empty and unarisen.
"Absence of intrinsic nature" means that the nature of each individual and their combination appears yet does not exist;

when analyzed, there is no combination, and it is not like the views of the non-Buddhists regarding dreams, floating hairs, mirages, or the various worldly phenomena of the *gandharva* city, which appear with characteristics despite lacking a cause.
This refutes those who argue for a cause and elucidates the meaning of non-arising. To elucidate non-arising is the flow of the Dharma.
This verse eternally severs the blazing terror of the non-causalists (ahetuvāda) among the various heterodox schools.
This establishment of "non-arising" by the Tathāgata differs from the "non-arising" of the heterodox schools;
for while those heterodox schools falsely cling to various causes of arising, [the Buddha] establishes non-arising both to refute their tenets and to establish his own.
In my own school, I teach that such dharmas can only be clearly understood by the noble ones (*ārya*) and cannot be known by ordinary, deluded people.
The reason for establishing "non-arising" is to refute the two types of conceptualization regarding existence and non-existence.
Since all phenomena are like cities of the *gandharvas*, dreams, and illusions, they are not without nature; therefore, I speak of them as being "without nature."
All that exists is non-existent and thus does not arise, because all phenomena lack the nature of existence (*bhāva*).
To speak of the nature of existence is to speak of something without cause; and that which is without cause likewise does not arise.

Now, since it has been stated that there is no arising and no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) is further spoken of—what is the reason for this? I shall explain it to you: it is because of those very phenomena.

Because the nature of conceptualization regarding the causes and conditions of conjunction no longer arises once one is free from them, it is said that emptiness is non-arising, and non-arising is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The reason for this lack of intrinsic nature is that all phenomena exist through the conjunction of causes and conditions;
if each is analyzed individually, none possess an intrinsic nature, and thus there is truly no such thing as a conjunction.
Unlike the non-Buddhists who falsely calculate that the twenty-three phenomena arise from the union of the primal nature (*prakṛti*) and the three qualities (*guṇas*),
and thus regard them as substantially existent, I teach that they are like dreams, illusions, falling hairs, mirages, and cities of the Gandharvas;
these metaphors illustrate that the things produced by causes and conditions in the world are fundamentally without intrinsic nature and are all empty.
Consequently, false appearances manifest of their own accord: first, to subdue the various causes of birth asserted by non-Buddhists;
second, to expound the meaning of the non-arising of my own school. If one expounds the meaning of my own school, it ensures that the flow of the Dharma will never be severed;
if one terrifies the non-Buddhists, it prevents them from daring to falsely establish their own erroneous causes. Therefore, that which I have taught is "non-existent."
Therefore, causes are identical in their path and course with emptiness, non-arising, and the lack of intrinsic nature;

they are not two different things. At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse: "What is it? What is its cause? By what reason does it arise? From where does it come? How do these combine to form the doctrine of no-cause?

At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse, observing conditioned phenomena: [The verse follows: "Conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a mirage, a reflection, and a city of the gandharvas. (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly after the introduction to the verse on conditioned phenomena. The translation reflects this.)
The Dharma is not without cause; the views of those who propound arising and ceasing based on causes are thereby extinguished.

The World-Honored One established the doctrine of non-arising (*anutpāda*) in order to refute the various causes of arising held by the heterodox (*tīrthika*), and he further spoke of the "blazing" doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*) in order to eliminate the various causes of arising held by the heterodox. Mahāmati, this is correct.

Fearing that this might be confused with the causeless theories of the non-Buddhists, he asked him: "All phenomena arise only because they have a cause, because they have a reason, and because they have a condition for their conjunction.
Why do you propound a theory of causelessness regarding that which has a cause, a reason, and a condition for its conjunction?
Does this not result in the doctrine of annihilationism? The Buddha replied: "I speak of 'causelessness' [in the sense that] I say..."
This is not the same as the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) doctrines of causality or non-causality based on the duality of arising and ceasing;
it is the refutation of both causality and non-causality, for all such views of arising and ceasing are entirely devoid of a true cause.
When I speak of "non-causality," I mean the extinguishing of the views of arising and ceasing—how could this possibly be compared to the non-causality of the non-Buddhists?
At that time, Mahāmati spoke in verse, asking: "What is meant by 'non-arising'? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature?
Or is it because one observes various conditions that a phenomenon is called 'non-arising'? This name should not be without meaning; please explain it for the sake of our discernment."

At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse: "It is not that there is no nature, nor is it that there is no arising; Nor is it that one looks toward various conditions, nor is it that there is a nature.
It is called 'name' though it is not a name, and it is not without meaning. This is not the realm of any outsiders, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, nor of those in the seventh stage.
This is called the mark of non-arising: it is far removed from all causes and conditions, and detached from all phenomena; there is only..."
When the subtle mind abides, both the perceiver and the perceived are abandoned; its body undergoes transformation, and I call this "non-arising.
There is no external nature, nor is there the absence of nature, nor is there any mental grasping. Having severed all views, I call this "non-arising.
Thus, one should distinguish non-self-nature, emptiness, and so forth: it is called empty because it is not empty, and it is called empty because it is non-arising.
At first, Mahāmati took non-arising (*anutpāda*) to mean the absence of phenomena (*abhāva*) and total annihilation; the World-Honored One answered that it is simply another name for the Tathāgata.
Later, Mahāmati took non-arising to mean the existence of phenomena (*bhāva*) and eternalism (*śāśvata*);

therefore, he answered by emphasizing the excellence of the signless (*animitta-darśana*). Because his doubts remained divided between these two paths, he asked again: "Ultimately, what is non-arising?"
Regarding the meaning [of "non-arising"]: do you mean that all phenomena necessarily lack intrinsic nature and are therefore exclusively non-existent, which is called "non-arising"?
Or do you mean that upon examining the various conditions, one finds they are not exclusively non-existent, yet there exists a distinct dharma named "non-arising"?

Since whatever has a name must have a meaning, where does this meaning reside? The Buddha said: "If it were the case that being exclusively devoid of intrinsic nature constitutes 'non-arising,' then..."
If one falls into the view of annihilation by observing that there is a separate dharma called "non-arising" among all conditions, then one falls into the view of eternalism.
When I speak of non-arising, it is not a lack of nature, nor is it a nature of existence; it is not even the meaning of non-existence. Yet they recklessly utter this name.
This meaning of non-arising is something that all non-Buddhists, followers of the Lesser Vehicle, and Bodhisattvas up to the seventh stage have not yet transcended.

The mind, thought, and consciousness are all unable to know this; only Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward—who have abandoned the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and have realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—are able to know its realm.
Because the characteristic of non-arising can be attained, it is named "non-arising. What is called the characteristic of non-arising refers to the eighth stage, which is free from the mind.

When all mundane and supramundane phenomena arising from causal conditions cease and no longer function, there remains only the subtle and wondrous true mind, revealed alone and distinct, with nothing else existing;
furthermore, both the perceiving subject and the perceived object are transcended.
One awakens to the self-nature of dharmas and attains the body born of intention (*manomaya-kāya*), moving everywhere without obstruction. This is what I call the oneness of body and mind.

This is non-arising (*anutpāda*). Furthermore, when one perceives all phenomena as being like a city of the *gandharvas* or a mirage and realizes the *māyopama-samādhi*, one does not perceive the two objects—existence and non-existence—as external objects of apprehension (*grāhya*), nor does one perceive the two minds—existence and non-existence—as internal subjects of apprehension (*grāhaka*).
Because all conceptual views and the false self have been severed, I say this is non-arising. Since it is non-existent...
When the meaning of arising is analyzed in this way, there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is likewise analyzed in this manner.
It is not that emptiness is taught because all phenomena are annihilated; rather, emptiness is taught because of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Nor is it that the absence of intrinsic nature is taught because all phenomena are annihilated; the absence of intrinsic nature is taught because of non-arising. This, then, is non-arising.
Meaning (*artha*) is precisely suchness (*tathatā*); how could it be like the annihilationism or non-arising of the non-Buddhists?
When the collection of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-saṃkhyā*) comes together, there is arising and ceasing; apart from these various causal conditions, there is no separate arising or ceasing.
To abandon the collection of causal conditions and claim there is a different nature is the false imagination (*parikalpa*) of the non-Buddhists, whether one speaks of identity or difference.

That which has the nature of existence or non-existence is not produced, being neither existent nor non-existent; apart from these numerical designations and their transformations, nothing at all can be apprehended.
There are only conventional designations that link together like a chain; apart from that causal chain, the meaning of production cannot be found.

Since production lacks intrinsic nature and does not arise, it is free from the errors of the non-Buddhists. Yet, when one speaks only of this causal chain, the foolish and ignorant are unable to comprehend it.
This clarifies that both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing are due to causes and conditions.
The causal laws of the world consist of twelve links, namely from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

If ignorance arises, the succession of conditions is not severed, and thus there is birth; if ignorance ceases, all conditions are detached, and thus there is cessation. This, then, is arising-and-ceasing.
All things arise solely through causes and conditions. If one were to abandon causes and conditions, there would be no other distinct phenomena for arising and ceasing.

If one were to claim that there is a phenomenon of arising distinct from these causes and conditions—such as the Sāṃkhya school’s calculation that the producer and the produced are identical, or the Vaiśeṣika school’s calculation that the producer and the produced are different—all such views fall into the deluded imaginings of non-Buddhists. Therefore, know this:

All worldly phenomena cannot arise from that which has an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor can they arise from that which lacks an intrinsic nature, nor from that which is neither existent nor non-existent, nor from that which is both existent and non-existent.

Apart from the transformations, arising, and ceasing within the enumeration of the twelve links of dependent origination, no further characteristic of arising and ceasing can be found; therefore, it is said that the characteristics of arising and ceasing merely follow worldly convention.
To speak metaphorically according to the truth, the twelve links of dependent origination arise and perish in succession like hooks and chains, forming an unbroken circle.
If one were to depart from these worldly causes and conditions, then every phenomenon would be liberated and there would be no mutual interaction;
how then could arising and perishing be found? Therefore, what I have taught—that dependent origination is without intrinsic nature and has never arisen—is not something separate [from reality].

The teaching of "arising" is intended to manifest "non-arising," precisely in order to distance oneself from the errors of the non-Buddhists who hold that there is arising and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If one were to speak only of the interlocking chain of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) without mentioning that what arises through conditions is devoid of intrinsic nature, how could those ordinary and deluded beings understand that causes and conditions are themselves non-arising, and that non-arising is itself causes and conditions? Thus, one should know that arising and ceasing...

Neither arising nor ceasing is ever apart from the principle of dependent origination; therefore it is said that all phenomena arise by way of causes and conditions, and all phenomena do not arise by way of causes and conditions.
If there were a nature of arising that existed apart from the chain of conditions, then it would follow the doctrine of causelessness, which destroys the meaning of the chain of conditions.

Just as a lamp reveals various forms when the chain of conditions is present, if this were so, then apart from the chain of conditions, there would be no further natures or non-natures, and no arising, being like the self-nature of empty space. Apart from the chain of conditions, wisdom has nothing to differentiate.
Furthermore, there is another non-arising dharma attained by the noble ones; that which arises as non-arising is the patience toward non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
If one causes all those in the world to observe the hook and the chain, they will all be freed from the hook and the chain, and from this they shall attain samādhi.

If one were to posit a cause of production distinct from the chain of dependent origination—such as a supreme, subtle atom (*paramāṇu*)—then one would fall into the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*) and destroy the meaning of the chain.

For example, just as a lamp’s light can reveal various forms, one should know that the manifestation of the body and its objects through the chain is likewise so; it cannot be revealed apart from the lamp.
Furthermore, it would follow that the various images could exist as distinct natures apart from the hook-and-chain [of causes and conditions].

Therefore, when I speak of the "theory of causelessness," I mean that it destroys the principle of the hook-and-chain. One should establish the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is all internal and external phenomena; the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they arise through conditions.
The reason (*hetu*) is: because the hook-and-chain is manifest. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like a lamp illuminating an image. If these were to exist apart from the hook-and-chain...

To assert that the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) constitutes non-arising (*anutpāda*), such that its self-nature is like empty space, is to fall into the partial emptiness of the Two Vehicles;

for this is a wisdom of non-arising sought apart from the "hook-and-chain" [interdependent] method, and thus cannot be taken as an object of cognition. Therefore, one should formulate the following formal inference (*pramāṇa*):
**Thesis:** All phenomena have existence as their subject matter, yet they lack intrinsic nature. **Reason:** Because they are without arising. **Example:** Like [the case of] empty space.
It is like space; beyond this, there is nothing further that is "unborn. This is the dharma attained by the Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sanctity.

Because they are able to penetrate that dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature, arising itself is non-arising; this is the true patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
It is said that there is only the subtle mind, wherein both the perceiver and the perceived are entirely transcended. Indeed, it is external...
The Way takes various causes to destroy the hook and the chain, yet it does not realize that all phenomena in the world are nothing other than hooks and chains;

they cannot be destroyed because they take [these conditions] as their cause. The foolish practitioners of the Two Vehicles desire to leave behind the hook and the chain to seek quiescence, yet they do not know that seeking quiescence while remaining apart from the hook and the chain is not the Great Samādhi. If one were to cause the entire world to be like the Worthy One...

The Noble Contemplation of the Hook and Chain: To realize that the twelve links of dependent origination are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature is to be within the hook and chain yet detached from the hook and chain, not being bound by the hook and chain.
From this, one attains samādhi and realizes non-arising, such that one may gallop alongside the worthy sages.
Ignorance, craving, various karmas, and so forth are called "internal hooks, locks, drills, fire-sticks, lumps of clay, wheels, seeds," and the like.
If there were another nature that arose from causes and conditions, it would not possess the meaning of a "hook" or "lock"; thus, it would not be established.
If that which arises lacks intrinsic nature, for whom would there be a hook or lock? Since they arise through mutual succession, one should understand the meaning of causes and conditions.

The phenomena of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion give rise to false conceptualizations in the ignorant; apart from these enumerations, there is no distinct dharma, which is what is meant by "the absence of intrinsic nature.

Just as a physician has no fixed theory regarding various ailments but prescribes diverse treatments according to the differences in the diseases, I likewise destroy the various afflictions for those sentient beings;
knowing the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, I preach to them the gateways of liberation.
It is not that because the roots of affliction differ there are various distinct dharmas; rather, the teaching of the Single Vehicle alone is the Mahāyāna.

What is called the "hook-and-chain" has both an internal and an external aspect: the internal hook-and-chain refers to the cycle through the three periods of time driven by ignorance, karma, and craving;
the external refers to such processes as obtaining fire by drilling wood, a lump of clay becoming a jar, or a seed producing a sprout.

If sprouts were to arise not with the hook and the clasp as their conditions, but rather with other natures as their conditions, then a tinder-igniter could produce sprouts and a seed could become a jar; birth, aging, sickness, and death would not arise from ignorance and craving.
Yet these things do not accord with the principle of the hook and the clasp; by what cause, then, could they be established?
Therefore, those doctrines asserting that things arise without cause are all mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

If one were to claim that all phenomena arise without cause and lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), then everyone would attain liberation; for whom, then, would there be a binding chain from which they could not be liberated?
That they do not attain liberation is entirely due to the successive arising of ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
One should know that the non-ceasing of saṃsāra is precisely the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); who could say it is without cause?

As for solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, the ignorant and deluded falsely imagine them to be the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and take them to be the causes of birth, thinking they can produce the four great elements.
Yet, when one examines these conditions, they are all found to lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). One fails to realize that these dharmas of the four great elements...
The water element arises from the false imagination of moisture; the fire element arises from the false imagination of capability for heating;
the earth element arises from the false imagination of cutting and severing; and the wind element arises from the false imagination of blowing and moving.

Thus, apart from these enumerated conditions, there is no other distinct phenomenon that serves as a cause of production. If there were a distinct phenomenon existing apart from these enumerated phenomena that served as a cause of production, [it would be untenable].
This would be the doctrine of annihilationism and the theory of causelessness; therefore, the establishment of non-arising has many meanings and is not without purpose.
First, it is non-arising by virtue of causes and conditions, which serves to refute the externalists' [notion of] a cause of arising.

Second, it is non-arising by virtue of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which serves to refute the externalists' calculation that the four great elements each possess their own intrinsic nature.
Third, because all things are empty, they do not arise; thus, views such as existence and non-existence, or identity and difference, are refuted.
For example, when a physician treats various illnesses, there is originally no manifold of theoretical discourse; rather, because illnesses differ, the methods of treatment also differ.
In the same way, I eliminate the disease of afflictions for sentient beings, distinguishing between the coarse and subtle levels of those afflictions.
Because there are differences in the superiority or inferiority of their faculties and dispositions, I teach them emptiness, non-arising, and the absence of self-nature to deliver them;
yet, it is not that the faculties and dispositions of afflictions truly have distinctions, nor is it that there truly exist various distinct remedial dharmas.
I simply use the dharma of the One Vehicle—emptiness, lack of nature, and non-arising—to guide sentient beings into [enlightenment].
"The patience regarding non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) is precisely what is called the Mahāyāna Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists give rise to the false discrimination of impermanence;
yet the World-Honored One also says that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent and are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing. What is the meaning of this?"
"What is meant by the heterodox and the orthodox? And how many kinds of impermanence are there? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All non-Buddhists maintain seven kinds of impermanence, which do not belong to my Dharma. What are the seven? Some among them say that once something has been created, it is then abandoned;
this is called impermanence. Some say that the destruction of form and location is impermanence. Some say that form itself is impermanence."

Some maintain that the state of transformation within form (*rūpa*) is called impermanence (*anitya*); others say it is the immediate disintegration of the thing itself, like the transformation of milk into curd, which cannot be seen during the interval.
Some say that all natures (*svabhāva*) undergo transformation through destruction; some say that nature itself is impermanent;
some say that the non-existence of nature is impermanent; and some say that the non-arising of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-anutpāda*) is impermanence, entering into oneness.
"All phenomena.
This means that because this cause is neither born nor extinguished, it consequently reaches [the state of] birth, extinction, and impermanence.

The intent is that since what the World-Honored One has taught regarding non-arising and non-extinction differs from that of the non-Buddhists, then all the various phenomena that the World-Honored One habitually teaches—

The practice of impermanence is a phenomenon of arising and ceasing; as for what is false and what is correct regarding the impermanence taught by non-Buddhists, and how many kinds of impermanence are there among the calculations of those non-Buddhists?

World-Honored One, you have briefly enumerated seven kinds of impermanence calculated by non-Buddhists, none of which are the characteristics of destruction or non-destruction spoken of in my teaching, as they merely revolve around one another.
When the cause perishes and the effect arises, and when the effect arises and the cause perishes, they are equal in their momentary rise and fall like the two ends of a scale;
this is impermanence (*anityatā*). Some say that to act and then abandon it is called impermanence—this reckons the agent as being impermanent.
Others say that the destruction of form and location is called impermanence. Still others say that form itself is impermanence.

All these [views] reckon that the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is impermanent, yet they are fundamentally unable to empty the four great elements themselves.
There are those who say that the "intermediate state" during the transformation of matter is called impermanent;

this means they reckon that while there exists something unchanging within the transformation of matter, both the primary producers (*bhūta*) and the derived products (*bhautika*) are permanent, with only a certain "impermanence" existing between the two states of matter.

The nature [of phenomena] causes the continuity of two colors to undergo transformation and disintegrate of its own accord, just as milk turns into curd, or wine and fruit undergo maturation and change;
yet, because they lack shape and cannot be perceived, they are said to be impermanent and to destroy all natures.
This is precisely because the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) is a subtle, profound, and hidden flux that cannot be fathomed, and is therefore invisible.

They reckon that within the intermediate state of the *tattva* of darkness (*mūla-tattva*), the continuity of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) remains uninterrupted, and they reckon this to be the divine self (*puruṣa*).
It is like a person who goes from youth to maturity, and from maturity to old age; although there is a constant flux from moment to moment, one does not perceive it oneself.
This is what is meant by the saying: "A strong man carries one on his back as he runs, yet the deluded do not realize it. There are those who say that the nature [of things] is impermanent.
This calculation posits that there is a self-nature of impermanence (*anityatā-svabhāva*) which is indestructible yet capable of destroying all natures;

it is said that this is what constitutes decay and killing, rather than being subject to decay and killing itself. Some speak of impermanence as both nature and non-nature, meaning that both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived elements (*bhautika*) are equally impermanent.
Others say that the impermanence of the non-arising of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-anutpāda*) enters into a single [principle].
As for all dharmas, this [view] calculates that arising and non-arising are two distinct poles;

it fails to realize that cessation is itself arising, and falsely claims that within the dharmas of arising and ceasing there exists something that neither arises nor ceases. That which is called "non-arising" is precisely that which is able to give rise to arising.

"Mahāmati, 'the impermanence of the non-existence of the nature of the great elements' refers to the destruction of the specific characteristics of the four great elements and their derivatives. The self-nature of the four great elements cannot be apprehended;
that they do not arise is what is meant by 'non-arising impermanence. This is not the impermanence of cessation; it is the fact that all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—do not arise.
Even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom (*paramāṇu*), nothing can be seen. This is the meaning of 'non-arising'; it is not arising, and this is its name."
If one does not realize that there is no characteristic of impermanence in arising, one falls into the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) view of the meaning of "arising-impermanence.
Since the seven types of impermanence held by non-Buddhists do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, the two types of annihilationism are mentioned first.
Regarding "nature and lack of nature" (svabhāva-asvabhāva), the Chinese translation says "thing and non-thing," referring to the things that create and the things that are created.
The self-nature of things perishes along with them: once the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) have produced derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), their own substance has already perished;

and since that which is derived is fundamentally not the four great elements, it likewise perishes along with them. Just as when a seed produces a sprout, both the seed and the sprout perish together, so too the nature of the four great elements cannot be found.
Since both nature and characteristics are non-existent, one knows that there is no arising. This is by way of nature.
To say that the cessation of characteristics constitutes non-arising, and that this non-arising impermanence enters into all phenomena—this is not the teaching of the Noble Ones.
It refers to the fact that both the permanent and the impermanent are equally non-arising.

They claim there is a certain "non-arising impermanence" that pervades all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, even when analyzing all phenomena as being either existent or non-existent. Until... [the analysis reaches its limit].
That even within a minute atom it cannot be seen is the meaning of its non-arising.
Because when all phenomena are analyzed, not even a hair’s breadth of a characteristic of arising can be found, this is called the characteristic of non-arising impermanence.
My disciples within the inner teaching should know that this "non-arising" is itself arising, for what they conceive as this non-arising impermanence is capable of producing [phenomena].
All phenomena of existence and non-existence are "non-arising" only in relation to "arising"; this is not a non-arising that transcends both existence and non-existence.
Therefore it is said: "If one does not awaken to this, one falls into the view of arising and impermanence."

Mahāmati, that which is called the impermanence of the intrinsic nature of great elements is merely the false discrimination of one's own mind; it is not the case that the intrinsic nature itself is impermanent.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of impermanence is indestructible. Mahāmati, this refers to the fact that all things are devoid of intrinsic nature due to impermanence.
Apart from impermanence, there is nothing else capable of rendering the intrinsic nature of all dharmas non-existent, such as a staff, a tile, or a stone that destroys various objects.
When things are perceived as appearing individually without distinction, this nature is impermanent; yet there is a difference between the entity and that which is produced by action.
This is impermanence; this is the entity produced by action. If there were no difference between the producer and the produced, then all natures would be eternal and without cause.

Mahāmati, that all natures are without intrinsic being yet arise from causes is not something known by ordinary, ignorant people; for it is not the case that dissimilar things are produced from non-causes.
If that which arises were such that all natures (*bhāva*) were entirely impermanent, this would be an inconsistent state:

there would be no distinction between the cause (*kāraṇa*) and the effect (*kārya*), yet they are both seen to be distinct. If nature were impermanent, it would fall into the category of being a causal nature (*kāraṇa-bhāva-lakṣaṇa*).

If it were to fall [into that], then all natures would not be ultimate; and if all natures fell into the characteristic of being a causal nature, then that which is itself impermanent should likewise be impermanent.

Because impermanence is itself impermanent, all natures (*dharmas*) would not be impermanent and should therefore be permanent. If impermanence were to enter into all natures, it would fall within the three periods of time;
for past form is co-existent with destruction, future form does not arise because it has not yet arisen, and present form is co-existent with the characteristic of destruction.
Form is a specific accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), consisting of the four great elements and their derivatives (*upādāya-rūpa*).
The intrinsic nature of form is indestructible, because it is free from being either different or non-different. Therefore, for all non-Buddhists, none of the four great elements are ever destroyed.
Furthermore, the four great elements and their derivative forms within the three realms of existence exist among the objects of knowledge as having arising and ceasing.

Apart from these four great elements and their derivative forms, what is there for all non-Buddhists to contemplate? Since the nature of the four great elements is impermanent, they do not arise; their self-nature and characteristics are non-existent.
Because it is subject to destruction.
This [view] conceives that the created is impermanent while the creator is permanent. Regarding the nature of impermanence, the Wei translation says:
"It is called impermanent because there is no substance. This is a false imagination of one's own mind, which falsely [perceives] that which is neither permanent nor impermanent.
When one considers all phenomena, it is not that impermanence exists within them as a distinct entity that causes phenomena to perish;

rather, it is the very nature of impermanence itself that remains unimpaired. This nature of impermanence is capable of bringing about the destruction and cessation of all phenomena as impermanent events.
If this nature of impermanence were removed, there would be nothing capable of causing all phenomena to reach destruction and cessation, just as [there would be no effect] without a staff.
Just as a hammer, stone, or other such objects can destroy various things while their own substance remains undestroyed, this nature of impermanence is likewise.

This is precisely what the Sāṃkhya school posits regarding the distinction between the primary cause (*pradhāna*) and its evolutes (*vikāra*). One should formulate the formal argument (*prayoga*) as follows:
**Thesis:** The nature of impermanence is indestructible. **Reason:** Because it destroys various objects. **Example:** Like a staff or a hammer.
Because the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that the potsherd and the stone are distinct from the external object, the Blessed One refuted this by stating they are not distinct.
If the nature of impermanence were capable of destroying all phenomena, then that destructive nature and the phenomena destroyed would necessarily be distinct;
however, we currently perceive that each is not distinct, and we do not observe any difference between the nature of impermanence and the various objects it destroys.
If there were indeed a distinction between them, one should be able to point out clearly that "this is the impermanence of the agent" and "this is the impermanent thing produced by it.

However, this is not the case; they cannot be said to be different. If one claims that the agent and the produced object are not different, then both the agent and the produced object must all be eternal, for one does not perceive any cause for their impermanence.
Because the nature [of things] destroys all entities, the thesis that the nature of impermanence acts as the cause [for that destruction] is not established;
thus, it is said that no dharma is seen to be able to render other dharmas impermanent.
Nevertheless, for all dharmas, whether they possess an intrinsic nature or lack one, their arising and destruction truly have causes, for they arise when conditions converge.
When conditions disperse, things perish; this is simply beyond the comprehension of the ordinary and foolish. Therefore, the Tang translation states:
"The disintegration and extinction of all phenomena truly have causes. Furthermore, where there is a cause, there must be an effect; cause and effect are necessarily similar.
If an effect were produced without its corresponding cause, it would mean that a dissimilar cause produced a dissimilar effect, which is termed "unrighteous" (non-dharma).
If things were to arise from dissimilar causes, such that a different cause produced a different effect, then all distinct phenomena would arise simultaneously from one another;

for instance, sowing millet would yield beans, and sowing hemp would yield wheat. Consequently, the relationship between those phenomena—the producer and the produced—would all be impermanent and devoid of distinction.
Yet, we currently observe that each phenomenon arises individually [from its own specific conditions].
Since distinct things each possess their own capacity for agency and their respective causes and effects are clearly evident, how could a different cause produce a different effect?
This would imply that not all natures are impermanent. Who, then, could claim that an impermanent nature can produce all things?
One should establish a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute this: "The subject, 'an impermanent nature,' lacks the capacity to produce various things."

The thesis and reason state: "Because cause and effect are not similar, it is like a peach tree being unable to produce a plum. Furthermore, he refutes [the opponent's view] by examining the characteristics of cause and effect:
if intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were impermanent, it would be a productive nature (*kāraka-svabhāva*) falling within the category of produced phenomena (*kṛtaka-dharma*).
If all phenomena were thus produced, then all produced phenomena would be non-final and entirely subject to destruction. There would be no [enduring] existence.

If the cause is always the effect, and if all natures fall within the category of causal natures, then the nature of impermanence itself should also be impermanent, because it follows that all produced phenomena are impermanent.
If that which produces the nature of impermanence is itself impermanent, then all phenomena produced by it should not be impermanent; they ought to be permanent.

Because the cause is like the fruit, [the opponent] subsequently refutes [this position] by arguing that, since the nature of impermanence falls within the dharmas of the three periods of time, it would result in annihilationism.
If one claims that the nature of impermanence enters into all dharmas, then that nature of impermanence itself should fall into the three periods of time and likewise undergo destruction.
If it enters the past, the form of the past is destroyed; if it enters the future, the future [form] does not exist.
If birth enters the present, it does not abide in the present; it is accompanied by the characteristics of momentary change, destruction, and decay.
Since matter (*rūpa*) itself decays, its nature of impermanence must likewise decay. How could the nature of impermanence alone remain undecayed?

Furthermore, matter is a specific differentiation of the accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and these four great elements are themselves the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of the four elements.
If the four great elements that act as the creators are not destroyed, then the nature of the derived matter they create is likewise not destroyed;
for the essential natures of the creator and the created are non-dual, being free from both difference and non-difference.
How could it be that the created is destroyed while the creator remains undestroyed? All non-Buddhists falsely imagine that all four great elements possess an inherent self-nature.
Without destroying [this understanding], one now contemplates that within all three realms of existence, all four great elements and their derived forms— wherever they may be—
are entirely known to possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing. Now, apart from these four great elements and derived forms,
what else could any outsider (tīrthika) possibly contemplate or seek as a "perishable impermanence" capable of destroying all things?
If you claim that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are unarisen and their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indestructible, I maintain that impermanence pervades all natures;

thus, everything falls within the three periods of time and ultimately converges upon destruction. Since they all converge upon destruction, the thesis (*pakṣa*) you have established—that [nature] is indestructible—is itself destroyed.
One should formulate a logical argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute it as follows: "The nature of impermanence" is the subject (*dharmin*).
The thesis and reason for refutation are as follows: because [the subject] falls within the three periods of time, it is like derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).

That which is devoid of initial creation and impermanence is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); furthermore, there are no other four great elements, because each has its own distinct characteristic and self-nature (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Since no differentiation can be found, they are without distinction; thus, these do not further create, nor do they perform the two types of skillful means (*upāya*).
One should know that this is impermanent.
Previously, you reckoned that the creator is permanent and that which is created is impermanent;

now you reckon that that which is created is permanent while the creator, having finished creating, immediately abandons it and is thus impermanent. The Buddha refuted him, saying: "You claim that the creator is impermanent."
Furthermore, is that which is produced eternal? If that which produces it were to depart from this [body], then the four great elements would no longer produce the four great elements;

how, then, could they be eternal? Since each of the four great elements has distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and their individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not seen to possess any difference that can be apprehended, the individual characteristics cannot produce [the result] alone, nor can the distinct characteristics produce it together.
Furthermore, it is not observed that the single water-element alone can produce earth, fire, or wind;
nor is it observed that earth, fire, and wind mutually produce one another or the water, fire, wind, and space elements.

Since the production of a single earth-element or wind-element from them is not seen, and since a single fire-element is produced by the co-arising of earth and water, those four great elements (mahābhūtas) are thus not observed to possess distinct self-characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) or different characteristics (vilakṣaṇa).
If the distinctions among the elements (*dhātu*) can be perceived, one knows that they do not further create different primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

This means that not only are the creators incapable of creating, but even if they were to cease their activity, they would be impermanent; furthermore, that which is created is likewise never again produced.
Thus, both the creator and the created—these two modes of operation—are entirely non-active and universally impermanent. How could this be?
That is to say: could it be that the derived [matter] is eternal while the primary elements are impermanent?
That which is impermanent due to the destruction of its form and location refers to the four great elements and their derived matter; they do not perish until the very end.

"Until the very end," Mahāmati, means analyzing them down to the subtlest atom; even when observed through such analysis, the four great elements and their derived matter do not perish, yet their forms and locations undergo transformation.

One cannot perceive length or shortness; they are not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), nor are the four great elements destroyed. When the locus of form is destroyed, it falls into the Samkhya school.
This school calculates that both the primary creators—the four great elements—and their derivatives are ultimately eternal. As for that which is ultimately destroyed:
When one analyzes form down to its subtlest atoms and observes that which is subject to disintegration, one finds that it is merely the four great elements and their derived forms;
the disintegration of shape and dimension—such as length—is perceived, but the essential nature of the four great elements and their derivatives does not disintegrate.
Therefore, the Buddha refuted this by saying: "The four great elements do not disintegrate; it is only the shape and dimension that disintegrate. This is precisely...

They fall into the view held by the Sāṃkhyas that the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) circulates through all realms of existence, being eternal and unchanging; thus they claim that the four great elements themselves are also eternal.

As for the statement that "form is impermanent," this means that form itself is impermanent; it does not mean that the spatial configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is impermanent while the four great elements are not.

If the four great elements were impermanent, then they would not be conventional designations; and if conventional designations were not of the nature [of things], one would fall into the view of the worldly theorists (Lokāyatika), who hold that all natures exist merely as verbal expressions and do not perceive the arising of their own-nature (svabhāva).
This [position] also maintains that both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) are impermanent; thus it says, "form is itself impermanent.

However, those Sāṃkhya teachers merely maintain that the configuration and location (*saṃsthāna-deśa*) are impermanent, not that the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta-svabhāva*) is also impermanent.
Therefore, it refutes them, saying: "If the nature of the four great elements were also impermanent, then there would be no conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)."

It is said that because conventional discourse does not transcend the four great elements, if one were to lack conventional discourse, one would fall into the Lokāyata view and become subject to annihilationism.

This is because such a view perceives all phenomena as being merely verbal designations and fails to see that they arise from their own true nature as they actually exist; thus, it results in annihilationism.

Regarding the impermanence of transformation (*pariṇāma-anityatā*): it refers to the manifestation of a change in the nature of form (*rūpa*), such that when gold is fashioned into an ornament, it manifests as a transformation, yet the nature of the gold itself does not perish;
rather, only the location of the ornament perishes. In this same way, the transformation of other natures and so forth is also like this.
When the fire of the various false imaginings (*vikalpa*) of the non-Buddhists regarding impermanence burns the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), [they maintain this].
If their own characteristics were not burned and each were to perish according to its own characteristic, then the four great elements and the derived matter they produce would have to be severed.

This [view] maintains that both the producers and the produced are eternal; however, between these two natures there exists an impermanent nature which causes material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) to continue and undergo transformation.
Thus, when any difference in the nature of all material things manifests, it is called "destruction" (*bhaṅga*).

It is not that the intrinsic nature of the four great elements perishes; rather, when a golden ornament undergoes transformation, it is said to have "perished," yet it is not the nature of the gold that perishes.
It is the same with the transformation of other natures: just as milk is made into ghee or curd, and though the ghee and curd undergo transformation, it is not the nature of the milk that perishes.
In this way, the various false conceptualizations of the non-Buddhists produce nothingness.

The first common view is that when one says fire burns the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of each of the four great elements is individually dispersed and destroyed;

however, their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not actually burned. If fire were able to burn the four great elements such that the characteristics of each of the four great elements were individually destroyed, then the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced by the four great elements would be severed; who then would be the creator and what would be the created? These are the four [objections] above.
Heterodox views maintain that the four great elements which possess form ultimately undergo extinction, whereas the four great elements which lack form can never be destroyed;
this is a doctrine of partial birth and partial extinction, and partial non-birth and non-extinction.
"Mahāmati, the arising of my Dharma is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this? It is because external natures are not fixed;
I speak only of the subtle mind of the three realms of existence, and not of various marks having birth and cessation, nor of the conjunction of the four great elements and their derivative forms.
Thus, one should know that the two kinds of deluded discrimination consist of the grasped and the grasper."

One who perceives that thoughts are free from the two views of existence and non-existence regarding external objects, and realizes that they are merely the manifestation of one's own mind, should understand that these conceptualizations arise from mental activity and do not arise without it.

Being free from the conceptualization of the mind as having the nature of existence or non-existence, one sees that all phenomena—mundane, supramundane, and the supreme supramundane—are neither eternal nor impermanent;
yet, failing to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind, one falls into the two extremes.
The continuity of evil views held by all non-Buddhists arises from their failure to realize that these are their own deluded imaginings;

these ordinary people lack any fundamental basis for what they call the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane. They claim these arise from deluded imagination, yet this is not something perceived by the foolish and ignorant.
These seven kinds of impermanence are all the false views of non-Buddhists and do not belong to my teaching.
What arises within my teaching speaks only of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the various sense objects as being neither permanent nor impermanent;

this is called true permanence, which transcends the mental constructs (*cittamātra*) of the non-Buddhists. Why is this? Because the non-Buddhists give rise to fixed views regarding external objects, or...

Whether calculating [the self] as permanent or calculating it as impermanent, one does not know that external objects are like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water, which cannot be said to be definitively existent or definitively non-existent.
Therefore, I teach only that the three realms are all the subtle and wondrous true mind;
I do not speak of various marks having arising and ceasing, for they exist only through the differentiation of the combination of causes and conditions of the four great elements.
Because of the four great elements and derived form, it is not that the four great elements and derived form are substantially existent dharmas;
rather, they all exist through the two kinds of false conceptualization of grasper and grasped. If one knows these two to be false conceptualizations, one does not perceive a grasper or a grasped;
one remains far removed from the two views of existence and non-existence regarding external natures and realizes only the One.
All phenomena are the measure of one's own mind, like flowers in a mirror or the moon in water; they cannot be reckoned as either existent or non-existent.
What is called "delusive thought" arises entirely from discursive reflection and mental attention; it does not arise from a state of no-thought, no-reflection, or non-attention.
If there were no mental attention, one would be free from the distinctions of existence and non-existence as manifested by one's own mind.
Furthermore, those who are able to thoroughly comprehend that the worldly, the world-transcending, and the world-transcending-supreme dharmas are neither eternal nor non-eternal—
those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), failing to realize that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds,

fall into dualistic conceptualization and further fall into two kinds of evil views with uninterrupted continuity, establishing seven types of theories on impermanence. These various non-Buddhists do not...
One realizes that all various deluded thoughts are merely the false discriminations of one's own mind, devoid of any fundamental basis;

yet, while claiming to have already attained the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane dharmas, they do not know that such assertions are all produced by the mental activity of deluded thought. How could they know what truly constitutes the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane?
The Dharma is not perceived through the mental attention of the deluded imaginings of ordinary fools, because they do not perceive their own imaginings and thus do not see the fundamental source.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Far removed from initial creation and..."
Regarding the difference in form and location, the nature of matter, and impermanence, the ignorant outsiders falsely imagine that all natures are subject to destruction.
Yet, the Great Self-nature remains; thus, the outsiders are submerged in various views through their notion of impermanence.

For those outsiders, there is neither arising nor ceasing, as the Great Nature is eternally constant. Why, then, do they harbor the notion of impermanence? All is merely the measure of mind; these two types [of views] are but mental constructs.
The mind’s流转 (pravṛtti), its grasping, and that which is grasped are devoid of self and what belongs to a self;
Brahmā is like the root and branches extending everywhere—thus I declare that all this is merely the measure of that mind.
The detailed analysis of the prose section is now complete; this shall further be summarized and analyzed as follows:
first, "abandonment after creation," meaning that the creator is impermanent because it abandons what is created, and thus is said to be "distant" from its initial act of creation;
second, "difference in form and location," meaning that both the creator and the created are eternal, differing only in their form and location; third, "impermanence of nature," meaning...

1. Calculating that the nature of impermanence can destroy all things; 2. The fourth is the impermanence of nature and non-nature, meaning that both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) are destroyed;
3. The fifth is that form itself is impermanent, meaning that while the derivatives are impermanent, the four great elements are permanent;
thus it is said that both nature and form are impermanent; 4. The sixth is that there is an intermediate state during transformation.
Because they are of a disintegrating nature, it is said that "all natures are without disintegration.

Seventh, because all dharmas are non-arising and universally enter into the four great elements whose self-nature is eternally abiding and indestructible, it is said that "the nature of the great elements is itself eternal.
Since it is said to be "indestructible" and "eternally abiding," yet one still forms the perception of impermanence—this arises from being submerged in various views.

For this reason, I have composed this treatise. Those various non-Buddhists all claim that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and that the natures of the four great elements are each indestructible and their nature is eternally abiding. If this were so, then everything would be eternal;
what dharma could then be impermanent such that one would form the notion of impermanence? This is not even worth discussing, for as for what they call "eternal":
If it were not true, even its own words would be self-contradictory; how then could its meaning be established?

If what I have taught—that all that exists within the three realms is merely the manifestation of one's own mind—is accepted, then because that dualistic deluded mind of grasper and grasped flows on without ceasing, one conceives of "I" and "mine. In reality, however, there is no such thing as a grasper.
That which is grasped as "mine" constitutes what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*).

However, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) further maintain that Brahmā first created sentient beings, regarding him as the root of all living things, just as a tree trunk gives rise to branches that spread throughout the world.
If this were the case, then the tree trunk would be the self and the branches would be what belongs to the self; for they have asserted it thus.
Therefore, I say that these are merely the mind’s own deluded imaginings (*vikalpa-citta-mātra*) and are not comprised within my [teachings on] dharmas.

If what I have taught—that the phenomena of the three realms, from the highest to the lowest, are created by this one mind alone and there is no second dharma—is understood, then this is called the "fundamental.
How could the Brahmā heavens or the *Viśeṣavat* gods be considered the fundamental?

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the characteristics of the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

If one is skillful in the characteristics of the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi, I and the other bodhisattvas shall never recklessly abandon the gate of the bliss of cessation-samādhi, nor fall into [the state of] one [who is not awakened]."
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this;
I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain it for me.

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "From the sixth stage onward, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in the seventh stage."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in every moment of thought, enters into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is free from all characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This meditative absorption is not that of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;

for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas enter into a meditative absorption characterized by the cessation of the marks of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka*) within the sphere of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-gati*).

Therefore, in the seventh stage, it is not a meditative absorption consisting of recollection, but rather the attainment of the non-differentiated characteristic of all phenomena, as opposed to the partial attainment of various distinct characteristics.

The nature of awakening to all phenomena—their wholesome and unwholesome characteristics—is right meditative attainment (*samyaksamādhi*). Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment involving wholesome thoughts.
Mahāmati, in the eighth stage, the conceptualizations of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*) are extinguished for Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
From the first stage up to the seventh stage, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas contemplate the measure of the mind, thought, and consciousness within the triple world and remain detached from them.
Due to the cultivation of false imaginings regarding "I" and "mine," they fall into the delusions of various external natures and signs;

these foolish people are directed toward the duality of their own mind—the grasped and the grasper—and remain ignorant and unawakened, being permeated by the habitual tendencies of falsehood and the faults of beginningless transgressions.

This is a detailed inquiry into the distinctions between the cultivation and realization of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Generally speaking, the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) can certainly lead one into either the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) or the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*);
it is that which is cultivated in common by all three vehicles and realized in common by all three vehicles.

Those who enter the meditative absorption of cessation to experience its bliss, yet become attached to it and fail to relinquish it, belong to the Small Vehicle; they do not give rise to [the resolve for] extinction and deliverance (*nirvāṇa*).
Manifesting various modes of deportment refers to Bodhisattvas entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) without losing their mental characteristics;

whereas for those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) who enter the meditative absorption of cessation, each moment is devoid of characteristics. Because they are Bodhisattvas, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"The Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the Two Vehicles only severs one type [of affliction], which is termed 'Noble Nature' (*ārya-gotra*). This means severing the conceptual grasping at a self (*parikalpita-ātma-grāha*) to realize the first fruit (*srota-āpanna*); from this point, one successively severs the eighty [afflictions] of the three realms."

When the afflictions of the first stage are extinguished and one attains the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one attains the four fruits [of the śrāvaka]. The Bodhisattva, seeing the path and completely severing the two types [of grasping], is called a "noble nature" (*ārya-gotra*).

This means that by severing the dualistic grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) through discrimination, one enters the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), which is termed the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). From this point on, one gradually severs the innate (*sahaja*) grasping at self and phenomena until reaching the eighth stage, where one attains the concentration of cessation.

Because what is seen is never different, yet what is practiced is never the same, a question is asked regarding the sequential characteristics of the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) of all three vehicles.

Furthermore, if one skillfully understands the characteristics of this sequential continuity of cultivation and abandonment, one will never recklessly abandon the bodhisattva’s meditative absorption (*nirodha-samāpatti*) or delight;
one will certainly not fall into the attachments or delusions of the two vehicles or external paths.

The Buddha taught that from the first to the sixth bhūmi, the bodhisattva’s entry into *nirodha-samāpatti* is indistinguishable from that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, due to the characteristics of their concentration.
Because they do not forget the process of emergence and entry, when they reach the seventh stage, they enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) in every thought-moment.
They remain far removed from the characteristics of concentration; that is, they possess the nature of nirvāṇa and its intrinsic characteristics, yet they do not grasp even these.

This is beyond the reach of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), for those of the two vehicles weary of saṃsāra and rejoice in nirvāṇa, falling into conditioned activity and possessing a subject that grasps.
Because they grasp at objects, they are unable to attain the samādhis of every thought-moment in the seventh stage;
because they perceive the various characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, they do not realize the non-differentiated nature of all phenomena.

Since they perceive all phenomena as having the goodness of nirvāṇa and the unwholesomeness of saṃsāra, and thus abandon the unwholesome while grasping for the wholesome, the two vehicles possess [such dualistic views].

In the seventh stage, there is no meditative absorption of wholesome thought (*kuśala-manasikāra-samādhi*); it is only upon reaching the eighth stage that one abandons the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Not only do all various marks (*nimitta*) cease, but even the conceptual marks of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*)—which are abandoned by those of the two vehicles—are all completely severed and extinguished.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "From the first stage up to the fifth..."
On the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is unable to abide for long in the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-darśana*); rather, the contemplation of signs (*sanimitta-darśana*) predominates.

Upon reaching the sixth stage, the contemplation of signlessness becomes frequent while the contemplation of signs becomes rare. On the seventh stage, although there is exclusively the contemplation of signlessness which flows continuously, it still involves preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and has not yet attained spontaneity (*anābhoga*) in manifesting signs and buddha-fields. From the eighth stage onward, one has attained the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*).
Constantly abiding in samādhi without the marks of entering or emerging, one is able to spontaneously manifest signs and lands;

the afflictions of the three realms never again arise, yet the subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness may still manifest, because the *vipāka* [consciousness] has not yet attained emptiness.
That which is called the cessation of the deluded conceptualizing consciousness is termed nirvāṇa; therefore, it is necessarily so.
As for the reason why the delusive appearances of mind, thought, and mental consciousness are extinguished upon reaching the eighth stage:

it is because from the first stage through the seventh stage, the contemplative practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas involve observing that the triple world is entirely manifested within the measure of the delusive constructs of mind, thought, and mental consciousness;
therein, there is fundamentally no self and nothing belonging to a self. Nevertheless, regarding the contemplation they cultivate...

Because their practice has not yet been forgotten and they have not transcended the mind-measure (*cittamātra*), they still cultivate through their own false imaginings; seeing external dharmas as existent, they fall into the various marks of external natures.
In reality, this is no different from the attachments of ignorant *śrāvakas* who cling to the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) within their own minds.
Due to their total lack of knowledge and failure to observe the flowing stream of false imaginings, they mistake a thief for their own son.

Because they have not awakened to the fact that they are permeated by the habitual tendencies of beginningless faults, evils, and falsehoods, it is only upon reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) that the delusive appearances of mind, thought,
and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*) are extinguished for those of the two vehicles.
Mahāmati, the *samādhi* of the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas at the eighth stage is called "Nirvāṇa" by the Bodhisattvas.
Because they are sustained by awakening, they find delight in the gateways of samādhi and do not enter parinirvāṇa;

yet if they were not so sustained, the stage of the Tathāgata would remain unfulfilled, all activities for the sake of sentient beings would be abandoned, and the lineage of the Buddhas would be severed.
Thus, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have revealed the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgatas, whereby śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain the bliss of the gateways of samādhi.

Because they are led astray, they falsely conceive of [the stages] as *nirvāṇa*. Mahāmati, I have divided the seven stages (*bhūmi*) so that [bodhisattvas] may skillfully cultivate the characteristics of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*);

skillfully cultivate the grasping of "self" and "mine," the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*), and the characteristics of arising and ceasing, as well as specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*);

and through the four kinds of unhindered analytical powers (*pratisaṃvid*), the power of certainty, and the gates of samādhi, they may enter the sequential continuity of the stages and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) without causing the bodhisattvas to fall into error.
The Mahāsattvas do not perceive the unwholesome common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the seven stages, for they would otherwise fall into the deviant paths of the non-Buddhists;

therefore, the sequence of the stages is established. Great Wisdom, in reality there is neither arising nor ceasing, apart from what is the mere manifestation of one's own mind (*svacitta-dṛśya-mātra*).
That which is called the continuity of the sequence of stages and the various activities within the triple world are not perceived by the deluded; they are not perceived by the deluded.
This refers to what I and all Buddhas have taught regarding the sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the various activities within the triple world (*tridhātu*).

This clarifies that while the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are identical in their cessation of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), the *nirvāṇa* they realize is fundamentally and utterly distinct;
for the Bodhisattvas are sustained by the power of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna-bala*) and do not [fall into] *nirvāṇa*.
Because they are intoxicated by the [false] nirvāṇa, although they are within nirvāṇa, they do not realize it as such.

If they were not sustained by the power of self-awakening wisdom, they would mistake the *pariṇāmanīya-nagara* (the conjured city) for the *ratnasthāna* (the place of jewels). Consequently, they would neither seek the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood above, nor deliver all sentient beings below;
thus, the lineage of the Buddhas would be permanently severed. Therefore, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, behold [this].

The Bodhisattva of the eighth stage does not arise from samādhi; through the three bridges and seven exhortations, he reveals the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata, causing them to advance further and not abide in nirvāṇa.
As for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who are intoxicated by the bliss of samādhi, they consider what is meager to be sufficient; therefore, within that state, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.
