To hear that the Nirvana-gathering is the perfection of dhyāna; to observe with the wisdom that the false imaginings of one’s own mind lack intrinsic nature and thus not fall into the two extremes;
and to attain the noble realization of self-awakening, which is superior to previous bodies and indestructible—this is the perfection of prajñā.
This refers to the practitioner who, having correctly entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and abiding in the True Dharma, attains the wisdom of the Tathāgata and asks [this question].
The meaning is that one who abides in meditative absorption immediately attains the correct wisdom of the Tathāgata and, by abiding in the True Dharma, realizes the Vajra-body.
Why, then, is it further said that one must fulfill the six *pāramitās* before attaining perfect enlightenment?
The Buddha stated that there are three distinctions regarding the *pāramitās*: first, the mundane, which refers to those practiced by humans and devas;
second, the supramundane, which refers to those practiced by followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); and third, the supreme supramundane, which refers to those practiced by Bodhisattvas.
As for the mundane *pāramitās*, they refer to the various ignorant ordinary beings who are attached to "self" and "what belongs to the self," and who calculate [existence] in terms of a self.

To be able to give while conceiving that there is something given, not being free from the two views of grasper and grasped, and seeking for the sake of future rebirth in superior realms as humans or devas to enjoy the pleasures of the five sensory objects such as form—this is called giving characterized by signs (*nimitta-sthita-dāna*).

This applies likewise to the remaining perfections (*pāramitā*). By means of this, one brings to fruition the five [perfections] through the production of outflowing causes (*sāsrava-hetu*) resulting in outflowing fruits (*sāsrava-phala*).

Although one may attain rebirth in the Brahma world by practicing the six perfections, if one does not transcend the mundane, these are the six perfections practiced by those of the realms of humans and devas.

As for the supramundane *pāramitās*, this refers to those of the Two Vehicles who, weary of birth and death, seek *nirvāṇa* and cultivate the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
they practice six types of inferior, untainted (*anāsrava*) conduct, seeking only their own [liberation].
Attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa and having no mind to share it with others—though this may be compared to the world as already being transcendent and superior, it is not ultimate;
this refers to the six pāramitās practiced by those of the two vehicles.
As for the "supreme mundane-to-transmundane pāramitās," these are the bodhisattvas’ profound realization of the dharma of suchness manifesting before them, awakening to all that exists.
All phenomena—whether outflowing or non-outflowing, conditioned or unconditioned—are merely the measure of false conceptualization manifested by one’s own mind;
fundamentally, they are not dual. It is only because of the mind’s own grasping that duality appears.

By awakening to this reality as it truly is, one does not give rise to false conceptualization. Thus, even while practicing the six perfections, one cannot fall into the destinies of humans, devas, or the two vehicles.
This is embraced by understanding that all forms and appearances are manifestations of one's own mind, thereby giving rise to no attachment;
it is practiced solely for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings.

One employs the most supreme skillful means in practicing generosity, yet perceives neither the giver, nor the recipient, nor the object given in between, because one knows that the essence of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of stinginess.
To practice in accordance with non-attachment is called the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) as intrinsic nature;

that is, practicing this giving without generating conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), and not giving rise to the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) regarding any objects. This is called the diamond-like ethical discipline (*vīrya-vajra-śīla*) as intrinsic nature;

that is, when those conceptual constructions do not arise, one knows reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), realizing that both the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Not contending with the mind is called the patience of the non-arising of self-nature (*svabhāva-anutpatti-kṣānti*).

Although one practices diligently without laziness throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, following the practice of skillful means as they truly are, yet the tree of the mind remains entirely unmoved; this is called the vigor of self-nature (*svabhāva-vīrya*).

Because one does not give rise to false conceptions and does not grasp at the nirvana of external paths or the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is [the patience of the non-arising of self-nature].

It is called "reaching the other shore" because its self-nature is established through the realization that the false imaginings manifested by one's own mind are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature.
By observing with wisdom, one does not fall into the evil views of the two extremes of existence and non-existence, thereby attaining the body of wisdom.
Progressing ever more excellently through each stage (*bhūmi*), it becomes indestructible; this attainment of the noble wisdom of self-realization is not the wisdom of the two vehicles.
That which can be reached is called "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*); its intrinsic nature is adamantine wisdom (*vajra-prajñā*).
Thus, one who practices to attain meditative absorption (*samādhi*), abides in the True Dharma, and is fully endowed with wisdom is one who possesses these six kinds of *pāramitās*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Empty, impermanent, and momentary—these are the deluded imaginings of the foolish.
Like a river, a lamp, or a seed, they conceive of 'momentariness. When moments cease, there is tranquility; it is peaceful and free from activity.
That all phenomena are unarisen—this is what I mean by the meaning of 'momentariness. When a thing arises, it then ceases; it does not [persist]."
The foolish say that the nature of uninterrupted continuity is perfumed by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and that ignorance (*avidyā*) is its cause, from which the mind arises.
[They ask: until form (*rūpa*) has arisen, what distinct characteristics of continuity exist in the interim?
How does a subsequent mind arise from that [preceding mind] when it does not abide in form? Since it arises from that, it is not as [the foolish claim].
How can it be that while the cause truly arises, there is nothing established, yet one knows the momentary destruction?

The practitioner, through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), perceives the vajra-like Buddha-relics, the palaces of the Light-Sound Heaven (*Ābhāsvara-deva*), and the imperishable phenomena of the world. Abiding in the True Dharma, he attains the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
as a bhikṣu, he attains equanimity. How does he perceive forms as being like moments, *gandharvas*, illusions, and so forth? They have no [inherent] existence.
There are those who, regarding momentary and unreal forms and so forth as if they were real—
this verse refers to both the momentary and the non-momentary— claim that because of such foolish commoners who perceive permanence in all phenomena which are impermanent,
I teach that all phenomena are unarisen and that all phenomena are momentary; this is entirely due to delusion.

Now, these metaphors—such as a flowing river, a lamp, and a seed—are employed because of the conventional designation of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), intended merely to shatter one's view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
How could you have imagined that I would then treat all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) as being momentary (*kṣaṇika*)?
Do you not know that when I speak of "momentariness," it is precisely to still the turbulence of deluded conceptualization and to cause one to see the original nature of all phenomena?
Quiescence is primordially free from activity and primordially unarisen; this is the meaning of "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) as I have taught it.
Since all phenomena arise by depending on causes and relying on conditions, they are born in that very place and perish in that very place.
Because this arising is itself non-arising, the moment is defined by non-arising, not by impermanence.

Because the foolish do not understand this, it is not explained to them. What are called "conditions" refer to the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). If these four conditions are not complete, arising and ceasing cannot be established.
Thus, arising occurs through conditions and ceasing occurs through conditions; how, then, could there ever be even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) in any phenomenon?

Is it not the case that what is called a "moment" (kṣaṇa) refers to the nature of continuity, wherein the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) acts as a guiding support, causing the preceding thought-moment to cease so that the succeeding thought-moment arises? However, this uninterrupted continuity cannot arise or cease of its own accord;
it exists solely because of the perfuming of deluded conceptualization (vikalpa). Thus, internally it takes ignorance (avidyā) as its cause, and externally...
If it is argued that the mind arises and ceases only by taking material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) as conditions, and thus arises from them—
then if there were an internal cause but no objective conditions consisting of the two types of objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*), namely the sense faculties and their objects,

upon what part would the nature of the intermediate continuity depend? If it is claimed that the continuity of the five consciousnesses actually ceases in accordance with the conditions of their respective objects...

Although the mind perishes in successive order, truly arising in accordance with objective conditions, and the mind likewise arises in successive order, yet the mind does not abide in form, nor does form abide in the mind;
each is unaware of the other, and each does not reach the other. Therefore, by what object could it be produced as an objective condition?
Thus, one knows that the mind is fundamentally without arising; this makes it clear that the mind is originally non-existent.
If arising arises from that [arising], one knows it does not truly arise from a cause.
Thus, even the characteristic of momentary arising cannot be found when sought; how then can the characteristic of momentary destruction be known?
This is what I mean by "momentary yet non-momentary. Furthermore, within all phenomena in a single moment, there is not even a moment.

How much more so for a practitioner who has realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and dwells in the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra*), even for a single moment?
Consider, for instance, gold, vajra, the relics of the Buddha, and the palaces of the Heaven of Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara-deva*);

since these are all worldly things possessing form and characteristics, they still possess various indestructible qualities—how much more so for a Bodhisattva who abides in the true Dharma of the Tathāgata!
How could those who possess the Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom, up to and including bhikṣus who have realized the equal nature of phenomena (dharmatā), perceive any characteristic of momentariness?

Because they see all phenomena as being like a city of the gandharvas, like a dream, or like an illusion—though they appear with formal characteristics, in reality no characteristic of momentariness can be found. How then could foolish people [perceive] in seeds...?
To regard the various unreal forms and so forth as real, falsely claiming they possess the characteristic of momentary destruction—
this is what I mean when I say that fools are unskilled in my teaching of intentional concealment (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*),
and thus conceive of all internal and external phenomena as being momentary.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the ultimate characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, consciousness, and the two kinds of non-self through their successive distinctions.

May I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, by means of this sequential and continuous discrimination of these dharmas across all stages, enter into all Buddha-dharmas. "To enter into all Buddha-dharmas" means... [text continues].
The Tathāgata, having attained the stage of self-realization, said to Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "So be it;

we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The five dharmas, the three natures (*svabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses, the two forms of selflessness, and the characteristics of the progression through discrimination—these refer to names, signs, conceptualization, right knowledge, and suchness. As for how a practitioner practices: [he practices] by means of these."

Entering the Tathāgata’s own realization of the noble path, free from views of annihilation, permanence, existence, non-existence, and so forth, one dwells in the present manifestation of the meditative attainment of happiness in the present life.

Mahāmati, ordinary beings do not realize that those five dharmas, the self-natures, the consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness, and external objects are merely manifestations of their own minds;
they are the false imaginings of ordinary people, not those of the noble ones. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what is meant by 'fools'?"
Now, false conceptualization arises; it is not [the case for] the noble ones or the Buddhas. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Fools are attached to conventional numbers, names, and signs, and their minds flow out and disperse. Once dispersed, they fall into various forms and appearances, falling into the views of 'I' and 'mine,' and longing with attachment for exquisite forms.
Having become attached, they are shrouded by ignorance and give rise to defiled clinging. Once defiled clinging has arisen, greed and anger are produced."

Having accumulated karma through repeated accumulation, one entangles oneself with false imaginings like a silkworm spinning its cocoon, falling into the ocean of birth and death and the wilderness of the various realms of existence.

Like a water-wheel drawing from a well, because of ignorance, one fails to realize that all things are like illusions, mirages, or the moon reflected in water, and that their intrinsic nature is free from "I" and "mine.
Thus, one gives rise to all manner of unreal imaginings regarding characteristics and the characterized, as well as arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Cessation arises from the conceptual constructions of one’s own mind; it is not produced by a creator god (*īśvara*), time, atoms, or primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
Foolish ordinary beings follow after names and signs.

Briefly distinguishing these, it is shown in general that the causes and effects of both the ordinary and the noble, as well as the false and the correct, all depend upon the five dharmas, the three natures, and the eight consciousnesses.

Having distinguished the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*) through consciousness, one now proceeds to subsume the eight consciousnesses, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the two selflessnesses within the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*).
Furthermore, it is revealed that these five dharmas do not transcend the single mind of quiescent extinction (*śānta-ekacitta*).

Therefore, he asks about the ultimate characteristics of the thorough discrimination (*parikalpa-lakṣaṇa*) regarding the five dharmas, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the two kinds of selflessness; for if one knows the ultimate characteristics of thorough discrimination, then one knows [the truth].

The Bodhisattva enters the successive stages of all the grounds through a continuous progression of characteristics, just as one enters the first ground by observing the names, meanings, intrinsic natures, and distinctions of the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*).

Therein, one first severs the dualistic grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) which are conceptual in nature, realizes the universally pervasive true suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*), and attains the wisdom that discerns the emptiness of both self and phenomena. From this point onward, one proceeds further by means of that wisdom of the two-fold emptiness.

By observing the co-arising of names, signs, and conceptualizations, one realizes the wisdom of the co-arising emptiness of both self and phenomena, thereby attaining entry into the two types of enlightenment—the Equal and the Sublime.

Furthermore, by the emptiness of the six consciousnesses and their associated self and phenomena, one enters the First Bhūmi; by the emptiness of the seventh consciousness and its associated self and phenomena, one enters the Eighth Bhūmi;
and by the emptiness of the eighth consciousness and its clinging to phenomena, one enters the Buddha-bhūmi. Thus, one knows the five dharmas and the three natures.
The eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness encompass all phenomena;

one who can discern these phenomena is able to enter all Buddha-dharmas, and only by entering all Buddha-dharmas does one attain the stages from the first bhūmi up to the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening.
Therefore, the World-Honored One demonstrated each of them one by one. What are called the "five dharmas" are set forth in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.

The treatise states: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings; it is said that the five kinds of dharmas do not transcend the single mind of quiescent extinction (*śānta-ekacitta*).
Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it means these three dharmas all flow forth from the self-nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Regarding the eight consciousnesses, it means that the eleven material phenomena are the objects of perception (*ālambana*), while the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*) are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)."
Phenomena that are associated are *vijñapti-mātra* as correspondence; phenomena that are dissociated are *vijñapti-mātra* as states; the eight consciousnesses are *vijñapti-mātra* as self-nature;
and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are *vijñapti-mātra* as the nature of consciousness. Therefore, the hundred dharmas all return to *vijñapti-mātra*.

These three types of phenomena all arise from false discrimination due to the two attachments to self and phenomena; thus, there are the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and mental factors (*manovijñāna*).

The various distinctions of names and characteristics are the conceptual constructions of consciousness; if one realizes the two kinds of emptiness, this is precisely right knowledge, suchness, and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Thus, as soon as there is the mark of self (*ātman*), all phenomena appear densely before one’s eyes;
yet if there is no mark of self, all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, all phenomena do not go beyond this.

These five dharmas encompass all dharmas. If a practitioner observes these five dharmas with clear and unerring vision and practices accordingly, they will gradually enter the noble realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

Without depending on others, they will penetrate the Buddha-dharma and be able to remain far removed from the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, as well as existence and non-existence, and will not fall into the trap of names and signs.

When one’s deluded thoughts regarding the present dharma-pleasure of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) are constantly present before them, one then attains the realization of the Tathāgata’s own-enlightened noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) and realizes suchness (*tathatā*).
If one does not awaken to the fact that the five dharmas, the three natures, and the eight consciousnesses are all devoid of self,
and if one does not know that all phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind, but instead falsely discriminates that there are real phenomena existing outside the mind— these are all...
The deluded thoughts and discriminations of ordinary fools are not those of the noble sages. Why is this?
All names and signs are merely conventional designations established by worldly consensus; they are fundamentally not real existents.

Yet, foolish people cling to these conventional numbers, names, and signs, and their minds consequently flow along with them, surging and scattering like water or wind, turbulent and impossible to restrain. Once set in motion...
Having scattered [the seeds], they again differentiate between various forms and appearances as beautiful or ugly, giving rise to signs of grasping and falling into attachment to "I" and "mine.
With these hopes and fixations, they regard them as exquisite forms; once they have become fixated, they are immediately shrouded and obstructed by ignorance, giving rise to delusive defilements.
Having become stained and attached, they give rise to craving toward agreeable objects and anger toward disagreeable objects.
With the two minds of greed and anger, one creates various evil karmas that accumulate day by day and month by month without ceasing.

Once these have accumulated, one is dragged away by karma and cannot liberate oneself; like a silkworm making a cocoon to entangle and bind itself, one falls into the great ocean of birth and death and the wilderness of the six realms of existence. Rising and falling, emerging and submerging, it is like drawing water from a well.
The wheel, the wheel, the wheel turning without interruption—thus the three wheels of affliction, karma, and suffering revolve incessantly.
All this arises from being shrouded by ignorance and clinging to names and appearances;

one does not know that all conventional designations and appearances are by nature like illusions, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, wherein there is originally no sovereign to act as a self, nor is there any "I" at all.
Relying upon a place of dependence, they conceive of it as "mine"; thus, fools give rise to all manner of unreal false imaginings regarding that which is devoid of self and what belongs to self.

They do not know that all dharmas are fundamentally free from the characteristic of the grasper and free from the characteristic of the grasped, and are also free from the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
How could there be various kinds of wondrous and wholesome forms? How could there be the arising of delusion or the creation [of karma]?
Regarding the matter of karma receiving its retribution, all these names and characteristics arise entirely from the delusive imaginings of one's own mind;

they do not arise from a creator god (Īśvara), time, atoms, or a supreme principle. Those who calculate that things arise from a creator god and so forth are all members of the class of ordinary people who cling to names and grasp at appearances;
they are not those who have realized that names and appearances are fundamentally empty.
Mahāmati, as for those "characteristics" (*nimitta*): that which is illuminated by the visual consciousness is called "form" (*rūpa*);

that which is illuminated by the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses is called "sound, odor, flavor, touch, and phenomena" (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharma*). These are what are called characteristics. Mahāmati, as for "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*):

it is the designation of various names and the manifestation of various characteristics; such as the names "elephant," "horse," "chariot," "infantry," "man," "woman," and so forth—these are what are called conceptual construction.
Mahāmati, when one possesses correct wisdom, names and signs are unattainable, like a passing guest;
the various consciousnesses do not arise, are neither interrupted nor severed, and one does not fall into the stages of any externalists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, by means of this correct wisdom, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva establishes neither names and signs nor the non-establishment of names and signs, having abandoned both views.
Establishing and denigrating are known as the non-arising of names and characteristics; this is called Suchness (*tathatā*).
Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, dwelling in Suchness, attains the realm of non-existence;
having attained the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), he is forever separated from all heterodox paths and evil destinies, and correctly abides in the supramundane path of the Dharma.

Having matured the characteristics of all phenomena—such as conceptualization and illusion—and having personally realized the nature of phenomena as being free from the marks of all false imaginings, one proceeds through the various stages up to the Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
Within this interval, through the power of samādhi, mastery, and the blossoming of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), one attains the stage of the Tathāgata.
Thereafter, by means of manifold transformations, one perfectly illuminates and manifests [the truth] to bring sentient beings to maturity.
Like the moon in water, having perfectly fulfilled the ten inexhaustible phrases, he expounds the Dharma through various analytical teachings for sentient beings with diverse understandings;
this Dharmakāya is free from mental constructions—this is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into that which is attained as Suchness (tathatā).
The previous statement that "name is itself appearance" reveals that appearance is itself name. Appearance and name refer to the two dharmas of form and mind:
that which has a shape capable of being observed is called appearance; that which expresses, designates, and invokes is called name.
For example, while the sense organs and their objects are both appearances, they are designated by the names "organs" and "objects. Thus, appearance is entirely name, and name is entirely appearance.
What is called "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) and "name" (nāma) always follow one another. "Delusive thought" (vikalpa) refers to being deluded by existence and deluded by non-existence;
it is called "delusive" because the mind arises from characteristics, and it is called "thought" because names do not name themselves and characteristics do not characterize themselves.

There must necessarily be an establishment and manifestation of provisional names and provisional characteristics, such as the names "elephant," "horse," "chariot," "infantry," "man," "woman," and so forth. This is called "delusive" because these names are not [inherently real].

That which is called a name but does not possess the characteristics of that [object] is termed "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). As it is said in the *Treatise*: "The mind is able to provide names for all phenomena;
if there were no mind, there would be no names at all. One should know that mundane and supramundane names all arise from the mind;
therefore, they are called the "object of mental verbalization" (*manojalpa-viṣaya*). Regarding "correct wisdom," it refers to the [wisdom] that functions within those conceptual constructions.
Displaying various names and signs, one minutely examines them to seek their true nature, yet finds them utterly unobtainable;
they are like travelers who have made a temporary halt. Thus, when "ox" is called, "ox" responds, and when "horse" is called, "horse" responds.
No further false conceptualization arises, and thus the various consciousnesses do not arise. Without giving rise to the two views, one does not fall into the two extremes of the non-Buddhists.
Riding upon biased and deviant wisdom is termed "correct wisdom. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Just as the names of all phenomena are merely provisional designations, throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, they come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Within all phenomena there are no names, and within names there are no phenomena; they are neither joined nor dispersed."
However, since these designations are merely provisional, why is this so? It is because all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) together with their names.

Thus, phenomena arise from the mind, while names are established based on phenomena. Since the phenomena that are produced have no place of origin, the mind that produces them is likewise non-existent.
Therefore, both mind and object are empty and both lack a locus; this is called right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). As for "suchness" (*tathatā*), it means:
By means of this correct wisdom, the bodhisattva observes that there is not a single thing to be established, because all phenomena are entirely real;
thus, they do not establish names or characteristics. They observe that there is not a single thing to be negated, because all phenomena are entirely suchness (tathatā);

thus, they do not negate names or characteristics. Because they do not establish anything, they do not fall into the view of establishment; because they do not negate anything, they do not fall into [the view of nihilism].

The view of slander is understood through the knowledge that names and characteristics are like passing travelers; they are fundamentally unarisen, and because they are unarisen, they are called "Suchness" (tathatā).

If a bodhisattva, while in the stage of the four preparatory practices (prayoga), gives rise to the four types of investigative wisdom (paryeṣaṇājñāna) to examine names, objects, intrinsic nature, and specific differences, and realizes that these do not exist apart from consciousness, they sever the dualistic attachments to a self and phenomena arising from conceptual discrimination and thereby attain realization.
By means of the *sarvatraga-tathatā* (all-pervading suchness), one attains entry into the realm of non-existence and tranquility, entering and abiding in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

While abiding in the first stage, one abandons the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*), forever leaves behind all births among externalists and in evil destinies, and truly dwells in the family of the Tathāgatas, correctly abiding in the supramundane path.
From the first stage, one observes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) up to the seventh stage.
Having matured in the pure contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*), knowing all phenomena to be like illusions and the like, one is no longer bound by signs;

realizing the Dharma of self-awakening, one proceeds to enter the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*). Therein, one leaves behind the various deluded views of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*) as well as the diverse characteristics of existence, non-existence, and difference in nature.
Proceeding sequentially through the stages up to the Cloud of Dharma stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one then attains the ten samādhis.
Through the sovereign power of their spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*), all flowers simultaneously bloom to adorn the Buddha-ground.
Having entered the stage of the Tathāgata, they immediately attain the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body) that is spontaneously born with its own kind and is free from volitional effort.

Consequently, they manifest various transformations and divisions of bodies, universally illuminating the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in infinite ways to bring sentient beings to maturity—like the moon reflected in water, neither emerging nor setting.
He enters skillfully into the ultimate fulfillment of the ten inexhaustible phrases, namely: the inexhaustibility of sentient beings, the inexhaustibility of worlds, and so forth.
For the sake of sentient beings with various inclinations and understandings, he preaches the Dharma according to their faculties and preferences;
though he manifests various bodies and speaks various teachings, his Dharma-body is fundamentally unmoving and free from all conditioned activity.
When one realizes that suchness is precisely what it is called, this is the realm entered by a bodhisattva through the attainment of suchness; that which is called the "five dharmas" is thus.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that the World-Honored One [teaches] the three natures?"
Regarding the entry into the five dharmas as each having its own specific characteristic, the Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness are all subsumed within the five dharmas. Mahāmati, those names and marks are the nature of parikalpita (imagined).
Mahāmati, when the mind and mental factors arise based on that parikalpita, they arise simultaneously, just as various rays of light arise simultaneously with the sun."

The distinct apprehension of individual characteristics is called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Mahāmati, because true wisdom and suchness (*tathatā*) are indestructible, they are called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the false discrimination of what is manifested by one’s own mind consists of eight kinds of conceptualization:

namely, the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses. These characteristics are unreal; they are the characteristics of false discrimination, and thus [the notions of] "self" and "mine" [are likewise unreal].
Because the two types of grasping are extinguished and the two types of selflessness arise, Mahāmati, these five dharmas—
the noble wisdom of self-realization of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, as well as the succession of the stages and all Buddha-dharmas—
are entirely contained within them.

The preceding exposition on the five dharmas is now complete; here, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*), and the two forms of selflessness (*dvividhanairātmya*) are all subsumed within these five dharmas.

Among those five dharmas, "name" (*nāman*) and "appearance" (*nimitta*) subsume the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) among the three natures, because it is due to the existence of names and appearances that pervasive conceptualization arises.
If names and appearances did not exist, pervasive conceptualization would likewise not exist; such is the reason for these names and appearances.
This subsumes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Among those five dharmas, the imagined [nature] subsumes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) within the three natures.

This is because, based on that imagination, the mind and mental factors arise with various names simultaneously, just as the sun and its light exist simultaneously. Since they arise simultaneously with various names, [it is so called].

Thus, there are various characteristics that appear individually; and among the various minds and mental factors that arise, those that possess discrimination and those that possess grasping are likewise each distinct.
These names and characteristics arise from false conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and are called the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
If there were no false conceptualization, dependent origination would not arise, for it is through false conceptualization that dependent origination occurs.

If they exist, they exist together; if they are absent, they are both absent. It is not that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) comes first and then false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), nor that false conceptualization comes first and then dependent origination. This is why false conceptualization subsumes the nature of dependent origination.

As for how correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) subsume the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*): it is because correct wisdom and suchness are far removed from the two kinds of delusion.
Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is realized through the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) as the principle of suchness, it is indestructible;
because it is indestructible, it is neither born nor extinguished. It is perfectly identical to the great void, lacking nothing and leaving no remainder.

This is how the suchness of correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna-tathatā*) subsumes and constitutes the intrinsic nature. As for what is called the "five dharmas subsuming the three intrinsic natures," these five dharmas likewise subsume the eight [consciousnesses].
The wise say that the perceived aspect (*nimitta*) and the perceiving aspect (*nāman*), which appear from within one's own mind, constitute "name" and "form.
Attachment to these gives rise to eight kinds of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), each taking its own object; this is what is called "delusive thought" (*parikalpita*).
One should understand that these eight distinct characteristics are all unreal, arising merely through the successive production of delusive conceptualization.
When consciousness has not yet been transformed, it is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), which is precisely the consciousness of names, marks, and false imaginings.

Once consciousness has been transformed, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* (womb of the Tathāgata), which is precisely right gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*). It is for this reason that these five dharmas subsume the eight consciousnesses.

Regarding how the five dharmas subsume the two selves and the two non-selves: if the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has not yet been shattered, one internally grasps the storehouse consciousness as a self.

Regarding external objects, when one takes the five sensory realms as discriminated by consciousness to be the self—this is what is called the attachment to the self (*ātma-grāha*)—once that is abandoned, one then takes the subject who abandons [the objects] to be the self, and takes that which is realized to be the self; this is what is called the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

These two forms of grasping at "self" and "mine" based on names and characteristics are mere conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). If these two types of appropriation are extinguished, then both are [extinguished].
The non-arising of self is precisely right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). In this way, these five dharmas subsume both the two selves and the two non-selves.

These five dharmas not only encompass the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two non-selves, but they are also capable of including all Buddha-dharmas—whether the four noble truths, that which is abandoned, that which is cultivated, or that which is realized; whether cause or fruit.
This is because they are subsumed within the non-emergence of the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is the single mind of quiescence.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the five dharmas—characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)—Mahāmati, regarding characteristics:
when locations, shapes, forms, colors, and so forth appear, these are called "characteristics. When there is such a characteristic, it is called [a name].

That which is designated as "a jar" and so forth—neither this nor anything else—is called a "name" (*nāma*) and a "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*). By means of various names, one manifests various characteristics such as "jars" and so on;

these mental states and mental factors are called "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). Those names and those characteristics are ultimately unattainable. From beginning to end, there is no awakening [to them].
To be free from the mutual succession of all phenomena and to be detached from unreal conceptual construction is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*), the true reality, the definitive, and the ultimate.
Ultimately, their intrinsic nature is unattainable; that is the mark of Suchness (*tathatā*), the point of entry for myself and all Buddhas to follow.
For the sake of all sentient beings, I have expounded it according to reality, established it, and revealed it.

By entering into that, one attains right awakening—neither annihilated nor eternal, where false conceptualization does not arise—and follows the noble path of self-realization, which is not shared by any outsiders, *śrāvakas*, or *pratyekabuddhas*.
The attainment of these marks is called right knowledge; great wisdom is what is meant by the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.
All Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within them. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should personally study through skillful means and also teach others, rather than following after others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—these entirely encompass the Mahāyāna.
Name, mark, and false discrimination constitute the nature of dependent origination; correct wisdom and suchness constitute the perfected nature. Thus it is established.
The above has integrated the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness entirely into the five dharmas.

However, since suchness (*tathatā*) and correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) are fundamentally not two separate entities, from the perspective of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*), suchness comes first and wisdom follows;

yet from the perspective of cultivation and realization, wisdom comes first and suchness follows. Therefore, while the preceding section used cultivation and realization to demonstrate that wisdom precedes suchness, this section [demonstrates it] from the perspective of the essence of phenomena.
Because the essence of phenomena (dharmatā) manifests first as suchness and subsequently as wisdom, it is further stated:

that which is called "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the forms, images, and physical appearances of those various phenomena. That which is called "name" (nāman) refers to the designation established upon those characteristics;
for example, the name "vase" is established upon the characteristic of a vase. This name is not that [other] name, and it cannot be transposed.

This is what is meant by "delusive conceptualization" (*vikalpa*): it refers to the mind and mental factors that are capable of establishing various names such as "vase" and manifesting various characteristics such as the "vase. What is meant by "suchness" (*tathatā*) is this:

the realization that among the various names and characteristics of things, the name does not correspond to the object and the object does not correspond to the name; since name and object do not correspond, both are without fixed determination.
If one thoroughly understands that designations are empty, then praise and blame cannot move them; thus, from beginning to end, there is no discrimination.
If one thoroughly understands that characteristics are empty, then beauty and ugliness cannot confuse them; thus, all phenomena do not undergo mutual transformation.

Because one understands that both names and characteristics are empty, one can depart from unreal conceptualization; because the various consciousnesses do not arise, names and characteristics are both like this—this is called "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Suchness (tathatā) is not only the ultimate reality in which all names and signs are suchness;

it is also the case that the self-nature of this ultimate suchness cannot be apprehended. It is not as if bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) all possess a self-nature of suchness to be realized—namely, that the very nature of suchness is itself the characteristic of suchness—and that this is what I and all others [possess].
This is the sphere entered by the Buddha in accordance with the nature of awakening, which is called "Right Knowledge.

By realizing this suchness (*tathatā*) as it truly is, he universally expounds it to sentient beings according to reality. These various names and characteristics are all conceptual constructs and provisional designations for manifestation;
they are entirely unattainable. Thus, he causes others to enter into the correct state in accordance with those very names and characteristics.

Since awakening does not destroy names and characteristics while entering cessation, nor does it cling to names and characteristics while falling into permanence, one remains far removed from the delusions of mind, thought, and consciousness;
thus, non-conceptualization arises, and one is able to accord with the noble path of self-realization.
This is precisely the characteristic that cannot be attained by any of the externalists or the followers of the two vehicles, for they do not transcend the mind and consciousness.
Because it is the mind of noble self-realized wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) and cannot be reached by the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), it is not something obtained by them.
Since it cannot be taken as an object by any consciousness, it is called "correct wisdom" (*samyagjñāna*). However, that which is not correct wisdom cannot accord with suchness (*tathatā*);
nor can one know it to be correct wisdom unless one accords with suchness. Therefore, there is no wisdom outside of suchness, and there is no suchness outside of wisdom.
To accord with suchness by means of the wisdom of suchness is precisely the realm realized through the noble wisdom of self-awakening;
this is what is called the five dharmas, which are able to encompass within them the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness, and all the Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, these five dharmas are not separate from ordinary daily life; you [should understand] this.
A bodhisattva should personally practice and train by means of the four immediate expedients (*catur-anantarya-upāya*), rather than following the shifting currents of others' words;
they should likewise teach others to practice and train for themselves, and not follow others either.

In the verse, the five dharmas first encompass the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*), so that all Buddha-dharmas are subsumed within the Mahāyāna.
Next, the verse [states] that the five dharmas subsume the three natures, as previously explained.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Regarding the statement made by the World-Honored One—that the Buddhas of the past are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise those of the future and the present—how is it, World-Honored One, that this is spoken in accordance with reality?"

"Venerable One, there is yet another meaning regarding 'reception' (*vedanā*); I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will explain it. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Do not take what is said literally regarding reception.
The measure of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is not like the sands of the Ganges. Why is this? Because it transcends worldly perspective and cannot be illustrated by any analogy.

It is because the foolish and ignorant, as well as the non-Buddhists who cling to permanence, nourish evil views through their false imaginings, and thus [the nature of] birth and death is without end."

Desiring to cause those who are exhausted by worldly desires to become weary of and detached from the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and to encourage them to strive with diligence for supreme progress, he says to them:

"The Buddhas are easy to encounter; they are not as difficult to see as the *udumbara* flower. However, when he observes that there are those to be converted who have ceased their skillful seeking, he again speaks thus: "A Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the *udumbara* flower. The *udumbara* [flower]...
Regarding the flower: there has been no past seeing, there is no present seeing, and there will be no future seeing of the Tathāgata; yet the world sees him everywhere.
This is not because he establishes his own realization through conventional means that one speaks of the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world being like the udumbara flower.

Mahāmati, those who establish their own realization through conventional means exceed worldly expectations and cannot be believed by ordinary fools; it is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, which is beyond [the world].

He considered that even such analogies are insufficient, for the true Tathāgata transcends the characteristics perceived by the mind, intellect, and consciousness, and thus cannot be illustrated by them.
Previously, it was stated that all phenomena are subsumed within the five dharmas and ultimately converge in *tathatā* (suchness);
this *tathatā* is the realm of the Dharmakāya. Now, desiring to manifest the eternal abiding of the Buddhas' Dharmakāya, Mahāmati raises worldly examples.

"World-Honored One, regarding what you have commonly taught—that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—is this to be accepted exactly as the Buddha has spoken, or is there further meaning beyond it? The Buddha said: "Do not accept it merely according to what was said.
The mental scope (*cittamātra*) of the Buddhas of the three periods is inexhaustible; it transcends all things and is without equal. It does not stop at being merely as [numerous] as [the sands]."
It is merely as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Why is this so? Because it transcends the world and is not of the world;
it is beyond the reach of the gaze and cannot be compared to any object within the world that can be known or seen.
Thus, a sutra says: "No phenomena existing or non-existing within the three realms can serve as a metaphor for the Buddha."
Furthermore, I employ this analogy because those foolish commoners and non-Buddhists who cling to views of eternalism or nihilism,
and who nourish such evil perspectives, revolve in the cycle of birth and death and are unable to perceive the realm of *tathatā*.

Desiring to cause them to become weary of and renounce the wheel of suffering within the six realms of existence, and to diligently practice the superior and progressive Dharma, I have thus spoken of these [dharmas].
The Buddhas are easy to encounter, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, unlike the udumbara flower which is difficult to see.
If one were to say that the Buddhas are as difficult to meet as the udumbara flower, people would surely give rise to despondency and cease their skillful means;

they would not produce the aspiration for excellence, and this cannot be called "skillful guidance. Therefore, I say that all Buddhas are easy to see, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, provided one's faculties are mature.

Those who have already been transformed may perceive [the Buddha] as giving rise to thoughts of indolence; at such times, he further says that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the *udumbara* flower, so that they may give rise to longing and a sense of rarity. This too is a skillful means and not a literal teaching.
The *udumbara* flower has not been seen, is not being seen now, and will not be seen; yet the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is fully known and fully perceived.

How could seeing [the truth] ever be compared to the udumbara flower? These two metaphors—one easy and one difficult—are both merely the Tathāgata’s skillful means to guide and encourage the ignorant;
they are not spoken for those who establish the ultimate penetration of self-nature.
For those who establish the ultimate penetration of self-nature, the radiance of their own awakened noble wisdom shines forth, so that it is present before their very eyes.
This realm of the Buddha is not like this; it transcends worldly expectations and is not something that ordinary, ignorant people can believe or understand.
Therefore, I borrow the example of the udumbara flower, which is difficult to encounter, to stimulate their birth of faith.

In reality, those who have attained the penetration of the essence of self-nature and the realm of self-realized noble wisdom transcend all metaphors—not only do they transcend them, but they are beyond comparison.
It cannot be compared to the sands of the Ganges, nor can it be likened to the udumbara flower. Why is this?
All that is visible in the world is not separate from mind, thought, and consciousness; thus, it can all be inferred and known.
If the true Tathāgata is beyond mind, thought, and consciousness, how could his manifested form be grasped by worldly means?
To know and see all of them is to use the sands of the Ganges as a metaphor.
Mahāmati, there is no fault in my speaking of the Buddhas as being like the sands of the Ganges. Mahāmati, for example, it is like the sands of the Ganges:
even when all kinds of fish, turtles, crocodiles, *śuśumāra* monsters, lions, elephants, horses, humans, and beasts trample upon the sand, the sand does not think or say: "I am being trampled."
They disturb me and give rise to deluded thoughts; yet the self-nature of purity is free from all defilement.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, with his noble wisdom, the Ganges-like great power, supernormal faculties, and mastery, is like the sands [of the river].
Although all non-Buddhists, humans, animals, and others may disturb him, the Tathāgata does not give rise to deluded thoughts in response. The Tathāgata remains tranquil and without [disturbance].

Because they possess the mindfulness and aspiration that, by means of the bliss of samādhi, they establish sentient beings in peace according to the original vows of the Tathāgata, they are free from affliction and disturbance;
they are no different from those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and furthermore, they have severed greed and anger.

Since the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is beyond all analogy, the Buddha’s frequent comparison of the Buddhas of the three periods to the sands of the Ganges does not entail the fault of self-contradiction, for there is a distinct meaning—as in the seven types [of analogies] below.

First, because the *dharmakāya* is free from conceptual thought (*niṣprapañca*), it is compared to the sands of the Ganges; this is because those sands of the Ganges are [inhabited by] all kinds of fish and turtles.

Even when fish, fishermen, lions, elephants, horses, and others kill or trample upon the sands, the sand does not give rise to the thought, "They are disturbing me," nor does it produce such delusive imaginings;
for its original nature is inherently pure and free from defilement.
Thus, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas have realized the noble wisdom of self-awakening, just as that Ganges River is fully endowed with virtuous characteristics.

With great power and mastery of supernormal faculties, like the sands of that river, all the celestial Māras and non-Buddhist practitioners—those foolish fish and turtles—disturb the Tathāgata with hearts of anger;
yet the Tathāgata does not give rise to even a single thought of delusion because of such disturbances.
This is because, through the vision of the Tathāgata, all phenomena are quiescent, free from the marks of mental objects, and devoid of conceptualization.

Consider this: since the Tathāgata’s original vow was to cause all sentient beings to be no different from himself and to cause them all to attain the bliss of samādhi, how could there be anyone who would instead produce affliction and disturbance? Therefore, although they may disturb the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata does not give rise to any thought of resentment;
for this reason, it is said that the Buddhas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and because they are free from greed and hatred.
Because they are free from greed, one honors them without adding joy; because they are free from hatred, one does not add anger even when provoked.
Since they do not give rise to discrimination—treating enemies and kin as equal and regarding self and others as one—it is said that the Buddhas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
As Huang Bi said: "Regarding 'the sands of the Ganges,' the Buddha said they are sands; yet the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Śakras, and Brahmās [are likewise so numerous]."
When the devas walk across it, the sand does not rejoice; when cattle, sheep, insects, or ants tread upon it, the sand does not feel anger.
It does not crave the fragrance of precious jewels, nor does it loathe the stench of excrement and urine.
This is the same principle.

For example, Mahāmati, the sands of the Ganges are the very nature of earth; when at the end of a kalpa all earth is consumed by fire, that element of earth does not abandon its own nature because it arises simultaneously with the element of fire.
Although other foolish people conceive the notion that the earth is burning, the earth itself is not burned, for fire is its cause.
In the same way, Mahāmati, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is indestructible like the sands of the Ganges.
Next, the indestructibility of the *dharmakāya* is illustrated by the analogy of the sands of the Ganges. These sands possess the intrinsic nature of earth;
even when the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, the sands do not abandon their own nature because they are co-arisen with the element of fire.
Foolish ordinary beings claim that the earth is burned, yet the earth is in reality not burned, for fire acts as its cause.
Because it arises [from conditions], the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is likewise. Fools delusively claim that the *dharmakāya* is destroyed when burned by the fire of ignorance;
they do not know that the *dharmakāya* is actually manifested through ignorance, for ignorance and Buddha-nature share the same single nature.
Therefore, the *dharmakāya* is indestructible, and like the sands of the Ganges, it is eternal. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The multitude..."
"When the kalpa comes to an end and is consumed by the great fire, my land remains peaceful and secure, constantly filled with devas and humans.
This reveals that the Dharma-body is never destroyed even amidst the fires of the kalpa-ending conflagration.
Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges are without limit, so too is the radiance of the Tathāgata without limit;
for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, it universally illumines all the assemblies of Buddhas.
Third, it is shown that because the *dharmakāya* does not fall into numerical categories, it is likened to the sands of the Ganges;

just as the sands of the Ganges are immeasurable, so too is the light of the Tathāgatas immeasurable. This is because the Tathāgata’s own essence possesses the light of great wisdom that universally illumines the *dharmadhātu*, and for the sake of maturing sentient beings, it shines everywhere throughout the Buddha-lands of the sands of the Ganges.
There are those among the assembly whose faculties have reached maturity; for them, he manifests this body and preaches the Dharma.
Because the worlds are infinite and sentient beings are infinite, his radiance is likewise infinite.
Mahāmati, it is just as when one seeks a sand grain distinct from the sands of the Ganges, it can never be found;
likewise, Mahāmati, for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there is no birth or death, nor arising and ceasing, because the causes and conditions [for such] have been severed.
Fourth, the analogy for the single characteristic of the *dharmakāya* is like the sands of the Ganges (in the Tang language, *hengsha*).
Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not change or transform into anything else, one can never find a different sand by seeking it elsewhere. The *tathāgata-dharmakāya* is also like this:
it eternally abides in a single characteristic, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing, and does not fall into the two types of birth—segmented or transformative.
Within death, because those causes and conditions for the three realms of existence are all completely severed and exhausted, there is no cause for birth and death;
thus, the Tathāgata has no distinct characteristics of birth and death, just as the sands of the Ganges have no difference between them.
Mahāmati, for example, it is impossible to perceive an increase or decrease in the sands of the Ganges;

in the same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s wisdom matures sentient beings without increasing or decreasing, because it is not a physical phenomenon (*kāyadharma*). Physical phenomena are subject to destruction, but the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata is not a physical phenomenon.
The fifth analogy concerns the Dharmakāya being without increase or decrease: it is like the sands of the Ganges;
when they are cast into the river, no increase is seen, and when they are taken out of the river, no decrease is seen. The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise:
it cannot be exhausted by taking from it, nor is it depleted by using it; one thereby brings sentient beings to maturity through the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The wisdom of sentient beings has never increased, nor has the wisdom of the Tathāgata ever decreased.

This is because the Dharmakāya is signless (*animitta*), whereas the physical body (*rūpakāya*) possesses form and characteristics. Since physical phenomena possess form, they may increase or decrease and are ultimately subject to destruction.
The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is not a physical phenomenon; it neither increases nor decreases, so how could it be destroyed?
Because the Dharma-body neither increases nor decreases, it is like the sands of the Ganges.
Just as one cannot obtain oil by pressing the sands of the Ganges, so too does the Tathāgata endure the oppression of all these beings in extreme suffering;
until all beings have attained Nirvāṇa, he does not abandon the Dharma-realm, but through his own samādhi, vows, and aspirations, he acts out of great compassion.

Therefore, the six similes illustrate that the Tathāgata is free from anger, like the sands of the Ganges. For example, if someone were to wish to obtain ghee or oil by pressing the sands of the Ganges, they would ultimately never obtain any, because there is no ghee or oil therein. Sentient beings are in the midst of extreme suffering; [yet] the Tathāgata...
By means of various skillful expedients, he seeks to bring them to liberation;
yet, because sentient beings are unwilling to accept transformation and fail to attain nirvana, they are oppressed by great suffering and affliction.

Although they do not accept transformation, the Tathāgata does not give rise to anger toward them, for he does not abandon the vast dharma-realm and is fully endowed with the joy of samādhi and great compassion.
Therefore, even though they do not receive transformation, they ultimately feel no anger or affliction; it is like pressing sand to seek oil—it can never be obtained.
Mahāmati, for example, the sands of the Ganges flow along with the water and are not without water.
In the same way, Mahāmati, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata flow toward nirvāṇa; for this reason, it is said that [the dharmas] are like the sands of the Ganges. The Tathāgata...
Mahāmati, "going" does not follow the flow of various migrations, for "going" has the meaning of destruction.
Since the original limit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is unknowable, Mahāmati, how can one speak of "going"? Mahāmati, "going" means cessation, yet the foolish do not understand this.
The seventh analogy is that the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma does not depart from nirvāṇa, being like the sands of the Ganges.
The Wei translation says: "For example, it is like the sands of the Ganges which flow along with the water; they are not without water.

So too, when the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, preach all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, there is nothing that does not accord with the flow toward nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is said to be like the sands of the Ganges flowing along."
Although it flows like water, it has never followed along with the current of birth and death;

for that current of birth and death revolves through the various realms of existence, which is the meaning of arising and ceasing. However, the original limit of birth and death is the very same as the original limit of nirvāṇa.
Since the original limit of nirvāṇa cannot be known, the original limit of birth and death likewise cannot be known. Because it cannot be known, [it is called] "limitless."
One should not say that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is a "flowing away. Why then do I say that birth-and-death has a flowing away?
What is called "flowing away" has the meaning of "severance"; it means that while the flow of birth-and-death can be severed, the flow of *nirvāṇa* is inexhaustible.
It is for this reason that birth-and-death is described as a "flowing away. Yet, foolish people do not understand this and claim that the Tathāgata also follows along with that flowing away.
They fall into the view of annihilationism because they do not understand that although the Tathāgata appears to flow within the cycle of birth and death, he constantly dwells in nirvāṇa;
it is just as when river sand flows along with the water, yet in reality there is no going.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, if the limit of birth and death for sentient beings cannot be known, how can liberation be known?

The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Because the causes—the beginningless habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of false delusions, faults, and conceptual constructions—are extinguished, one realizes that external objects are merely manifestations of one’s own mind.

When the body of conceptual construction is transformed, this is liberation; it is not [liberation] through non-extinction. Therefore, [the limit of birth and death] is boundless, yet it is not entirely non-existent.”
All those which are the infinite various names for that false imagination—whether observed internally or externally—are devoid of false imagination.
There is no other sentient being; wisdom and suchness, all dharmas, are entirely quiescent.
Because one does not recognize them as the manifestation of one's own mind, false imagination arises; if one recognizes them, it ceases.

Mahāmati’s thought was this: "If the primordial limit of birth and death is unknowable because it has the sense of being 'annihilated,' then liberation must likewise have the sense of being 'annihilated' and would also be unknowable. How, then, can liberation be known?
What is called liberation is the total extinction of the habitual tendencies of beginningless false discrimination; it is not being subject to such discrimination."
Enveloped by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one further realizes that external natures are all manifestations of one’s own mind;

thus, one does not give rise to discrimination and is no longer bound by the activity of deluded thoughts (*parikalpita*). This transformation of the body of deluded thoughts within birth and death is called liberation.
Yet, since liberation is in reality not a cessation, it is said that liberation has no boundaries; this does not mean that birth and death are extinguished and then liberation occurs.
Because liberation is entirely extinguished and utterly non-existent, it cannot be known;
yet, to speak of "boundless liberation" is merely another name for the boundless delusions of saṃsāra that have been transformed.
In reality, the original limit of saṃsāra is none other than the original limit of nirvāṇa; they are not different in essence. Therefore, it is said: "Form is boundless."
One should know that prajñā is likewise boundless. It is not only that birth-and-death does not exist apart from deluded conceptualization;
when one observes the internal body and external objects with wisdom, apart from deluded conceptualization, even the mark of a sentient being cannot be found.
Thus, from the observing wisdom itself to the observed objects, all are utterly quiescent; therefore, deluded conceptualization is extinguished.
One attains infinite liberation because one does not know that all phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind;
by grasping at one's own mind with one's own mind, delusive thoughts arise, which constitute the very root of birth and death.

If one realizes that there is only mind, then delusive thoughts are extinguished, and one immediately attains infinite liberation. How could it be said, then, that liberation is a state of annihilation?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Observe all the Guides as being like the sands of the Ganges:
they are neither destroyed nor do they depart, nor are they ultimately finite; this is what constitutes equality.
Observe all the Tathāgatas as being equal to the sands of the Ganges: they are entirely free from all faults, and though they follow the stream, their nature is eternal."
The Buddha is the Perfectly Awakened One.
The Guide observes that those who are like the sands of the Ganges are not destroyed by fire, do not depart following the stream, and are likewise not subject to the dharma of ultimate annihilation;
this reveals that the equal Dharma-body is indestructible, non-departing, and unborn.
Furthermore, one observes that the Tathāgatas are like the sands of the Ganges;

that is to say, they are like the sands of the Ganges in being without thought, free from the faults of love and hatred, without differentiation, and because they are free from causes and conditions, they are without oil and free from the affliction of suffering.
Abiding eternally in their own nature as they flow toward *nirvāṇa*, this is the perfect enlightenment of the Buddha. Thus, the single analogy of the sands of the Ganges possesses various [meanings].
How could the meaning of "categories" imply that a number as vast as the sands of the Ganges is sufficient to match the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata?
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has prophesied that Arhats shall attain [Buddhahood]..."
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is equal and without distinction from all bodhisattvas; for all dharmas of sentient beings, there is no nirvāṇa.

Who then attains the Buddha-way? From the Buddha until parinirvāṇa, not a single word is spoken therein, nor is there any answer, because the Tathāgata is eternally in samādhi, having neither thought nor deliberation; it is the emanation-buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) [who acts].

If he performs such Buddha-works through transformation, why does he speak of the mark of the momentary, successive destruction of consciousness; why are Vajrapāṇi and his retinue constantly following and guarding him;

why does he not establish a fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*); why do Māra, the deeds of Māra, and the retribution of evil karma appear—such as the case of the brahmin student Cincā-Māṇava and the woman Sundarī, who departed with empty bowls—and why do the obstructions of evil karma manifest? How is it that the Tathāgata attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
Yet they do not escape all faults. The Buddha said to Mahāmati: “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it;
I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
Since the previous discussion of the single analogy of the Ganges possesses many meanings, there is no contradiction with one's own words;
this passage, moreover, extensively cites various contradictory statements to pose questions. First, it asks:

if śrāvakas of fixed nature are like the rotten seeds of a plantain sprout that will never become Buddhas, for what reason did the World-Honored One further bestow upon them the prediction of attaining bodhi? And [why] bodhi...
"Are these two statements not contradictory—that the Tathāgata has no difference [between himself and others], and that it is impossible for any sentient being not to become a Buddha?

Furthermore, the World-Honored One has already stated that all sentient beings can attain Buddhahood, yet you also say that the Dharma-nature of all beings does not enter nirvana; ultimately, who is it that becomes a Buddha?
Moreover, the World-Honored One has stated that from beginning to end he preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, delivering over three hundred assemblies of sutras."
Yet you say that in the interim he never spoke a single word nor ever gave a single answer—is this not a contradiction?
Since the Tathāgata was in meditative concentration, without deliberation or discernment, he should not have manifested any buddha-activities;
why then do you say that transformation-buddhas and emanations pervaded the ten directions to extensively perform buddha-activities—is this not a contradiction?

Fourth Question: Since the Tathāgata has already taught that the *ālayavijñāna* is the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is pure by nature and fundamentally free from arising and ceasing, why does he further speak of the mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as perishing moment by moment? Is this not a contradiction?
Fifth Question: Since it is said that the Tathāgata is without marks (*animitta*) that can be perceived, why does he further say that the Vajrapāṇi always [protects him]? Is this not a contradiction?

1. Is it not contradictory that he is attended by guards? 2. Since it was stated that the "original limit" (pūrvakoṭi) is not established, why is it further said that he knows liberation—is this not a contradiction?

3. Since the Tathāgata has realized the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) and is free from all faults and evils, how is it that he is not free from faults and yet possesses various forms of suffering and affliction—is this not a contradiction?

The celestial Māra raising an army is a demonic deed (*mārakarma*). The Brahmin Ciñcā tying a wooden bowl to her waist and joining with the heretic Sundarī to falsely slander the Buddha is an evil deed (*akuśalakarma*).

Furthermore, when the Buddha went to the village of Pāṭaligrāma to beg for alms and departed with an empty bowl, as well as his eating of horse-gram and his suffering from headaches and backaches caused by a wooden stake, [these were also results of past karma].
The injury to the foot by a poisoned thorn, Devadatta’s pushing of the mountain to crush the Buddha, the fire pit, the intoxicated elephant, and the poisoned food—all these were karmic retributions.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I have spoken of these for the sake of *nirvāṇa without remainder*, in order to encourage and advance those who practice as Bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, in other worlds, there are those practicing as bodhisattvas who take delight in the nirvāṇa of the śrāvaka vehicle;

in order to cause them to leave the śrāvaka vehicle and advance toward the Mahāyāna, the *nirmāṇakāya* buddha bestows predictions of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas. This is not done by the *dharmakāya* buddha.
Mahāmati, for this reason, it is said that the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are no different. Mahāmati, "no different" means that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas are not distinct.
The Tathāgata’s liberation through the severance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is of a single flavor; it is not [merely] the severance of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

O Mahāmati, those who see the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) attain a supreme purity. As for the afflictive hindrances, they are severed by first practicing the vision of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), whereby the seven consciousnesses are extinguished.
The liberation from the hindrance of phenomena is the ultimate purity resulting from the extinction of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Regarding the reason for bestowing the prediction of Buddhahood upon śrāvakas, there are two meanings:
first, because some śrāvakas seek their own parinirvāṇa with remainder, [the Buddha] desires to urge them forward so that they may enter the parinirvāṇa without remainder;

second, because those in this world or other directions who have resolved their minds and practice as bodhisattvas originally intended to seek the Buddha-way, yet hear only that the Buddha-way is long and distant.
Having endured diligent toil for a long time, one might finally achieve success, yet then experience a retreat because of a fondness for the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna.

Therefore, in order to entice and advance those who practice the Bodhisattva path, causing them to abandon the Small Vehicle and turn toward the Great [Vehicle] so that they may realize *nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*, the Buddha bestows upon them a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
This is a prediction bestowed by a *nirmāṇakāya-buddha* for the sake of *śrāvakas*, not one bestowed by a *dharmatā-buddha*.
Because this cause has been explained, it is said that the Tathāgata’s bestowing of predictions upon śrāvakas is no different from that for bodhisattvas;

this is not intended merely to encourage them. Furthermore, the reason why śrāvakas are not different from bodhisattvas is that, when compared with all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, both vehicles have already exhausted the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within the three realms and the four stages of abiding, thereby attaining the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

The liberation through taste and the liberation through sameness are identical; it does not mean that the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are also severed such that one would be no different from a Buddha or a Bodhisattva.

If the cognitive obscurations were severed, one would transcend the grasping at phenomena by seeing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which is far more exceptionally pure than merely attaining the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).
As for those who have severed the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they have only begun their cultivation and severed them [at that initial stage].

Although one may have realized the selflessness of persons regarding the afflictions and delusions, if one has not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it is not ultimate purity;

for while the preceding seven consciousnesses—the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*manovijñāna*), and the sensory consciousnesses—have ceased their activity and the grasping at a self has been suddenly severed, this is called attaining the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, and it does not involve the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
