If, however, one severs the obstacles to phenomena and attains liberation through phenomena...
Thus, when the ālayavijñāna—which contains the beginningless habitual tendencies of false ignorance—is entirely eliminated, it is called the "pure white consciousness" (amala-vijñāna).
This is termed the attainment of the wisdom of dharma-emptiness, through which one first achieves ultimate purity.

Since this is certainly beyond the knowledge of the followers of the Two Vehicles, how could they possibly be said to be no different from Bodhisattvas, as if they were racing side by side? Such a claim would be contradictory.
Indeed. Because of the principle of the primordially abiding dharma (*pūrvasthita-dharma*), there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in terms of priority or posteriority.
I have said that all sentient beings do not understand the dharma, and I have also said that from beginning to end, not a single word has been spoken.
It means that because all sentient beings are from the very beginning in the state of quiescent extinction and do not undergo further extinction, it is said that there is no Buddha to be realized;
and because all phenomena are from the very beginning beyond the realm of verbal expression, it is said that there is no dharma to be taught.

If there were a Buddha to be realized, that would be called slandering the Buddha; if there were a dharma to be taught, that would be called slandering the Dharma. This is because they abide in their original nature.
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is eternally abiding; whether dharmas exist or do not exist, the dharma-realm is eternally abiding.

Because it is fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) throughout the past and future, one speaks of "non-existence" when establishing non-existence. How could such a statement be contradictory?
Because his original vows are inexhaustible, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma without deliberation or investigation; because he is transformed by right knowledge, his mindfulness is not deluded;
because he has severed the habitual tendencies of the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance, he has abandoned the two afflictions and is detached from the two deaths;
and because he has awakened to the selflessness of persons and phenomena and severed the two obstacles.
When the Tathāgata is in meditative concentration, he has no deliberation nor investigation; yet it is said that he manifests transformation-buddhas to perform the buddha-work.

Because the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible original vows protect and deliver sentient beings, although he remains in concentration without mind or objective conditions, he is able to respond to all their minds and conditions by preaching various dharmas. All that he speaks thus proceeds from the ocean of right gnosis.
Emerging from the midst of the stream, one speaks without depending on deliberation;

the reason for being without thought or deliberation is that the five abodes have been thoroughly exhausted, the two deaths have forever ceased, the two voids are simultaneously realized, and the two obstructions are completely severed.
Thus, although there is no deliberation or examination, one is able to manifest buddha-works—how could this be contradictory?
Mahāmati, the seven moments—the mind, the intellect, the mental consciousness, and the visual consciousnesses—have as their cause the habitual tendencies of the wholesome and untainted categories;
being free from these, they no longer undergo cyclic existence. Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both cyclic existence and nirvana, and of suffering and happiness;
it cannot be realized by those of deluded intellect and foolish ordinary people whose minds are distracted by emptiness.
I say that the Tathāgatagarbha is pure by nature, yet I also speak of the various consciousnesses as perishing moment by moment in succession—

namely, the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the seven preceding types of consciousness— which flow and shift from moment to moment without abiding for even an instant.

Because they contain the seeds of false habitual tendencies within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the storehouse consciousness arises simultaneously with these seven types of consciousness.
Cessation occurs because one has not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*); thus there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

If those noble ones (*ārya*) abide in samādhi and presently attain the wholesome and untainted, they are then able to distance themselves from mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), and no longer undergo moment-to-moment cycling.
This, however, is merely the cessation of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), not the cessation of the Tathāgatagarbha. For although the Tathāgatagarbha exists within the consciousness...

Because the *tathāgatagarbha* is primordially pure yet capable of acting as the cause for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), nirvāṇa, suffering, and happiness according to conditions, it enters into birth-and-death through defiled conditions; yet the *tathāgatagarbha* remains pure, unchanging, and self-abiding.
Likewise, it enters into nirvāṇa through pure conditions; yet the *tathāgatagarbha* remains pure, unchanging, and self-abiding.
Because it is thus, one knows that the Tathāgatagarbha is empty yet not empty, and not empty yet empty.
However, because those foolish ordinary beings have their minds distracted by emptiness and their wisdom confused by emptiness, they perceive it only as empty and do not know its non-emptiness.
Therefore, I say that the various consciousnesses perish moment by moment in succession, and yet I also say that the Tathāgatagarbha is primordial.
How could this not be consistent with their coming forth in purity?
Mahāmati, those whom the Vajrapāṇi guardians follow and protect are merely *nirmāṇa-buddhas* (emanation buddhas), not the true Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, the true Tathāgata is beyond all faculties and measures, and transcends all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists.

Because the faculties and measures are entirely extinguished through the attainment of the patience of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) regarding the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), one is not protected by the Vajrapāṇis.
All emanation-buddhas (*nirmāṇabuddha*) do not arise from karma; those who are not emanation-buddhas are nonetheless not separate from the Buddha.

Like the wheel of a potter and other such things produced by sentient beings, they teach the Dharma through signs; yet they do not speak of their own self-realized realm as a place of personal communication.
Furthermore, when I say that the Vajrapāṇi spirits constantly follow and attend me, they are attending the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha (the transformation Buddha), not the *dharmakāya* Buddha.

This is because the *dharmakāya* Buddha is far removed from all sense faculties, all numerical measures, and the faculties and measures of all ordinary people, *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and non-Buddhists; these have all been utterly extinguished. Therefore, [it is not attended by] any ordinary beings or *śrāvakas*.
None are able to know or see it; what is seen by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).

Because they do not know that it is manifested from the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), they perceive it as coming from the outside, grasping at its spatial limits and being unable to know it exhaustively.
Therefore, only those who practice according to reality personally realize *tathatā* (suchness), see the *dharmakāya*, and attain the bliss of the present dharma.

Abiding in the accomplishment of the uninterrupted knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the uninterrupted patience regarding phenomena (*dharmanirvedhabhāgīya-kṣānti*), this is precisely the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Because the Dharmakāya Tathāgata dwells eternally within the diamond concentration, he does not require protection by the Vajrapāṇi spirits;
those who are protected are merely the *nirmāṇa-buddhas* (emanation buddhas). As for what is called "emanation," it means that [the emanation] does not arise from oneself.
All those born through the power of their own karma appear in accordance with the roots of goodness of sentient beings; therefore, they are called "emanations" (*nirmāṇa*).
Although these emanation Buddhas are not the ultimate Buddha, they are nonetheless the ultimate Buddha appearing in accordance with conditions, and thus they do not depart from the ultimate Buddha.
It is like the vessels produced by a potter: through the transformation of the wheel, the string, clay, water, and human effort, various objects are manifested.

The vessel [of the body] exists to respond to the needs of sentient beings; the True Buddha and the emanated Buddhas likewise manifest according to the activities and characteristics of sentient beings as their cause, appearing with the thirty-two marks to preach the Dharma in response to the minds of sentient beings.
Therefore, there are faculties and measures; however, in the state that transcends self-communication and is free from faculties and measures, one speaks of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
Because it is within the sphere of experience, I say that those guarded by the Mallas are transformation Buddhas; how could this be contradictory?

Furthermore, Mahāmati, fools give rise to the view of annihilation based on the cessation of the seven consciousnesses; because they do not realize the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to the view of permanence.
Due to their own false imaginings, they do not know the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi); through the cessation of the wisdom of their own false imaginings, they attain liberation.

The reason why the "original limit" (*pūrvakoṭi*) is not established is that those deluded worldlings, relying on the seven bodies of consciousness which perish moment by moment, give rise to the view of annihilationism;

furthermore, failing to realize the subtle arising and ceasing of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), they instead cling to its continuous flow as being truly eternal, thereby giving rise to the view of permanence.
They do not know that calculating annihilation and calculating permanence are both merely portions of one's own false conceptualization.

It is not that one truly does not know the ground of the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), which is neither born nor extinguished; rather, it is because one does not establish that original limit for them.

If one can distance oneself from discursive thought (*vikalpa*) and the cessation of consciousness (*vijñāna*), then the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*), and one thereby understands liberation.
Thus, while it is said that the original limit is unknowable, the statement that one knows liberation—how could these two be contradictory?
Because the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) have been severed, all faults are eliminated.

To say that one realizes the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) yet is not free from various faults means that while the Tathāgata has exhausted the five stages and is truly free from all evils and transgressions, he nevertheless does not escape various karmic retributions; this precisely demonstrates that determinate karma (*niyatavedanīyakarman*) cannot be avoided.
This can be transformed so as to serve as an example for all humans and devas; it does not mean that the Tathāgata has not abandoned all faults and evils—how could this be contradictory?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The Three Vehicles are also not vehicles; the Tathāgata..."

The unceasingly indestructible teachings proclaimed by all Buddhas, which are free from all faults and evils, are intended to encourage those of inferior capacity toward uninterrupted wisdom and nirvana without remainder;

therefore, they are taught in a concealed manner. The wisdom arising from all Buddhas is the analytical exposition of the various vehicles and paths, yet these are not the ultimate vehicle, nor are they true nirvana. They are taught as the realms of desire, form, and existence, and as views.

They teach that the consciousness arising from the mental consciousness of the four stages of abiding—the dwelling place of the mind, the mind itself, and the visual consciousness and so forth—is subject to cessation and impermanence;
yet they speak of it as eternal, viewing it as nirvana.
This verse conveys a single meaning: it signifies that within the realm of *tathatā* (suchness), there are fundamentally no three vehicles (*triyāna*).

Since the three vehicles are, in reality, not vehicles at all, there is no matter of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). Thus, even for the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata, there is no such thing as entering *nirvāṇa*;
hence it is said that the Tathāgata does not perish. Furthermore, since the three vehicles do not exist, to speak of bestowing predictions upon them is likewise [unfounded].

A "Buddha" refers to one who has already severed the afflictions and abandoned all faults and evils; by guiding and advancing others, he enables them to enter the wisdom of the uninterrupted Dharma (*anantarya-dharma*) and realize *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
Therefore, it was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that those of the three vehicles can all become Buddhas.
Furthermore, because all Buddhas appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kāraṇa*), it is thus...
The wisdom arising from all Buddhas teaches that all phenomena are not non-existent; this is the analysis of this path, for there is no other vehicle beyond it.
Thus, it is said that the three vehicles are all provisional teachings. Even the *nirvāṇa* realized therein is not ultimate reality.
The reason it is not ultimate is that they have merely severed the afflictions of the four stages of abiding (*catur-vāsabhūmi*). These are as follows:

The four afflictions—the ground of abiding in desire-attachment, the ground of abiding in form-attachment, the ground of abiding in existence-attachment, and the ground of abiding in all views—are precisely the two delusions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*).
These arise from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), taking the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as their dwelling place and depending upon the manas for their abode.
Thus, the seventh manas firmly clings to the eighth consciousness as a self, thereby constituting the basis for the fragmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*).
Because it is the seed of birth and death, it is called that which arises from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); it is the abode of consciousness and the dwelling place of the mind (*manas*).
Those of the Two Vehicles see only the mind and the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, and consider them to be subject to severance and extinction.
They reckon them to be impermanent, asserting that the cessation of this impermanence is itself the eternal Nirvāṇa; they do not know that [Nirvāṇa] is merely the exhaustion of what is falsely named.

Regarding the fact that Nirvana has not yet been attained as its own-nature—emptiness—the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata—at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati asked in verse: "As for those bodhisattvas who are resolved to seek the Buddha-way, how should they regard wine, meat, and onions?
I pray only that the Unsurpassed Honored One, out of compassion, will explain this for me."
"What is it that fools greedily crave—foul, filthy, and ill-reputed, yet sweet to tigers and wolves—which can be eaten?
To eat it gives rise to all manner of faults; to not eat it is a source of merit and goodness. I pray that you will explain for me the faults and merits of eating and not eating.
After the Bodhisattva Mahāmati had spoken these verses in question, he again addressed the Buddha, saying: "I pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us."
Regarding the merits of not eating meat and the faults of eating meat, I and all the bodhisattvas, in the present and the future,
shall expound the Dharma in various ways for those sentient beings who desire to eat meat, so that those beings may turn toward one another with a mind of loving-kindness;
having attained such a mind of loving-kindness, each shall clearly understand their respective stages of abiding and swiftly attain ultimate, unsurpassed Bodhi.
Even the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, having brought their own stages to rest, have attained unsurpassed Bodhi;
yet even those heterodox practitioners of evil and false doctrines, who hold the inverted views of eternalism and nihilism and are attached to them, still maintain prohibitions against eating meat.
How much more so for the Tathāgata, the protector of the world, who has perfected the True Dharma—could he possibly eat meat? The Buddha told Mahā-...
“Wisdom, excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
[The Buddha continued: “One aspect of eating meat is that it is the habitual karma of yakṣas; therefore, I shall explain this so that they may understand it.”
Because one must sever evil through self-restraint, those bodhisattvas who aspire to seek the Buddha-way first take the precept against killing as their primary rule.

Therefore, I pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately expound upon this; for if its evils were not explained, those foolish people would not know to feel weary of them or renounce them, and their attachment to foul and impure merit would cause their fortune to diminish daily while their reputation would also decline—how much more so [if they do not renounce it]!
As for meat, it is a thing that tigers and wolves delight in with wholehearted craving.
How can those who stand alongside Heaven and Earth as the most spiritually gifted among all beings share the same cravings as tigers and wolves, and likewise eat it with such wholehearted pleasure?
Furthermore, there are many kinds of faults in eating meat; in the present life, the first is that one will frequently suffer from illness.
Second, regarding short life spans: if this occurs in the future, then from lifetime to lifetime one will be devoured by others without end;

yet if one does not eat [meat], there are likewise many kinds of meritorious virtues. Just as in the present life one is free from illness and enjoys long life, in the future one will be born in a favorable realm and enjoy all manner of blessings and happiness. If the Tathāgata were to explain at length the faults of eating meat—
Having understood this meaning—the faults [of killing] and the merit of abstaining from eating—I and the bodhisattvas shall not allow various murderous thoughts to arise.
Causing them to face one another with loving-kindness, and having attained that mind of loving-kindness, they shall further cherish all sentient beings as if they were an only child.
Each, within their respective stages of dwelling, shall attain purity and clarity, giving rise to no attachment and swiftly [attaining liberation].

Having attained unsurpassed bodhi, they further cause those of the two vehicles who have ceased their practice and entered extinction— those unwilling to protect living beings and deficient in the mind of compassion—
to likewise turn their minds toward unsurpassed bodhi. Moreover, even among the various non-Buddhists who dwell in false views, reckoning in nihilism or eternalism,
and who hold perverted attachments such as the cow- or dog-vows, there are still prohibitions that do not permit the eating of meat.
How much less could the Tathāgata— having rescued and protected sentient beings through the pure True Dharma and enabled them to achieve the pure and white Brahma-conduct—
permit them to eat meat without establishing prohibitions against it?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat; however, I shall now briefly explain them for you.
That is to say, all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, been related to one another through a succession of causes and conditions as our six kinds of kin.

Because they have always been our kin, one should not eat meat. [This includes] the flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, horses, humans, wild beasts, and so forth. Thus spoke the butcher.
Meat should not be eaten because it is sold in mixed markets; meat should not be eaten because it grows from impure elements;
meat should not be eaten because when sentient beings smell its odor, they all become terrified—just as dogs see outcasts such as Caṇḍālas and Taṃbas and, loathing them, bark together in fear;
furthermore, meat should not be eaten because it prevents the compassionate mind of a practitioner from arising.
One should not eat meat because it is a delicacy craved by the foolish and ignorant, being foul-smelling, impure, and lacking a good reputation;

one should not eat meat because it causes the failure of various mantras and rituals; one should not eat meat because those who kill living beings perceive the form and give rise to consciousness, becoming deeply attached to its flavor;
and one should not eat meat because such meat-eaters are abandoned by the devas.
One should not eat meat because it causes foul breath; one should not eat meat because it results in many evil dreams;
one should not eat meat because tigers and wolves will smell its scent in secluded forests; one should not eat meat because it leads to a lack of moderation in eating and drinking;
and one should not eat meat because it prevents the practitioner from developing a sense of revulsion [for the world]. I shall now speak of all that...
When eating and drinking, one should regard the food as the flesh of one's own children and as medicine being taken; therefore, one should not eat meat.
There is no basis for permitting the consumption of meat.
The Buddha briefly set forth its faults and perils: first, because all beings have been mutual relatives and kin, they share the same essence.
Because one's parents should not be eaten, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings of the six realms have been my parents;
to kill and eat them is to kill my own parents and to kill my own body.

How can one who eats the flesh of their parents and simultaneously eats their own flesh be called a human? Second, regarding the flesh of humans and animals: [the text continues that these are likewise forbidden].

First, when a butcher sells various meats, would anyone with a human heart fail to feel sorrow and instead eat them with relish? Second, all meats are composed of the essence of blood and the impure, foul-smelling elements of life; how could those who seek purity consume them? Third, for one who eats meat, all sentient beings who smell its odor will be struck with terror. Fourth, [the meat is the food of demons]. Fifth, [it obstructs the path to liberation]. Sixth, [it violates the precepts]. Seventh, [it causes rebirth among carnivorous animals]. Eighth, [it prevents the attainment of the Buddha's wisdom]. Ninth, [it is contrary to the conduct of the noble ones]. Tenth, [it is not the practice of the Buddhas]. Eleventh, [it leads to a foul odor]. Twelfth, [it brings about a bad reputation]. Thirteenth, [it results in a stinking mouth]. Fourteenth, [it causes the body to emit a foul stench]. Fifteenth, [it leads to being reviled by the wise]. Sixteenth, [it results in being shunned by the virtuous]. Seventeenth, [it causes one to be born in the hells]. Eighteenth, [it leads to birth as a hungry ghost]. Nineteenth, [it results in birth as an animal]. Twentieth, [it prevents rebirth in the heavens]. Twenty-first, [it obstructs the attainment of the Path]. Twenty-second, [it prevents the realization of Nirvana]. Twenty-third, [it causes one to be separated from the Three Jewels]. Twenty-fourth, [it prevents one from seeing the Buddhas]. Twenty-fifth, [it obstructs the hearing of the Dharma]. Twenty-sixth, [it prevents the sight of the Sangha]. Twenty-seventh, [it obstructs the cultivation of the roots of goodness]. Twenty-eighth, [it prevents the planting of the seeds of enlightenment]. Twenty-ninth, [it obstructs the perfection of the paramitas]. Thirtieth, [it prevents the fulfillment of the bodhisattva vows]. Thirty-first, [it obstructs the attainment of the ten powers]. Thirty-second, [it prevents the realization of the four fearlessnesses]. Thirty-third, [it obstructs the eighteen unique qualities]. Thirty-fourth, [it prevents the attainment of the great compassion]. Thirty-fifth, [it obstructs the eighty minor marks]. Thirty-sixth, [it prevents the attainment of the thirty-two major marks]. Thirty-seventh, [it obstructs the attainment of the dharanis]. Thirty-eighth, [it prevents the mastery of the samadhis]. Thirty-ninth, [it obstructs the attainment of the eloquence of the Buddhas]. Fortieth, [it prevents the realization of the ultimate truth]. Forty-first, [it obstructs the attainment of the unconditioned]. Forty-second, [it prevents the realization of the nature of emptiness]. Forty-third, [it obstructs the attainment of signlessness]. Forty-fourth, [it prevents the realization of wishlessness]. Forty-fifth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-arising]. Forty-sixth, [it prevents the realization of non-cessation]. Forty-seventh, [it obstructs the attainment of non-birth]. Forty-eighth, [it prevents the realization of non-death]. Forty-ninth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-suffering]. Fiftieth, [it prevents the realization of non-self]. Fifty-first, [it obstructs the attainment of non-purity]. Fifty-second, [it prevents the realization of non-impurity]. Fifty-third, [it obstructs the attainment of non-defilement]. Fifty-fourth, [it prevents the realization of non-purification]. Fifty-fifth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-attachment]. Fifty-sixth, [it prevents the realization of non-hatred]. Fifty-seventh, [it obstructs the attainment of non-delusion]. Fifty-eighth, [it prevents the realization of non-clinging]. Fifty-ninth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-grasping]. Sixtieth, [it prevents the realization of non-discrimination]. Sixty-first, [it obstructs the attainment of non-conceptualization]. Sixty-second, [it prevents the realization of non-mindfulness]. Sixty-third, [it obstructs the attainment of non-recollection]. Sixty-fourth, [it prevents the realization of non-forgetfulness]. Sixty-fifth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-perception]. Sixty-sixth, [it prevents the realization of non-cognition]. Sixty-seventh, [it obstructs the attainment of non-knowledge]. Sixty-eighth, [it prevents the realization of non-insight]. Sixty-ninth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-wisdom]. Seventieth, [it prevents the realization of non-enlightenment]. Seventy-first, [it obstructs the attainment of non-liberation]. Seventy-second, [it prevents the realization of non-nirvana]. Seventy-third, [it obstructs the attainment of non-extinction]. Seventy-fourth, [it prevents the realization of non-permanence]. Seventy-fifth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-impermanence]. Seventy-sixth, [it prevents the realization of non-suffering]. Seventy-seventh, [it obstructs the attainment of non-bliss]. Seventy-eighth, [it prevents the realization of non-self]. Seventy-ninth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-purity]. Eightieth, [it prevents the realization of non-impurity]. Eighty-first, [it obstructs the attainment of non-defilement]. Eighty-second, [it prevents the realization of non-purification]. Eighty-third, [it obstructs the attainment of non-attachment]. Eighty-fourth, [it prevents the realization of non-hatred]. Eighty-fifth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-delusion]. Eighty-sixth, [it prevents the realization of non-clinging]. Eighty-seventh, [it obstructs the attainment of non-grasping]. Eighty-eighth, [it prevents the realization of non-discrimination]. Eighty-ninth, [it obstructs the attainment of non-conceptualization]. Ninetieth, [it prevents the realization of non-mindfulness]. If one who gathers sentient beings is like a butcher, a hunter, or a dog—objects of loathing and fear that bark at the herd—how could he eat?
Fifth, if the mind of killing has once stirred and the mind of compassion does not arise, how could one who cultivates the mind of compassion eat?
Sixth, if it is something craved by the ignorant and foul with stench and impurity, how could my disciples consume meat?
It is just as when the foolish and ignorant, who delight in what is foul and impure, cause pure conduct to degenerate, leading all people in the world to cry out:
"How can there be a true śramaṇa practicing pure conduct who eats meat? How could one who cultivates pure conduct eat such things?
Seventh, whether in cemeteries or at the foot of trees, they may either maintain incantations or seek liberation.
Because eating meat creates all manner of obstacles, how could those who seek supreme fruition eat it?

Eighth: for those who have long eaten meat, the impulse to kill has become habitual; seeing the form and color of sentient beings, they develop a deep craving for their flavor and harbor the intent to devour them.
How could one who regards and protects sentient beings as they would their own eyes eat such meat?
Ninth, to abandon the flavor of the Dharma-food consumed by the noble ones and instead eat the flesh of sentient beings is to be associated with rākṣasas and rejected by the devas;

how could such things be fit for consumption? Tenth, just as the foul stench of a burning corpse is impure, how could it be smelled and brought into the mouth? All meats cause the breath to smell foul; how could they [be eaten]?
Eleventh: For those who eat meat, the intent to kill increases;
their dreams are restless, and they frequently see various evil things in their sleep, their body hair standing on end. How could one who seeks peace of mind eat such food?
Twelfth: Those who eat meat lack all wholesome powers; when they dwell in secluded places, there are many non-human beings (amanuṣya) present.
13. When they watch for an opportunity, tigers, wolves, and lions also come to watch and seek to eat their flesh;
how can those who seek security and peace in safety eat such things? 14. Those who eat meat are never satisfied by what they eat, which increases their illnesses;
how can those who practice the art of maintaining life (āyurveda) eat such things? 15. The Bodhisattva practices...
To emerge from birth and death, one should view all food and drink as pus and blood, fix the mind upon the Noble Path, and not give rise to craving for flavors.
If one gives rise to attachment, one cannot achieve weary detachment; how could one who is weary of birth and death eat such things?
Therefore, I have always said that even when an ordinary person consumes pure food for the sake of a pure livelihood, they should still practice the six [reflections].
One should regard meat as food for one's parents and as food for one's children; one should view it as taking medicine when one is ill. How much less could one eat meat?
For there is no possibility that those who permit the eating of meat could ever be [righteous].
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasaudāsa who ate various kinds of meat until he eventually...
When subjects and citizens find it unbearable to provide food, they will immediately plot rebellion;
therefore, by cutting off their stipends, those who eat blood incur such faults as these, and for this reason one should not eat meat.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all those who kill for the sake of profit slaughter and trade in living beings; those foolish beings who eat meat use money as a net to catch various meats.
Those who take life—whether by means of wealth, hooks, or nets—kill various beings that move through the air, water, or on land, slaughtering and selling them for profit.
Mahāmati, there is no fish or meat that is not taught, sought, or imagined [by such people];
for this reason, one should not eat meat. Mahāmati, at times I have prohibited five kinds of meat, or I have forbidden them altogether.
"O Mahāmati, in this sutra, ten kinds [of meat] have been excluded in every way and at all times; all skillful means have been completely severed.
Even the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not consume food, let alone eat fish or meat.
Furthermore, because they are preceded by great compassion, they regard all sentient beings as their only child; therefore, they do not permit it."
[The Buddha] commanded him to eat the flesh of his own son.
The former statement—that eating meat entails various faults—refers to the manifest retribution for eating meat;
therefore, he cites King Sutasoma, who was so addicted to the taste of meat that he eventually ate human flesh and consequently lost his kingdom, as proof.

In the language of Tang, this is called Śakra Devānām Indra. While occupying the position of King of Devas, due to residual habits from past lives of eating meat, he transformed his body into a hawk and pursued a dove.
At that time, I was a king named Śibi; out of compassion for the dove, I cut flesh from my own body to take its place in death.
O Mahāmati, if even the residual habits of Śakra still cause distress to sentient beings, how much more so [the habits of others]?
Those others who, lacking shame, constantly eat meat should know that eating meat brings suffering to oneself and distress to others; therefore, a Bodhisattva should not eat meat.
Mahāmati, in the past there was a king who was riding a horse while hunting when the horse became startled and bolted, entering a perilous mountain pass.
Having no way to return and being far removed from human habitation, he encountered a female lion with whom he shared a dwelling place.
He subsequently engaged in loathsome conduct and begot several sons; the eldest was named Pāda-paṅka (Spotted-foot).

Later, he became king and ruled over seven hundred million households. Due to the residual habit of eating meat, he would not eat anything that was not flesh. Initially he ate birds and beasts, but later he began eating humans.
All the sons and daughters born to him were rākṣasas. After this body perished, he was reborn as a lion and a jackal.
Among wolves, tigers, leopards, eagles, vultures, and the like, it is ultimately impossible to seek human birth; how much less can one escape birth and death to enter the noble path of nirvāṇa?
Those who eat meat have such faults as these, yet the foolish and ignorant do not realize it, claiming that because eating meat does not involve the act of killing, it is without fault.
They do not know that for the most part, those who kill living beings [do so for food].
Whether people eat it or do not eat it, there is likewise no act of killing; therefore, eating meat is a crime equal to killing.
Those killers, though they do not eat it themselves, kill living beings for the sake of profit and sell them; thus, they slaughter for the sake of wealth.
Those who eat meat, though they do not kill themselves, capture various meats for the sake of flavor. Thus it is.
Driven by money, those who eat meat cast their nets; driven by wealth, those who kill for profit gain their taste.

Because of the taste of wealth, they employ every kind of expedient—setting snares on mountains, spreading nets in valleys, damming rivers and canals—to harm all beings whether moving on land, in water, or through the air.
If one claims, "I do not kill myself, nor do I instruct others to kill, and I have no doubt regarding killing," [one is still implicated].

Furthermore, among those things that may be eaten, there is nothing in the world that can be considered "pure meat" fit for consumption without being taught to take it, without seeking the object, and without imagining its flavor, yet where fish and meat arrive spontaneously without cause.
Therefore, I have elsewhere in other sūtras stated that five kinds of pure meat are not permitted to be eaten: namely, that which has not been seen, heard, or suspected.
One must not doubt that birds killed by themselves or those left over from scavengers should be forbidden from being eaten;
or, one may prohibit ten types—namely, humans, snakes, elephants, horses, dragons, foxes, pigs, dogs, lions, and monkeys—and thus forbid their consumption.
These were all gradual prohibitions taught as skillful means. Now, in this assembly, the eating of meat of any kind whatsoever is entirely forbidden. As for what was mentioned previously...
Establishing expedient and provisional teachings, all are illuminated and entirely severed. Why is this?
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not a body sustained by mixed food; it takes the Dharma as its body and does not consume anything, much less impure things such as fish and meat.
In instructing his disciples, he teaches them only to partake of the flavor of the Dharma, and never to eat fish or meat.
Furthermore, because I have purified my habitual tendencies and take great compassion as my foremost practice,
regarding all sentient beings as if they were my only child, how could I ever teach my disciples to eat their own children's flesh? For this reason,
this sutra prohibits it entirely.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past, [all beings] were one's own kin; they are base, filthy, and impure, produced by various impurities. Upon smelling their odor, all are struck with terror.
All meats, as well as leeks, scallions, garlic, and the like, along with various intoxicants that lead to heedlessness—one who practices the path should keep far away from these."
One should also always avoid sesame oil and beds with perforated slats, for within them there are minute insects that are extremely terrified.

When food gives rise to negligence (*pramāda*), negligence gives rise to discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), and from discursive thoughts arises sensual desire (*kāmarāga*). Therefore, one should not eat such things.

From eating arises sensual desire; sensual desire causes the mind to become deluded and intoxicated; this intoxication increases craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and because of craving, one is not liberated from birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
To kill sentient beings for profit, or to purchase meat with wealth—both are evil karmas that lead to rebirth in the Raurava Hell.
If there is no instruction, no perception, and no seeking, then the three kinds of pure meat do not exist; since they cannot exist without these causes, one should not eat them.
For this reason, all those practitioners have completely distanced themselves from such acts, as every World-Honored Buddha of the ten directions has individually rebuked them.

Passing from one state to another, they devour one another and die, falling into the species of tigers, wolves, and the like; they find no loathing for foul odors and filth, and their births are always characterized by ignorance.
They are frequently born among the Caṇḍālas, hunters, and Taṃbas, or among the Dāyinīs and various flesh-eating Rākṣasas, pigs, wildcats, and so forth, being born everywhere within such realms.
Previously, the faults and afflictions of eating meat were briefly explained in verse; here they are further elucidated in detail: one should not eat meat because it was once a relative;

one should not eat it because it is loathsome, vile, and impure; one should not eat it because it is mixed with humans and livestock; one should not eat it because it is unsuitable as animal flesh that causes terror upon sight;
and one should not eat it because of its impurity. Not only should meat not be eaten, but by extension, one should also refrain from eating onions.
Garlic, the five pungent herbs, and alcohol—if eaten when cooked, they incite lust; if eaten raw, they incite anger; if indulged in through drinking, they give rise to heedlessness.
One should therefore distance oneself from them because they cause terror to sentient beings.

Not only does the sound of barking and howling startle those who eat meat, but even sesame oil and perforated beds harbor minute insects; one should likewise distance oneself from these out of concern for their terror. If...
It may still be acceptable to feel shame and remorse upon eating and drinking, rather than giving rise to negligence;
however, if one gives rise to negligence, then perverse thoughts will arise. Once thoughts have become perverse, greed arises. When there is greed, the mind becomes deluded;
when deluded, one becomes attached; when attached, one is bound; and when bound, one cannot escape the cycle of birth and death. This, then, is the desire for birth and death.

Since the roots [of unwholesome conduct] all have the five pungent vegetables and the indulgence in wine and food as their auxiliary causes, one who wishes to excise the fundamental nature must first eliminate these auxiliary causes.
It might still be tolerable if they failed to attain liberation but did not fall into the evil realms;
however, those who kill living beings do so for the sake of profit, and those who crave flavors do so by means of nets for the sake of profit.
Although the one who kills and the one who eats are different, they share equally in the karma of killing and both fall into the Raurava Hell.
If there were fish or meat that arrived of its own accord—without being taught, sought, or thought of—it might be permissible to eat.
However, since it is not the case that these three types of "pure meat" appear without cause, how could they possibly exist? Therefore, [they cannot be eaten].
All so-called "pure meat" is obtained through the practitioner's conceptualization and seeking; in the final analysis, it is identical in fault to killing living beings.
Therefore, one should not eat it. This is why practitioners distance themselves from it and why the Tathāgata censures it.
Even if one were to escape the suffering of hell and avoid retribution, it would still be unacceptable, for due to the habituation of killing—
Failing to repay their karmic debts, they are born in the same place where they prey upon one another;
subsequently, they may be born among humans as butchers, hunters, or rākṣasas, never escaping their state of ignorance.
Upon death, they fall again into the ranks of tigers, wolves, cats, and wildcats. Since such is the retribution, how can it not be forbidden?
In the *Bandhanamukta*, the *Mahāmegha*, the *Aṅgulimālīya*, and this *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, I have entirely prohibited the eating of meat.
It is censured by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas; those who eat it without shame will be perpetually dull-witted and ignorant in every birth.

Having previously declared that meat is forbidden based on what is seen, heard, or suspected, they do not realize that all such conceptualizations of meat-eating have been severed, and thus they are born into places where meat is consumed.
Just as sensual desire is an obstacle to noble liberation, so too are wine, meat, onions, leeks, and garlic all obstacles to the Noble Path.
Sentient beings of future ages will be deluded regarding meat and will say, "This is pure and without fault; the Buddha permitted us to eat it.
One should eat with the thought that it is like taking medicine, or like eating the flesh of one's own son, maintaining contentment, generating revulsion, and practicing the alms-round.
I declare that one who dwells in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is always free from fear when among tigers, wolves, and other evil beasts, and may always dwell together with them.
However, sentient beings are all terrified whenever they see those who eat flesh and blood. Therefore, a practitioner should not eat meat out of a mind of loving-kindness.
To eat meat is to lack compassion; it is to turn one's back forever on true liberation and to contradict the outward signs of a noble one (*ārya*). For these reasons, one should not eat meat.
To be born into a family of brahmins or other such practitioners, or into a household of wisdom and wealth— this results from abstaining from eating meat.
Since the retribution for eating meat is such as this, I have at times spoken of various sūtras, such as the *Gajasūkara-parivarta*, as well as this present sūtra,
wherein I have entirely prohibited and forbidden meat, because it is that which all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all worthy sages collectively condemn.

Those who eat meat are shameless and unashamed people who, throughout kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, are perpetually deluded and perpetually obscured because they do not know propriety and righteousness, nor do they recognize the grace of others.
Therefore, I have previously stated that one must not eat meat whether it has been seen being killed, heard to have been killed, or suspected to have been killed;
this is the severing of all meat-eating. How could there be anything in the world that is not seen, not heard, or not suspected?
How could such meat be fit for consumption? Ordinary, deluded people, shrouded by false imaginings, fail to perceive and do not understand;

they falsely claim that the Tathāgata permitted the eating of the "three kinds of pure meat. Consequently, they give rise to the thought of eating meat, their minds racing toward places where meat is eaten.
This is no different from the fault of lustful desire; it truly constitutes an obstacle to liberation. It is upon this very basis that [the path] is founded.
Therefore, the five pungent herbs and intoxicating liquor, when serving as auxiliary causes, are all obstacles to the Noble Path.
Yet, sentient beings of the末法 (mofa / final age) delusively consume meat and offer foolish arguments, saying: "These three kinds of pure meat are without fault;
the Buddha permitted me to eat them. This may be called a failure to properly discern the Tathāgata’s hidden intent (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
I am unaware that I have ever instructed my disciples in practices such as contentment and the dhūta austerities;

even regarding the practice of eating but one meal per day, I have taught them to regard it as taking medicine or as eating the flesh of their own children, so as not to give rise to attachment and to lead them toward renunciation.
I have taught them to constantly practice the conduct of begging for food—how could I ever permit the eating of meat? Therefore, [it is not so].

One who eats meat dwells securely in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*); when entering among beasts, they do not disturb the herds, and when entering among birds, they do not disrupt their flight.
Even with fierce predators such as tigers and wolves, one may roam together. Yet if one eats meat, dogs will startle upon smelling it and wild beasts will flee upon seeing it;
how could this be appropriate for a practitioner? Therefore, one who cultivates the noble path should abide in a mind of loving-kindness and should not [eat meat].
Regarding the eating of meat: if one who eats meat does not contemplate that all sentient beings share the same essence, they lack the mind of compassion (*maitrī-citta*).
Since the cause—the mind of compassion—is absent, how can there be the fruit of liberation? Since the fruit of sainthood is absent, there is also no majestic deportment for protecting living beings.
Because the manifest signs of the noble ones are intended to transform and benefit sentient beings, practitioners should not eat meat. If they do not eat it...
By abstaining from meat, one is born into the pure lineage of a Brahmin;
by following the teachings, one is constantly born in places of pure practice; by abandoning ignorance, one is constantly born with wisdom;
and by severing greedy craving, one is constantly born into wealth and nobility—all of these result from not eating meat. Is it not so for those who have renounced the consumption of meat?
